Here when a bond e between$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$is cut into a free end$e _ { 1 }$at$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and a fixed end$e _ { 2 }$at$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$, we always impose the condition$z _ { e } = z _ { e _ { 1 } } = z _ { e _ { 2 } } ;$see Figure 2. This is merely a diagrammatic representation of Fubini’s theorem.

With the above conventions, it is straightforward to verify that

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}}\tag{2.10}
$$

where in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } }$, we are integrating in the variables of free ends and bonds of$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$, treating the variables of fixed ends as frozen in the integral. In fact, (2.10) follows from the calculation

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \bigg (\underset {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} {\prod} \pmb {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}} \bigg) \cdot Q \mathrm{d} \pmb {z} _ {\mathcal {E}} \mathrm{d} \pmb {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}} \\ & {\quad = \underbrace {\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {1} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {1} |}} \bigg (\underset {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M} _ {1}} {\prod} \pmb {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}} \bigg)} _ {\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}}} \cdot \underbrace {\bigg (\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {2} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {2} |}} \bigg (\underset {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M} _ {2}} {\prod} \pmb {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}} \bigg) \cdot Q \mathrm{d} \pmb {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {2}} \mathrm{d} \pmb {t} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} \bigg)} _ {\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} (Q)} \mathrm{d} \pmb {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {1}} \mathrm{d} \pmb {t} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}}} \\ & {\quad = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} (Q).} \end{array}\tag{2.11}
$$

In general, in (2.10), M is allowed to have fixed ends, and the definitions of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$(and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } } )$in (2.8) is modified by replacing$\mathcal { E }$with E := {bonds and free ends}. The proof of (2.10) in full generality is presented in Proposition 8.14.

In our cutting algorithm, presented in Section 2.3.2 below, we will repeatedly cut M into smaller molecules until all of them becomes elementary molecules$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$, such that each of them contains only one or two atoms, so the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { j } }$can be calculated explicitly. We can then control$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$by$\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } ) \leq \| Q _ { \mathbb { M } } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } . } \end{array}$ $\Pi _ { j } \parallel \mathcal { L } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { j } } \parallel _ { L ^ { \infty }  L ^ { \infty } }$

There are four major types of elementary molecules, denoted by {2}, {3}, {4} and {33}, indicated by the degree (i.e number of bonds plus free ends, not counting fixed ends) of each atom. See Figure 15 (Section 8.2) for a picture of elementary molecules and Definition 8.11 for its rigorous definition. Note that {33} molecules are divided into types {33A} and {33B}, and we also allow {44} molecules which play minor roles and will not be discussed here.

The key observation is that, for each {33} molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$that occurs in the cutting process (see$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$in Figure 2), we have the operator norm bound$\| \mathcal { L } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { i } } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } \to L ^ { \infty } } \le \varepsilon ^ { v }$for some positive constant υ, at least in typical cases. For this reason, we define each {33} molecule to be good, and each {3} and {2} molecule to be normal. In fact, a {3} molecule corresponds to a normal collision, a {2} molecule corresponds to a recollision, and a {33} molecule (which can be further decomposed to a {3} and a {2} molecule) corresponds to a recollision that follows a normal collision, which constitutes the basic unit of gain, as already observed in [20] in the context of wave turbulence. Finally, we define a {4} molecule to be bad as it “wastes” one integral and leads to losses$\| \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { j } } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } \to L ^ { \infty } } \le \varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) }$. See Definition 9.4 for the precise version of classification of elementary molecules.

Returning to the estimate of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$, suppose there exists a cutting sequence that decomposes a molecule M into a collection of molecules$( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$. Then, by the discussion above and the fact that$Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$is bounded (say $\| Q _ { \mathbb { M } } \| \le 1 )$), we obtain

$$
\| | \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} | (\boldsymbol {z} _ {H}) \| _ {L ^ {1}} = \varepsilon^ {(d - 1) | H |} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q _ {\mathbb {M}}) \leq \prod_ {j} \| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {j}} \| _ {L ^ {\infty} \to L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {v \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} + (d - 1) (| H | - \# _ {\mathrm{bad}})},\tag{2.12}
$$

where we gain a factor of$\varepsilon ^ { v }$for each good molecule and lose a factor of$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) }$for each bad molecule. By (2.12), it is clear that (1.24) would follow if we can construct a cutting sequence satisfying

$$
v \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} + (d - 1) \cdot (| H | - \# _ {\mathrm{bad}}) \geq c \cdot \rho .\tag{2.13}
$$

This inequality is stated in Proposition 9.7, and is the main goal of the combinatorial part of this paper. We discuss the algorithm of constructing the cutting sequence, in Section 2.3.2 below.

The discussion and estimates of elementary molecules are contained in Section 9.1, see Propositions 9.1–9.3 and Definition 9.4. The proof of (1.24) (as part of Proposition 6.2, see (9.53)) is contained in Section 9.2, using also the auxiliary results (Propositions 9.8–9.9) in Section 9.3.

2.3.2. The cutting algorithm. Finally we discuss the proof of (2.13) stated as Proposition 9.7. This is the main technical ingredient of the proof, and will occupy Sections 11–13. The idea is to maximize the numbe of good (i.e. {33}) molecules and minimize the number of bad (i.e. {4}) molecules, and balance between them if needed. Below we discuss the main ideas and a few important points in this construction.

Toy models. The full algorithm, see Sections 12–13, is quite complicated. In Section 11, we will neglect a few technicalities by making the simplifying assumptions that (i) M has no O-atoms, and (ii) each layer $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$is precisely a forest. Moreover, we define the toy models (I, I+, II and III, see Definitions 11.2, 11.9, 11.15, 11.20 and Figure 20) to be specific cases of two layer molecules M: it has an upper layer$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and a lower layer$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, each of which is a tree. The$\rho$in (2.13) is comparable to the number of bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$ and M<sub>D</sub>.

The proof in Section 11 (under the simplifications$( \mathrm { i } ) { - } ( \mathrm { i i } ) )$will consist of two parts: reducing general multi-layer molecules M to one of the toy models (via layer selection), and designing a cutting algorithm for each individual toy model.

The UP algorithm. We start with a simple algorithm called UP, see Definitions 11.10. Basically, in this algorithm we select a lowest degree 3 atom n, and cut the atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(the set of descendants of n) from high to low, see Figure 28 (Section 11.3).

We can show that all the molecules resulting from UP are elementary by preserving the key monotonicity property: each atom either has no top fixed end or no bottom fixed end, see Proposition 11.12 (1). Moreover, this algorithm minimizes$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$(the number of {4} molecules) by allowing only one {4} molecule per connected component of M.

The drawback is that, the UP algorithm does not necessarily maximize$\# \{ 3 3 \}$(the number of {33} molecules), so it is not directly useful in our proof. However, it is still useful in “finishing of” unimportant parts of the molecule where we do not expect any gain. Moreover, in some important cases, one can actually make special adaptations to UP to guarantee the abundance of {33} molecules; this leads to the important algorithms 2CONNUP and 3COMPUP below.

Toy model I. The feature of toy model I, see Definition 11.2, is that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has exactly one bond with$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. In this case, the cutting algorithm is defined in Definition 11.4. It combines a trivial algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(always cutting lowest) with a greedy algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(cutting a {33} molecule, and the related {343} molecule, whenever possible). See Figure 22 (Section 11.2).

In this algorithm, one can show that the number of {4} molecules is minimized, i.e.$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1$; moreover the greedy algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$guarantees the abundance of {33} molecules, i.e.$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \gtrsim \rho _ { ; }$see Proposition 11.7. This relies on the fact that we never get any degree 2 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(Lemma 11.8), which crucially uses that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest.

Toy model I+. Toy model I+ (Definition 11.9) is similar to toy model I, but only a subset$X \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { U }$of atoms has one bond with$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and the others have none. Moreover, in toy model I+ we assume the number of connected components of X satisfies$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \ll \rho .$

In this case the algorithm (which is essentially the MAINUD algorithm) is defined in Definition 11.13, and is similar to Definition 11.4, see Figures 30–31 (Section 11.3). The only diference is that we only apply the naive “cutting lowest” algorithm in X, and instead apply UP in the rest of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, to minimize the number of {4} molecules. In fact this guarantees that$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \lesssim \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$, which is negligible compared to the gain $\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \gtrsim \rho ,$see Proposition 11.14.

Toy model II. In toy model II (Definition 11.15), we have the same assumptions as toy model I, but with$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \gtrsim \rho .$In this case the algorithm is defined in Definition 11.17. Basically we first remove$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ and cut it using DOWN the dual of UP, and then cut$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$using a special variant of UP which is called the 3COMPUP algorithm, see Figure 34 (Section 11.4).

The idea here is that, after removing$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, the degree 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are precisely those in X. Then,$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$ will satisfy the key property that the degree 3 atoms are separated by degree$\it 4$atoms, i.e. the number of connected components of degree 3 atoms satisfies$\# _ { 3 \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } = \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \gtrsim \rho .$Under this assumption, one can design a special variant of UP (basically choosing two lowest deg 3 atoms n instead of one), namely the 3COMPUP, to guarantee the abundance of {33} molecules, see Proposition 11.19.

Toy model III. In toy model III (Definition 11.20), we assume there exists$\gtrsim \rho$atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, each having two bonds with$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ;$they are called 2-connections. In this case, we simply apply the DOWN algorithm (dual of UP in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, see Definition 11.21 and Figure 38 (Section 11.5). In the process, each 2-connection atom n will naturally occur as a {33} molecule, which we then cut it to obtain a good component. Consequently we get$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \gtrsim \rho$and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$, see Proposition 11.22.

Reduction to toy models. With the algorithm constructed for each toy model, it now remains to reduce general multi-layer molecules M (under the assumptions$( \mathrm { i } ) { - } ( \mathrm { i i } ) )$to one of the toy models. The first step is to reduce M to a two-layer molecule by a process called layer selection.

Since we have ignored the recollisions within each layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$by assuming each layer is a forest, we know that the recollisions in M must happen across diferent layers. These recollisions come from the condition (4) in Section 2.1.1: this condition implies that the particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$are connected both within layer $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 }$and within layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \le \ell ^ { \prime } } : = \cup _ { \ell ^ { \prime \prime } \le \ell ^ { \prime } } \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime \prime } }$, resulting in cycles.

The idea of layer selection is as follows. First choose a layer$\ell _ { 1 }$such that$s _ { \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } = | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } ) | \gtrsim \rho .$, and that$s _ { \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } \gg s _ { \ell _ { 1 } } ;$this means that the particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } )$are connected to each other (with negligible exceptions) within layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } }$. Now, choose the highest layer$\ell _ { 2 } < \ell _ { 1 }$such that suficiently many particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } )$are connected to each other within$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { 2 } : \ell _ { 1 } - 1 ] } : = \cup _ { \ell _ { 2 } \leq \ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell _ { 1 } - 1 } \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Then, by putting together layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \left( \ell _ { 2 } < \ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell _ { 1 } \right)$into$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(and removing a negligible number of exceptions), and defining$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 2 } } : = \mathbb { M } _ { D }$ we obtain a two layer molecule where each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a tree (or forest), and there exist$\gtrsim \rho$bonds between them. For details see Definition 11.23 and Proposition 11.24, and Figure 40 (Section 11.6).

Once we are in the two layer setting, we then consider the dichotomy determined by the quantities #<sub>2conn</sub> (the number of 2-connections as defined above) and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$(the number of connected components of$X )$ where X is the set of atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that have exactly one bone with$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. By definition, if$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \gtrsim \rho$then M is toy model III. If$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \ll \rho ,$then the 2-connections will be negligible and we may assume$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$ Then, M will be toy model I+ or II, depending on whether$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \ll \rho \mathrm { o r } \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \gtrsim \rho .$This completes the proof in Section 11.

The full algorithm. Finally we discuss the extra ingredients in the full algorithm in Sections 12–13, in addition to those in Section 11. These are summarized in Section 11.7 and include the followings:

• The O-atoms: in the general case we need to replace the relevant notions (adjacency, connectedness etc.) by the ones associated with ov-segments, and modify the cutting algorithms accordingly. For example, the algorithms UP (Definition 11.10), 2CONNUP (Definition 11.21), 3COMPUP (Definition 11.17) and MAINUD (Definition 11.13), have their full versions defined in Definitions 12.1, 13.1, 13.6 and 13.12 respectively.

• Layer refinement: this is discussed in Definition 12.8 (Section 12.3), and is needed to treat the possible recollisions within each layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. We further sub-divide each$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$into finitely many subsets, such that each of them is precisely a forest, which recovers assumption (ii). This also leads to an extra step in the layer selection process, see Definition 12.12.

• The strong an weak resonances: these are exceptional cases where {33} molecules do not gain powers, see Definitions 12.4 and 12.16. In reality, if this efect becomes significant, we shall perform alternative cutting algorithms that exploit such degeneracies to gain powers of$\varepsilon$in a diferent way, see Propositions 12.5 and 12.17.

• The pre-processing step: this is discussed in Definition 13.10 (Section 13.3). This additional step is needed to deal with possible fixed ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$for the two-layer molecule M, which may cause trouble to the greedy algorithm in the toy model I+.

For a summary of the ingredients of the proofs in Sections 12–13 and their logical relations, see Figure 41 (Section 11.7).

2.4. The Boltzmann approximation and truncation error. In Sections 2.1–2.3 above, we have focused on the proof of the$E _ { H }$estimates in (1.21) (see Proposition 6.2). Now it remains to prove the approximation of$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$by the Boltzmann solution, see Proposition 6.1.

By discussions in Section 2.1, we know that$f ^ { \mathcal { A } } ( \ell \tau )$is given by an explicit series expansion of iterated time integrals that involve only$f ^ { \mathcal { A } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$, therefore this part follows from essentially the same arguments in the short-time theory. We identify those leading terms that do not contain recollision, and those sub-leading terms that contain recollision. We then match each leading term with the corresponding term that occurs in the Duhamel expansion of$f ( \ell \tau )$in terms of$f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$; note that the cluster expansion (see (3.16)) actually leads to extra terms in addition to those occurring in Boltzmann Duhamel expansions, but these extra terms turn out to cancel each other, as shown in Proposition 14.2. As for the sub-leading terms, they can be proved to be vanishing by applying a very simple special case of the cutting algorithm in Sections 11–13 (see Section 14.3, Point 5), since we only have one single layer and the number of recollisions in each cluster is bounded by Γ. All these are contained in Section 14.

Finally we discuss the estimate for the error term$f _ { s } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$caused by the truncated dynamics. This estimate is stated in Proposition 6.3 and is proved in Section 15. Here again we reduce the estimate to the construction of a cutting algorithm. However, as we now have many recollisions, one new dificulty arises due to the possibility that a small group of particles within distance$O ( \varepsilon )$of each other producing many recollisions within time$O ( \varepsilon )$. To treat this, we rely on a new ingredient, namely the absolute upper bound on the number of collisions given the number of particles, which is proved in Burago-Ferleger-Kononenko [15]. Basically, if Γ is suficiently large, then these Γ recollisions must involve suficiently many particles, with each new particle providing a {33} molecule in a suitable algorithm.

The algorithm in Section 15 is similar to the one in Sections 11–13, and is based on a two-layer molecule formed by$A ^ { + }$and A where A is (almost) a tree and$A ^ { + }$is arbitrary; see Proposition 15.4 (which actually involves three layers A<sup>+</sup>, A and$A ^ { - }$, but in reality we only exploit two of them). The main algorithm, called MAINTRUP, is similar to the MAINUD algorithm in Section 13.4, where each time we cut a lowest atom in$A ^ { + }$, and keep cutting any {33} or {343} structure in A that occur. This will then guarantee a lower bound for the number of {33} molecules, provided we have a lower bound for the number$\# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { + }$of bonds connecting an atom in A to an atom in a specific subset$X ^ { + } ( A ) \subseteq A ^ { + }$. This last lower bound is then provided by (the inverse function of) the Burago-Ferleger-Kononenko upper bound in [15], see Proposition 15.2. For more details of the algorithm, see Definition 15.9 and Proposition 15.10.

2.5. Comparison between wave and particle systems. As mentioned in Section 1.2, the proof in this paper is deeply inspired by that in the wave setting by the first two authors [23]. Here we make a brief comparison between the two proofs, in terms of their similarities and diferences. In the case of wave kinetic theory, the microscopic system in [23] is given by the nonlinear Schr¨odinger (NLS) equation on a torus$\mathbb { T } _ { L } ^ { d }$ of size L, with a nonlinearity of strength α. The lowest-order nontrivial statistical quantity is the second moment of the Fourier modes$\mathbb { E } | \widehat { u } ( t , k ) | ^ { 2 }$, where$\widehat { \boldsymbol { u } } ( t , \boldsymbol { k } )$is the Fourier transform of the solution$u ( t , x )$to the NLS equation, which is to be approximated by the solution of the (homogeneous) wave kinetic equation (1.19), in the limit$L \to \infty$and$\alpha  0$. This kinetic limit is taken under an appropriate choice of scaling law between L and$\alpha ,$namely$\alpha = L ^ { - \gamma }$, where$\gamma \in ( 0 , 1 )$in the homogeneous setting, see [23].

At a conceptual level, the two proofs are very similar. The fundamental dificulty represented by the divergence of the series expansion on the long time interval$[ 0 , t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } ]$is the same, and the same goes for the need to create an arrow of time where, in both cases, the microscopic system is time-reversible but the limiting kinetic equation is irreversible. The idea of performing a partial expansion, where one refrains from expanding the lowest order statistic (the$f ^ { A }$here, and the second moments in the wave case) but expands the cumulants all the way to time$t = 0$, is also the same. This keeps track of all the relevant collisions or interactions on the long time interval$[ 0 , t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } ]$that afect the cumulants at time$t _ { \mathrm { f i n } }$

Even at a more technical level, there are uncanny similarities between the two proofs. First, both proofs start with a truncation of the dynamics in order to control the size of the diagrams appearing in the cumulant expansions. Also, in both proofs, the needed cumulant estimate is reduced to a combinatorial problem that is resolved through an elaborate algorithm. This combinatorial problem, in both cases, involves th combinatorial structure of molecules, which are formed by atoms that represent collisions or interactions. While the algorithms are vastly diferent in the wave case and particle case, there is an important similarity in the gain mechanism. As shown in Section 2.3, the basic unit of gain here is the special structure of {33} molecules; similarly, in the wave case, the basic unit of gain also comes from the {33} molecules and the associated five-vector counting problem.

All this being said, the analogy between the particle and wave kinetic theories has its limitations, and despite the above similarities, each proof carries its own distinct set of challenges. In the wave case, a large box limit needs to be performed to go from the discrete Fourier space of$\mathbb { T } _ { L } ^ { d }$to the continuum setting of the wave kinetic equation (1.19). This links the wave kinetic theory to some deep number theory problems, which seems to be absent in the particle setting. Also, the Feynman diagram expansion for the NLS equation turns out to converge only conditionally and not absolutely, and requires highly nontrivial cancellations between arbitrarily large diagrams, which is another distinctive feature and novelty of [23]. On the other hand, the cumulant expansion in the particle setting is technically more involved, due to the application of inclusion exclusion principle and the resulting notion of overlaps, which does not seem to be have an analog in the wave case. Also the main algorithm in the particle case seems to be conceptually more complicated than the corresponding algorithm in the wave case, which may be due to the singular nature of the δ integrals in $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$compared to the counting problems in [23].

2.6. The rest of this paper. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Note that, although the notion of cutting and cutting algorithm is the main novelty and central to the proof, they have to wait until Section 8 (cutting) and Section 11 (algorithm) to appear, due to the necessary preparations in Sections 3–7.

• Part I: Sections 3–5 are devoted the statement and proof of Proposition 3.25.

• In Section 3 we define all the relevant notions (molecules, topological reduction etc.) in Sections $3 . 1 \mathrm { - } 3 . 4 ,$and then state Proposition 3.25 in Section 3.5.

• In Section 4 we define the truncated dynamics (Definition 4.3) and its properties, which are needed in the proof of Proposition 3.25.

• In Section 5 we prove Proposition 3.25.

• Interlude I: Section 6 contains the statement of the main propositions, Propositions 6.1–6.3, of this paper. We also prove that these propositions imply Theorem 1.

• Part II: Sections 7–9 are devoted to the first half of the proof of Proposition 6.2, where we reduce it to Proposition 9.7.

• In Section 7 we make the necessary preparations, and reduce the the expression$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$occurring in the upper bound of$E _ { H }$to the local integration$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$

• In Section 8 we define the notion of cutting (Definition 8.3), study its properties, and how the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$behaves under cutting (Proposition 8.14).

• In Section 9 we state the main result concerning cutting algorithms, i.e. Proposition 9.7, and prove that it implies Proposition 6.2.

• Interlude II: Section 10 contains a few simple reductions and reiterations of properties of the molecule M, in preparation of the proof of Proposition 9.7.

• Part III: Sections 11–13 are devoted to the second half of the proof of Proposition 6.2, i.e. the proof of Proposition 9.7.

• In Section 11 we study the two-layer toy models, namely toy models I, I+, II and III (in Sections 11.2–11.5 respectively). In Section 11.6 we define layer selection in the toy model case, and in Section 11.7 we sketch the additional ingredients needed in the full algorithm.

• In Section 12 we present the first half of the proof of Proposition 9.7, where we reduce it to Proposition 12.18. This section contains the UP algorithm (Definition 12.1), strong and weak degeneracies (Definitions 12.4, 12.16), layer refinement (Section 12.3) and layer selection (Section 12.4).

• In Section 13 we finish the proof of Proposition 12.18. In Sections 13.1–13.4 we introduce the algorithms 2CONNUP, 3COMPUP, pre-processing and MAINUD respectively. Finally, in Section 13.5 we finish the proof of Proposition 12.18 by invoking the dichotomy and reducing to one of the toy model cases in Section 11.

• The Finale: Sections 14–15 are devoted to the proof of Propositions 6.1 and 6.3.

• Appendices: Appendix A–C contain auxiliary results and tables summarizing important notions.

## 3. The cumulant expansion formula

In this section, we will state the main cumulant formula in Proposition 3.25, which has form

$$
f _ {s} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \sum_ {H \subseteq [ s ]} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (\ell \tau)) ^ {\otimes ([ s ] \setminus H)} \cdot E _ {H} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {H}) + (\text { error   terms }),\tag{3.1}
$$

$$
| E _ {H} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {H}) | \leq \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} ] \in \mathcal {F} _ {\boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {\ell}}} | \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} | (\boldsymbol {z} _ {H}).\tag{3.2}
$$

Here$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$is an approximate solution to the Boltzmann equation, and M is a molecule (Definition 3.1). Also $\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$is a collection of molecules (Definition 3.20) and$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$is an integral expression associated with the molecule M (Definition 3.23), which represents the densities given by trajectories that topologically reduce to M (Definition 3.8).

The statement of Proposition 3.25 involves many concepts that need to be defined. We define these notions in Sections 3.1–3.4, which are related to molecules M and topological reductions. Then, in Section 3.5 we define the set$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { i } }$and the associated integral$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } | ( z _ { H } )$in (3.2), and then state Proposition 3.25. This will be the main goal in the first part of the paper, whose proof will occupy Sections 4–5.

3.1. Molecules. We start with the definition of molecules. As seen in Figure 5 (Section 3.2), molecules are topological reductions of actual particle trajectories (see Definition 3.8 for precise formulation).

Definition 3.1 (Molecules). We define a (layered) molecule to be a diagram demonstrated by Figure 3. More rigorously, we define a (layered) molecule$\mathbb { M } = ( \mathcal { M } , \mathcal { E } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { L } )$to be a diagram as follows. For the correspondence between molecule pictures and physical particle pictures, see Table 3 in Appendix B.

![](images/page_24_chart_8.jpg)

Figure 3. An example of molecules.

(1) Atoms, edges, bonds and ends. M is a set of nodes referred to as atoms, and$\mathcal { E }$is a set of edges consisting of bonds and ends to be specified below. For convenience, below we will abuse notation and use M instead of M to denote the set of atoms in M.

(a) An atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$is either a C-atom (collision) or an O-atom (overlap), denoted respectively by ◦ and • as in Figure 3. Each atom is assigned with a unique layer$\ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ]$which is an integer in$\left[ \underline { { \ell } } : \ell \right] .$, where ℓ is the highest layer and ℓ is the lowest layer of M. Define$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$to be the set of atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$of layer$\ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] = \ell ^ { \prime }$. The boundaries between layers are indicated by horizontal lines, as in Figure 3.

(b) Each edge in E is either a bond between two atoms n and${ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ,$or an end emanating from one atom n, or an empty end that does not involve any atom. Each edge is either top or bottom when viewed at each involved atom n; a top (resp. bottom) edge is drawn above (resp. below) the atom, as in Figure 3. Moreover, each end is also either free or fixed, with fixed ends indicated by a$\times ,$as shown in Figure 3. We understand by convention that empty ends are always free, and count as both top and bottom.

(c) For two atoms n and${ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ,$if a bond exists between n and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$that is bottom at n and top at${ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ,$we say n is parent of${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$is child of n.

(2) Particle lines.$\mathcal { P }$is a collection of paths: each path starts from a bottom end at an atom, then keeps connecting to a parent by a bond, until reaching a top end at another atom. Each chain$\pmb { p } \in \mathcal { P }$is called a particle line. We require that each edge belongs to a unique particle line; in particular, each empty end is also viewed as a particle line by convention. For a top edge and a bottom edge at an atom n, we say they are serial if they belong to the same particle line. Note that each particle line p contains a unique bottom end and a unique top end. We will identify particle lines with physical particles, see Table 3.

Recall ℓ defined in (1a). We may define a start layer$\ell _ { 1 } [ p ] \in [ \underline { { \ell } } : \ell ]$and finish layer$\ell _ { 2 } [ p ] \in [ \underline { { \ell } }$ $\ell + 1 ]$for each particle line$\mathbf { \nabla } _ { \pmb { p } } .$. As$\pmb { p }$contains a unique bottom (and unique top) end, we may also equivalently write$\ell _ { 1 } [ e ]$(resp.$\ell _ { 2 } [ e ] )$for each bottom (resp. top) end e instead of$\ell _ { 1 } [ p ]$and$\ell _ { 2 } [ \pmb { p } ]$. We refer to the interval$[ \ell _ { 1 } [ { \pmb p } ] : \ell _ { 2 } [ { \pmb p } ] ]$as the lifespan of the particle line$\mathbf { \delta } _ { p . }$In Figure 3, the lifespan of ${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$and$\pmb { p } _ { 2 }$are$\left[ 1 : 3 \right]$and$[ 1 : 2 ]$, respectively. For${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$, its finish layer is$\ell _ { 2 } [ p _ { 1 } ] = \ell + 1 = 3$, which is above the highest layer$\ell .$To indicate this, we draw it penetrating the top horizontal line.

(3) Initial links. Finally, L is a collection of pairs of bottom ends$( e , e ^ { \prime } )$with$\ell _ { 1 } [ e ] = \ell _ { 1 } [ e ^ { \prime } ] = 1$(provided $\underline { { \ell } } = 1 )$. Since each particle line has a unique bottom end by (2), we can equivalently view$\mathcal { L }$as a collection of pairs of particle lines with start layer 1. Each pair in$\mathcal { L }$is called an initial link. In Figure 3, L contains a single pair$( e _ { 4 } , e _ { 9 } )$, which is indicated by a dashed line connecting them.

(4) Ov-segments. For later use, we also define an ov-segment to be a path between two atoms (or ends) such that all intermediate atoms in this path are O-atoms (except the possible endpoints), and this path is contained in a single particle line. We say an ov-segment is maximal if it is not contained in other ov-segments. In Figure$^ { 3 , }$the path consisting of edges$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 2 } .$, and atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 3 }$ is an example of a maximal ov-segment. Note that each edge in M belongs to a unique maximal ov-segment. Also each bond in M is a special case of ov-segment (not necessarily maximal).

(5) The objects$( \mathcal { M } , \mathcal { E } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { L } )$satisfies the following requirements.

(a) Each atom has exactly 2 top edges and exactly 2 bottom edges.

(b) Starting from any atom n, it is impossible to get back to n by iteratively taking parent or by iteratively taking child.

(c) If n is a parent of$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$then we must have$\ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] \geq \ell [ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ]$. If n belongs to a particle line p then we must have$\ell _ { 1 } [ { \pmb p } ] \leq \ell [ { \pmb n } ] \leq \ell _ { 2 } [ { \pmb p } ]$

Definition 3.2 (Full molecules). If a molecule M has no fixed end, we say M is a full molecule.

In the statement of the cumulant formula, we will need to label diferent particles to distinguish them. Also the particles corresponding to$z _ { s }$or$z _ { H }$in$f _ { s } ( \ell \tau , z _ { s } )$or cumulant$E _ { H } ( \ell \tau , z _ { H } )$, i.e. the root particles, will play a special role.

Definition 3.3 (Label and root particle lines). Given a molecule M, we may assign labels (which takes values in N) to each particle line$\pmb { p }$of M. This makes M a labeled molecule. Note that two labeled molecules with the same molecule structure (Definition 3.1) but diferent labelings are regarded as diferent.

For any molecule M, define the set of all particle lines in M to be$p ( \mathbb { M } )$. Define a particle line$\pmb { p }$to be a root particle line, if its finish layer$\ell _ { 2 } { [ } p { ] } = \ell + 1$, where ℓ is the highest layer in M. Define the set of root particle lines to be$r ( \mathbb { M } )$, and the set of non-root particles to be$( p \backslash r ) ( \mathbb { M } ) : = p ( \mathbb { M } ) \backslash r ( \mathbb { M } )$

For two labeled molecules M and M<sup>′</sup> with ℓ layers, we define them to be equivalent, denoted$\mathbb { M } \sim \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$ if they have the same molecule structure (Definition 3.1) and the same labels for root particle lines. Define [M] to be the equivalence class of M, which is obtained by relabeling non-root particle lines in M.

In Figure$^ { 3 , }$we can label$\mathbf { \psi } _ { p _ { 1 } } , \mathbf { \psi } _ { p _ { 2 } }$and$\mathbf { \mathit { p } _ { 3 } }$by 1, 2 and 3 respectively, where$\pmb { p } _ { 1 }$is the root particle line.

Remark 3.4. Clearly an equivalence class [M] is uniquely determined by an unlabeled molecule M, and a fixed labeling of all root particle lines. In the proof of the cumulant expansion formula (Proposition 3.25) in Sections 4–5, it is important that we use M to represent labeled molecules and sum over equivalence classes [M] (see relevant notations in Definition 1.6 (6)). Once this proof is finished, in subsequent analysis of the $| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$terms, the labeling will not play any role, so we will ignore it and use M to denote unlabeled molecules in Sections 6–15 (we still need to label the root particles, which will not play a major role, see Remark 3.26).

We introduce some additional notions associated with molecules, which will be used in the proof below.

Definition 3.5 (Ordering of atoms). Let M be a molecule and${ \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \in \mathbb { M }$be atoms.

(1) Descendants and ancestors. If n is obtained from n<sup>′</sup> by iteratively taking parents, then we say n is an ancestor of${ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ,$and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$is a descendant of n. We use$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(resp.$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$to denote the set of descendants (resp. ancestors) of n. By convention we understand that${ \mathfrak { n } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(and${ \mathfrak { n } } \in Z _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$

(2) The partial ordering of atoms and edges. We also define a partial ordering between all atoms, by defining$\mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \prec \mathfrak { n }$if and only if$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } \ne \mathfrak { n }$and is a descendant of n (equivalently n is ancestor of n<sup>′</sup>). In particular n$^ { \prime } \prec \mathfrak { n }$if n<sup>′</sup> is a child of n (equivalently n is parent of n<sup>′</sup>).

(3) Given any subset$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$, we can define a lowest atom in A to be any atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$that satisfies n<sup>′</sup> ̸∈ A for each${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } \prec { \mathfrak { n } } \left( { \mathrm { i . e . ~ } } { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } \right) = { \mathfrak { n } }$is descendant of n). Define highest atoms in the same way. These are just minimal and maximal elements of A under the partial ordering ≺, and note that they need not be unique for general A.

Definition 3.6 (Various sets associated with molecules). Let$\mathbb { M } = ( \mathcal { M } , \mathcal { E } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { L } )$be a molecule.

(1) Sets$\mathcal { E } _ { * }$and$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } }$. Define E<sub>∗</sub> to be the set of all edges that are either bonds or free ends (i.e. not counting fixed ends). Define also the sets$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } }$(resp.$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } , \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + } )$to be the set of all ends (resp. bottom ends, top ends). Note that empty ends belong to$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { \pm }$by convention.

Note that the sets$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$and$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + }$are in bijection with the set$p ( \mathbb { M } )$of all particle lines, see Definition 3.1 (2).

(2) Number of atoms and particle lines. We will use$| \mathbb { M } | , \ | \mathbb { M } | _ { \mathrm { O } } , \ | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } , \ | \mathbb { M } | _ { r }$and$\| \mathbb { M } | _ { p \backslash r }$to denote the number of atoms, O-atoms, particle lines$\displaystyle ( \mathrm { i . e . } \ | p ( \mathbb { M } ) | )$), root particle lines$\left( \mathrm { i . e . } \ | r ( \mathbb { M } ) | \right)$, and non-root particle lines (i.e.$| ( p \backslash r ) ( \mathbb { M } ) | )$of M respectively.

3.2. Topological reduction. In this section, we rigorously formulate the notion of topological reduction. We start with the notion of admissible trajectories, which generally occur from modifications of hard sphere dynamics where certain collisions are neglected according to certain rules (see Definition 3.15).

Definition 3.7 (Admissible trajectories). Let$z ( t ) = z _ { N } ( t ) = ( z _ { j } ( t ) ) _ { j }$be any particle trajectory (a priori with no equation or restriction). We say it is admissible (see Figure 4), if

![](images/page_26_image_12.jpg)

Figure 4. Admissible trajectories (Definition 3.7), where it is allowed to have$| x _ { i } - x _ { j } | < \varepsilon$ but two particles reaching distance ε from “inside” will not collide and not change velocity, as they do not satisfy the pre-collisional condition.

(1) Each$z _ { j } ( t ) = ( x _ { j } ( t ) , v _ { j } ( t ) )$is piecewise linear,$x _ { j } ( t )$is continuous and$v _ { j } ( t )$is left continuous, with a discrete set of times of velocity discontinuity referred to as collisions;

(2) At each collision time t, there exist two and only two particles whose velocities are discontinuous, their positions$( x _ { i } , x _ { j } )$and velocities$( v _ { i } , v _ { j } )$satisfy (1.2) with$x _ { i } ( t ) - x _ { j } ( t ) = \varepsilon \omega ( \omega \in \mathbb { S } ^ { d - 1 } )$, and $( v _ { i } ( t ) - v _ { j } ( t ) ) \cdot \omega \leq 0$. We refer to this set of conditions as the pre-collisional condition.

(3) Additionally, we define an overlap to be a time when$x _ { i } ( t ) - x _ { j } ( t ) = \varepsilon \omega \left( \omega \in \mathbb { S } ^ { d - 1 } \right)$and$( v _ { i } ( t ) -$ $v _ { j } ( t ) ) \cdot \omega \leq 0$, but the velocities$v _ { i }$and$v _ { j }$are continuous at time t.

Definition 3.8 (Topological reduction). Let$z ( t )$be an admissible trajectory for$t \in [ 0 , \ell \tau ]$, and M be a molecule with ℓ layers (Definition 3.1). We say z(t) topologically reduces to M, if there is a bijection between maximal ov-segments of M (Definition 3.1 (4)) and maximal linear pieces of the trajectory z(t), see Figure 5, which satisfies the following requirements:

(1) If two maximal ov-segments intersect at a C-atom, then the corresponding linear pieces of$z ( t )$have a collision. If they intersect at an O-atom, then the corresponding linear pieces have an overlap.

(2) The induced correspondence between atoms and collisions/overlaps preserves order (i.e. if n is parent of$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$then the corresponding collision/overlap happens later in time), and is bijective on collisions (it is injective on overlaps by time ordering, but might not be surjective).

(3) If two maximal ov-segments belong to the same particle line in M, then the corresponding linear pieces belong to the trajectory of the same particle.

(4) The collision/overlap corresponding to an atom in layer ℓ must occur in the time interval$[ ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , \ell \tau ]$ For a summary of correspondence of concepts in molecules and physical trajectories, see Table 3. In Figure 5, the overlap in [τ, 2τ] of the red and green particles corresponds to the O-atom on layer 2, and the collision in [0, τ] of the red and green particles corresponds to the C-atom on layer 1.

![](images/page_27_image_5.jpg)

Figure 5. An illustration of topological reduction.

Remark 3.9. The topological reduction M of a given trajectory$z ( t )$may not be unique, since we do not require a bijective correspondence between O-atoms and the actual set of overlaps. The O-atoms may represent only an arbitrary subset of all overlaps. However there is always a unique topological reduction that is C-molecule (i.e. contains only C-atoms).

3.3. Clusters. As seen in Definition 3.8, O-atoms correspond to overlaps that do not afect the dynamics. Ignoring all such overlaps leads to the definition of clusters.

Definition 3.10 (Create and delete an O-atom). Given a molecule M, we define the following operations, see Figure 6. The particle lines and ov-segments will not be broken after these operations.

(1) Delete an O-atom. Let o be an O-atom with 4 edges$e _ { i } ( 1 \leq i \leq 4 )$connected to other atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } .$ where$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 3 }$are serial and same for$e _ { 2 }$and$e _ { 4 }$. By deleting the O-atom o, we remove o and the 4 edges$e _ { j }$from$\mathbb { M } ,$and add two bonds$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 3 } .$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$between$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 4 } .$, with the same top/bottom assignment as$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 3 } )$and$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 4 } )$. Here if some${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i }$is absent, say$e _ { 3 }$is a free end at${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$then the bond$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 3 } )$should be replaced by a free end at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } .$, etc.

(2) Create an O-atom. Given two edges$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 3 }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 4 } .$we can create an O-atom o by reverting the above process: add a new O-atom${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$remove$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$, add the bonds $e _ { j }$between o and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$with the same top/bottom assignment as$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { . } }$and make$e _ { 1 }$serial with$e _ { 3 }$ and$e _ { 2 }$serial with$e _ { 4 }$. We also refer to this as joining$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$by$\mathfrak { o }$.

![](images/page_28_image_0.jpg)

Figure 6. Creating and deleting O-atoms as in Definition 3.10. Note that each atom${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$ can be either C- or O-atoms, or absent.

Definition 3.11 (Clusters). Given a molecule M, we obtain a new molecule$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$by deleting all O-atoms from M as in Definition 3.10, leaving only C-atoms. The connected components$( \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mathbb { M } _ { k } )$of M<sup>′</sup> are called the clusters of M. We say that an O-atom o joins$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } }$if the two particle lines at o connects the C-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and in$\mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } }$respectively. We also define the auxiliary cluster graph to be the graph with nodes being clusters$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$, and an edge is drawn between$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } }$for each O-atom joining them. See Figure 7 for an illustration.

![](images/page_28_image_3.jpg)

Figure 7. An example of clusters and O-atoms joining them as in Definition 3.11, and the corresponding cluster graph. Here we have 3 clusters$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$, with$( \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } )$and$( \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } )$each joined by an O-atom.

Definition 3.12 (C-molecule). A molecule consists of only C-atoms are referred to as C-molecules. Clusters are always C-molecules.

Definition 3.13 (Recollision number). Given a subset$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$, we define its recollision number by$\rho ( A ) =$ $\# \mathrm { b o n d } ( A ) - | A | + \# \mathrm { c o m p } ( A )$, where${ \# } _ { \mathrm { b o n d } ( A ) }$and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( A ) }$are respectively the number of bonds between atoms in A, and the number of connected components of A. We say a set A is recollisional (or equivalently cyclic) if$\rho ( A ) > 0$

Remark 3.14. Recollision number is an important notion and will be used frequently later. It equals the circuit rank which is the number of (independent) cycles in A. It is easy to see that$\rho ( A ) \geq 0$for any A.

3.4. Molecule prescribed dynamics. In Proposition 3.25, the quantity$\mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } }$basically represents an integral over the non-root particle variables, under the restriction that the particle trajectories under certain dynamics topologically reduces to M. In order to exclude the possible efects of other collisions, we need to introduce the molecule prescribed dynamics (Definition 3.17), which ignores any possible collision that does not come from the molecule. This is an example of general modified dynamics, which we introduce below.

Definition 3.15 (Modified dynamics). We define the modified dynamics, which is governed by a given property Pro, as follows.

(1) Governing property. Pro is a property, which can be expressed in terms of an admissible trajectory γ and two particles${ \pmb p } , { \pmb p } ^ { \prime }$. This means that, given any admissible trajectory$\gamma$and particles${ \pmb p } , { \pmb p } ^ { \prime }$, we can uniquely determine whether Pro$( \gamma , p , p ^ { \prime } )$equals True or False.

(2) Modified dynamics. Given initial configuration$z ^ { 0 } = z _ { N } ^ { 0 }$, we define the dynamics$z ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t ) = z ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t , z ^ { 0 } )$ governed by Pro, as follows:

(a) We have$z ^ { \mathsf { P r o } } ( 0 ) = z ^ { 0 }$

(b) Suppose$z ^ { \mathsf { P r o } } ( t ^ { \prime } )$is known for$t ^ { \prime } \in [ 0 , t ]$. Let$\gamma$be the admissible trajectory$z ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t ^ { \prime } ) \left( t ^ { \prime } \in [ 0 , t ] \right)$ If two particles satisfy the pre-collisional condition (Definition$3 . 7 \ ( 2 ) )$at time$t ,$and also Pro$\begin{array} { r l } { \phantom { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ) ( \gamma , p , p ^ { \prime } ) = } \end{array}$True for the molecule$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$and the particle lines${ \pmb p } , { \pmb p } ^ { \prime }$corresponding to these two particles, then they collide as in (1.2).

(c) If a particle does not satisfy (2b) with any other particle, then it does not have any collision and moves linearly by (1.3).

(3) Flow map and flow operator. We define the flow map$\mathcal { H } ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t ) = \mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t )$by

$$
\mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{Pro}} (t): \mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}, \quad \mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{Pro}} (t) (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z} ^ {\mathrm{Pro}} (t)\tag{3.3}
$$

where$z ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t ) = z _ { N } ^ { \mathrm { P r o } } ( t )$is defined in (2). The mapping$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ( t )$need not be injective; however, we can still define the flow operator$S ^ { \mathsf { P r o } } ( t )$by

$$
\mathcal {S} ^ {\mathrm{Pro}} (t) f (\boldsymbol {z}) = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}: \mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{Pro}} (t) (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}).\tag{3.4}
$$

(4) Collision and overlap. The notions of collisions and overlaps for any trajectory of modified$\mathrm { { d y } \mathrm { { - } } }$ namics, are defined as in Definition 3.7.

(5) Label of particles. In this definition, we assume that particles are labeled by$[ N ] = \{ 1 , \cdots , N \}$(see the convention in Definition 1.6 (4)). For a general labeling set$\lambda ,$the formulation remains the same, except that the subscript N in expressions like$z _ { N } ( t ) , \mathcal { H } _ { N } ( t ) , S _ { N } ( t )$etc. is replaced by λ.

Remark 3.16. We make a few remarks regarding Definition 3.15. First, up to Lebesgue zero sets, the modified dynamics is well-defined just as Definition 1.1, and produces admissible trajectories in Definition 3.7. Also, we allow$| x _ { i } - x _ { j } | < \varepsilon$and do not restrict to$\mathcal { D } _ { N }$, and only allow collisions under pre-collisional condition.

Second, the modified dynamics can be described as “collision ⇔ pre-collisional and property Pro holds”, in particular the dynamics is completely determined by the condition Pro. Examples of this Pro include the molecule prescribed dynamics (Definition 3.17), extended dynamics (Definition 4.1) and truncated dynamics (Definition 4.3).

Definition 3.17 (Molecule prescribed dynamics). Given a C-molecule M, the dynamics prescribed by M is a modified dynamics as in Definition 3.15, with particle set being$p ( \mathbb { M } )$, and governing property given by

$\operatorname* { P r o } ( \gamma , p , p ^ { \prime } ) = \mathtt { T r u e } \Leftrightarrow \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } \subseteq \mathbb { M }$, and p and$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$intersects at a C-atom$\mathfrak { n } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} \subseteq \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$

Here M<sup>′</sup> is the unique C-molecule which is topological reduction$\boldsymbol { \mathrm { \ell } } ^ { 6 }$of$\gamma$as in Definition 3.8 (the uniqueness is guaranteed by Remark 3.9),$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the set of descendants of n (Definition 3.5), and$\pmb { p }$and$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$are viewed as particle lines in M. See Figure 8.

If M contains O-atoms, the the dynamics prescribed by M is defined to be the dynamics prescribed by ${ \widetilde { \mathbb { M } } } .$which is the C-molecule formed by deleting all the O-atoms in M.

Definition 3.19. Let$\pmb { p } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbf { \mathit { p } } _ { 2 }$be two particle lines, and$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$be a set. We say:

${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$intersects$A ,$, if an atom exists that belongs to both${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$and A.

•${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$is connected to a cycle within A, if${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$intersects a component of A that contains a cycle;

${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$forms an initial link within A, if there exists a particle line${ \pmb p } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$which either equals${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$or is connected to${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$via$A ,$such that the bottom end in${ \pmb p } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$is involved in an initial link.

Remark 3.21. We briefly explain the ideas behind the items in Definition 3.20. Here (1a) comes from the truncation of dynamics (Definition 4.3) and the truncation in the Penrose argument, and (1c) also comes from the construction in the Penrose argument. Next, (1b) follows from the fact that we only expand the particles that are connected to root particles, and (1d) follows from the condition for the cumulant$E _ { H }$. The other conditions$( 2 ) - ( 4 )$are similar but with modifications associated with single layer or error terms.

Definition 3.22 (Associated transport operators). Let M be a molecule. We define the following objects:

(1) Prescribed dynamics and flow operators. We use$z _ { \mathbb { M } } ( t )$to denote the M-prescribed dynamics in Definition 3.17, with$\mathcal { H } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( t )$and$S _ { \mathbb { M } } ( t )$etc. defined accordingly as in Definition 3.15. Note that the subscript N is omitted, as$N = | \mathbb { M } | _ { p }$can be inferred from M.

(2) Indicator functions$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } }$and$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$. We define the indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( z ^ { 0 } )$such that $\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( z ^ { 0 } ) = 1 \Leftrightarrow$the trajectory$z _ { \mathbb { M } } ( t )$, with initial configuration$z ^ { 0 }$, topologically reduces to M.

(3.8)

Define also the indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$, associated with the initial link structure${ \mathcal { L } } ,$by

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} = \prod_ {(e _ {1}, e _ {2}) \in \mathcal {L}} \mathbb {1} _ {e _ {1} \sim \mathrm{in} e _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon} \qquad \mathrm{and} \qquad \mathbb {1} _ {e _ {1} \sim \mathrm{in} e _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & | x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} | \leq \varepsilon , \\ \varepsilon^ {v} & | x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} | \geq \varepsilon , \end{array} \right.\tag{3.9}

where$v = 3 ^ { - d - 1 }$(Definition 1.6 (3)).

Remark 3.24. We make a few remarks on Definitions 3.22–3.23.

## 4. Truncation of dynamics

We now start the proof of Proposition 3.25. In this section we will define the truncated dynamics and establish the decomposition (3.14). This is needed in order to control the number of particles and recollisions in each cluster in each time layer, that occur in the molecule expansion (for example in Definition 3.20 (1a), the number of particles in layer ℓ<sup>′</sup> is bounded by$\Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 } A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$

Recall from (1.10) and (1.11) that$f ( t , z _ { s } )$is given by

$$
f (t, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \varepsilon^ {(d - 1) s} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} \int (\mathcal {S} _ {s + n} (t) W _ {0, s + n}) (\boldsymbol {z} _ {s + n}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]},\tag{4.1}
$$

so the correlation$f ( t , z _ { s } )$is determined by the collisions in the dynamics$S _ { s + n } ( t )$, for which we will define the truncation.

4.1. The extended and truncated dynamics. In this subsection, we define the extended and truncated dynamics as two instances of modified dynamics in Definition 3.15.

Definition 4.1 (The extended dynamics). We define the extended dynamics (or E-dynamics), denoted by$z ^ { E } ( t )$, to be the modified dynamics in Definition 3.15, with the governing property$\mathtt { P r o } ( \gamma , p , p ^ { \prime } ) \equiv \mathtt { T r u e }$

Remark 4.2. In the E-dynamics, we have a collision whenever the pre-collisional condition is satisfied. In particular, if the distance of any two particles becomes$\geq \varepsilon .$then this separation is preserved thereafter.

The E-dynamics is a natural extension of the original dynamics (Definition 1.1) from$\mathcal { D } _ { N }$to the whole space$\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 d N }$. If we restrict the initial data of the E-dynamics to$\mathcal { D } _ { N }$, then the trajectory stays in$\mathcal { D } _ { N }$forever, and the E-dynamics coincides with the O-dynamics (see Proposition 4.5 below).

Definition 4.3 (The truncated dynamics). Let$( \Lambda , \Gamma )$be fixed. We define the truncated dynamics (or $( \Lambda , \Gamma ) -$, or T-dynamics), denoted by$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$, to be the modified dynamics in Definition 3.15, with the governing property$\mathrm { P r o } ( \gamma , p , p ^ { \prime } )$given by

$$
\operatorname{Pro} (\boldsymbol {\gamma}, \boldsymbol {p}, \boldsymbol {p} ^ {\prime}) = \text { True } \Leftrightarrow \text { either   } (\mathbb {M} _ {i} = \mathbb {M} _ {j} \text {   and   } \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {i}) \leq \Gamma - 1),
$$

$$
\text { or } (\mathbb {M} _ {i} \neq \mathbb {M} _ {j} \text { and } | \mathbb {M} _ {i} | + | \mathbb {M} _ {j} | \leq \Lambda \text { and } \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {i}) + \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {j}) \leq \Gamma),\tag{4.2}
$$

where${ \mathbb M } _ { i } ~ ( \mathrm { r e s p . } ~ { \mathbb M } _ { j } )$is the connected components of M in which the particle line$\pmb { p } \ ( \mathrm { r e s p . } \ p ^ { \prime } )$occurs, and M is the unique C-molecule which is topological reduction of$\gamma$.

Remark 4.4. In the (Λ, Γ)-truncated dynamics, we force the property that each cluster has size$\le \Lambda$and recollision number$\leq \Gamma$(Proposition 4.5 (5)), by neglecting any collisions that may violate this property.

Proposition 4.5. The E- and$( \Lambda , \Gamma )$-dynamics (Definitions 4.1 and 4.3) satisfy the following properties.

(1) Up to some Lebesgue zero set of$z ^ { 0 }$, the E- and T- dynamics in Definitions 4.1 and 4.3 are well-defined and produces admissible trajectories in Definition 3.7.

(2) Define$( \mathcal { H } ^ { E } , S ^ { E } )$and$( \mathcal { H } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } , S ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } )$as special cases of (3.3) and (3.4). Then, when the initial data $z ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { D } _ { N }$, the E-dynamics coincides with the O-dynamics in Definition 1.1, i.e.$z ^ { E } ( t ) = z ( t )$and $\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t ) ( z ^ { 0 } ) = \mathcal { H } _ { N } ( t ) ( z ^ { 0 } )$. Moreover, we have$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t ) f =  { S _ { N } } ( t ) f$if f is supported in$\mathcal { D } _ { N }$

(3) The$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$and$S _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$defined in (2) satisfy the following flow or semi-group property for$t , s \geq 0 :$

$$
\mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t + s) = \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (s), \qquad \mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t + s) = \mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) \mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (s).\tag{4.3}
$$

In general, the$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$and$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$might not satisfy the flow property.

(4) Both transport operators$S _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$and$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$preserve the$L ^ { 1 }$integral:

$$
\int (\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) f) \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} v = \int (\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) f) \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} v = \int f \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} v.\tag{4.4}
$$

(5) In the (Λ, Γ)-dynamics, suppose a trajectory topologically reduces to a C-molecule M. Then each connected component$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$of M satisfies$| \mathbb { M } _ { j } | _ { p } \le \Lambda$and$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) \leq \Gamma$, (recall the notions of) Moreover, for O-, E- and (Λ, Γ)-dynamics, the number of collisions |M| has an absolute upper bound that depends only on d and N.

4.2. The truncated domain. In this subsection, we introduce the domain$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$, which characterizes the initial data such that the truncated dynamics coincide with the extended dynamics.

Definition 4.6 (The truncated and error domain$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$and$\mathcal { E } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } )$. Given$( \Lambda , \Gamma )$, we define the truncated domain$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$as follows:

$$
\mathcal{D}_{N}^{\Lambda ,\Gamma} = \bigcup_{k = 1}^{N}\bigcup_{\substack{\{\lambda_{1},\dots ,\lambda_{k}\} \in \mathcal{P}_{N}^{k}\\ |\lambda_{j}|\leq \Lambda}}\Bigg\{\boldsymbol{z}^{0}\in \mathbb{R}^{2dN}:p(\mathbb{M}_{j}) = \lambda_{j}\text{and}\rho (\mathbb{M}_{j})\leq \Gamma \text{for each} 1\leq j\leq k\Bigg\} ,\tag{4.5}
$$

where$\mathbb { M } _ { j } \left( 1 \leq j \leq k \right)$are the components of the (unique) C-molecule topological reduction of the admissible trajectory$\boldsymbol { z } ^ { E } ( t ) \left( t \in [ 0 , \tau ] \right)$with initial configuration$z ^ { 0 }$. We also refer to these$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$as clusters.

We also define the error domain$\mathcal { E } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$as

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} := \mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N} \backslash \mathcal {D} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma}.\tag{4.6}
$$

Their indicator functions are denoted by$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } }$and$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { E } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } }$, and we have$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { E } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } } = 1 - \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } }$

The following proposition ensures that the E- and (Λ, Γ)-dynamics coincide on$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$

Proposition 4.7. For each$z ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$and$t \in [ 0 , \tau ]$we have$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ( z ^ { 0 } ) = \mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t ) ( z ^ { 0 } )$. Moreover, if f is supported in$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$, then we have$\bar { S _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \bar { \Gamma } } } ( t ) f = S _ { N } ^ { E } ( t ) f$. For general f we have

$$
\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) \big (\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma}} \cdot f \big) = \mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) \big (\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma}} \cdot f \big).\tag{4.7}
$$

Proof. Suppose$z ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$. By definition of$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$, in the whole E-dynamics$z _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$for$t \in [ 0 , \tau ]$, the size $| \mathbb { M } _ { j } |$of each cluster$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$(under the E-dynamics) never exceeds Λ, and the recollision number$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$never exceeds Γ. Therefore, whenever a collision happens in the E-dynamics, we must also have a collision in the (Λ, Γ)-dynamics. This implies that the E-dynamics$z _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$and (Λ, Γ)-dynamics$z _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$have exactly the same collisions, and thus coincide because they have the same initial data.

Now assume f is supported in$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$, then

$$
(\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) f) (\boldsymbol {z}) = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} \in \mathcal {D} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} \in \mathcal {D} _ {N} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = (\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) f) (\boldsymbol {z}).\tag{4.8}
$$

Then (4.7) follows because$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } } \cdot f$is supported in$\mathcal { D } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$

## 5. Proof of the cumulant formula

We already have (3.14), with$\widetilde { f } _ { s }$and$f _ { s } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$defined in (4.17) and (4.18) respectively. To complete Proposition 3.25, in this section, we prove the upper bound for$f _ { s } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } } \left( t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } , z _ { s } \right)$in (3.20), and the cumulant expansion formula (3.15) for$\widetilde { f _ { s } } ( \ell \tau )$, with bounds$( 3 . 1 6 ) \ – ( 3 . 1 9 )$. This is done in several steps.

Recall that the definition of$\bar { W } _ { N }$and$\widetilde { f } _ { s }$involves the transport operator$S _ { N } ^ { \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } , \Gamma } ( \tau )$defined by the truncated dynamics. In Sections 5.1–5.2 we will prove a crucial decomposition formula for this operator, namely Proposition 5.10. Then in Sections 5.3–5.4, we will use this decomposition to prove Proposition 5.16. This is the key inductive step, which establishes the cumulant decomposition (3.15) at time$\ell \tau$provided the same expansion holds at time$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$, and expresses the cumulant$E _ { H } ( \ell \tau )$in terms of$E _ { H } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$and a molecule $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell }$with single layer$\ell .$Then in Sections 5.5–5.6, by induction in ℓ using Proposition 5.16, and using the initial cumulant formula (time$t = 0$, see Proposition 5.18), we complete the proof of Proposition 3.25.

Remark 5.4. We explain the idea behind Definition 5.3 (3). Lemma 5.6. Let M be a molecule with connected components$\{ \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \cdots , \mathbb { M } _ { k } \}$and$p ( \mathbb { M } ) = [ N ]$. Let S be the set of initial configurations$z ^ { 0 }$defined by the above conditions. If$z ^ { 0 } \in { \mathfrak { S } }$and$f$is supported in$\mathfrak { S } .$, then for$t \in [ 0 , \tau ]$we have

Proof. We divide the proof into 4 parts. Recall$z _ { \lambda } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$is the partial dynamics, and$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda }$is obtained from selecting the particles in λ from the full dynamics$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$; in general they are not equal.

Proof part 1. In this part we prove that, if no particle in λ collides with particle in$\lambda ^ { c }$in the full dynamics$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$, then we have$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda } = z _ { \lambda } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$

To prove this fact, define

$$
t _ {*} = \sup \left\{t: (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t)) _ {\lambda} = \boldsymbol {z} _ {\lambda} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) \right\},
$$

it sufices to show that$t _ { * } = \tau . \mathrm { ~ I f ~ } t _ { * } < \tau ,$by left continuity we have$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda } = z _ { \lambda } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$for all$t \leq t _ { * }$. Let the C-molecule topological reduction of$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$and$z _ { \lambda } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( \dot { t } )$(up to time$t _ { * } )$be M and$\mathbb { M } _ { \lambda }$, since no collision occurs between particles in$\lambda$and$\lambda ^ { c }$, we know that$\mathbb { M } _ { \lambda }$is just a connected component of M consisting particle lines in λ. Consider the possible collision in either$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda } ~ \mathrm { o r } ~ z _ { \lambda } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$at time$t _ { * }$. By Definition 4.3 of the (Λ, Γ)-dynamics, we know that, whether this collision is allowed is determined only by properties of the molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { \lambda }$, in both cases. As such, the two dynamics must follow the same scattering rule at$t _ { * }$. Moreover, up to a zero measure, no other collisions occur for$t > t _ { * }$suficiently close to$t _ { * }$. Therefore, the two dynamics remain identical for such$t ,$contradicting the maximality of$t _ { * }$. This contradiction shows that we must have$t _ { * } = \tau$, as desired.

Proof part 2. In this part, we show that (1) and (2) hold under the assumption that$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$topologically reduces to M. In fact, this assumption implies that no collision happens between any particle in$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$and any particle in$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } )$in the full dynamics$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$. By Part 1, we know that

$$
\boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {j})} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) = (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t)) _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {j})} \quad \text {and} \quad \boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {j}) \cup p (\mathbb {M} _ {j ^ {\prime}})} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t) = (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {\Lambda , \Gamma} (t)) _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {j}) \cup p (\mathbb {M} _ {j ^ {\prime}})}.
$$

Clearly the first equation above implies (1). The second equation implies that there is also no collision between$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$and$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } )$in the partial dynamics$z _ { p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) \cup p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } ) } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$, which is (2).

Proof part 3. In this part, we show that (1) and (2) implies that$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$topologically reduces to M. Let$\lambda _ { j } = p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$and$\lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } } = p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } )$. We first show that under (1) and (2), there is no collision between any$\lambda _ { j }$and$\lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } } \mathrm { ~ i n ~ } z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$. Assume the contrary, there must exist a first collision time$t _ { * }$between some$\lambda _ { j }$ and$\lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } }$. Let the next collision time in$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$be$t _ { * } + \delta .$, then in the time interval$[ 0 , t _ { * } + \delta ]$, there is no collision between particles in$\lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } }$and$( \lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } } ) ^ { c }$. By Part 1, we know that$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } } } = z _ { \lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j } } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$ for$t \in [ 0 , t _ { * } + \delta ]$, which is impossible because there is a collision between$\lambda _ { j }$and$\lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } }$in$( z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t ) ) _ { \lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } } }$while there is no collision between$\lambda _ { j }$and$\lambda _ { j ^ { \prime } }$in$z _ { \lambda _ { j } \cup \lambda _ { j } } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$by (2).

Now assume$z ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } ( t )$topologically reduces to$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, we only need to show$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M }$. 5.2. Penrose argument and molecule representation. In this subsection, we start from (5.6) in Lemma 5.5, and treat the product$\prod \mathbb { 1 } _ { ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } , e ) \sim ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } , e ^ { \prime } ) }$using the Penrose argument which introduces the O-atoms, with the goal of proving (5.17) in Proposition 5.10. Definition 5.7. Let Λ and Γ be fixed. The molecules M and$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$in this definition have only one layer$\ell ,$but may contain O-atoms. Here$\{ \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \cdots , \mathbb { M } _ { k } \}$are clusters of M obtained by deleting all O-atoms (Definition 3.11), and e and $e ^ { \prime }$are edges in$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } }$respectively (obtained from deleting O-atoms) that are joined by an O-atom in M. The indicator function$1 _ { \prec }$indicates that if${ \mathfrak { o } } \prec { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime }$are O-atoms of M that belong to the same ov-segment, then the overlap corresponding to o occurs earlier than that of${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime }$.

(2) The operator$( S \circ \mathbb { I } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } }$. Recall the operators$( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } }$and$| ( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } |$defined in (3.10) (with$( \ell - \underline { { \ell } } + 1 ) \tau$ replaced by τ as M has only one layer):

We now define the operator$( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } }$which is variant of$( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } }$. Lemma 5.9. For any molecule M we have$\mathbb { I } _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma } \le \mathbb { I } _ { \mathbb { M } }$

Proof. First assume M is C-molecule (so$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$is as in Definition 5.3). where$| O _ { 1 } ( A ) | \le A$(see Definition 1.6 (7)).

where$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } }$is C-molecule, and$\{ \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } , \cdots , \mathbb { M } _ { k } \}$are connected components of$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } }$

We divide the proof into 4 parts.

Proof part 1: preparations. Let the labeled C-molecule${ \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } } .$, and the clusters$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$, be fixed for now. Note that$p ( { \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } } ) = [ N ]$, and also fix the root particles set to be [s]. A cluster$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$is called a root cluster if it contains a root particle.

The M on the right hand side of (5.17) will be formed by selecting certain clusters$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and joining them by certain O-atoms. To treat the product$\prod \mathbb { 1 } _ { ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } , e ) \sim ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } , e ^ { \prime } ) }$in (5.18), we apply the Penrose argument in the spirit of [8]. By writing$\mathbb { 1 } _ { ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } , e ) \sim \langle \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } , e ^ { \prime } \rangle } = 1 - \mathbb { 1 } _ { ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } , e ) \sim ( \mathbb { M } _ { j ^ { \prime } } , e ^ { \prime } ) }$and expanding, we get

$$
\prod \mathbb {1} _ {(\mathbb {M} _ {j}, e) \not \sim (\mathbb {M} _ {j ^ {\prime}}, e ^ {\prime})} = \sum_ {G \in 2 ^ {E}} (- 1) ^ {| G |} \mathbb {1} _ {G}, \quad \mathbb {1} _ {G} = \prod_ {(e, e ^ {\prime}) \in G} \mathbb {1} _ {(\mathbb {M} _ {j}, e) \sim (\mathbb {M} _ {j ^ {\prime}}, e ^ {\prime})}.\tag{5.19}

(2) We show that, for each$F \in { \mathcal { F } } \cup { \mathcal { F } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$that belongs to the range of$\pi ,$one can define a forbidden set $F B ( F )$, such that for any$G \in 2 ^ { E }$we have

The mapping π will be constructed (with properties (2)–(3) proved) in Part 4 of the proof below. In this and the next part, we use only these properties to finish the proof of (5.17). The point is that we rewrite the sum in (5.19) as

$$

$$

Before defining π, we first make some preparations. For each root particle line$r \in [ s ]$ let$\mathbb { Q } _ { \boldsymbol { r } }$<sub>r</sub> be the (root) cluster containing$r ,$and$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } ( r )$be the component of${ \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } } _ { G }$containing$r$(and$\mathbb { Q } _ { r } )$, and $\operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$be the corresponding component of$\operatorname { C l } _ { G }$. For each cluster$\mathbb { Q } \in \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$, consider the graph theoretic distance between$\mathbb { Q }$and$\mathbb { Q } _ { r }$(i.e. the length of shortest path connecting them), and define$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( r )$to be the set of$\mathbb { Q } \in \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$with the above distance being$q \geq 0$

Algorithm defining π. For each root particle$r \in [ s ]$, let$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } ( r )$and$\operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$be defined above. We distinguish two cases:

Case$1 \colon \ i f \ | \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ) | < \Lambda$for each r. We perform the following steps:
