(2) Consider all the elements$\mathfrak { o } = ( e , e ^ { \prime } ) \in G \ ( \mathrm { i . e }$. O-atoms in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } )$that join a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( 1 )$and a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( 1 )$for some$q \geq 0$. We order them first in the increasing order in$q ,$and then in the increasing order in o (following the linear order defined above).

(3) Start with the set$S : = \{ \mathbb { Q } _ { 1 } \}$. Each time, select the smallest$\mathfrak { o } = ( e , e ^ { \prime } )$in (2) that still remains in $\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } ( 1 )$. Let K be the cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( 1 )$that is joined by o to a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( 1 )$, we add {K} to the set$S ,$and delete all other elements of G (i.e. O-atoms) that join K to another cluster in$S .$Repeat until S exhausts all clusters in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( 1 )$, then stop working in this component.

(4) Then, select the next smallest root particle r that does not belong to any previously operated component, and repeat$( 1 ) - ( 3 )$until all root clusters have been accounted for. Finally, delete all O-atoms that do not belong to any$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } ( r )$. Define the result to be$F = \pi ( G )$

Case 2: if$| \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ) | \geq \Lambda$for some r. We perform the same steps as in Case$^ { 1 , }$except at the first time when $| \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ) | \geq \Lambda$. At this time we perform$( 1 ) - ( 3 )$as in Case$^ { 1 , }$but terminate early when$| S | = \Lambda$(without adding the next atom to S). Then we delete all the o that still remains in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { G } ( r )$and do not join two clusters in S. After this, stop exploring (even if there are still root clusters) and delete all O-atoms that do not belong to any previously operated component. Define the result to be$F = \pi ( G )$

It is easy to verify the following properties of$\pi ( G ) = F ;$in particular, they imply that$F \in { \mathcal { F } } \cup { \mathcal { F } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$by definitions in Part 1.

• The cluster graph$\mathrm { C l } _ { F }$is a forest. This is because in our construction (3), each new cluster in$S$has only one overlap (after deletion) joining it to earlier clusters in S.

• If$| \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ) | < \Lambda$, then$\operatorname { C l } _ { F } ( r ) = \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$and$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( r )$. This is because in our construction$( 3 )$ the set S remains connected in the cluster graph, and each cluster in$S \cap \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( r )$is always connected to$\mathbb { Q } _ { r }$by a path of length q even after the deletions.

• In Case$\mathcal { Q } , \mathrm { C l } _ { F }$has a unique component$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$that contains Λ clusters; each component$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$ that is operated before$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$contains$< \Lambda$clusters, and each component other than$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$and $\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$contains only one cluster. This is clear from the construction in Case 2.

Definition of$F B ( F )$. Now we define the set$F B ( F )$as follows.

Case 1: when$| \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ) | < \Lambda$for each r. We define${ \mathfrak { o } } \in F B ( F )$if and only if

(1) o joins two clusters in two diferent components$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r )$;

(2) o joins a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r )$and a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q ^ { \prime } } ( r )$with$| q - q ^ { \prime } | \geq 2 ;$or

(3)${ \mathfrak { o } } \notin F$joins a cluster$\mathbb { Q } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r )$and a cluster$\mathbb { K } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q + 1 } ( r )$, and the unique${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime } \in F$joining$\mathbb { K }$to a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r )$satisfies${ \mathfrak { o } } < { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime }$in the linear ordering; or

(4) o joins a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r )$and a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F }$not in any$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$

Case 2: when$| \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } ) | = \Lambda$. We define the components$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$and previously operated components $\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$as above, and let their union be$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( \leq r _ { 0 } )$. Consider also the last cluster K reaching$| S | = \Lambda$in Case 2 of the algorithm; assume it belongs to$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q _ { 0 } } ( r _ { 0 } )$and the associated smallest o is${ \mathfrak { o } } _ { 0 }$. Then, we define ${ \mathfrak { o } } \in F B ( F )$if and only if

(5) o satisfies one of (1)–(3) holds within${ \mathrm { C l } } _ { F } ( \leq r _ { 0 } ) ;$; or

(6) o joins one cluster K outside$\mathrm { C l } _ { \leq r _ { 0 } }$and another cluster$\mathbb { Q } .$which either belongs to$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$for some $r ^ { \prime }$as above, or belongs to$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r _ { 0 } )$for some$q < q _ { 0 } - 1$, or belongs to$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q _ { 0 } - 1 } ( r _ { 0 } )$and${ \mathfrak { o } } < { \mathfrak { o } } _ { 0 }$

Proof of (2)–(3) in Part 2. Now, with the mapping π and the set$F B ( F )$defined as above, we can prove the properties (2)–(3) in Part 2.

The main point is to show (5.20). Recall the properties$( 1 ) - ( 6 )$in the definition of$F B ( F )$above. We first show that if$\pi ( G ) = F$then$F B ( F ) \cap G = \emptyset$(as$F \subseteq G$is obvious). Assume$\mathfrak { o } \in F B ( F ) \cap G$for contradiction, and consider each of the cases$( 1 ) - ( 6 )$

(1) If o joins a clusters in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r )$and a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } ) \ne \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r )$, then we have$\operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r ) = \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r ^ { \prime } )$ because of${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$but this is contradiction because$\operatorname { C l } _ { F } ( r ) = \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$and$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ^ { \prime } )$

(2) If o joins a clusters in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r )$and a cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q ^ { \prime } } ( r )$with$q ^ { \prime } \geq q + 2$, then this latter cluster belongs to $\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( r )$or lower because of${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$but this is contradiction because$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( r ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q + 1 } ( r )$is disjoint with$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q ^ { \prime } } ( r )$

(3) If o joins$\mathbb { Q } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r )$and$\mathbb { K } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q + 1 } ( r )$, and satisfies${ \mathfrak { o } } \leq { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime }$where${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime } \in F .$, then consider the time when we add {K} into S. By the construction in (3) of the algorithm, we would select o and delete${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \prime } .$so the result will not be$F ,$, contradiction.

(4) If o joins one cluster in$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r )$to a cluster K not in any$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$, then$\mathbb { K } \in \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$because of${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$, but this implies$\mathbb { K } \in \operatorname { C l } _ { F } ( r )$, contradiction.

(5) This case is basically the same as (1)–(3) but restricted to$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$and$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$

(6) Assume o joins K$\notin \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( \leq r _ { 0 } )$and Q as specified. If$\mathbb { Q } \in \operatorname { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$for some$r ^ { \prime }$in the definition of $F B ( F )$above, then we have$\mathbb { K } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ^ { \prime } ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } )$due to o, which is a contradiction. If$\mathbb { Q } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r _ { 0 } )$for $q < q _ { 0 } - 1$, then similarly$\mathbb { K } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( r _ { 0 } ) \subseteq \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r _ { 0 } )$(the subset relation is because$q + 1 < q _ { 0 }$, so all clusters in$\mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q + 1 } ( r _ { 0 } )$must have been exhausted in the construction in (3) of the algorithm before reaching$| S | = \Lambda )$ which is also contradiction. Finally if$\mathbb { Q } \in \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q _ { 0 } - 1 } ( r _ { 0 } )$and${ \mathfrak { o } } < { \mathfrak { o } } _ { 0 }$, then again the in construction we would select o at some point before selecting${ \mathfrak { o } } _ { 0 }$, so the result will not be$F ,$contradiction.

We next show that if$F \subseteq G$and$F B ( F ) \cap G = \emptyset$, then we must have$\pi ( G ) = F$. This is basically done by reverting the proof in cases$( 1 ) - ( 6 )$above, which we carry out below.

Assume first that$| \mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ) | < \Lambda$for each r. Then, using the absence of elements in (1) and (4), we deduce that$\operatorname { C l } _ { F } ( r ) = \operatorname { C l } _ { G } ( r )$for each$r ;$using the absence of elements in (2), we can inductively show that $\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( r )$for each r and$q .$Finally, using the assumptions for (3), we see that the choice of edges in the construction of$\pi ( G )$exactly leads to those edges already in$F .$

The case when some$| F _ { r _ { 0 } } | = \Lambda$is similar. The same arguments above implies that$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( r ^ { \prime } ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ( r ^ { \prime } )$for those$r ^ { \prime }$in the definition of$F B ( F )$above, and$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ^ { q } ( r _ { 0 } ) = \mathrm { C l } _ { G } ^ { q } ( r _ { 0 } )$for$q < q _ { 0 }$, and the result up to this point coincides with$F .$. Then, when we execute (3) of the algorithm and each time choosing a smallest remaining ${ \mathfrak { o } } ,$the absence of elements in (6) guarantees that we cannot add anything outside$\mathrm { C l } _ { F } ( \leq r _ { 0 } )$into S. So the result coincides with$F ,$as desired.

Finally, we prove the properties of$A L ( F )$in (3) in Part 2. In fact, the first two properties (5.21)–(5.22) follow immediately from the definition of$F B ( F )$(and thus$A L ( F ) )$above. The last property concerning relabeling is also obvious, because the set$A L ( F )$is constructed using the linear ordering for o, which is invariant under the said relabelings.□

5.3. Recurrence formula for${ \widetilde { f } } _ { s } .$. In this subsection we apply the decomposition of$\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } } _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$, i.e. (5.17) in Proposition 5.10, to obtain a representation formula of$\widetilde { f _ { s } } ( \ell \tau )$at time$\ell \tau$, in terms of single-layer molecules M and the same quantity$\widetilde { f } _ { s }$at time$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$. See Proposition 5.12.

Definition 5.11 (Sets$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$and$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } } )$. Given$\Lambda _ { \ell } ,$, define$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$(resp.$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } } )$to be the set of equivalence class [M] of labeled molecules M of single layer$\ell ,$such that$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$(resp.$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } } )$as in Definition 5.7 (3). Note that the$\mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { i } }$in Definition 3.20 (3) is a special case of this$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda , \ell }$with only one root particle (the$\mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$is unrelated to$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$, though.)

Proposition 5.12 (Recurrence formula for$\widetilde { f } _ { s } )$. Recall$\widetilde { f _ { s } } ( \ell \tau , z _ { s } )$defined in (4.14) and (4.17). For M with one layer$\ell ,$define

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {f} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\ell \tau , \pmb {z} _ {r (\mathbb {M})}) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} | _ {p \setminus r}} \int (\mathcal {S} \circ \mathbb {1}) _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}} \big (\widetilde {f} _ {| \mathbb {M} | _ {p}} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \pmb {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M})} ^ {\prime}) \big) d \pmb {z} _ {(p \setminus r) (\mathbb {M})},} \\ & {\widetilde {f} _ {\mathbb {M}, \mathrm{upp}} (\ell \tau , \pmb {z} _ {r (\mathbb {M})}) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} | _ {p \setminus r}} \int | (\mathcal {S} \circ \mathbb {1}) _ {\mathbb {M}} | \big (| \widetilde {f} _ {| \mathbb {M} | _ {p}} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \pmb {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M})} ^ {\prime}) | \big) d \pmb {z} _ {(p \setminus r) (\mathbb {M})}.} \end{array}\tag{5.32}
$$

Then we have the following formula

$$
\begin{array}{c} \widetilde {f} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} ] \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}}, r (\mathbb {M}) = [ s ]} \widetilde {f} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) + \mathrm{Err} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}), \\ | \mathrm{Err} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) | \leq \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} ] \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}} ^ {\mathrm{err}}, r (\mathbb {M}) = [ s ]} \widetilde {f} _ {\mathbb {M}, \mathrm{upp}} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}). \end{array}\tag{5.33}
$$

Remark 5.13. The expressions in (5.32) are just like those in (3.11)–(3.12) in Definition 3.23, with the transport operator$( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } }$(and its variant) associated with the molecule M, and integration in the non-root particles. Here the molecule M has single layer ℓ, as we evolve from time$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$to time$\ell \tau$. The input function is the density$\widetilde { f } _ { | \mathbb { M } | _ { \mathcal { F } } }$at time$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$, with$z _ { p ( \mathbb { M } ) } ^ { \prime }$being the states of the particles at time$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$ Note also that$\ell _ { 1 } [ { \pmb p } ] - \underline { { \ell } } = 0$in (3.11)–(3.12) because M has only one layer$\ell .$

We remark that the$f _ { \mathbb { M } }$in (5.32) is not constant on each equivalence class [M] due to the$( S \circ \mathbb { I } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } }$factor (in fact this is the only instance of non-constant cases throughout this paper). By Definition 1.6 (6), we should interpret the sum as

$$
\sum_{[\mathbb{M}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}) = [s]}(\dots):= \sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ p(\mathbb{M}) = [|\mathbb{M}|_{p}],r(\mathbb{M}) = [s]}}\frac{1}{(|\mathbb{M}|_{p} - s)!} (\dots).\tag{5.34}
$$

Here note that$\mathrm { ( i ) }$we may always restrict$p ( \mathbb { M } ) = [ | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } ]$in each equivalence class [M], without afecting the expression$\widetilde { f _ { \mathrm { M } } }$or the average in [M] (thanks to Definition$5 . 7 \ ( 2 \mathrm { c } ) )$), and (ii) once$p ( \mathbb { M } ) = [ | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } ]$is fixed, the size of the equivalence class equal$| [ \mathbb { M } ] | = ( | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } - s ) !$due to permuting the$\| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } - s$non-root labels.

Proof. In the summation below we only consider the sum over$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$and$[ \mathbb { M } ] \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } .$, as the the remaining sum over$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$and$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$is similar (in fact easier as$\widetilde { f } _ { \mathrm { M , u p p } }$is invariant under equivalence relation).

By (4.14) and (4.17), we have

$$
\widetilde {f} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \varepsilon^ {s (d - 1)} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d n}} \mathcal {S} _ {s + n} ^ {\Lambda_ {\ell}, \Gamma} (\tau) \widetilde {W} _ {s + n} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s + n} ^ {\prime}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}.\tag{5.35}
$$

Here, for distinction, we used a diferent set of variables$z _ { s + n } ^ { \prime }$for the states at (ℓ − 1)τ . Inserting (5.17), we get the decomposition

$$
\begin{array}{l}\widetilde{f} (\ell \tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{s}) = \varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ p(\mathbb{M})\subseteq [s + n],  r(\mathbb{M}) = [s]\\ }}\frac{1}{n!}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2dn}}(\mathcal{S}\circ \mathbb{1})_{\mathbb{M}}^{\mathrm{Pen}}\circ \mathcal{S}_{[s + n]\setminus p(\mathbb{M})}\widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{s + n}^{\prime})  \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}_{[s + 1:s + n]}\\ \\ +( \operatorname{Err}), \end{array}\tag{5.36}
$$

where (Err) represents the sum over$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$. By Definition$5 . 7 \ ( 2 \mathrm { c } )$, in the summation (5.36), we may always restrict$p ( \mathbb { M } ) = [ | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } ]$, with an additional factor$\binom { n } { | { \mathbb { M } } | _ { p } - s }$(this fixes the set of labels of non-root particles, but not the label of each individual particles). This leads to the expression

$$
\begin{array}{l}\widetilde{f} (\ell \tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{s}) = \varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ p(\mathbb{M}) = [|\mathbb{M}|_{p}],  r(\mathbb{M}) = [s]}}\frac{1}{(|\mathbb{M}|_{p} - s)!(n - |\mathbb{M}|_{p} + s)!}\\ \\ \times \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d n}}(\mathcal{S}\circ \mathbb{1})_{\mathbb{M}}^{\text{Pen}}\circ \mathcal{S}_{[s + n]\setminus p(\mathbb{M})}^{\Lambda_{\ell},\Gamma}\widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{s + n}^{\prime})  \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}_{[s + 1:s + n]} + (\text{Err}). \end{array}\tag{5.37}
$$

Upon switching the order of summation, we get

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\widetilde {f} (\ell \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \varepsilon^ {s (d - 1)} \sum_ {\substack {\mathbb {M} \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}} \\ p (\mathbb {M}) = [ | \mathbb {M} | _ {p} ], r (\mathbb {M}) = [ s ]}} \frac {1}{(| \mathbb {M} | _ {p} - s) !} \int (\mathcal {S} \circ \mathbb {1}) _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}}} \\ & {\Bigg (\sum_ {n = | \mathbb {M} | _ {p} - s} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{(n - | \mathbb {M} | _ {p} + s) !} \int \mathcal {S} _ {[ | \mathbb {M} | _ {p} + 1: s + n ]} ^ {\Lambda_ {\ell}, \Gamma} \widetilde {W} _ {s + n} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {s + n} ^ {\prime}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ | \mathbb {M} | _ {p} + 1: s + n ]} \Bigg) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {(p \setminus r) (\mathbb {M})} + (\mathrm{Err}).} \end{array}\tag{5.38}
$$

Consider the parenthesis in the second line in (5.38). Using the$L ^ { 1 }$invariance of${ \mathcal { S } } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$(Proposition 4.5 (4)) and (1.11), we conclude that this parenthesis equals$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } } \widetilde { f } _ { | \mathbb { M } | _ { p } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , z _ { p ( \mathbb { M } ) } ^ { \prime } )$. This implies that

$$
\widetilde{f} (\ell \tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{s}) = \sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ p(\mathbb{M}) = [|\mathbb{M}|_{p}],  r(\mathbb{M}) = [s]}}\frac{\varepsilon^{-(d - 1)(|\mathbb{M}|_{p} - s)}}{(|\mathbb{M}|_{p} - s)!}\int (\mathcal{S}\circ \mathbb{1})_{\mathbb{M}}^{\mathrm{Pen}}\widetilde{f}_{|\mathbb{M}|_{p}}((\ell -1)\tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{p(\mathbb{M})}^{\prime})  \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}_{p(\mathbb{M})} + (\mathrm{Err}).\tag{5.39}
$$

Now, using (5.34) and note that$s = | \mathbb { M } | _ { r }$, we see that the main term in (5.39) exactly matches that in (5.33). Since the error term (Err) can be treated in the same way, this completes the proof of Proposition 5.12. □

5.4. Recurrence formula for cumulants. In this subsection, starting from (5.33) in Proposition 5.12, we shall insert the ansatz (3.15) for$\widetilde { f _ { s } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$and subsequently derive the same expansion for$\widetilde { f _ { s } } ( \ell \tau )$. This also includes a recurrence formula for both$f ^ { A }$and$E _ { H }$in (3.15), see Proposition 5.16. This is the main step in the proof of Proposition 3.25; with it, we simply proceed by induction in ℓ, and use the initial cumulant expansion for$\ell = 0$(Proposition 5.18 in Section 5.5), which is done in Section 5.6.

Definition 5.14. Given a molecule M and$H \subseteq p ( \mathbb { M } )$, we define$r ( \mathbb { M } ) \searrow H$, if each particle line$r \in r ( \mathbb { M } )$ belongs to a component of M, which contains either another particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } )$, or a particle line in H.

Remark 5.15. Using Definition 3.19, the condition$r ( \mathbb { M } ) \searrow H$can also be expressed as “each particle line in $r ( \mathbb { M } )$is connected to either another particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } )$via$\mathbb { M } ,$or connected to a particle line in H via M, or belongs to$H ^ { \ast }$, in the same manner as Definition 3.20 (1d).

In reality,$r ( \mathbb { M } ) = r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$will be the root particle set of a certain layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, and$H = r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 } )$will be the root particle set of the previous layer. The symbol$r ( \mathbb { M } ) \searrow H$means that$r ( \mathbb { M } )$is either connected “horizontally” to itself, or “vertically” to H in the previous layer.

Proposition 5.16. Fix ℓ and$( A _ { \ell } , \Lambda _ { \ell } )$defined in (1.32). Assume for each set$Q _ { \ell - 1 }$with$s ^ { + } = | Q _ { \ell - 1 } | \leq \Lambda _ { \ell } ^ { 2 } A _ { \ell }$，we have cumulant expansion at$t = ( \ell - 1 ) \tau$

$$
\widetilde {f} _ {s ^ {+}} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {Q _ {\ell - 1}}) = \sum_ {H _ {\ell - 1} \subseteq Q _ {\ell - 1}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} ((\ell - 1) \tau)) ^ {\otimes (Q _ {\ell - 1} \setminus H _ {\ell - 1})} \cdot E _ {H _ {\ell - 1}} ((\ell - 1) \tau) + \operatorname{Err} ((\ell - 1) \tau , \boldsymbol {z} _ {Q _ {\ell - 1}}),\tag{5.40}
$$

where$E _ { H _ { \ell - 1 } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$is a function of$z _ { H _ { \ell - 1 } }$(with$E _ { \mathcal { O } } = 1$by convention) and is symmetric in its variables, $f ^ { \mathcal { A } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$is a single variable function of$\boldsymbol { z } = ( x , v )$), and the tensor product$( f ^ { A } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau ) ) ^ { \otimes ( Q _ { \ell - 1 } \setminus H _ { \ell - 1 } ) }$is a function of$z _ { Q _ { \ell - 1 } \backslash H _ { \ell - 1 } } .$

Then for each$Q _ { \ell }$with$s = | Q _ { \ell } | \leq A _ { \ell } .$, we have the cumulant expansion at$t = \ell \tau \colon$

$$

$$

then$f ^ { A } , E _ { H _ { \ell } }$and Err in (5.41) are explicitly given by the following formulas:

Note that the right hand side of (5.43) is also a function of a single variable$z { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } | r ( \mathbb { M } ) | = 1$

(2) The cumulant$E _ { H _ { \ell } } ( \ell \tau , z _ { H _ { \ell } } )$satisfies

$$
|E_{H_{\ell}}(\ell \tau ,\boldsymbol{z}_{H_{\ell}})|\leq \sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = H_{\ell}\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}),  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}|\mathcal{I}\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell},H_{\ell -1}}|(  \boldsymbol{z}_{r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})}  ).\tag{5.44}
$$

$$
\| \mathrm{Err} ^ {2} (\ell \tau) \| _ {L ^ {1}} \leq \varepsilon^ {- 2 (d - 1) \Lambda_ {\ell} ^ {2} A _ {\ell}} \cdot \| \mathrm{Err} ((\ell - 1) \tau) \| _ {L ^ {1}}.\tag{5.46}
$$

Remark 5.17. We make a few remarks regarding Proposition 5.16. First, the function$E _ { H } ( \ell \tau )$depends only on$| H |$and is symmetric in its variables, and the functions Err,$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 1 } }$and$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 2 } }$are symmetric in all their variables. By (5.34), we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}\sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})}}\bigcirc = \sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}),  p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [| \mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p}]}}\frac{1}{(|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} - s)!}\cdot \bigcirc \\ \\ = \sum_{n_{\ell} = s}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n_{\ell} - s)!}\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}),  p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [n_{\ell}]}}\bigcirc \\ \\ = \sum_{n_{\ell} = s}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n_{\ell} - s)!}\sum_{H_{\ell}\subseteq [s]} \sum_{\substack{(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r))_{r\notin H_{\ell}}\\ \mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}} \prod_{r}\bigcirc_{r}\cdot \sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\\ p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [n_{\ell}],  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}) = H_{\ell}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}\bigcirc^{\prime}. \end{array}\tag{5.64}
$$

By Definition 5.7 (2c), we know that the summand ⃝ remains invariant under any relabeling that preserves the order of labels within each component. Now consider the summation in (5.64) with$n _ { \ell } , H _ { \ell }$and$\big | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ^ { \prime } \big | _ { p \setminus r } : =$ $m ^ { \prime }$fixed, and with$| \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r ) | _ { p \backslash r } : = m _ { i }$fixed for each r. The number of choices for the non-root particle sets of each$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r )$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ^ { \prime }$is given by the multinomial coeficient$\binom { n _ { \ell } - s } { m _ { 1 } , \cdots , m _ { r } , m ^ { \prime } }$. For each fixed choice of these sets, we have

$$
\sum_{\substack{(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r))_{r\not\in H_{\ell}}:p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r))\text{fixed}\\ \mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}} \prod_{r}\bigcirc_{r} = \prod_{r\not\in H_{\ell}}\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}:p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r))\text{fixed}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}} \bigcirc_{r} = \prod_{r\not\in H_{\ell}}m_{r}! \sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)]\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}:|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)|_{p\setminus r} = m_{r}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}} \bigcirc_{r},\tag{5.65}
$$

where the last equality is because diferent choices of$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r ) )$do not afect the expression$\bigcirc _ { r }$or the average in the equivalence class$\textstyle \left[ \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r ) \right]$by the above invariance property. Similarly we have

$$
\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\\ p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\text{fixed},r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}) = H_{\ell}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}\bigcirc^{\prime} = (m^{\prime})!\sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}:|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}|_{p\setminus r} = m^{\prime},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}) = H_{\ell}\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}),  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}\bigcirc^{\prime}.\tag{5.66}
$$

By inserting (5.65)–(5.66) into (5.64), and first summing in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r )$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ^ { \prime }$and then in the non-root particle sets and finally in$m _ { r }$and$m ^ { \prime } { . }$, we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} (5.64) = \sum_{n_{\ell} = s}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n_{\ell} - s)!}\sum_{H_{\ell}\subseteq [s]}\sum_{\substack{(m_{r})_{r\not\in H_{\ell}},m^{\prime}\\ m^{\prime} + \sum_{r}m_{r} = n_{\ell} - s}}\binom {n_{\ell} - s}{m_{1},\dots ,m_{r},m^{\prime}}\\ \\ \times \prod_{r\not\in H_{\ell}}m_{r}!\sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)]\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}:|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)|_{p\setminus r} = m_{r}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}} \bigcirc_{r}\cdot (m^{\prime})!\sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}:|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}|_{p\setminus r} = m^{\prime},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}) = H_{\ell}\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}),  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}\bigcirc^{\prime}. \end{array}\tag{5.67}
$$

Using the multinomial formula, we see that the combinatorial factors in (5.67) exactly cancel. Let the summations in the second line of (5.67) be$X _ { m } ,$and$Y _ { m ^ { \prime } }$respectively, then

$$
\begin{aligned} (5.64) = & \sum_{H_{\ell}\subseteq [s]}\sum_{n_{\ell} = s}^{\infty}\sum_{\substack{(m_{r})_{r\notin H_{\ell}},m^{\prime}\\ m^{\prime} + \sum_{r}m_{r} = n_{\ell} - s}}\prod_{r\notin H_{\ell}}X_{m_{r}}\cdot Y_{m^{\prime}}\\ & = \sum_{H_{\ell}\subseteq [s]}\sum_{(m_{r})_{r\notin H_{\ell}},m^{\prime}}\prod_{r\notin H_{\ell}}X_{m_{r}}\cdot Y_{m^{\prime}} = \sum_{H_{\ell}\subseteq [s]}\prod_{r\notin H_{\ell}}\left(\sum_{m_{r}}X_{m_{r}}\right)\cdot \left(\sum_{m^{\prime}}Y_{m^{\prime}}\right) \end{aligned} \tag{5.64}\tag{5.68}
$$

where we have changed the order of summation. Finally, by definition of$X _ { m _ { r } }$and$Y _ { m ^ { \prime } }$we have

$$
\sum_{m_{r}}X_{m_{r}} = \sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)]\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)) = \{r\}}}\bigcirc_{r} = \sum_{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}(r)]\in \mathcal{T}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}}\bigcirc_{r},\qquad \sum_{m^{\prime}}Y_{m^{\prime}} = \sum_{\substack{[\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}]\in \mathcal{F}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}) = H_{\ell}\\ H_{\ell -1}\subseteq p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime}),  r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}^{\prime})\searrow H_{\ell -1}}}\bigcirc^{\prime}\tag{5.69}
$$

(note that$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ( r )$has only one root particle, and renaming it into r or anything else does not afect the expression$\bigcirc _ { r }$or the average in the equivalence class). By putting together (5.68) and (5.69), we have proved (5.61). This completes the proof of Proposition 5.16.□

5.5. The initial cumulant expansion. In this subsection we prove the initial cumulant expansion (5.41) for$\ell = 0$, without the Err term, see Proposition 5.18. The initial cumulants$E _ { H _ { 0 } } ( 0 )$correspond to the closeness scenarios$| x _ { p _ { 1 } } - x _ { p _ { 2 } } | \leq \varepsilon$which, stem from the$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } _ { N } }$indicator functions in (1.7).

Proposition 5.18 (Initial cumulant expansion). Assume that the initial density function$W _ { 0 , N } ( z _ { N } )$is given by (1.7). Then for each set$Q _ { 0 }$with$\left| Q _ { 0 } \right| \leq A _ { 0 } \left( A _ { 0 } \right)$is defined in (1.32)), we have initial cumulant expansion at t = 0:

$$
f (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {Q _ {0}}) = \sum_ {H _ {0} \subseteq Q _ {0}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes (Q _ {0} \setminus H _ {0})} \cdot E _ {H _ {0}} (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {H _ {0}}),\tag{5.70}
$$

where$f ^ { A } ( 0 , z ) = f _ { 0 } ( z )$and$E _ { H _ { 0 } } ( 0 , z _ { H _ { 0 } } )$satisfies the following upper bound

$$
| E _ {H _ {0}} (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {H _ {0}}) | \leq (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H _ {0}} \sum_ {\mathcal {L}: p (\mathcal {L}) = H _ {0}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon}.\tag{5.71}
$$

Here$\mathcal { L }$is a collection of pairs$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$with$p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } \ \in \ H _ { 0 }$(cf. Definition 3.1 (3), where bottom ends are identified with particle lines). This$\mathcal { L }$is a forest with no isolated vertex, when viewed as a graph over vertex set$H _ { 0 }$. Moreover,$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$is defined by

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} = \prod_ {(p _ {1}, p _ {2}) \in \mathcal {L}} \mathbb {1} _ {p _ {1} \sim_ {\mathrm{in}} p _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon} \qquad \text {and} \qquad \mathbb {1} _ {p _ {1} \sim_ {\mathrm{in}} p _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \quad | x _ {p _ {1}} - x _ {p _ {2}} | \leq \varepsilon , \\ \varepsilon^ {v} & \quad | x _ {p _ {1}} - x _ {p _ {2}} | \geq \varepsilon . \end{array} \right.\tag{5.72}
$$

where$v = 3 ^ { - d - 1 }$, as in (3.9).

Proof. The following proof is an adaptation of the proof of [49], Proposition A.1. To start with, we introduce the following notations:

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {A \not \sim B} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{| z _ {p} - z _ {p ^ {\prime}} | \geq \varepsilon , \forall p \in A \text {and} p \neq p ^ {\prime} \in B \}} \quad \text {and} \quad \mathbb {1} _ {p \sim B} = \mathbb {1} _ {\{\exists p ^ {\prime} \in B, \text {such that} | z _ {p} - z _ {p ^ {\prime}} | \leq \varepsilon \}}.\tag{5.73}
$$

Without loss of generality, we assume that$Q _ { 0 } = [ s ]$. By (1.7), (1.8) and (1.11), we have

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \frac {1}{\mathcal {Z}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) n}}{n !} \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {s + n}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ s + n ]} (\boldsymbol {z} _ {s + n})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}, \\ \mathcal {Z} = 1 + \sum_ {N = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) N}}{N !} \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {N}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ N ]} (\boldsymbol {z} _ {N})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {N}, \end{array}\tag{5.74}
$$

which implies that

$$
f (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ s ]} \mathbb {1} _ {[ s ] \not \sim [ s ]} \cdot \frac {1}{\mathcal {Z}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) n}}{n !} \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}} \mathbb {1} _ {[ s ] \not \sim [ s + 1: s + n ]} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ s + 1: s + n ]} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}.\tag{5.75}
$$

Note that

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {[ s ] \not \sim [ s + 1: s + n ]} = \prod_ {p \in [ s ]} \mathbb {1} _ {p \not \sim [ s + 1: s + n ]} = \sum_ {H _ {1} \subseteq [ s ]} (- 1) ^ {| H _ {1} |} \cdot \prod_ {p \in H _ {1}} \mathbb {1} _ {p \sim [ s + 1: s + n ]}.\tag{5.76}
$$

We will fix$H _ { 1 }$and define$M = [ s ] \backslash H _ { 1 }$, then put aside the factors$\mathbb { 1 } _ { H _ { 1 } \times H _ { 1 } } \cdot \mathbb { 1 } _ { H _ { 1 } \times M }$that occur in the$\mathbb { 1 } _ { [ s ] \times [ s ] }$ in (5.75), and focus on${ \mathbb { 1 } } _ { M \not \sim M }$. Here we apply a Penrose type argument in the setting of Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 5.10, by setting

$E = \{ ( p , p ^ { \prime } ) : p \neq p ^ { \prime } \in M \}$, so subsets of$E$are identified with graphs over vertex set$M ,$and denote $\mathbb { 1 } _ { A _ { o } } : = \mathbb { 1 } _ { p \sim p ^ { \prime } } { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } \mathfrak { o } = ( p , p ^ { \prime } )$

• There is no$\mathcal { F } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$, and$\mathcal { F }$is the set of$F \subseteq E$whose corresponding graph are forests;

• The mapping$\pi : 2 ^ { E }  \mathcal { F }$is any algorithm of generating a spanning forest$F = \pi ( G )$from a graph G. For example, we can fix a linear ordering of elements of E based on labels of particles, then apply the same procedure that is applied to the graph$\operatorname { C l } _ { G }$in (3) in the definition of the algorithm in Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 5.10.

It is easy to see, as in Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 5.10, that (5.20) is true for the above-defined$\mathcal { F }$ and$\pi .$Then we get

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {M \not \sim M} = \prod_ {\mathfrak {o} \in E} (1 - \mathbb {1} _ {A _ {\mathfrak {o}}}) = \sum_ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathcal {L} _ {2} |} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}},\tag{5.77}
$$

where$\mathcal { L } _ { 2 }$is a graph over vertex set$M = [ s ] \backslash H _ { 1 }$that is a forest (corresponding to$F \in { \mathcal { F } }$above),$| { \mathcal { L } } _ { 2 } | = | F |$ is the number of edges in the graph$\mathscr { L } _ { 2 } , p ( \mathscr { L } _ { 2 } )$is the set of non-isolated vertices in$\mathcal { L } _ { 2 }$, and

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} ^ {\text {Pen}} := \prod_ {(p, p ^ {\prime}) \in \mathcal {L} _ {2}} \mathbb {1} _ {p \sim p ^ {\prime}} \prod_ {(p, p ^ {\prime}) \in A L (F)} \mathbb {1} _ {p \not \sim p ^ {\prime}}; \qquad \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} ^ {\text {Pen}} \leq \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} := \prod_ {(p, p ^ {\prime}) \in \mathcal {L} _ {2}} \mathbb {1} _ {p \sim p ^ {\prime}}.
$$

Inserting (5.76) into (5.75), and letting$H _ { 1 } \cup p ( \mathcal { L } _ { 2 } ) = H _ { 0 }$, we get

$$
f (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) = \sum_ {H _ {0} \subseteq [ s ]} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes ([ s ] \backslash H _ {0})} \cdot E _ {H} (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {H _ {0}}),\tag{5.78}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {H} (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {H _ {0}}) = (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H} \frac {1}{\mathcal {Z}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) n}}{n !} \sum_ {(H _ {1}, \mathcal {L} _ {2}): H _ {1} \cup p (\mathcal {L} _ {2}) = H _ {0}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathcal {L} _ {2} | + | H _ {1} |} \mathbb {1} _ {H _ {1} \not \sim H _ {1}} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {H _ {1} \not \sim ([ s ] \backslash H _ {1})} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} ^ {\text {Pen }} \\ \times \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}} \prod_ {p \in H _ {1}} \mathbb {1} _ {p \sim [ s + 1: s + n ]} \cdot (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ s + 1: s + n ]} d \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ s + 1: s + n ]}. \end{array} \tag {5}\tag{5.79}
$$

Recall$v = 3 ^ { - d - 1 }$. Let$K \subseteq [ s + 1 : s + n ]$be the set of$p ^ { \prime }$such that$p ^ { \prime } \sim p$for some$p \in H _ { 1 }$. Since each$p ^ { \prime }$ corresponds to at most$( 3 v ) ^ { - 1 } = 3 ^ { d }$diferent p (the number of non-intersecting unit balls that all intersect a given unit ball cannot exceed$3 ^ { d }$, due to a simple covering argument), we conclude that$| K | \geq 3 v | H _ { 1 } |$, thus

Denote the integral in (5.79) by (Int), then by (5.80) we have

Here in the third line we have used$\begin{array} { r } { \int \mathbb { 1 } _ { p ^ { \prime } \sim H _ { 1 } } f ^ { \boldsymbol { A } } ( 0 , z _ { p ^ { \prime } } ) \mathrm { d } z _ { p ^ { \prime } } \le | H _ { 1 } | \varepsilon ^ { d - 1 } \le \varepsilon ^ { d - \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \end{array}$. Finally, inserting (5.81) into (5.79), we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} | E _ {H _ {0}} (0, \boldsymbol {z} _ {H _ {0}}) | \leq (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H _ {0}} \frac {1}{\mathcal {Z}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) n}}{n !} \sum_ {(H _ {1}, \mathcal {L} _ {2}): H _ {1} \cup p (\mathcal {L} _ {2}) = H _ {0}} \mathbb {1} _ {H _ {1} \not \sim H _ {1}} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {H _ {1} \not \sim ([ s ] \setminus H _ {1})} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} ^ {\text {Pen}} \\ \times \sum_ {3 v | H _ {1} | \leq m \leq n} \varepsilon^ {(d - \frac {1}{2}) m} \binom {n} {m} \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {[ n - m ]}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ n - m ]}   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ n - m ]} \\ = (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H _ {0}} \sum_ {H _ {1} \cup p (\mathcal {L} _ {2}) = H _ {0}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} \sum_ {m \geq 3 v | H _ {1} |} \frac {\varepsilon^ {\frac {m}{2}}}{m !} \frac {1}{\mathcal {Z}} \underbrace {\left(\sum_ {n = m} ^ {\infty} \frac {\varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) (n - m)}}{(n - m) !} \int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {[ n - m ]}} (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes [ n - m ]}   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {[ n - m ]}\right)} _ {= \mathcal {Z}, \text {by (1.8) and the change of variable N = n - m}} \\ = (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H _ {0}} \sum_ {H _ {1} \cup p (\mathcal {L} _ {2}) = H _ {0}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} \sum_ {m \geq 3 v | H _ {1} |} \frac {\varepsilon^ {\frac {m}{3}}}{m !} \leq \sum_ {H _ {1} \cup p (\mathcal {L} _ {2}) = H _ {0}} \varepsilon^ {v | H _ {1} |} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L} _ {2}} \\ \leq (f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (0)) ^ {\otimes H _ {0}} \sum_ {\mathcal {L}: p (\mathcal {L}) = H _ {0}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon}. \end{array}\tag{5.82}

5.6. Proof of Proposition 3.25. In this subsection, we put together Propositions 5.16 and 5.18, to prove Proposition 3.25.

Proof of Proposition 3.25. We divide the proof into 5 parts.

Proof part 1. We prove there exists$E _ { H } = E _ { H } ( \ell \tau , z _ { H } )$that verifies (3.15). In fact, this follows immediately by induction on$\ell ,$using Proposition 5.18 (base case$\ell = 0 )$and Proposition 5.16 (inductive step).

Proof part 2. We prove that$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$in (3.15) satisfies (3.16). In fact, we have$f ^ { \mathcal { A } } ( 0 ) = f _ { 0 }$by Proposition 5.18; by 5.43), we see that$f ^ { \mathcal { A } } ( \ell \tau )$satisfies

$$
f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (\ell \tau , z) = \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} ] \in \mathcal {T} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}}} \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}, \varnothing} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}} (z)\tag{5.83}
$$

with$z = z _ { r ( \mathbb { M } ) }$. Moreover, by first line of (5.42), we see that$\mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } , \mathcal { O } } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } } ( z )$is given by

$$
\mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}, \varnothing} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}} (z) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} | _ {p \setminus r}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathbb {M} | _ {p \setminus r}}} (\mathcal {S} \circ \mathbb {1}) _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {\mathrm{Pen}} \left[ \left(f ^ {\mathcal {A}} ((\ell - 1) \tau)\right) ^ {\otimes (p (\mathbb {M}))} \right] \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {(p \setminus r) (\mathbb {M})}.\tag{5.84}
$$

Recall also the quantity$\mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( z )$defined in (3.11) in Definition 3.23; using that$\mathbb { I } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon } = 1 \ ( [ \mathbb { M } ] \in \mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$has no initial link) and$\ell _ { 1 } [ p ] - \underline { { \ell } } = 0$(M has only one layer$\ell ) .$, we see that$\mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( z )$is the same as$\it { \Delta } T \mathcal { N } _ { \mathbb { M } , \it { \Delta } \alpha } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } } ( z )$but with $( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \mathrm { P e n } }$in (5.84) replaced by$( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } }$. Similarly, the quantity$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } , \emptyset } | ( z )$defined in (5.42) is identical with the quantity$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } | ( z )$defined in (3.12).

Now, by inserting (5.13) into (5.84), we get

\begin{array}{l} \| f _ {s} ^ {\mathrm{err}} (t _ {\mathrm{fin}}, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) \| _ {L _ {\boldsymbol {z} _ {s}} ^ {1}} = \varepsilon^ {s (d - 1)} \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {\mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} \big \| \big [ (\mathcal {S} _ {s + n} ^ {E} (\tau)) ^ {\mathfrak {L} - \ell} \circ \mathcal {S} _ {\ell , s + n} ^ {\mathrm{err}} (\tau) \big ] (\widetilde {W} _ {s + n} ((\ell - 1) \tau)) \big \| _ {L ^ {1}} \\ \qquad \leq 2 \varepsilon^ {s (d - 1)} \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {\mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{n !} \big \| \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {s + n} ^ {\ell}} \cdot \widetilde {W} _ {s + n} ((\ell - 1) \tau) \big \| _ {L ^ {1}} \\ \qquad \leq 2 \varepsilon^ {s (d - 1)} \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {\mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {\mathbb {M} _ {\ell} \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}} ^ {\mathrm{trc.err}}, r (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}) = [ s ]} \frac {1}{n !} \big \| \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}} \cdot \widetilde {W} _ {s + n} ((\ell - 1) \tau) \big \| _ {L ^ {1}}. \end{array}\tag{5.98}
$$

In the sum (5.98), we argue as in the proof of Proposition 5.12: by symmetry we may always restrict $p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) \ : = \ : [ | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } | _ { p } ]$with an additional factor$\binom { n } { | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } | _ { p } - s }$. Using also (5.34) which is also true in the current setting, we obtain that

$$
\begin{array}{l}\| f_{s}^{\mathrm{err}}(t_{\mathrm{fin}},\boldsymbol{z}_{s})\|_{L^{1}_{\boldsymbol{z}_{s}}}\\ \leq 2\varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{\ell = 1}^{\mathfrak{L}}\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\sum_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}\in \mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{trc.err}}_{\Lambda_{\ell}},r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]} \frac{1}{n!}\big\| \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}}\cdot \widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau)\big\|_{L^{1}}\\ \\ \leq 2\varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{\ell = 1}^{\mathfrak{L}}\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}\in \mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{trc.err}}_{\Lambda_{\ell}}\\ p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p}],r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]}} \frac{1}{n!}\binom {n}{|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} - s}\big\| \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}}\cdot \widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau)\big\|_{L^{1}}\\ \\ = 2\varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{\ell = 1}^{\mathfrak{L}}\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty}\sum_{[ \mathbb{M}_{\ell}] \in \mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{trc.err}},r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]} \frac{1}{(n - |\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} + s)!}\big\| \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}}\cdot \widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau)\big\|_{L^{1}}\\ \\ = 2\varepsilon^{s(d - 1)}\sum_{\ell = 1}^{\mathfrak{L}}\sum_{[ \mathbb{M}_{\ell}] \in \mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{trc.err}},r(\mathbb{M}_{\ell}) = [s]} \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d|\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p}}}\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{M}_{\ell}}(\boldsymbol{z}_{p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})})  \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}_{p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})}\\ \\ \times \sum_{n = |\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} - s}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n - |\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} + s)!}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d(n - |\mathbb{M}_{\ell}|_{p} + s)}} \widetilde{W}_{s + n}((\ell -1)\tau)  \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{z}_{[s + n]\setminus p(\mathbb{M}_{\ell})}. \end{array}\tag{5.99}
$$

Since the summation in (5.99) is equal to$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 2 ) | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } | _ { p } } \widetilde { f } _ { | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } | _ { p } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , z _ { p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) } )$by (4.17), and using also the$L ^ { 1 }$ preserving property of${ \mathcal { S } } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } }$, we conclude that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| f _ {s} ^ {\mathrm{err}} (t _ {\mathrm{fin}}, \boldsymbol {z} _ {s}) \| _ {L _ {\boldsymbol {z} _ {s}} ^ {1}} \leq 2 \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {\mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} ] \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}} ^ {\mathrm{trc.err}}, r (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}) = [ s ]} \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} | _ {p \setminus r}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} | _ {p}}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}} \cdot \widetilde {f} _ {| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} | _ {p}} ((\ell - 1) \tau)   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell})} \\ \leq 2 \sum_ {\ell = 1} ^ {\mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {[ \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} ] \in \mathcal {F} _ {\Lambda_ {\ell}} ^ {\mathrm{trc.err}}, r (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}) = [ s ]} \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} {|} _ {p \setminus r}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} | _ {p}}} | (\mathcal {S} \circ \mathbb {1}) _ {\mathbb {M} _ {\ell}} | | \widetilde {f} _ {| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell} | _ {p}} ((\ell - 1) \tau)   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell})}. \end{array}\tag{5.100}
$$

The$\widetilde f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$term in (5.100) contains a main term and an error term Err as in (3.15). The contribution of Err leads to the second term on the right hand side of (3.20), using$| \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } | _ { p \setminus r } \le 3 \Lambda _ { \ell }$and following the proof of (5.46) in Part 1 of Proposition 5.16. For the contribution of the main term in (3.15), we repeat the same arguments as in the proof of (3.17) and (3.18) in Parts 3 and 4 above (i.e. expand$\tilde { f } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$into previous layers and putting all diferent layers into a multi-layer molecule M; note we have extra integration in particle$r ( \mathbb { M } ) = [ s ]$here). This then leads to the first term on the right hand side of (3.20), where $[ \mathbb { M } ] \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { t r c . e r r } }$because$[ \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ] \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { t r c . e r r } }$, see Definition 3.20 (4). This proves (3.20), and finally finishes the proof of Proposition 3.25.□

Remark 5.19. With Proposition 3.25 proved, in the rest of this paper, we need to estimate the quantities$\mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } }$ and$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$on the right hand side of (3.16)–(3.20). Note that these quantities are constant in equivalence classes [M]. Thus, as said in Remark 3.4, for the rest of this paper, we will use M to denote unlabeled molecules only (plus labelings of root particles only).

for any$H \neq \emptyset$, and

Now we prove Theorem 1 assuming Propositions 6.1–6.3.

Proof of Theorem 1 assuming Propositions$6 . 1 \mathrm { - } 6 . 3 .$The goal is to prove (1.18) for$f _ { s } \left( t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } , z _ { s } \right)$(recall we have set$t = t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } = \mathfrak { L } \tau )$, with$s \leq | \log \varepsilon | = A \underline { { s } }$. which is negligible thanks to our choice of the sequences$( \Lambda _ { \ell } )$and$\left( A _ { \ell } \right)$in (1.33) in Definition 1.6 (3), which ensures that$\Lambda _ { \ell } \gg \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 } A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$if$\ell ^ { \prime } > \ell$and$\tau ^ { \Lambda _ { \ell } / 1 0 } \cdot \varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 } A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } } \ll 1$.
