## 7. Preparations for$E _ { H }$estimates

From this section until Section 13, we will prove Proposition 6.2 (and the associated Proposition 9.7). We start from the upper bounds of$E _ { H }$and$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 1 } }$in (3.17)–(3.18) in Proposition 3.25, which have the form $\sum _ { \mathbb { M } } | { \mathcal { T } } { \mathcal { N } } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$(here and below we will replace [M] by M as M now represents unlabeled molecules, see Remark 5.19). To bound these terms, it sufices to (i) control the number of terms M in the summation, and (ii) control the size of$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$for each individual M.

In this section, first in Section 7.1 we prove an upper bound (Proposition 7.2) on the number of choices of M, and then in Section 7.2 we reduce the$L ^ { 1 }$norm of$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$to an integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$involving Dirac δ functions that localizes each individual collision and overlap (Proposition 7.5). The estimates of this quantity $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$will then occupy Sections 8–9.

7.1. Upper bounds of combinatorial factors. In this subsection we prove an upper bound on the number of molecules M in Proposition 7.2. For this we need to introduce the following parameter$\rho$for molecules M:

Definition 7.1 (The parameter$\rho )$. Given a molecule M with highest layer ℓ and lowest layer 1, with layer $\ell ^ { \prime }$denoted by$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Define the parameters$s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$by$s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } : = | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) \rrangle$and$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } : = \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for$\ell ^ { \prime } \in [ 1 : \ell ] ;$ also define$s _ { 0 } = | H _ { 0 } |$where$H _ { 0 }$is the initial cumulant set (see (5.87)), i.e. those particles involved in initial links. Now define the parameter$\rho$by

$$
\rho = \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime} = 0} ^ {\ell} s _ {\ell^ {\prime}} + \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime} = 1} ^ {\ell} \mathfrak {R} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}.\tag{7.1}
$$

We interpret the quantity$\rho$as the sum of$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(the total number of recollisions within each single layer), together with the sum of$s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(the total number of particles lines crossing diferent layers).

We now state and prove the main combinatorial upper bound in this section.

Proposition 7.2. Let M be a molecule and$\rho$be as in Definition 7.1. Assume H is a set and$| H | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$ Consider all molecules$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$(recall that we are summing over non-labeled molecules M) that satisfy $r ( \mathbb { M } ) = H$, with the size |M| of M fixed, and the$\rho$defined in Definition 7.1 also fixed. Then the number of choices for M, together with the labelings of root particles, is bounded by

$$
\sum_ {\mathbb {M}} 1 \leq C ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \rho}.\tag{7.2}
$$

The same result is true if we replace$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$by$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$or$\mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$or$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { t r c . e r r } }$

Proof. We only consider the case$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ,$as the other cases are similar. Note that M is constructed from its layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$by the following process, see Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 3.25 and Figure 11:

• Label the root particles, and draw a molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$with a single layer$\ell ^ { \prime } ,$, for each$\ell ^ { \prime } \in [ 1 : \ell ] ;$

• For each$\ell ^ { \prime } \in [ 1 : \ell - 1 ]$, identify a subset of$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$with a subset of$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } )$, call this identified subset$H _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and$| H _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | = s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ;$

• For each particle line in$H _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, merge the corresponding top end in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and bottom end in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 }$to form a bond;

• Finally choose a set$H _ { 0 } \subseteq p ( \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } )$, and fix the initial links L between particle lines in$H _ { 0 }$as in Proposition 5.18.

We now estimate the number of choices for M, by considering each of the above steps.

Proof part 1. In this part we prove that$| \mathbb { M } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$and$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$. In fact, by Definition 3.20 (1a)–(1b) we know that each cluster of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$has at most$\Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$particle lines and at most$\Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } + \Gamma$collisions (using the upper bound of Γ for the recollision number). Then each component has at most$\Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 }$particle lines and at most$2 \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 }$collisions (as each component has at most$\Lambda _ { \ell }$clusters). Then each$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$has at most $A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 }$particle lines and$2 A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \Lambda _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { 2 }$collisions (as each component must contain a root particle line, and there are$s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \leq A _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$of them). All these values are bounded as$\leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$by Definition 1.6 (3), hence the result.

Proof part 2. In this part we consider the first step of labeling and constructing individual$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Note that labelings lead to$| H | ! \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$choices as$| H | = | r ( \mathbb { M } ) | = | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) | = s _ { \ell } \le \rho .$. Next we may fix the values of$( \left| \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \right| ) _ { \ell ^ { \prime } \in [ 1 : \ell ] }$. As these numbers add up to the fixed |M|, we have at most$2 ^ { | \mathbb { M } | }$choices which is acceptable in (7.2). Similarly, we can also fix the values of$\left( s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \right)$and$\left( \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) \right)$at an acceptable price. Now, note that each$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$is a graph with each atom having at most 4 bonds; moreover it is formed by adding at most$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$edges to a forest.

It is known that the number of trees (and forests) with$\left| \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \right|$atoms and each atom having at most 4 bonds can be bounded by$1 0 ^ { | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | }$(the result for forests follows from that for trees; for trees, we may fix a root and turn the tree into a rooted, at most ternary tree, and use the well-known counting upper bound for the number of binary and ternary trees).

Once the tree parts are fixed, we add in the$\le \rho$extra edges one by one; each edge has at most$| \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | ^ { 2 } \le$ $| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$choices, which leads to | log ε|<sup>C ρ(M</sup>ℓ<sup>′</sup> <sup>)</sup> choices in total. All these factors are acceptable in (7.2) even after accounting for diferent$\ell ^ { \prime }$(for example$\begin{array} { r } { \prod _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } 1 0 ^ { | \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | } = 1 0 ^ { | \mathbb { M } | } ) } \end{array}$

Proof part 3. In this part we consider the steps of matching and merging particle lines/ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 }$, see Figure 11. Recall that$| H _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | = s _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$; selecting a set of this cardinality in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 }$leads to at most

$$
\binom{| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} | _ {p}}{s _ {\ell^ {\prime}}} \binom{| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime} + 1} | _ {p}}{s _ {\ell^ {\prime}}} \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} s _ {\ell^ {\prime}}}
$$

choices. Putting diferent$\ell ^ { \prime }$together, we again get a factor of$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$which is acceptable.

Proof part 4. In this part we consider the last step of constructing$H _ { 0 }$and${ \mathcal { L } } .$Note that$| H _ { 0 } | = s _ { 0 }$, and $| \mathcal { L } | \ ( \mathrm { i . e }$. the number of initial links in$\mathcal { L } )$is bounded by$2 | H _ { 0 } |$as$\mathcal { L }$is a forest. The number of choices of$H _ { 0 }$ and$\mathcal { L }$is then trivially bounded by$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } s _ { 0 } }$, which is also acceptable.

By putting Parts 1–4 above together that accounts for all steps in the construction of$\mathbb { M }$, we have proved (7.2) and Proposition 7.2.□

7.2. Reducing to the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$. In this subsection, we rewrite the integrals$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$in Proposition 3.25 as integrals$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$involving Dirac functions that localize each individual collision and overlap, see Definition 7.3 and Proposition 7.5. As we will see in Section$^ { 8 , }$this representation behaves well under the cutting operation, and allows us to obtain eficient estimates.

Definition 7.3 (Associated operator of a molecule). Consider the molecule$\mathbb { M } = ( \mathcal { M } , \mathcal { E } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { L } )$, we define the following objects.

(1) Associated variables$z _ { \mathcal { E } }$and$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } }$. We associate each atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$with a time variable$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and each edge$e \in { \mathcal { E } }$with a position-velocity vector$z _ { e } = ( x _ { e } , v _ { e } )$. We refer to them as associated variables and denote the collections of these variables by$z _ { \mathcal { E } } = ( z _ { e } : e \in \mathcal { E } )$and$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } } = ( t _ { \mathfrak { n } } : \mathfrak { n } \in \mathbb { M } )$

(2) Associated distributions$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. Given an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, let$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$and$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$be the two bottom edges and top edges at n respectively, such that$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$(resp. e and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$are serial. We define the associated distribution$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } } = \Delta = \Delta ( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } , z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } , t _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$as follows.

(a) If n is an C-atom, then

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \boldsymbol {\Delta} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) := & \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {1}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {1}}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {2}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \big) \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {-} \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {1}} + [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {2}} - [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big), \end{array}\tag{7.3}
$$

where$\omega : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { e _ { 1 } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } } + t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) )$is a unit vector, and$z _ { - } = - \operatorname* { m i n } ( z , 0 )$

(b) If n is an O-atom, then

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \boldsymbol {\Delta} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) := & \boldsymbol {\delta} (x _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {1}}) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} (x _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {2}}) \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {-} \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {1}} \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} - v _ {e _ {2}} \big) \end{array}\tag{7.4}
$$

where ω is as above. Note that (7.4) forces$z _ { e _ { 1 } } = z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$and$z _ { e _ { 2 } } = z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$

(3) The associated domain D. The associated domain D is defined by

$$
\mathcal {D} := \left\{\boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}} = (t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \in (\mathbb {R} ^ {+}) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}: (\ell^ {\prime} - 1) \tau <   t _ {\mathfrak {n}} <   \ell^ {\prime} \tau \text {if} \mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}; t _ {\mathfrak {n}} <   t _ {\mathfrak {n} ^ {+}} \text {if} \mathfrak {n} ^ {+} \text {is parent of} \mathfrak {n} \right\}.\tag{7.5}
$$

(4) The associated operator$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$. With the associated variables$z _ { \mathcal { E } } = ( z _ { e } : e \in \mathcal { E } )$and$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } } = ( t _ { \mathfrak { n } } : \mathfrak { n } \in \mathbb { M } )$ we define the associated integral operator$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$by

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) := \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) (| \mathcal {E} _ {*} | - 2 | \mathbb {M} |)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {*} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}} Q (\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E}}, \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {*}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}.\tag{7.6}
$$

Here$\mathcal { E } _ { * }$is the set of edges of M that are bonds or free ends (i.e. not counting fixed ends; for full molecules M this makes no diference). Note that in (7.6) we are only integrating in the variables $z _ { \mathcal { E } _ { \ast } }$for bonds and free ends, thus$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$is a function (or distribution) of all fixed ends of M.

## Remark 7.4. We make a few remarks concerning Definition 7.3.

(1) The time variables$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$represent the collision or overlap time of n. The vector variables$\boldsymbol { z _ { e } } = ( x _ { e } , v _ { e } )$ are associated with the linear piece of trajectory along edges$e ,$where$v _ { e }$is the velocity (which is constant along this piece), and$x _ { e }$is the position transported backwards to time 0 (so the actual position of the particle at time t in this linear piece is$x _ { e } + t v _ { e } )$

(2) The Dirac functions in$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } }$prescribes the collision or overlap by forcing the elastic collision formula in (7.3) and forcing the same velocity in (7.4). In (7.6), we treat all the variables$z _ { e }$for fixed ends e as fixed, so the result of this integral is a function (or distribution) or these fixed variables.

(3) In (7.5) we have the natural (partial) time ordering, consistent with the atom ordering in Definition 3.5: the time$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$for n must be before the time$t _ { { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + } }$for${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$(its parent, or equivalently the next collision). Moreover collisions in layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$must happen in time interval$[ ( \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 ) \tau , \ell ^ { \prime } \tau ]$,which leads to natural orderings between diferent layers. These time orderings will occasionally be useful in the proof below. Apart from these, we do not assume any total ordering of collision times (except in an auxiliary step in the proof of Proposition 7.5 below).

We now state the main result of this subsection.

Proposition 7.5. Let M be a full molecule (so$\mathcal { E } _ { * } ~ = ~ \mathcal { E } )$with$r ( \mathbb { M } ) = H$. Let$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$be the associated integral of M defined in (3.12). Then, we have

$$
\left\| \left| \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} \right| \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {H}\right) \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} = \varepsilon^ {(d - 1) | H |} \cdot \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} \left(Q _ {\mathbb {M}}\right).\tag{7.7}
$$

where$Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$is the function given by

$$
Q _ {\mathbb {M}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D}} (\boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}) \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} (\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E}}) \cdot \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {end}} ^ {-}} \left| f ^ {\mathcal {A}} \big ((\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau , x _ {e} - (\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau \cdot v _ {e}, v _ {e} \big) \right|.\tag{7.8}
$$

Here in$( 7 . 8 ) , \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$is the set of bottom ends of M (including empty ends, see Definition 3.6 (1)), and$\ell _ { 1 } [ e ]$is the initial layer for bottom end e in Definition 3.1 (2). The indicator functions$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } }$is defined in (7.5), and $\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$is defined in (3.9).

Proof. We divide the proof into 3 parts.

Proof part 1. In this part, we make some simplifications to (7.7) and reduce it to (7.10). First we prove$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = | \mathcal { E } | - 2 | \mathbb { M } | .$. This is because each atom in M has exactly 4 edges; by adding them together and noticing that each bond (between two atoms) is counted twice and each end is counted once, we obtain $4 | \mathbb { M } | = 2 | \mathcal { E } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + } |$(ignoring empty ends; however this equality remains true even with empty ends). Using also that$| \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } | = | \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + } | = | \mathbb { M } | _ { p }$(as each particle line has a unique top end and a unique bottom end, see Definition$3 . 1 \ ( 2 ) )$, we conclude that$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = | \mathcal { E } | - 2 | \mathbb { M } |$, as desired.

By$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = | \mathcal { E } | - 2 | \mathbb { M } |$, and note that$| H | = | \mathbb { M } | _ { r } .$, we see that the powers of$\varepsilon$on both sides of (7.7) match. Next, in the definition of$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$in (3.12), by integrating in the$z _ { r ( \mathbb { M } ) }$variables, using the definition$| ( S \circ \mathbb { 1 } ) _ { \mathbb { M } } |$ in (3.10) and the$L ^ { 1 }$preserving property of${ \mathcal { S } } _ { \mathbb { M } }$, we see that

$$
\left| \left| \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} \right| \right| \bigg | _ {L ^ {1}} = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | \mathbb {M} | _ {p \setminus r}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathbb {M} | _ {p}}} \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M}} \cdot | (| Q (\boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M})} ^ {\prime}) |) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {p (\mathbb {M})} ^ {\prime},\tag{7.9}
$$

where$Q$is as in (3.13). We may identify a particle line$p \in p ( \mathbb { M } )$with its bottom end$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$, and note also that$Q _ { \mathbb { M } } = | Q | \cdot \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { D } } ( t _ { \mathbb { M } } )$; as such, we see that (7.7) would follow if we can prove

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} \setminus \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} | \times \mathcal {D}} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} \setminus \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M}} \big (\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \big), a. e.,\tag{7.10}
$$

where we identify$p \in p ( \mathbb { M } )$with the bottom end$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$and identify$z _ { p } ^ { \prime }$in (7.9) with$z _ { e }$. (Indeed, once we prove (7.10), we simply integrate both sides against$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) \left| \mathbb { M } \right| _ { p \setminus r } } \cdot \left| Q \right|$; the right hand side becomes (7.9), while the left hand side becomes$\varepsilon ^ { ( d - 1 ) | H | } \cdot \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } \big ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } \big )$using the above identification, relation between |Q| and $Q _ { \mathbb { M } } .$, and the restriction$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } } \in \mathcal { D }$in (7.10).)

In the rest of this proof, we focus on proving (7.10).

Proof part 2. In this part, we introduce an extension of (7.10) for the purpose of induction. This extension contains two extra parameters$\ell _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$and$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } } \in [ ( \ell _ { \mathrm { m i n } } - 1 ) \tau , \ell _ { \mathrm { m i n } } \tau ]$, and an (extra) total ordering ≺ for all atoms in M, which is an extension of the partial ordering in Definition 3.5. For each such total ordering ≺ and each$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$, define the extension of (7.10) as follows.

In this extension, we require that$\ell [ \mathfrak { n } ] \geq \ell _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$for all atoms in${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$(we still view the lowest layer of M as 1). Moreover, define the new indicator function

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M}, \prec , t _ {\mathrm{min}}} \left(\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}}\right)\tag{7.11}
$$

to be the same indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } } .$, but with the additional requirements that (i) each collision and overlap happens after time$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$, and (ii) if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } \prec { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$in the total ordering, then the collision/overlap corresponding to ${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$happens before that of$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$. Similarly, we also define the new domain

$$
\mathcal {D} _ {\mathrm{tot}} := \left\{t _ {\mathbb {M}}: t _ {\min} <   t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {1}} <   t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {2}} \text {for any} \mathfrak {n} _ {1} \prec \mathfrak {n} _ {2} \right\}.\tag{7.12}
$$

Then, the extension is written as

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} \setminus \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-} |} \times \mathcal {D} _ {\mathrm{tot}}} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} \setminus \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathbb {M}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M}, \prec , t _ {\min}} (\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}}), a. e.\tag{7.13}
$$

If we can prove (7.13) for each fixed$\prec ,$then (7.10) follows by setting$\ell _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = 1 , t _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = 0$and summing over all diferent choices of the total ordering ≺. In the rest of this proof, we focus on proving (7.13).

Proof part 3. In this part, we prove (7.13) by induction on the number of collisions and overlaps.

If M has no collision or overlap, then$\mathbb { M } = \emptyset$and both sides of (7.13) are vacuously 1. Now suppose (7.13) is true for molecules with fewer collisions and overlaps than M. For M, we choose the smallest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in$M under the total ordering$\prec$. We will assume n is a collision happening between two particles$p _ { 1 }$and$p _ { 2 } ;$the overlap case is similar and much easier (where the incoming velocity coincide with the outgoing ones).

Consider the C-atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$. It has no child as it is the smallest atom, which means it has two bottom ends$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$. Let the corresponding serial top edges at n be$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$, and let$p _ { j }$be the particle line that$e _ { j }$ and$e _ { j } ^ { \prime }$belong to. We will assume$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$are both bonds; the case when one or both of them are ends only requires trivial modifications. Now, if we remove the atom n and turn$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$to two bottom ends at the other atoms they connect to, we will reduce M to another molecule$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$(with the extra total ordering inherited from M).

On the left hand side of (7.13), we may first fix$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and$( x _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , x _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } , v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } )$, and integrate in the remaining variables. By induction hypothesis for$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, the integral in the remaining variables equals

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}, \prec^ {\prime}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}} \left(x _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, x _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, (z _ {e}) _ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-} \setminus \{e _ {1}, e _ {2} \}}\right),\tag{7.14}
$$

where the indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \widetilde { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \prime } , \prec ^ { \prime } , t _ { n } }$is defined for the molecule M<sup>′</sup> with the total ordering$\prec ^ { \prime }$inherited from$\prec ,$and$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$replaced by$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. We then integrate in the variables$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and$( x _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , x _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } , v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } )$; regarding this integral, we claim (for any function$Q \geq 0 )$that

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {4 d} \times I} \Delta (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot Q (z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \mathrm{d} z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} \mathrm{d} z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathfrak {n}}} \\ & {\qquad = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathrm{col}} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot Q \big (x _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1} - t _ {\mathrm{col}} \cdot v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1}, v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1}, x _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2} - t _ {\mathrm{col}} \cdot v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2}, v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2}, t _ {\mathrm{col}} \big).} \end{array}\tag{7.15}
$$

Here$I = [ ( \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] - 1 ) \tau , \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] \tau ] \cap [ t _ { \mathrm { m i n } } , + \infty ) , \ \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$is the indicator function that a collision happens between particles p<sub>1</sub> and p<sub>2</sub> with initial position and velocity$\left( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } \right)$, at collision time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } \in I$, and$z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } = ( x _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } , v _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } )$ for$j \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$are the position and velocity of the particles$p _ { 1 }$and$p _ { 2 }$right after the collision; note that$z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { \mathcal { I } }$ and$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$are both functions o$\left( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } \right)$

The proof of (7.15) follows from first integrating in x ′ and x ′ , then in v ′ and v ′ , and then in$\boldsymbol { x } _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$$\boldsymbol { x } _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$$v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$$v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. Note that:

(i) The Dirac δ functions imply that a collision happens between particles$p _ { 1 }$and$p _ { 2 } ;$

(ii) The factor$[ ( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) \cdot \omega ] _ { - }$<sub>−</sub> supported in$( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) \cdot \omega \leq 0$implies that the particles form a pre-collisional configuration at collision time;

(iii) The collision time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$is the unique time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$satisfying$| ( x _ { e _ { 1 } } + t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } v _ { e _ { 1 } } ) - ( x _ { e _ { 2 } } + t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) | = \varepsilon$and the pre-collisional condition;

(iv) The value of$z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } = ( x _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } , v _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } ) = ( x _ { e _ { j } ^ { \prime } } + t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } v _ { e _ { j } ^ { \prime } } , v _ { e _ { j } ^ { \prime } } )$equals the outgoing position and velocity of particles$p _ { j }$immediately after the collision, which is uniquely determined by$\left( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } \right)$;

(v) Once$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$and v ′ are fixed, the integral in$\boldsymbol { v } _ { \boldsymbol { e } _ { j } ^ { \prime } }$$\boldsymbol { x } _ { e _ { i } ^ { \prime } }$contains a single δ factor, and once$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$is fixed, the integral in$\boldsymbol { v } _ { \boldsymbol { e } _ { j } ^ { \prime } }$also contains a single δ factor. Finally it is easy to check that

$$
\left| \left(v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}\right) \cdot \omega \right| \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \left(\left| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} \left(v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}\right) \right| - \varepsilon\right) = \boldsymbol {\delta} \left(t _ {\mathfrak {n}} - t _ {\mathrm{col}}\right),
$$

so integrating in the order of$\boldsymbol { x } _ { e _ { j } ^ { \prime } }$then$\boldsymbol { v } _ { \boldsymbol { e } _ { j } ^ { \prime } }$and$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$then proves (7.15).

Now, by (7.15) and induction hypothesis, we know that the left hand side of (7.13) equals

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathrm{col}} (z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}, \prec^ {\prime}, t _ {\mathrm{col}}} \big (x _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1} - t _ {\mathrm{col}} \cdot v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1}, v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {1}, x _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2} - t _ {\mathrm{col}} \cdot v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2}, v _ {\mathrm{out}} ^ {2}, (z _ {e}) _ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-} \setminus \{e _ {1}, e _ {2} \}} \big).\tag{7.16}
$$

The indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$is equivalent to the requirement that the particles$p _ { 1 }$and$p _ { 2 }$collide in the layer $[ ( \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] - 1 ) \tau , \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] \tau ]$and after time$t _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$. The indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { M } ^ { \prime } , \prec ^ { \prime } , t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } }$is equivalent to requiring that, if particle$p _ { j } \left( j \in \{ 1 , 2 \} \right)$) had initial position$x _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j } - t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } \cdot v _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j }$and initial velocity$v _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { j }$, and other particles had the same initial position and velocity given by the corresponding$z _ { e } ~ ( e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } \backslash \{ e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } \} )$, then the exact collisions and overlaps in the M<sup>′</sup>-prescribed dynamics (with total ordering$\prec ^ { \prime } )$would happen, and they would all happen (in the corresponding time layer and) after time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$

Note that the position and velocity of$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$at time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$, with the above virtual initial configuration, is exactly$( z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { 1 } , z _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { 2 } )$, which equals the same outgoing position and velocity of$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$at time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$right after the first collision n, with the actual initial configuration$z _ { e } ~ ( e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } )$. Since we are restricting all collisions and overlaps other than n to happen after$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$, we know that$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { M } ^ { \prime } , \prec ^ { \prime } , t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } }$is equivalent to requiring that the exact collisions and overlaps in the M-prescribed dynamics (other than n, with total ordering ≺) all happen (in the corresponding time layer and) after the collision time$t _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$for n. Therefore, the product indicator function$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } } \cdot \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { M } ^ { \prime } , \prec ^ { \prime } , t _ { \mathrm { c o l } } }$equals$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathbb { M } }$in (7.13). This proves (7.13) and hence Proposition 7.5.□

Remark 7.6. By (7.7) and (7.9), we know that changing the value of$Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$on Lebesgue zero sets does not afect the value of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$. Below we will exploit this to make sure that the functions$Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$integrated in (7.6) are everywhere defined Borel functions, and their support satisfy that no two collisions happen at the same time, and no collision happens at any$\ell \tau$

Remark 7.7. Note the following diference between C-atoms and O-atoms. In (7.3), the distribution$\pmb { \Delta }$is symmetric under permutation$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )  ( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$, and also$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )  ( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$except for the$[ ( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) \cdot \omega ]$<sub>−</sub> factor. In other words, for any C-atom we must distinguish top and bottom edges, and also distinguish serial edges, in order for (7.3) to be well-defined; however there is also symmetry between $^ { \mathrm { 6 6 } } \mathrm { t o p } ^ { \mathrm { 9 } }$and “bottom” in the case when the$\left[ \left( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } \right) \cdot \omega \right] .$factor does not play a role

On the other hand, in (7.4), the distribution$\pmb { \Delta }$is symmetric under permutation exchanging$e _ { 1 }$with$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$, or exchanging$e _ { 2 }$with$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ,$, or exchanging$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$with$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$. Therefore, for any O-atom we do not need to distinguish top and bottom edges, as long as the serial edges (or particle lines) are properly distinguished.

## 8. Operations on molecules

From this section until Section 9, we will prove Proposition 6.2 (pending Proposition 9.7 which will be proved in Sections 10–13). Thanks to the preparations in Section$^ { 7 , }$we only need to estimate the quantity $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$in (7.7)–(7.8) for a fixed molecule M.

In Section 8.1, we define several operations on the molecule M, which reduce it to smaller and simpler elementary molecules (see Definition 8.11). In Section 8.2 we study the behavior of the quantity$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$under these operations, see Propositions 8.13–8.14. With these, it then sufices to estimate the$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$integrals for elementary molecules, which are done in Section 9.

8.1. Cutting, deleting and splitting. The operations we will define include cutting (see Definition 8.3; this is the main operation that breaks M into two smaller molecules, which corresponds to rewriting the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$in$( 7 . 6 )$as an iterated integral), deleting (see Definition 8.1; this forgets the overlap condition at an O-atom), and splitting (see Definition 8.9; this restricts to diferent sub-domains in the integral, or equivalently the support of$Q$in (7.6)).

The notion of deleting an O-atom is already defined as part of Definition 3.10. We repeat here for the reader’s convenience, together with a few more notions for molecules.

Definition 8.1 (Deleting and various other notions). We define the following notions for a molecule M.

(1) Delete an O-atom. Let o be an O-atom with 4 edges$e _ { i } ( 1 \leq i \leq 4 )$connected to other atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } .$ where$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 3 }$are serial and same for$e _ { 2 }$and$e _ { 4 }$. By deleting the O-atom o, we remove o and the 4 edges$e _ { j }$from$\mathbb { M } ,$and add two bonds$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 3 }$, and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$between$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 4 } .$, with the same top/bottom assignment as$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 3 } )$and$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 4 } )$. Here if some${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i }$is absent, say$e _ { 3 }$is a free end at o, then the bond$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 3 } )$should be replaced by a free end at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$, etc.

(2) Degree. Define the degree of n (abbreviated deg) to be the number of edges at n that are not fixed ends (counting only bonds and free ends). Note that any atom has deg at most 4, and every atom has deg 4 if and only M is full.

(3) Sub-molecules. Let$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } \subseteq \mathbb { M }$be a subset of atoms. We will regard$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$as a molecule (referred to as a sub-molecule of M), by viewing each bond between an atom in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$and an atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$as a free end at the atom in M<sup>′</sup>.

Next we define the important notion of regular molecules, which is an important property that governs our treatment of O-atoms and definition of cutting (Definition 8.3) below.

Definition 8.2. We say M is regular, if for any O-atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, any fixed end at n must be serial with a free end at n (we say they form a simple pair), see Figure 12. This property will be assumed for all the molecules studied below, and will be preserved throughout the reduction process.

![](images/page_67_image_4.jpg)

Figure 12. Structures allowed and not allowed at O-atoms in regular molecules. The simple pair is formed by a fixed end and serial free end at an O-atom as shown on the left.

Now we introduce the operation of cutting. For some intuitions see Remark 8.6.

Definition 8.3 (Cutting). Let M be a regular molecule and$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$be a set of atoms. The operation of cutting A as free (resp.$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$as fixed) turns M into a new molecule$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$which is the disjoint union of two molecules, i.e.$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \sqcup \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$. For convenience, we may also say that M is “cut into two smaller molecules$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { ^ { , * } } }$. We understand that all empty ends belong to$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } ;$as for the atoms and other edges, we describe the procedure as follows, see Figure 13. For some intuitions see also Remark 8.6.

(1) The atom sets of$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$are A and$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$respectively. If M contains only C-atoms (so each maximal ov-segment is just a bond), then we simply break each bond e between an atom in A and an atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash A ,$, by removing it and drawing a free end$e _ { 1 }$(resp. fixed end$e _ { 2 } )$at the corresponding atom in A (resp.$\mathbb { M } \backslash A )$. We form$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$(resp.$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } )$by atoms in A (resp.$\mathbb { M } \backslash A )$and these edges.

(2) Now, suppose M contains O-atoms. For each maximal ov-segment σ that contains an atom in A and an atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$(other maximal ov-segments are not afected), let the highest and lowest atoms of $\sigma$be${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$and$\mathfrak { n } ^ { - }$, and let$\left( \mathfrak { p } _ { 1 } , \cdots , \mathfrak { p } _ { s } \right)$be the atoms in$A \cap \sigma$(ordered high to low). Then, we take the following steps, which extend the steps in (1) from bonds to ov-segments, see Figure 13:

(a) First remove every bond in$\sigma .$. Then, for$1 \leq j \leq s - 1$, draw a bond between${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j + 1 }$ Then, if${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$, draw a top free end at$\mathfrak { p } _ { 1 } ; \mathrm { i f } \ \mathfrak { p } _ { s } \ne \mathfrak { n } ^ { - }$, draw a bottom free end at${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { s }$. Let$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$ be formed by atoms in A and these edges (constructed from diferent$\sigma )$

(b) Next, if${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + } \in { \sigma } \backslash A$, draw a bottom fixed end at${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + } ;$; if${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { - } \in \sigma \backslash A$, draw a top fixed end at$\mathfrak { n } ^ { - }$ Then, for any${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \pm } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } \in { \sigma } \backslash A$, draw a simple pair at n consisting of a free and and a (serial) fixed end. Let$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$be formed by atoms in$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$and these edges (constructed from diferent σ).

Note that, deleting O-atoms does not afect the correspondence between molecular and physical pictures under topological reduction. However, this correspondence will break down after cutting. Therefore, we will only talk in the molecule language after performing any cutting. For example, notions like p will only be referring to particle lines as in Definition 3.1 (2), instead of physical particles.

In connection with the notion of cutting, we define the notion of ov-adjacency and a few more naturally related notions, see Figure 14:

![](images/page_68_image_0.jpg)

Figure 13. Example of cutting (Definition 8.3). Left: simple case of cutting without Oatoms. Right: cutting in the presence of O-atoms (showing only one maximal ov-segment $\sigma )$. Here green atoms belong to$A$and become$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$after cutting, while blue atoms belong to$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$and become$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$after cutting. The${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \pm }$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$are as indicated.

Definition 8.4 (Ov- notions). Recall molecules M and ov-segments in Definition 3.1.

(1) Ov-adjacency. We define two atoms n<sub>1</sub> and n<sub>2</sub> to be ov-adjacent, if they are connected by an ov-segment; if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$is an ancestor (resp. descendant) of$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$along this ov-segment, we say it is an ov-parent (resp. ov-child) of$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$.

(2) Ov-connectedness. For a subset$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$, we say it is ov-connected if for any two atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \in A$ there exist atoms$\mathfrak { n } _ { j } \in \mathbb { M } \left( 0 \leq j \leq q \right)$such that$( \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { q } ) = ( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$is ov-adjacent with${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j + 1 }$ The maximal ov-connected subsets of A are called ov-components of A.

(3) Ov-distance. Finally, define the ov-distance of two subsets$B , B ^ { \prime } \subseteq \mathbb { M }$to be the minimal q such that there exist atoms$\mathfrak { n } _ { j } \in A \left( 0 \le j \le q \right)$such that$( \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { q } ) \in B \times B ^ { \prime }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$is ov-adjacent with ${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j + 1 }$. Note that the ov-distance is 0 if$B \cap B ^ { \prime } \neq \emptyset$, and is ∞ if they are contained in diferent connected components<sup>10</sup> of M.

Figure 14. The ov- related notions in Definition 8.4. Here A is the set of colored atoms, which has 3 ov-components$A _ { j }$represented by 3 diferent colors (as opposed to 7 connected components). The ov-distance between$A _ { 1 }$and$A _ { 2 }$is 2, while the ov-distance between$A _ { 1 }$ and$A _ { 3 }$is$\infty$

Lemma 8.5. Regularity is preserved after deleting an O-atom or cutting a subset A as fixed or free.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">A ⊆ M</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>10</sup>The ov-components of the whole molecule M are the same as the components. However the ov-components of subsets might not be the same as its components.</span></small>

Proof. Simply note that, the forbidden configuration, where a fixed end at an O-atom is serial with another fixed end or a bond, cannot be constructed in the deleting or cutting process. This can be directly verified for each step in Definitions 8.1 and 8.3.□

Remark 8.6. We make a few remarks concerning Definitions 8.3–8.4.

(1) The way to understand cutting is the following: suppose we cut A as free (and$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$as fixed) and consider a maximal ov-segment σ as in Definition 8.3 (2), see Figure 13. Then, in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$(which has atom set$\mathbb { M } \backslash A )$, every possible bond in$\sigma$is broken, and each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$has a new fixed end. We may simply say that “the ov-segment σ is broken in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { ^ { , * } } }$. On the other hand, in$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$(which has atom set$A )$, the ov-segments are preserved and the atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \cap \sigma$are still ov-adjacent along σ (with the$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$atoms between them neglected) and they do not have any new fixed end.

(2) In particular, if we cut A as free, then this cutting generates (one or more) fixed end at every atom ${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash A$that is ov-adjacent to an atom in A, and not at any other atom. When n is C-atom, this fixed end is bottom (resp. top) if n is ov-parent (resp. ov-child) of an atom in A (as for O-atoms, the bottom/top distinction is less important, but it is important that M is regular, see Remark 8.7).

Remark 8.7. Recall Definition 8.2 or regular molecules. This regularity will be retained in all algorithms: any simple pair formed by fixed end at O-atom and the serial free end is completely unrelated to the rest of the molecule (and this O-atom gets detached from both its neighbors). Some simple consequences of this will be used frequently below: (i) any O-atom of deg 2 must not be adjacent to any other atom, and cutting it does not afect the rest of the molecule; (ii) for any O-atom n of deg 3, it can be connected to other atoms along one ov-segment. All ov-parents and ov-children of n (if any) must belong to the same (maximal) ov-segment and are ov-adjacent to each other.

Remark 8.8. Note that, deleting O-atoms (Definition 8.1) does not afect the correspondence between molecular and physical pictures under topological reduction. However, after cutting, this correspondence will break down, and we will only talk in the molecule language afterwards (for example notions like p will only be referring to particle lines as in Definition 3.1 (2)), instead of physical particles.

We now discuss the operation of splitting into sub-cases. This is not an operation on the molecule M but rather an operation on the domain of integration (or equivalently on the support of$Q )$in the integral (7.6). In reality, it is used to classify the various degenerate and non-degenerate cases witch will require diferent strategy in the algorithm (cf. Remark 9.5).

Definition 8.9. In splitting, we do not change M but split the support of Q in (7.6) as follows: decompose 1 into finitely many indicator functions$1 = \textstyle \sum _ { j } { \mathbb { 1 } } _ { S _ { j } }$, and decompose$\begin{array} { r } { Q = \sum _ { j } Q \mathbb { 1 } _ { S _ { j } } } \end{array}$. Each of these terms corresponds to a sub-case where we make extra restrictions on the support of$Q$provided by the conditions defining$S _ { j }$. Examples of such defining conditions include$| x _ { e } - x _ { e ^ { \prime } } | \geq \lambda$(or oppositely$| x _ { e } - x _ { e ^ { \prime } } | \leq \lambda )$ $| v _ { e } - v _ { e ^ { \prime } } | \geq \lambda$or$\vert t _ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \vert \geq \lambda$(or opposite) etc., where$( e , e ^ { \prime } )$are any two given edges,$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$are any two given atoms, and λ is any given quantity, cf. the definition of good molecules in Definition 9.4.

Now we define the notion of operation sequences, which are sequences consisting of operations of deleting, cutting and splitting:

Definition 8.10 (Operation sequence). Given a molecule M and$Q ,$define an operation sequence to be a sequence of operations acting on M or$Q ,$such that each one is either cutting a subset of M as in Definition 8.3, or deleting an O-atom in M as in Definition 8.1, or splitting into finitely many sub-cases (by decomposing 1 into indicator functions) as in Definition 8.9. We require that all the deletings must occur before all the cuttings (splittings can occur anywhere in the sequence). If an operation sequence does not contain splitting, then we call it a cutting sequence.

Finally, we define the elementary molecules, which are the result of the cutting sequences we will construct in the algorithms below, and the main object of study in Section 9:

Definition 8.11 (Elementary molecules). We define a molecule M to be elementary, if it satisfies one of the properties, see Figure 15:

(1) {2} molecules: M contains one atom of deg 2, with both fixed ends being top (or both being bottom) in the case of C-atom, and with the two fixed ends not serial in the case of O-atom.

(2) {3} molecules: M contains one atom of deg 3.

(3) {4} molecules: M contains one atom of deg 4.

(4) {33} molecules: M contains two atoms connected by a bond, which are both deg 3. We say M is {33A} molecule if we can cut one atom as free such that the other atom becomes a {2} molecule as defined above. Otherwise we say M is {33B} molecule.

(5) {44} molecules: M contains two atoms connected by a bond, which are both deg 4.

![](images/page_70_image_6.jpg)

Figure 15. The elementary molecules as in Definition 8.11. Note the good/normal/bad property of this molecule depends on the extra restrictions on the variables due to splitting, see Definition 9.4; the edges$e _ { j }$and atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$are marked as will be used in the proof of Propositions 9.1–9.3.

8.2. Operations on associated operators. In this subsection, we study the behavior of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$in (7.6) under the cutting, deleting and splitting operations. Namely, we will prove${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q ) \leq { \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q )$after deleting (Propositions 8.13) and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q ) = \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } } \circ \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } } ( Q )$after cutting (Proposition 8.14).

Recall the integral (7.6), where Q is a function of$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } }$and$z _ { \mathcal { E } }$. If we perform deleting or cutting to M and turn it into M<sup>′</sup> or$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \sqcup \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$, then we will get a new set of vector variables$z _ { e }$associated with the new molecule (the time variables remain the same as atoms are not afected by cutting). In order to define $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q )$and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } } \circ \mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } } ( Q )$for the same$Q { \mathrm { . } }$, we need to match the vector variables for$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$with those for M. More precisely, we need to define the following two mappings:

• A mapping from the set of bonds plus free ends of M to that of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } ;$this decides how we transform the function$Q$in (7.6) between the integral variables of M and those of M<sup>′</sup>.

• A mapping from the set of new fixed ends of$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$to the set of new bonds plus free ends of$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } ;$this decides, while evaluating$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } } ( Q )$, the value that$z _ { f }$is fixed to be, for each fixed end$f$of$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$

In Definition 8.12 below, we will construct these mappings under deleting and cutting operations, which provides the correspondences between vector variables$z _ { e }$

Definition 8.12 (Transformation of associated variables under cutting and deleting). Suppose$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$is formed from M by deleting or cutting. Define the following mappings:

(1) The case of deleting. Let$e _ { j }$and$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$be as in Definition 8.1 (1), we define the mapping$e _ { 1 } , e _ { 3 } \mapsto e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$ and$e _ { 2 } , e _ { 4 } \mapsto e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$. This means, we identify the variables$z _ { e 1 }$and$z _ { e _ { 3 } }$before deleting, with$z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$after deleting, and same for$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 4 } )$.

(2) The case of cutting: no O-atoms. As in Definition 8.3 (1), for each bond e between A and$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$ that is turned into a free end$e _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and a fixed end$e _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$, we define the mapping$e \mapsto e _ { 1 }$and $e _ { 2 } \mapsto e _ { 1 }$. This means, we identify$z _ { e }$before cutting with$z _ { e _ { 1 } }$after cutting, and also fix the fixed end variable$z _ { e _ { 2 } }$to be$z _ { e _ { 1 } }$

(3) The case of cutting: general. Let σ and related notions be as in Definition 8.3 (2), we define the mapping as follows. For each bond$e \in \sigma ,$, consider the two atoms of e, and the one that is closer to ${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } ;$we then map e to the free end$e ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$at this atom. For each fixed end$e \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$, we map it to the same bottom edge$e ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \cap \sigma$at p (it could be a free end or a bond). For example, in Figure 16, we have$e _ { j } \mapsto e _ { j } ^ { \prime }$and$f _ { j } \mapsto e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$. We also identify and fix the relevant variables as in (1)–(2).

![](images/page_71_image_2.jpg)

This picture shows the case of the example shown in Figure 13, where $e _ { j } \mapsto e _ { j } ^ { \prime }$and$f _ { j } \mapsto e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$in the notation of the mapping in Definition 8.12. Note that all the$z _ { e }$ variables for edges e coming from this ov-segment are all equal to each other, see the proof of Proposition 8.14.

Proposition 8.13. Let M<sup>′</sup> be formed from M by deleting one O-atom (Definition 8.1). Then we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \leq \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q), \quad \forall Q \geq 0.\tag{8.1}
$$

Proof. Note that the power$| \mathcal { E } _ { * } | - 2 | \mathbb { M } |$in (7.6) is the same for M and$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, as we have 1 less atom and 2 less bonds/free ends when going from M to M<sup>′</sup>. Now let$e _ { j }$and$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$be as in Definition 8.1 (1), then we have$z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } = z _ { e _ { 1 } } = z _ { e _ { 3 } }$by the mapping in Definition 8.12 (1) and the Dirac factors in (7.4), and similarly $z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } = z _ { e _ { 2 } } = z _ { e _ { 4 } }$. Concerning the integral in (7.6), using the identification of variables in Definition 8.12, we see that$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$is the same as$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q )$but with the extra integral

$$
\int \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {3}} - z _ {e _ {1}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {4}} - z _ {e _ {2}}) \pmb {\delta} \big (| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {2}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega ] _ {-} \mathrm{d} z _ {e _ {3}} \mathrm{d} z _ {e _ {4}} \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathfrak {n}}.
$$

By (7.15) we know this integral equals an indicator function, which is$\leq 1$, hence${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q ) \leq { \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q )$

Proposition 8.14. Assume that a molecule M is cut into$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$(Definition 8.3), where$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$ are cut as free and fixed respectively. Then we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} (Q).\tag{8.2}
$$

Proof. Recall the formula (7.6). Let$\mathcal { E } _ { * , j }$and$\mathcal { E } _ { * } ^ { \prime }$be the$\mathcal { E } _ { * }$sets for$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$and$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$respectively, then it is easy to see that$| \mathbb { M } | = | \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } | + | \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } |$and$| \mathcal { E } _ { * } | = | \mathcal { E } _ { * , 1 } | + | \mathcal { E } _ { * , 2 } | = | \mathcal { E } _ { * } ^ { \prime } |$, so the powers on both sides of (8.2) match. Below we will neglect these powers of ε for simplicity. Now by (7.6), we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {*} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \left(\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}}\right) \cdot Q   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {*}}   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}.\tag{8.3}
$$

On the other hand, by Fubini we have

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {1, *} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {1} |}} \bigg (\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} _ {1} \in \mathbb {M} _ {1}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {1}} \bigg) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {1, *}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {2, *} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {2} |}} \bigg (\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} _ {2} \in \mathbb {M} _ {2}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {2}} \bigg) \cdot Q   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {2, *}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}}} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {*} ^ {\prime} |} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \bigg (\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {\mathfrak {n}} \bigg) \cdot Q   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {*} ^ {\prime}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}.} \end{array}\tag{8.4}
$$

Here in the second line in (8.4), we are identifying the variables$z _ { \mathcal { E } _ { \ast } ^ { \prime } }$with the variables$z _ { \mathcal { E } _ { \ast } }$, and fixing each fixed end variable$z _ { e }$in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$to be the corresponding free end variable$z _ { e ^ { \prime } }$in$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$, by the mapping in Definition 8.12. it then sufices to show that (8.3) equals (8.4) under the above identification and assignments.

No O-atom case. Assume M has no O-atom, then we are in the simpler scenario in Definition 8.3 (1). In this case, each new free end$e _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$is paired with a new fixed end$e _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$and they come from breaking a bond$e \in \mathbb { M } ;$by Definition 8.12 (2) we see that the integration in (8.3) and (8.4) are the same. Moreover, the$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and Q factors are also the same under the above identification and assignments, so trivially (8.3) equals (8.4).

General case. In the general case with O-atoms, the identification and assignments of variables and more complicated. We only need to consider a fixed maximal ov-segment$\sigma$(along with the relevant notions ${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j } )$as in Definition 8.3 (2). Let the bonds in σ be$e _ { j } , ( 1 \leq j \leq q )$from top to bottom, then in view of the Dirac factors in (7.4), we know the integral (8.3) involves the Dirac factors

$$
\prod_ {j = 1} ^ {q - 1} \delta (z _ {e _ {j + 1}} - z _ {e _ {j}}).\tag{8.5}
$$

On the other hand, for each${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { i } \in A \cap \sigma$, consider the bond connecting${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { i }$to its child in$\sigma ,$and let it be $e _ { j _ { i } }$. Then, by the identification and assignments as in Definition 8.12 (3), we know that the integral (8.4) involves the Dirac factors

$$
\prod_ {i = 1} ^ {s - 1} \delta \big (z _ {e _ {j _ {i + 1}}} - z _ {e _ {j _ {i}}} \big) \cdot \prod_ {e \not \in \{e _ {j _ {i}} \}} \delta \big (z _ {e} - z _ {e _ {j _ {1}}} \big)\tag{8.6}
$$

It is easy to see that$( 8 . 5 ) { = } ( 8 . 6 )$, as both sides are exactly the Dirac mass supported on the linear subspace $\{ z _ { e _ { 1 } } = \cdot \cdot \cdot = z _ { e _ { q } } \}$. For example, in the context of Figure 16, where$( j _ { 1 } , j _ { 2 } , j _ { 3 } ) = ( 1 , 4 , 5 )$, we have

$$
\pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {1}} - z _ {e _ {2}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {2}} - z _ {e _ {3}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {3}} - z _ {e _ {4}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {4}} - z _ {e _ {5}}) = \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {1}} - z _ {e _ {4}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {4}} - z _ {e _ {5}}) \cdot \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {2}} - z _ {e _ {1}}) \pmb {\delta} (z _ {e _ {3}} - z _ {e _ {1}}).
$$

Finally, note that all the Dirac functions in (8.5) and (8.6) imply that all the variables$z _ { e _ { j } }$are equal, so by inserting them into the rest of the$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and$Q$factors in (8.3) and (8.4), we conclude that these remaining factors are also the same for (8.3) and (8.4). This then shows that (8.3) equals (8.4), and completes the proof of Proposition 8.14.□

Remark 8.15. In general, (8.2) holds with both sides being interpreted in the sense of distributions. However, in this paper, we will only encounter the case where$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$is a function whenever$Q$is, in which case (8.2) holds classically. The condition that$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$is a function is really a condition on the molecule M, which restricts the number and places of its fixed ends, and will always be satisfies throughout the algorithm. That being said, one can still interpret (8.2) in bigger generality in the sense of distributions as follows: If one replaces all the delta functions appearing in the definition of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$by approximations of identity, then the analog of formula (8.2) holds with no ambiguity. The same result then holds by taking the limits of those approximations of identity (in the appropriate distributional sense).

Note that the operators$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } }$and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } }$in Proposition 8.14 in general do not commute (unless M has no fixed end). Therefore, it is important to order the resulting components after cutting, such that$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$which is cut as free always occurs to the left of$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$which is cut as fixed (i.e. the operator$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { 2 } }$is applied first, and the corresponding variables are integrated first in the iterated integral). This ordering is defined in the following definition.

Definition 8.16 (Ordering components after cutting). Suppose a molecule M becomes a new molecule M<sup>′</sup> after a sequence of cutting operations; we refer to the connected components of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$as final components. We define a total ordering${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$between these final components inductively, as follows (see Figure 46 for an example):

(1) In the first cutting operation, suppose$\mathbb { M }$is cut into$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$(as free) and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$(as fixed). Then for any final component$\mathcal { X } , \mathcal { y }$of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, we require that$\mathcal { X } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { Y } \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } \mathcal { X } \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$and$\mathcal { V } \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$

(2) For the final components that are contained in$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$(resp. in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } )$, order them inductively using${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$ defined for the subsequent sequence of cutting operations applied to$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$(resp. to$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } )$).

If M<sup>′</sup> is the result of M after (deleting and) cutting, and$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$is the disjoint union of its final components, i.e.$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \sqcup \cdots \sqcup \mathbb { M } _ { k }$with$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathbb { M } _ { k }$, then we define the associated integral operator by

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} \circ \dots \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {k}}.\tag{8.7}
$$

Remark 8.17. As explained above, i$\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { ~ f ~ } \mathbb { M } _ { i } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathbb { M } _ { j } . } \end{array}$, then the operator$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { j } }$is applied first, and the$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$variables are integrated first. In many cases of the algorithm below, each time we will cut an elementary component as free, and work on the remaining molecule (cf. Remark 10.7 below); in this case${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$is just the order of being cut, i.e.$\mathcal { V } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { X }$if and only if$\mathcal { V }$is cut before$\mathcal { X }$. This ordering will be useful in identifying a good molecule after splitting, see Definition 9.4 (3a), (3e).

Suppose we have a cutting sequence, and one of the cuttings breaks a maximal ov-segment$\sigma$as in Definition 8.3 and creates free and fixed ends. Then for any such fixed end$e ,$there always exists a free end or bond$e ^ { \prime }$such that$z _ { e } = z _ { e ^ { \prime } }$, and we have$\mathcal { V } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { X }$where$\mathcal { X }$and$\mathcal { V }$are the final components containing e and$e ^ { \prime }$respectively. In fact, we can choose$e ^ { \prime }$to be the image of e under the mapping in Definition 8.12 (3), then$\mathcal { V } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { X }$follows from Definition 8.16 (1). This will also be helpful in getting good molecules below.

By putting together Definition 8.9, Proposition 8.13 and Proposition 8.14, we arrive at the main conclusion of this section, namely

Proposition 8.18. Start with a full molecule M and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$as in (7.7), where$Q = Q _ { \mathrm { M } }$as in (7.8). If we apply any cutting sequence (Definition 8.10) to M and turn it to$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, with the associated variables transformed as in Definition 8.12, then we always have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \leq \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q),\tag{8.8}
$$

where$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$) is defined as in (8.7) with$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathbb { M } _ { k }$being the final components of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$

If we apply any operation sequence (including also splitting which operates on the support of$Q )$to$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$ and get a contribution$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q ^ { \prime } )$for each sub-case, then we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \leq \sum_ {\text { sub - cases }} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime}),\tag{8.9}
$$

where the summation is taken over all sub-cases. Note that$Q ^ { \prime } = Q \cdot \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { P } }$for some$\mathcal { P }$representing the restriction in this sub-case (see Definition 8.9).

Proof. We only need to prove (8.8). In fact, for any splitting$\begin{array} { r } { Q = \sum _ { j } Q \mathbb { 1 } _ { S _ { j } } } \end{array}$as in Definition 8.9, we trivially have$\begin{array} { r } { \mathbb { Z } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q ) = \sum _ { i } \mathbb { Z } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q \mathbb { 1 } _ { S _ { j } } ) } \end{array}$, so (8.9) follows from (8.8).

Now to prove$\left( 8 . 8 \right)$, using Proposition 8.13, we can treat the deleting operation and only need to consider cuttings, in which case we will prove the equality in (8.8). We proceed by induction: the case of one cutting follows from Proposition 8.14. Now for any M, say the first cutting cuts$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$as free and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$as fixed. In subsequent cuttings, assume$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 }$is cut into$\mathbb { M } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } = \sqcup _ { j } \mathbb { M } _ { 1 j }$(in increasing${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$order) and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 }$is cut into$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } =$ $\sqcup _ { j } \mathbb { M } _ { 2 j }$(in increasing${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$order), then the final result of the cutting sequence is$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \left( \sqcup _ { j } \mathbb { M } _ { 1 j } \right) \sqcup \left( \sqcup _ { j } \mathbb { M } _ { 2 j } \right)$ in increasing${ \prec } _ { \mathrm { c u t } }$order, due to Definition 8.16. Then by induction hypothesis we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1}} \circ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2}} (Q) = \left(\prod_ {j} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {1 j}}\right) \circ \left(\prod_ {j} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} _ {2 j}}\right) (Q) = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q),
$$

which completes the proof.

## 9. Estimating the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$

In this section, we complete the proof of Proposition 6.2, pending the proof of the pure combinatorial Proposition 9.7 (which is in Sections 10–13). Starting from Proposition 3.25, using Propositions 7.2, 7.5 and 8.18, we can reduce Proposition 6.2 to the estimate of quantities of form$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q ^ { \prime } )$, where M<sup>′</sup> (and$Q ^ { \prime } )$are possible results of an operation sequence applied to M (and$Q = Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$, corresponding to possible sub-cases.

The operation sequence is constructed in Proposition 9.7 using the algorithms in Sections 10–13. In Proposition 9.7 we can guarantee that:

• The number of sub-cases is acceptable$( \mathrm { i . e . } ~ \le C ^ { | \mathbb { M } | } \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$in Proposition 9.7);

$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$is formed by elementary molecules (Definition 8.11);

• We have adequate control of these elementary molecules (and associated support information of$Q ^ { \prime } )$ in terms of good and bad molecules (Definition 9.4 and (9.51)).

The goal of this section is to use the above information to prove an estimate for$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q ^ { \prime } )$, namely (9.53). Note that this$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } }$is a composition of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { j } }$where$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$are components of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$which are elementary molecules. In Section 9.1 we will estimate each$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } _ { i } }$, and classify them as good, normal, and bad in Definition 9.4. Then in Section 9.2, we put together these local estimates and apply Proposition 9.7, to prove (9.53) and thus finish the proof of Proposition 6.2. These arguments rely on some technical estimates concerning volumes of $( v _ { e } )$and cross-sections in (7.6), which we leave to Section 9.3.

9.1. Integrals for elementary molecules. In this subsection, we prove upper bounds for$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$for an elementary molecule M, in Propositions 9.1–9.3. We will use${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$and$e _ { j }$to denote atoms and edges in M, and abbreviate$t _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ~ : = ~ t _ { j }$and$z _ { e _ { j } } : = z _ { j }$. For future reference, let us explicitly write out the support of $\begin{array} { r } { \Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } , z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } , t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) = \Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } , z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } , t _ { 1 } ) } \end{array}$, which is defined in (7.3) and (7.4), as follows:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} x _ {2} = x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) - \varepsilon \omega , \\ x _ {3} = x _ {1} + t _ {1} \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \\ v _ {3} = v _ {1} - \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \quad \text {if \mathfrak {n} is C - atom}; \\ x _ {4} = x _ {2} - t _ {1} \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \\ v _ {4} = v _ {2} + \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \end{array} \right. \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} x _ {2} = x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) - \varepsilon \omega , \\ x _ {3} = x _ {1}, \\ v _ {3} = v _ {1}, & \text {if \mathfrak {n} is O - atom}. \\ x _ {4} = x _ {2} = x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) - \varepsilon \omega , \\ v _ {4} = v _ {2} \end{array} \right.\tag{9.1}
$$

Proposition 9.1 (Upper bounds for one-atom$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } )$. Let$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$be defined as in$( 7 . 6 )$, where M contains only one atom n with 4 edges$e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { 4 }$, see Figure 15. We assume that$e _ { 1 } ~ ( \mathrm { r e s p . } ~ e _ { 2 } )$is serial with$e _ { 3 } ~ ( \mathrm { r e s p . } ~ e _ { 4 } )$ Let$Q$be a function supported in$| v _ { j } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$and$| x _ { j } - x _ { j } ^ { 0 } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, where$( x _ { j } , v _ { j } ) = z _ { e _ { j } }$and$x _ { j } ^ { 0 }$are fixed vectors, and also$\mathbf { \delta t _ { M } } \in \mathcal { D }$with D as in (7.5).

(1) Suppose M is a {2} molecule as in Definition 8.11, i.e. the two fixed ends are either both bottom or both top, by symmetry we may assume$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$are fixed and$( e _ { 3 } , e _ { 4 } )$are free. Then

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathrm{col}} (z _ {1}, z _ {2}) \cdot Q.\tag{9.2}
$$

Here in (9.2), the indicator$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$is defined to be 1 if and only if there exists a unique$t _ { 1 }$such that

$$
| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | = \varepsilon , \quad (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \leq 0,\tag{9.3}
$$

where$\omega : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { 1 } - x _ { 2 } + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) )$is a unit vector. We also have the following estimate

$$
\left\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \left\| Q \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}}\tag{9.4}
$$

Moreover, in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$, the function$Q$depends on$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } , z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } , t _ { 1 } )$. On the right-hand side of (9.2), $Q$becomes a function of$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } )$, obtained by a change of variables applied to the original Q. This change of variables is determined as follows:$t _ { 1 }$is expressed as a function of$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } )$via (9.3), and $( z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } )$is defined as a function of$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } )$, either by the last four equations in the left half of (9.1) if M is a C-atom, or by$( z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } ) = ( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } )$if M is an O-atom.

(2) Suppose M is a {3} molecule as in Definition 8.11, by symmetry we may assume$e _ { 1 }$is fixed and $( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 3 } , e _ { 4 } )$are free. Then

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \left[ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {-} \cdot Q \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {2}.\tag{9.5}
$$

Here in (9.5),$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } , z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } , t _ { 1 } )$in the input variables of$Q$are functions of the integral variables $( t , \omega , v _ { 2 } )$given by$( 9 . 1 )$, with$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } )$fixed. In the integral (9.5) the domain of integration can be restricted to$t _ { 1 } \in [ ( \ell [ { \mathsf { n } } ] - 1 ) \tau , \ell [ { \mathsf { n } } ] \tau ]$since supp$( Q ) \subseteq { \mathcal { D } }$

(3) Suppose M is a {4} molecule as in Definition 8.11. Then

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times (\mathbb {R} ^ {d}) ^ {3}} \left[ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {-} \cdot Q \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} x _ {1} \mathrm{d} v _ {1} \mathrm{d} v _ {2}.\tag{9.6}
$$

Here in (9.6),$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } , z _ { 3 } , z _ { 4 } , t _ { 1 } )$in the input variables of$Q$are functions of the integral variables $( t , \omega , x _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } , v _ { 2 } )$given by (9.1). In the integral (9.6) the domain of integration can be restricted to $t _ { 1 } \in [ ( \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] - 1 ) \tau , \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] \tau ]$since supp$Q \subseteq { \mathcal { D } }$. We also have the following estimate

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.\tag{9.7}
$$

(4) Suppose M is an empty end. Then

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) := \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d}} Q \mathrm{d} z _ {e}.\tag{9.8}
$$

We also have the following estimate

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.\tag{9.9}
$$

Proof. We may assume$\| Q \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } = 1$. We divide the proof into several parts.

Proof of (1). We start with (9.2) and consider the C-atom case (the O-atom case is similar and much easier). Note that here we are fixing$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , v _ { 2 } )$and integrating in$( x _ { 3 } , v _ { 3 } , x _ { 4 } , v _ { 4 } )$and$t _ { 1 }$, which is the same as in (7.15) in the proof of Proposition 7.5.
