Then (9.4) follows directly from (9.2).

Proof of (2). Now consider (9.5); again consider the C-atom case, and note that here we are fixing $( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } )$and integrating in$( t _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , v _ { 2 } , x _ { 3 } , v _ { 3 } , x _ { 4 } , v _ { 4 } )$, i.e.

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {6 d}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {4} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {4} - v _ {2}) \big) \\ \quad \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {4} - v _ {2} - [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \\ \quad \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {-} \cdot Q (x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {4}, v _ {4}, t _ {1})   \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {4} \mathrm{d} x _ {j} \mathrm{d} v _ {j}, \end{array}\tag{9.10}
$$

where$\omega : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { 1 } - x _ { 2 } + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) )$is a unit vector. In (9.10), once we fix$( x _ { 2 } , v _ { 2 } )$, then the integral in $( x _ { 3 } , x _ { 4 } , v _ { 3 } , v _ { 4 } )$is given by a change of variables in the function$Q ,$, so we have

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \left(| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} \left(v _ {1} - v _ {2}\right) | - \varepsilon\right) \cdot \left[ \left(v _ {1} - v _ {2}\right) \cdot \omega \right] _ {-} \cdot Q \left(x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {4}, v _ {4}, t _ {1}\right) \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} x _ {2} \mathrm{d} v _ {2},\tag{9.11}
$$

where ω is as above, and

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} x _ {3} = x _ {1} + t _ {1} \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \\ v _ {3} = v _ {1} - \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \\ x _ {4} = x _ {2} - t _ {1} \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega , \\ v _ {4} = v _ {2} + \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] \omega . \end{array} \right.\tag{9.12}
$$

Now in (9.11), we may fix$v _ { 2 }$and make the change of variables$x _ { 2 }  \omega _ { : }$which leads to

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d}} \boldsymbol {\delta} (| \omega | - 1) \cdot \left[ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {-} \cdot Q (x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {4}, v _ {4}, t _ {1}) \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {2},\tag{9.13}
$$

where$x _ { 2 } = x _ { 1 } + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) - \varepsilon \omega$, which matches (9.1) together with (9.12). The integral in$\omega$in (9.13) is done on the unit sphere$\omega \in \mathbb { S } ^ { d - 1 }$, which then gives (9.5).

Proof of (3). By integrating in the variables$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } )$in (9.5), we also obtain (9.6). Then (9.7) immediately follows from (9.6) and the fact that$\left[ \left( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } \right) \cdot \omega \right] _ { - } \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$on the support of$Q$(which is due to our support assumptions for$v _ { e } )$

Proof of (4). This immediately follows from (7.6) and the support assumptions for$x _ { e }$and$v _ { e }$.□

Proposition 9.2 (Better upper bounds for one-atom$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } )$. Consider the same setting (with$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$for an oneatom molecule M etc.) as in Proposition 9.1 above, but with extra restrictions on the support of$Q ,$which are specified below.

(1) Suppose M is a {3} molecule (by symmetry we may assume$e _ { 1 }$is fixed and$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 3 } , e _ { 4 } )$are free), and we further restrict the support of Q to be a subset of

$$
| t _ {1} - t ^ {*} | \leq \varepsilon^ {\upsilon} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | v _ {i} - v _ {j} | \leq \varepsilon^ {\upsilon} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | x _ {j} - x ^ {*} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - \upsilon} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | x _ {i} - x _ {j} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - \upsilon}\tag{9.14}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / 2$. Here$( x ^ { * } , v ^ { * } , t ^ { * } )$are some external parameters (it is possible that$x ^ { * }$or$v ^ { * }$ coincide with$x _ { 1 } \ \mathrm { o r } \ v _ { 1 } )$, and the support of$Q$may depend on these parameters. Moreover, in the second and fourth cases in (9.14), we require$i \neq j ,$, and also$\{ i , j \} \neq \{ 1 , 3 \} , \{ 2 , 4 \}$when M is an O-atom. In the third case we require$j \neq 1$, and also$j \neq 3$when M is an O-atom.

Then we have the following estimate (uniform in all parameters):

$$
\left\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {v} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.\tag{9.15}
$$

(2) Suppose M is$\mathrm { ~ a ~ } \{ 4 \}$molecule, and we further restrict the support of$Q$to be a subset of

$$
| x _ {i} - x _ {j} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | x _ {i} - x ^ {*} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | v _ {i} - v _ {j} | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}\tag{9.16}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / 2$. Here$x ^ { * }$is an external parameter as in (1). Moreover we require$i \neq j$, and also$\{ i , j \} \neq \{ 1 , 3 \} , \{ 2 , 4 \}$when M is an O-atom. Then we have the following estimate (uniform in all parameters):

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) + v} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}\tag{9.17}
$$

(3) Suppose M is an empty end with an edge$e _ { 1 }$and associated variable$z _ { 1 } = ( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } )$, and we replace the$Q$in (7.6) by$\mathbb { 1 } _ { * } ^ { \varepsilon } \cdot Q$, where

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {*} ^ {\varepsilon} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \quad | x _ {1} - x ^ {*} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}, \\ \varepsilon^ {v} & \quad | x _ {1} - x ^ {*} | \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}, \end{array} \right.\tag{9.18}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / 2$. Here$x ^ { * }$is an external parameter as in (1). Then we have the following estimate (uniform in$x ^ { * } )$

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\mathbb {1} _ {*} ^ {\varepsilon} \cdot Q) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) + v} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.\tag{9.19}
$$

(4) Suppose M is {3} or {4} molecules, and we do not make any restriction on the support of$Q$as in (1)–(2), but replace$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$with$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( \mathbb { 1 } _ { * } ^ { \varepsilon } Q )$where

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {*} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \quad | x - x ^ {\prime} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}, \\ \varepsilon^ {v} & \quad | x - x ^ {\prime} | \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \end{array} \right.\tag{9.20}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / 2$. Here$( x , x ^ { \prime } )$is either$( x _ { i } , x ^ { * } )$or$( x _ { i } , x _ { j } ) , x ^ { * }$is an external parameter, and the indices i and$j$also satisfy the requirements in (1) and (2) respectively. Then the estimates (9.15) and (9.17) hold true.

Proof. We may assume$\| Q \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } = 1$. We divide the proof into several parts.

Proof of (1) and (2). Recall that the expression of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$is given by (9.5) and (9.6), where the variables $( x _ { i } , v _ { i } )$are given by (9.1). Consider the conditions (9.14) and (9.16). The case$| t _ { 1 } - t ^ { * } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$in (9.14) is trivial as we gain$\varepsilon ^ { v }$in the integral in$t _ { 1 }$in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$, which proves (9.15). Next assume$| v _ { i } - v _ { j } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$in (9.14)

and M is a C-atom (the O-atom case is the same as long as$\{ i , j \} \ne \{ 1 , 3 \} , \{ 2 , 4 \}$; let$v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } : = u$and $u - ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega : = u ^ { \perp }$, then we have

$$
\mathrm{either} | u | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}, \mathrm{or} | u \cdot \omega | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}, \mathrm{or} | u ^ {\perp} | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}, \mathrm{or} | u - 2 (u \cdot \omega) \omega | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}.\tag{9.21}
$$

Note that$| u - 2 ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega | = | u |$, and$| u | ^ { 2 } = | u \cdot \omega | ^ { 2 } + | u ^ { \perp } | ^ { 2 }$, we may reduce to one of the cases$| u \cdot \omega | \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$2 or$| u ^ { \perp } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$. With fixed ω (say$\omega = ( 1 , 0 , \cdots , 0 )$by symmetry), in either case, at least one coordinate of u is bounded by$\varepsilon ^ { v }$, and all the other coordinates (as well as the weight$( ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) \cdot \omega ) _ { - } )$are bounded by $| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, which implies (9.15) by this volume gain.

Next, assume$| x _ { j } - x ^ { * } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$(or similarly$| x _ { i } - x _ { j } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon } )$in (9.14), then since the distance between any two$x _ { j } + t _ { 1 } v _ { j }$is at most$\varepsilon ,$we must have$| ( x _ { 1 } - x ^ { * } ) + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { j } ) | \leq 2 \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon } ;$; by dyadically decomposing $| t _ { 1 } |$and gaining from both the support of$t _ { 1 }$and the restriction on$v _ { 1 } - v _ { j }$as above, we can obtain a volume gain which is$\varepsilon ^ { v }$, and this is enough to prove (9.15). The cases of (9.16) involving$x _ { i } - x _ { j }$and$v _ { i } - v _ { j }$follow similarly, and the case involving$x _ { i } - x ^ { * }$is trivial as we gain from integrating in$x _ { 1 }$

Proof of (3) and (4). The bound in (3) is immediate (we gain from the$x _ { 1 }$integral in (9.8) if$| x _ { 1 } - x ^ { * } | \leq$ $\varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon } )$. For (4), the case$| x - x ^ { \prime } | \geq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$is also immediate. For the case$| x - x ^ { \prime } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$, the estimate follows by the same argument as in the$| x _ { j } - x ^ { * } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$case from the proofs of (1) and (2).□

Proposition 9.3 (Better upper bounds for two-atom$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } )$. Let$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$be defined as in (7.6), where M is a regular molecule containing only two atoms$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$with 7 edges$e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { 7 }$, see Figure 15. We also denote by e the edge between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } .$, which equals some$e _ { j }$. Let Q be a function supported in$| v _ { j } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$and $| x _ { j } - x _ { j } ^ { 0 } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, and also$\mathbf { \delta t _ { M } } \in \mathcal { D } .$, as in Proposition 9.1. Consider the following cases:

(1) Suppose M is a {33A} molecule with atoms$( \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } )$. Let e be the bond connecting them and$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 7 } )$ be the two fixed ends at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$respectively. Assume moreover that either$\mathrm { ( i ) } \ \ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } ] \neq \ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } ]$for the two atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } .$or (ii) the support of Q is a subset of

$$
\max (| x _ {1} - x _ {7} |, | v _ {1} - v _ {7} |) \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - \upsilon} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | \geq \varepsilon^ {\upsilon}\tag{9.22}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / 3$

(2) Suppose M is a {33B} molecule with two C-atoms. Assume the support of$Q$is a subset of

$$
\left| t _ {1} - t _ {2} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {v} \quad \text { and } \quad \left| v _ {i} - v _ {j} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {v} \quad \text { for   any   edge } (e _ {i}, e _ {j}) \text { at   the   same   atom },\tag{9.23}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / ( 6 d )$

(3) Suppose M is$\mathrm { ~ a ~ } \left\{ 4 4 \right\}$molecule with atoms$( \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } )$and$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 7 } )$being two free ends at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$ respectively, such that M becomes a {33A} molecule after turning these two free ends into fixed ends. Moreover assume the support if Q is a subset of

$$
\max (| x _ {1} - x _ {7} |, | v _ {1} - v _ {7} |) \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \text { and } \quad | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | \leq \varepsilon^ {v}.\tag{9.24}
$$

for some$0 < v < 1 / ( 4 d )$

Then, in any of the above cases (1)–(3), we have

$$
\left\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \varepsilon^ {v} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot \| Q \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.\tag{9.25}
$$

Proof. We may assume$\| Q \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } = 1$. We divide the proof into several parts.

Proof of (1). Since M is a {33A} molecule (Definition 8.11), by symmetry, we may assume that$\left\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \right\}$ becomes a {2} molecule after cutting${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$as free. First assume (ii) is true. To calculate$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$, we cut${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$as free to obtain${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q ) = { \mathcal { T } } _ { \{ { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } \} } \circ { \mathcal { T } } _ { \{ { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } \} } ( Q )$. By assumption, we know that$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$becomes a deg 2 atom with two top fixed ends. The inner integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \} }$can be computed using (9.2) in Proposition 9.1.

Let the bond between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$be e, denote the edges at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$by$( e _ { 1 } . \cdot \cdot , e _ { 4 } )$as in Proposition 9.1, then $e = e _ { j }$for some$j \in \{ 2 , 3 , 4 \}$and${ j \neq 3 \ \mathrm { i f } \ \mathsf { n } _ { 1 } }$is an O-atom (because M is regular, a fixed end cannot be serial with a bond at O-atom). After plugging in the above formula for the inner integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \} }$, we can reduce $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$to an integral of form$\mathcal { T } _ { \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } \} }$as described in (2) of Proposition 9.1, namely

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \left[ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {-} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathrm{col}} (z _ {j}, z _ {7}) \cdot Q \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {2},\tag{9.26}
$$

where the input variables of$Q$are explicit functions of$( t _ { 1 } , \omega , v _ { 2 } )$and$( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 7 } )$using Proposition 9.1 and the fact that$z _ { j }$satisfies (9.1). To prove (9.25) for (1), it sufices to control the volume of the support of$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$ (which is a set depending on$z _ { 1 }$and$z _ { 7 } )$

By definition (9.3) of$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } }$, we know this restriction implies that

$$
\left| \left(x _ {j} - x _ {7}\right) \wedge \left(v _ {j} - v _ {7}\right) \right| \leq \varepsilon | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}\tag{9.27}
$$

for some$2 \leq j \leq 4 .$, where$j \neq 3$if n is O-atom. Let$v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } = u$and$u - ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega = u ^ { \perp }$. Plugging in the formula (9.1), and noting that$| x _ { j } - ( x _ { 1 } + t _ { 1 } u _ { j } ) | \leq \varepsilon$where$u _ { j } = v _ { 1 } - v _ { j }$and$( u _ { 2 } , u _ { 3 } , u _ { 4 } ) = ( u , ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega , u ^ { \perp } )$ if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$is a C-atom and$( u _ { 2 } , u _ { 4 } ) = ( u , u )$if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$is an O-atom, we obtain that

$$
\left| \left(x _ {1} - x _ {7} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {7})\right) \wedge u _ {j} - \boldsymbol {g} \right| \leq \varepsilon | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}\tag{9.28}
$$

for some constant 2-form$\mathbf { \pmb { g } }$depending only on$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } , x _ { 7 } , v _ { 7 } )$

In (9.28), by dyadic decomposition, we may assume$| x _ { 1 } - x _ { 7 } + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 7 } ) | \sim \varepsilon ^ { \beta }$(say with$0 < \beta < 1$, the endpoint cases are treated in the standard way), then with fixed$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } , x _ { 7 } , v _ { 7 } )$and$t _ { 1 }$, the vector$u _ { j }$must belong to a one-dimensional tube in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$which has length$\leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$and width$\varepsilon ^ { 1 - \beta } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$. Note that $u _ { j } \in \{ u , ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega , u - ( u \cdot \omega ) \omega \}$, by elementary calculations, we see that this restriction on$u _ { j }$implies that $( u , \omega )$must belong to a subset of$\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { S } ^ { d - 1 }$with volume$\leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \beta } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$. This already implies (9.25), if $\beta \le 1 - v$

Now suppose

$$
\left| x _ {1} - x _ {7} + t _ {1} \left(v _ {1} - v _ {7}\right) \right| \sim \varepsilon^ {\beta}, \quad \beta > 1 - v,
$$

we shall exploit the$t _ { 1 }$integral in (9.26). If$| v _ { 1 } - v _ { 7 } | \gtrsim \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$, then$t _ { 1 }$belongs to an interval of length$\leq \varepsilon ^ { \beta - 1 + \upsilon }$ which then implies (9.25) together with the above volume bound for$( u , \omega )$. If$| v _ { 1 } - v _ { 7 } | \ll \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$, then we must also have$| x _ { 1 } - x _ { 7 } | \ll \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$, while by the support of$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { c o l } } ( z _ { j } , z _ { 7 } )$we also get

$$
\left| x _ {j} - x _ {7} + t _ {2} \left(v _ {j} - v _ {7}\right) \right| = \varepsilon , \quad \left| x _ {j} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} \left(v _ {j} - v _ {1}\right) \right| \in \{0, \varepsilon \},\tag{9.29}
$$

which implies$\left| t _ { 2 } - t _ { 1 } \right| \cdot \left| v _ { j } - v _ { 1 } \right| \lesssim _ { * } \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$given that$( x _ { 7 } , v _ { 7 } )$is close to$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } )$. Since now we must have $| t _ { 2 } - t _ { 1 } | \geq \varepsilon ^ { v }$by (9.22), we conclude that$| v _ { j } - v _ { 1 } | \lesssim _ { * } \varepsilon ^ { 1 - 2 v }$which again implies (9.25) as in the proof of Proposition 9.1 (2).

Finally, assume (i) is true but (ii) is not, by the above proof, we may assume that$Q$is supported in the set where$| t _ { 1 } - t _ { 2 } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$. But since$t _ { 1 }$and$t _ { 2 }$must belong to disjoint time intervals in view of$\ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } ] \neq \ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } ]$ we conclude that$t _ { 1 }$itself must belong to a fixed interval of length at most$\varepsilon ^ { v }$. Then (9.25) follows from exploiting the volume of support of$t _ { 1 }$. This completes the proof of (1).

Proof of (2). Now consider the case of {33B} molecules. Recall that in this case both atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$are C atoms, the higher atom${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$has one top fixed end, and the lower atom$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$has a bottom fixed end. Concerning the serial relations of edges and up to symmetry, there are 3 cases for the molecule M (see Figure 15), which we list below.

Case 1. This is the case when both fixed ends are serial with the common edge e. Here

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {1 0 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {4} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {4} - v _ {2}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {4} - v _ {2} - [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {+} \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {6} - x _ {5} + t _ {2} (v _ {6} - v _ {5}) \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {3}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {6} - v _ {5} + [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {7} - v _ {3} - [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {5} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta \big ] _ {+} \cdot Q (x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {7}, v _ {7}, t _ {1}, t _ {2}) \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {6}   \mathrm{d} x _ {j}   \mathrm{d} v _ {j}   \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2}   \mathrm{d} t _ {j}, \end{array}\tag{9.30}
$$

where$\omega : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { 1 } - x _ { 2 } + t _ { 1 } ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) )$and$\eta : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { 5 } - x _ { 3 } + t _ { 2 } ( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } ) )$are two unit vectors. Here we first integrate in$( x _ { 4 } , v _ { 4 } , x _ { 6 } , v _ { 6 } )$, then make the change of variables$x _ { 5 }  \eta$to reduce to

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {4 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \\ \qquad \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | - \varepsilon \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {3}) \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {+} \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {3} \mathrm{d} x _ {j} \mathrm{d} v _ {j} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2} \mathrm{d} t _ {j} \\ \qquad \times \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {7} - v _ {3} - [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta \big ] _ {+} \cdot Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} \eta \mathrm{d} v _ {5}, \end{array}\tag{9.31}
$$

where the exact expressions of the input variables of$Q$are omitted for simplicity. Note that in (9.31), the $\delta$functions imply that$\eta = ( v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } ) / | v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } |$and$( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } ) \cdot \eta = ( v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } ) \cdot \eta _ { ; }$, we may decompose$v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 }$ into$[ ( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } ) \cdot \eta ] \eta$, and a vector$w \in \Pi _ { \eta } ^ { \perp }$which is orthogonal to$\eta .$. This leads to

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {4 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | - \varepsilon \big) \\ \qquad \times \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {+} \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {3}) \big) | v _ {7} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {3} \mathrm{d} x _ {j} \mathrm{d} v _ {j} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2} \mathrm{d} t _ {j} \cdot \int_ {\Pi_ {\eta} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} w, \end{array}\tag{9.32}
$$

where$\eta = ( v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } ) / | v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } |$as above,$\Pi _ { \eta } ^ { \perp }$is the orthogonal complement of$\eta ,$and the input variables of $Q$are again omitted. The factor$| v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 } | ^ { - ( d - 2 ) }$comes from the factor$\left[ \left( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } \right) \cdot \eta \right] _ { + }$, together with the Jacobian coming from viewing$[ ( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } ) \cdot \eta ] \eta$as the polar coordinates of$v _ { 7 } - v _ { 3 }$. Now for fixed$( x _ { 3 } , v _ { 3 } )$，we make the change of variables$x _ { 2 }  \omega ,$and argue similarly as above (namely decomposing$v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 }$into $[ ( v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 } ) \cdot \omega ] \omega$and a vector$\theta \in \Pi _ { \omega } ^ { \perp }$orthogonal to$\omega )$, to get

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {3}) \big)} \\ & {\qquad \times | v _ {7} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \mathrm{d} x _ {3} \mathrm{d} v _ {3} \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} t _ {2} \cdot \int_ {\Pi_ {\eta} ^ {\perp} \times \Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots) \mathrm{d} w \mathrm{d} \theta ,} \end{array}\tag{9.33}
$$

where$\omega = - ( v _ { 3 } - v _ { 1 } ) / | v _ { 3 } - v _ { 1 } |$and$\Pi _ { \omega } ^ { \perp }$is the orthogonal complement of$\omega .$. Finally, by integrating the$\pmb { \delta }$ functions in (9.33), first in$x _ { 3 }$and then in$v _ { 3 }$and then in$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } )$, we get

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2}} | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | ^ {- d} | v _ {7} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)}   \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} t _ {2} \int_ {\Pi_ {\eta} ^ {\perp} \times \Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} w \mathrm{d} \theta ,\tag{9.34}
$$

where each of$( v _ { 3 } , \eta , \omega )$is a function of$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } )$and the fixed parameters. The weight$| t _ { 1 } - t _ { 2 } | ^ { - d } | v _ { 7 } -$ $v _ { 3 } | ^ { - ( d - 2 ) } | v _ { 1 } - v _ { 3 } | ^ { - ( d - 2 ) }$in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$is bounded above by$\varepsilon ^ { - 1 / 2 }$due to (9.23) and$0 < v < 1 / ( 6 d )$, and can be absorbed by$\varepsilon ^ { d - 1 }$, and hence (9.25) follows.

Case 2. This is the case when the top fixed edge is serial with$e ,$but the bottom fixed edge is not. Here

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {1 0 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {4} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {4} - v _ {2}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {4} - v _ {2} - [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {+} \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {5} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {5}) \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {6} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {6} - v _ {3}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {7} - v _ {5} + [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {6} - v _ {3} - [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {5} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta \big ] _ {+} \cdot Q (x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {7}, v _ {7}, t _ {1}, t _ {2}) \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {6}   \mathrm{d} x _ {j}   \mathrm{d} v _ {j}   \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2}   \mathrm{d} t _ {j}, \end{array}\tag{9.35}

where$\omega$and η are as above. ω), to reduce

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {6 d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {5} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {5}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {6} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {6} - v _ {3}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {7} - v _ {5} + [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {6} - v _ {3} - [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {5} - x _ {3} + t _ {2} (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {5} - v _ {3}) \cdot \eta \big ] _ {+} \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \prod_ {j \in \{3, 5, 6 \}} \mathrm{d} x _ {j} \mathrm{d} v _ {j} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2} \mathrm{d} t _ {j} \cdot \int_ {\Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} \theta , \end{array}\tag{9.36}
$$

where$\omega = - ( v _ { 3 } - v _ { 1 } ) / | v _ { 3 } - v _ { 1 } |$and$\Pi _ { \omega } ^ { \perp }$is the orthogonal complement of$\omega .$Now in (9.36), we argue as in (2) of Proposition 9.1, namely make the change of variables$x _ { 6 }  \eta _ { : }$, noting that

as well as$( v _ { 5 } - v _ { 3 } ) \cdot \eta = ( v _ { 6 } - v _ { 7 } ) \cdot \eta ,$to reduce it to

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d} \times \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \left[ (v _ {6} - v _ {7}) \cdot \eta \right] _ {+} \mathrm{d} v _ {6} \mathrm{d} \eta \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} t _ {2} \cdot \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \cdot \int_ {\Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots) \mathrm{d} \theta ,\tag{9.37}
$$

where$( x _ { 3 } , v _ { 3 } )$is determined by$( v _ { 6 } , \eta , t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } )$and the fixed parameters. Note that with fixed$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \eta )$, we have

x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) = \gamma + (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) \sigma

where$\gamma$depends only on$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \eta )$and the fixed parameters, and$\sigma$is the projection of$v _ { 6 } \mathrm { ~ - ~ } v _ { 7 }$to the orthogonal complement$\Pi _ { \eta } ^ { \perp }$of$\eta .$. Then the δ function in (9.37) can be written as$\pmb { \delta } _ { \mathbb { R } } ( \gamma \cdot \eta ) \pmb { \delta } _ { \Pi _ { n } ^ { \perp } } ( \gamma + ( t _ { 1 } - t _ { 2 } ) \sigma )$ where$\Pi _ { \eta } ^ { \perp }$is the orthogonal complement of$\eta .$The latter$\delta _ { \Pi _ { \pi } ^ { \perp } }$yields$| t _ { 1 } - t _ { 2 } | ^ { - ( d - 1 ) }$upon integrating in$\sigma _ { : }$ and leaves us with the remaining component$\alpha : = ( v _ { 6 } - v _ { 7 } ) \cdot \eta$from the integral in$v _ { 6 }$. Note also that

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\gamma \cdot \eta = \eta \cdot \left[ (x _ {3} + t _ {1} v _ {3}) - (x _ {1} + t _ {1} v _ {1}) \right] = \eta \cdot \left[ (x _ {3} + t _ {2} v _ {3}) - (x _ {1} + t _ {1} v _ {1}) + (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) v _ {3} \right]} \\ & {\qquad = \eta \cdot \left[ (x _ {7} + t _ {2} v _ {7}) - \varepsilon \eta - (x _ {1} + t _ {1} v _ {1}) + (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) v _ {3} \right] = \eta \cdot \zeta - \varepsilon ,} \end{array}
$$

where$\zeta : = ( x _ { 7 } + t _ { 1 } v _ { 7 } ) - ( x _ { 1 } + t _ { 1 } v _ { 1 } )$, and we have used that$v _ { 3 } \cdot \eta = v _ { 7 } \cdot \eta$. We also have$| \zeta | \geq \frac { 1 } { 2 } \varepsilon ^ { 2 v }$since

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {(x _ {7} + t _ {1} v _ {7}) - (x _ {1} + t _ {1} v _ {1}) = (x _ {7} + t _ {2} v _ {7}) - (x _ {1} + t _ {1} v _ {1}) + (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) v _ {7}} \\ & {\qquad = (x _ {3} + t _ {2} v _ {3}) + \varepsilon \eta - (x _ {3} + t _ {1} v _ {3}) + (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) v _ {7} = (t _ {1} - t _ {2}) (v _ {7} - v _ {3}) + \varepsilon \eta} \end{array}\tag{9.38}
$$

due to (9.23). As a result, we now have that

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {\times} \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \max (\alpha , 0) \cdot | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | ^ {- (d - 1)} | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \boldsymbol {\delta} (\eta \cdot \zeta - \varepsilon)   \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \eta \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} t _ {2} \cdot \int_ {\Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} \theta ,\tag{9.39}
$$

where$v _ { 3 }$and ω are determined by$\left( \alpha , \eta , t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } \right)$and the fixed parameters. The integral in η can be performed by decomposing η into a vector$\eta ^ { \circ }$parallel to$\zeta$and a vector$\eta ^ { \perp }$orthogonal to$\zeta .$The part of integrand involving$\eta ^ { \circ }$is$\begin{array} { r } { | \xi | ^ { - 1 } \delta _ { \mathbb { R } } ( \eta ^ { \circ } - \frac { \varepsilon \zeta } { | \zeta | ^ { 2 } } ) } \end{array}$, and the integral in$\eta ^ { \perp }$can be reparametrized into an integral on the unit sphere$\mathbb { S } ^ { d - 2 }$in the orthogonal complement of$\zeta$up to a multiplicative factor of$( 1 - \varepsilon | \zeta | ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { d - 2 } \sim 1$. Thus

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {S} ^ {d - 2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \max (\alpha , 0) | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | ^ {- (d - 1)} | v _ {1} - v _ {3} | ^ {- (d - 2)} \frac {| \zeta | ^ {- 1}}{(1 - \varepsilon | \zeta | ^ {- 1}) ^ {d - 2}}   \mathrm{d} \alpha \mathrm{d} \eta^ {\perp} \mathrm{d} t _ {1} \mathrm{d} t _ {2} \int_ {\Pi_ {\omega} ^ {\perp}} Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} \theta ,\tag{9.40}
$$

where$\eta$is determined by$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \eta ^ { \perp } )$and the fixed parameters, and$v _ { 3 }$and ω are determined by$\left( \alpha , \eta , t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } \right)$ and the fixed parameters. The weight$\lvert t _ { 1 } - t _ { 2 } \rvert ^ { - ( d - 1 ) } \lvert v _ { 1 } - v _ { 3 } \rvert ^ { - ( d - 2 ) } \lvert \zeta \rvert ^ { - 1 }$in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$are bounded by$\varepsilon ^ { - 2 / 3 }$due to (9.23) and can be absorbed by$\varepsilon ^ { d - 1 }$, and hence (9.25) follows.

Case 3. This is the case when neither fixed end is serial with e. Here, we define the unit vectors ω and η similar to the above, but instead of substituting, we shall keep both$( \omega , \eta )$and the original$( x _ { j } , v _ { j } )$variables in the same integral, but with additional δ factors. This leads to the integral (note that the$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) }$is turned into$\varepsilon ^ { d - 1 }$due to introducing the two$\omega$and η variables)

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {1 0 d} \times (\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}) ^ {2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {3} - x _ {1} + t _ {1} (v _ {3} - v _ {1}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {4} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {4} - v _ {2}) \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} - v _ {1} + [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {4} - v _ {2} - [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {6} - x _ {4} + t _ {2} (v _ {6} - v _ {4}) \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {7} - x _ {5} + t _ {2} (v _ {7} - v _ {5}) \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {6} - v _ {4} + [ (v _ {4} - v _ {5}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {7} - v _ {5} - [ (v _ {4} - v _ {5}) \cdot \eta ] \eta \big) \\ \quad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {1} - x _ {2} + t _ {1} (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) - \varepsilon \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {4} - x _ {5} + t _ {2} (v _ {4} - v _ {5}) - \varepsilon \eta \big) \\ \quad \times   \left[ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {+} \left[ (v _ {4} - v _ {5}) \cdot \eta \right] _ {+} \cdot Q (x _ {1}, v _ {1}, \dots , x _ {7}, v _ {7}, t _ {1}, t _ {2}) \prod_ {j = 2} ^ {6}   \mathrm{d} x _ {j}   \mathrm{d} v _ {j} \cdot   \mathrm{d} \omega   \mathrm{d} \eta \cdot   \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2}   \mathrm{d} t _ {j}. \end{array}\tag{9.41}
$$

Now let$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } )$be fixed, then$\boldsymbol { y } ^ { * } : = \boldsymbol { x } _ { 1 } + t _ { 1 } \boldsymbol { v } _ { 1 }$and$z ^ { * } : = x _ { 7 } + t _ { 2 } v _ { 7 }$are also fixed, and the$\delta$functions occurring in (9.41) that involve$x _ { j }$(there are six of them) can be rearranged as

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {2} + t _ {1} v _ {2} - (y ^ {*} - \varepsilon \omega) \big) \cdot \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {3} + t _ {1} v _ {3} - y ^ {*} \big) \cdot \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {4} + t _ {1} v _ {4} - (y ^ {*} - \varepsilon \omega) \big)} \\ & {\times \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {4} + t _ {2} v _ {4} - (z ^ {*} + \varepsilon \eta) \big) \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {5} + t _ {2} v _ {5} - z ^ {*} \big) \pmb {\delta} \big (x _ {6} + t _ {2} v _ {6} - (z ^ {*} + \varepsilon \eta) \big).} \end{array}\tag{9.42}
$$

Therefore, once$\omega , \eta$and$v _ { j }$are fixed for some$j \in \{ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 \}$, the corresponding δ factor will take care of the integration in$x _ { j }$, except that the two δ factors involving$x _ { 4 }$in (9.42) will lead to the new δ factor

$$
\delta ((t _ {2} - t _ {1}) v _ {4} + y ^ {*} - z ^ {*} - \varepsilon (\omega + \eta)).
$$

Now, suppose$( \omega , \eta , v _ { 4 } )$are fixed, we shall integrate the remaining four δ functions in (9.41) involving only$v _ { j } .$, in the variables$( v _ { 2 } , v _ { 3 } , v _ { 5 } , v _ { 6 } )$, as follows. The integration in$( v _ { 3 } , v _ { 6 } )$result in substitution, and for the integration in$( v _ { 2 } , v _ { 5 } )$we note that

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \pmb {\delta} \big (v _ {4} - v _ {2} - [ (v _ {1} - v _ {2}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \cdot \widetilde {Q} (v _ {2}) \mathrm{d} v _ {2} = \pmb {\delta} \big ((v _ {4} - v _ {1}) \cdot \omega \big) \cdot \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \widetilde {Q} (v _ {4} + \alpha \omega) \mathrm{d} \alpha\tag{9.43}
$$

for any function${ \cal \widetilde Q } ,$which is easily proved by assuming ω is a coordinate vector. The same holds for the integration in$v _ { 5 }$, and putting them together, we can reduce

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {(\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}) ^ {2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} \max (\alpha_ {1}, 0) \max (\alpha_ {2}, 0) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \boldsymbol {\delta} ((t _ {2} - t _ {1}) v _ {4} + y ^ {*} - z ^ {*} - \varepsilon (\omega + \eta)) \\ \qquad \times   \boldsymbol {\delta} \big ((v _ {4} - v _ {1}) \cdot \omega \big) \boldsymbol {\delta} \big ((v _ {4} - v _ {7}) \cdot \eta \big) \cdot Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} v _ {4} \cdot \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} \eta \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2}   \mathrm{d} t _ {j} \mathrm{d} \alpha_ {j}. \end{array}\tag{9.44}
$$

Next, with$v _ { 4 }$fixed, we integrate in η and ω using the formula

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \boldsymbol {\delta} (X \cdot \omega) f (\omega) \mathrm{d} \omega = | X | ^ {- 1} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 2}} f (R _ {X} \omega^ {\prime}) \mathrm{d} \omega^ {\prime}, \qquad X \in \{v _ {4} - v _ {1}, v _ {4} - v _ {7} \}
$$

where$\mathbb { S } ^ { d - 2 }$is the unit sphere in the orthogonal complement of a fixed coordinate vector$e ,$and$R _ { X }$is the rotation such that$\begin{array} { r } { R ( e ) = \frac { X } { | X | } } \end{array}$. This follows from applying the spherical coordinates. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {(\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 2}) ^ {2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {2}} | t _ {1} - t _ {2} | ^ {- d} | v _ {4} - v _ {1} | ^ {- 1} | v _ {4} - v _ {7} | ^ {- 1} \max (\alpha_ {1}, 0) \max (\alpha_ {2}, 0) \\ \qquad \times \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \delta \bigg (v _ {4} + \frac {y ^ {*} - z ^ {*} - \varepsilon (R _ {v _ {4} - v _ {1}} \omega^ {\prime} + R _ {v _ {4} - v _ {7}} \eta^ {\prime})}{t _ {2} - t _ {1}} \bigg) \cdot Q (\dots)   \mathrm{d} \omega^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} \eta^ {\prime} \mathrm{d} v _ {4} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {2}   \mathrm{d} t _ {j} \mathrm{d} \alpha_ {j}. \end{array}\tag{9.45}
$$

Now, with$( t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , \omega ^ { \prime } , \eta ^ { \prime } )$fixed, we evaluate the integral in$v _ { 4 }$by first changing variables into$v _ { 4 } \to \xi$where ξ is the argument of the δ. Since$\varepsilon ^ { 1 / 2 } \ll | t _ { 2 } - t _ { 1 } |$by assumption, the Jacobian of this change of variables is close to 1, so (9.25) follows, using the lower bounds in (9.23).

Proof of (3). This is easy and follows from (1): simply note that$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } , x _ { 7 } , v _ { 7 } )$belongs to a set of volume $\varepsilon ^ { 2 d ( 1 - v ) } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { \dot { C } ^ { * } }$with$0 < v < 1 / ( 4 d )$. Once$( x _ { 1 } , v _ { 1 } , x _ { 7 } , v _ { 7 } )$is fixed, we can perform the the integration in the remaining variables just as in the {33A} molecule case in (1). This leads to the desired bound (9.25). □

Now we define the normal, good, and bad components, based on Propositions 9.1–9.3. The cutting algorithm aims to produce good components while avoiding bad ones. These properties depend not only on the molecule M, but also on the restriction on the support of Q, which comes from splitting (Definition 8.9).

Definition 9.4 (Normal, bad and good molecules). Suppose$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$is formed from a full molecule M by an operation sequence (Definition 8.10) and picking one sub-case at each splitting, and$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$contains only elementary molecules. The initial link structure$\mathcal { L }$between the bottom ends of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$are inherited from that of M (as the operations do not afect any bottom end). Note also that in the splitting steps, by selecting a sub-case each time, we may have made certain extra restrictions to the support of Q in (7.6).

Based on all this information, we now define the notions of good, normal and bad molecules. Below, for any one-atom molecule$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } \}$, we denote the 4 edges by$e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { 4 }$, where$e _ { 1 }$is serial with$e _ { 3 }$, and$e _ { 2 }$is serial with$e _ { 4 }$. For two-atom molecule$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$, we denote the 7 edges by$e _ { 1 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , e _ { 7 }$with$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 7 }$being the fixed ends in the case of {33} molecules, see Figure 15. Recall also the constant$v : = 3 ^ { - d - 1 }$

(1) The following molecules are normal:

(a) Any {2} molecule.

(b) Any {3} molecule, except those described in (3a) below.

(c) Any {33A} molecule, except those described in (3b) below.

(2) The following molecules are bad:

(a) Any {4} molecule.

(b) By convention, we also view any empty end as bad.

(3) The following molecules are good:

(a) Any {3} molecule${ \mathcal { X } } = \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$with fixed end$e _ { 1 }$, where either the extra restriction includes one of the following conditions:

$$
\left| t _ {\mathfrak {n}} - t _ {\mathfrak {n} ^ {\prime}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {\upsilon} \quad \text {or} \quad \left| v _ {e _ {i}} - v _ {e _ {j}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {\upsilon} \quad \text {or} \quad \left| x _ {e} - x _ {e ^ {\prime}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - \upsilon} \quad \text {or} \quad \left| x _ {e _ {i}} - x _ {e _ {j}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - \upsilon}\tag{9.46}
$$

or$( e _ { i } , e _ { j } ) \in \mathcal { L }$, or$( e , e ^ { \prime } ) \in \mathcal { L }$(i.e. the relevant pair of ends are initial linked as in Definition 3.1; see also the$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$factor in Definition 7.3).

Here in (9.46) we assume that (i) n<sup>′</sup> is an atom in a molecule Y with$\mathcal { V } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { X }$(Definition 8.16), and$e ^ { \prime }$is a free end or bond at${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } ; ~ ( { \mathrm { i i } } ) ~ e$is a free end at n and$e _ { i } \neq e _ { j }$are two ends at n; (iii) if n is O-atom, then$e ^ { \prime }$is not serial with$e _ { 1 }$, and$e _ { i }$not serial with$e _ { j }$. In this case,$t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } }$and $x _ { e ^ { \prime } }$are fixed variables, so the extra restrictions (or initial link) makes X good.

(b) Any {33A} molecule$\mathcal { X } = \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$with fixed ends$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 7 } )$, where either the extra restriction includes one of the following conditions:

$$
\left| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {7}} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad \left| v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {7}} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad \left| t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {1}} - t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {2}} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {v},\tag{9.47}
$$

or$\ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } ] \neq \ell [ \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } ]$. In this case$\mathcal { X }$is good as a$\mathrm { \{ 3 3 A \} }$molecule without strong degeneracy.

(c) Any {33B} molecule$\mathcal { X } = \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$of two C-atoms with fixed ends$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 7 } )$, where the extra restriction includes both of the following conditions:

$$
\left| v _ {e _ {i}} - v _ {e _ {j}} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {v} \quad \text { and } \quad \left| t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {1}} - t _ {\mathfrak {n} _ {2}} \right| \geq \varepsilon^ {v}.\tag{9.48}
$$

Here$( e _ { i } , e _ { j } )$are two diferent ends at the same atom$\left( \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } \ \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \right)$. In this case$\mathcal { X }$is good as a {33B} molecule without weak degeneracy.

(d) Any {44} molecule${ \mathcal X } = \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$, where the extra restriction includes both of the following conditions:

$$
| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {7}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{and} \quad | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {7}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}.\tag{9.49}
$$

Here$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 7 } )$are two free ends at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and n<sub>2</sub> respectively, such that M becomes a {33A} molecule after turning these two free ends into fixed ends. In this case the strong extra restrictions (9.49) makes X good.

(e) Any {4} molecule${ \mathcal { X } } = \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$, where either the extra restriction includes one of the following conditions:

$$
| v _ {e _ {i}} - v _ {e _ {j}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | x _ {e} - x _ {e ^ {\prime}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \mathrm{or} \quad | x _ {e _ {i}} - x _ {e _ {j}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v},\tag{9.50}
$$

or$( e _ { i } , e _ { j } ) \in \mathcal { L }$, or$( e , e ^ { \prime } ) \in \mathcal { L }$(i.e. the relevant pair of ends are initial linked as in Definition 3.1; see also the$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$factor in Definition 7.3).

Here in (9.50) we assume that (i)${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$is an atom in a molecule Y with$\mathcal { V } \prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \mathcal { X }$(Definition 8.16), and$e ^ { \prime }$is a free end or bond at${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } ; ~ ( { \mathrm { i i } } ) ~ e$is a free end at n; (iii)$( e _ { i } , e _ { j } )$are two diferent ends at${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$and are non-serial when n is O-atom. In this case,$x _ { e ^ { \prime } }$is a fixed variable, so the extra restrictions (or initial link) makes X good.

(f) Finally, by convention, we also view an empty end e as good, if$( e , e ^ { \prime } ) \in { \mathcal { L } }$for some$e ^ { \prime } ,$i.e. e is involved in some initial link. In this case the initial link condition (see the$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$factor in Definition 7.3) will ensure the gain and thus we view e as good.

Remark 9.5. We explain the classification of elementary molecules in Definition 9.4 as follows:

(1) Note that Definition 9.4 allows for some {4} molecules and empty ends to be both good and bad; this will not cause any confusion, because in practice the property of good/non-good and bad/non-bad are always exploited independently. The rule of thumb is that, each good molecule leads to a power$\varepsilon ^ { v }$gain in the estimate of the integral$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q )$in (7.6), and each bad molecule leads to a power $\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) }$loss in this integral (and each normal molecule leads to no gain or loss). These gain and loss estimates easily follow from Definition 9.4 and Propositions 9.1–9.3.

(2) Note that the definition of good molecules depends on various extra restrictions imposed in Definition 9.4. In fact, these extra restrictions (corresponding to degeneracy and non-degeneracy conditions) are what motivates the splitting steps in the operation sequence. Basically, we may split into degenerate and non-degenerate sub-cases, and exploit diferent good molecules based on the extra restrictions in each diferent sub-case. We may also design diferent cutting strategies based on diferent sub-cases, which will be clear in the algorithm below (cf. the strongly and weakly degeneracies in Propositions 12.5 and 12.17, where we have a diferent cutting strategy from the main case).

Remark 9.6. Most of the elementary molecules that will occur in the algorithm (Sections 11–13) are {2}, {3}, {4} and {33A} molecules. In fact, {33B} molecules will occur only in the MAINUD algorithm (Definition 13.12), and the {44} molecule will occur only in Choice 1 in the proof of Proposition 12.5. Our construction will guarantee that the {33B} and {44} molecules are always good every time they occur.

9.2. Proof of Proposition 6.2. In this subsection we finish the proof of Proposition 6.2, assuming Proposition 9.7 below, which states that there exists an operation sequence that satisfies the nice property (9.51). This condition is natural in view of the gains and losses associated with good and bad molecules (see Remark 9.5; the choice of$\upsilon / 2$instead of υ is due to the need to cover certain log losses).

The construction of the operation sequence in Proposition 9.7 will be left to Sections 10–13. The proof in this subsection relies on Propositions 3.25, 7.2, 7.5, 8.18 and 9.1–9.3. We also rely on two estimates for $( v _ { e } )$volume and cross sections in (7.6), namely Propositions 9.8 and 9.9. The proof of these estimates are technical, and we leave it to Section 9.3.

Proposition 9.7. Let$\mathbb { M } = ( \mathcal { M } , \mathcal { E } , \mathcal { P } , \mathcal { L } )$be a full (unlabeled) molecule as in Definition 3.20, which belongs to either$\mathcal { F } _ { \pmb { \Lambda } _ { i } }$or$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$. Let$r ( \mathbb { M } ) = H$and$Q = Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$as in (7.8). Let also$\rho$be defined as in (7.1) in Definition 7.1.

Then, there exist an operation sequence (Definition 8.10) which produces at most$C ^ { | \mathbb { M } | } \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$total sub-cases, such that in each sub-case the M<sup>′</sup> contains only good, normal and bad elementary molecules (Definition 9.4). Moreover, if$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$, we have the following estimate (recall$v = 3 ^ { - d - 1 } )$:

$$
(v / 2) \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} + (d - 1) (| H | - \# _ {\mathrm{bad}}) \geq (C _ {1 3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho ,\tag{9.51}
$$

where$\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } }$and$\# _ { \mathrm { b a d } }$are the number of good and bad molecules respectively. If$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$, then (9.51) holds with an extra term$- C ^ { * } | H |$on the right hand side.

Proof. The proof will occupy Sections 10–13, and will be finished in Section 13.5 (after reducing to Proposition 12.18 at the end of Section 12).□

Proof of Proposition$6 . 2$assuming Proposition 9.7. We first make some reductions. By Proposition 3.25, we can estimate$\lvert E _ { H } \rvert$and$| \mathrm { E r r } ^ { 1 } |$by sum of$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$over$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$and$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$respectively. We can bound the number of choices of M by Proposition 7.2, and reduce the$L ^ { 1 }$norms of$| \mathcal { T N } _ { \mathbb { M } } |$to$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$by$\mathrm { B y }$Proposition 7.5. We then apply the operation sequence to M as in Proposition 9.7 (which includes the upper bound on the number of sub-cases produced), and apply Proposition 8.18 to reduce to estimating$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q ^ { \prime } )$for each sub-case. In summary, we get

$$
\| E_{H}\|_{L^{1}}\leq \sum_{m;\rho \geq |H|}C^{m}|\log \varepsilon |^{C^{*}\rho}\cdot_{\varepsilon^{(d - 1)|H|}}\sup_{\substack{\mathbb{M}\in \mathcal{F}_{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{\ell}}:r(\mathbb{M}) = H\\ |\mathbb{M}| = m,  \rho   \text{fixed}}}\sup_{\substack{\text{sub - cases}\\ }}\mathcal{I}_{\mathbb{M}^{\prime}}(Q^{\prime}),\tag{9.52}
$$

and the same for$\| \mathrm { E r r } ^ { 1 } \| _ { L ^ { 1 } }$but with$\mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda }$replaced by$\mathcal { F } _ { \Delta _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$. Here note that$| H | \leq \rho$because$\begin{array} { r } { | H | = | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) | = s _ { \ell } ; } \end{array}$ moreover, for$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$we must have$| \mathbb { M } | \geq \Lambda _ { \ell }$(as there exists a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that has exactly$\Lambda _ { \ell }$ clusters, see Definition 3.20 (2)).

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime}) \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} | / 9} \cdot \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | H | + (2 v / 5) + (5 C _ {1 3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \rho}\tag{9.53}
$$

for any$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { i } }$and any sub-case in the operation sequence that leads to$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$and$Q ^ { \prime }$. The rest part of this proof is devoted to the proof of (9.53). We divide into 6 parts.

Proof part 1: properties of final components. In this part, as a preparation, we prove a simple fact for the (elementary) final components in M<sup>′</sup> after the operation sequence. More precisely, we will show that

$$
\# _ {\neg \mathrm{N} \{3 \}} \leq C (\# _ {\text { good }} + \rho),\tag{9.54}
$$

where$\# _ { \neg \mathrm { N } \{ 3 \} }$is the number of final components in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$that are either nor normal or not {3} molecules, and $\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } }$and$\# _ { \mathrm { b a d } }$are the number of good and bad final components in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$respectively.

To prove (9.54), we will consider the quantity$3 | \mathbb { M } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { * } |$under the operation sequence. It is easy to see that this quantity decreases by 1 under deleting, and does not change under cutting. The latter is obvious when there is no O-atom (since a bond is cut into a free and a fixed end, and fixed ends do not count in $| \mathcal { E } _ { * } | )$; in general it can be directly verified using Definition 8.3 (2)).

Next consider the initial value of$3 | \mathbb { M } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { * } |$for M (for which${ \mathcal { E } } = { \mathcal { E } } _ { * }$as there is no fixed end). In Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 7.5, we have proved that$4 | \mathbb { M } | = 2 | \mathcal { E } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + } |$. Note that each edge in E is classified as either bond, or top end in$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + }$, or bottom end in$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$, and each empty end counts as both top end end bottom end, we deduce that

$$
3 | \mathbb {M} | - | \mathcal {E} | = | \mathcal {E} | - | \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-} | - | \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {+} | - | \mathbb {M} | = \# _ {\mathrm{bond}} - | \mathbb {M} | - \# _ {\mathrm{ee}},\tag{9.55}
$$

where$\# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } }$and$\# \mathrm { { e e } }$are the number of bonds and empty ends in M respectively. Note that$\# _ { \mathrm { e e } } \geq 0$, and the number of bonds between diferent layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$is bounded by$\textstyle \sum _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) |$(as each such bond corresponds to a particle line crossing two diferent layer which will be in some$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) )$, we see that the initial value

$$
3 | \mathbb {M} | - | \mathcal {E} | \leq \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime}} | r (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}) | + \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime}} (\# _ {\mathrm{bond} (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}})} - | \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} |) \leq \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime}} | r (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}) | + \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime}} \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}) \leq \rho\tag{9.56}
$$

using also Definition 3.13.

Now we prove (9.54). By the above discussions, we see that$3 | \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { * } ^ { \prime } | \le \rho$for the final result$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$(and corresponding$\mathcal { E } _ { * } ^ { \prime } )$. Note that this value equals 0 for {3} molecules, equals −1 for {2} and {33} molecules, and equals 1 for {4} and {44} molecules and empty ends, so we conclude that

$$
\# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 \}} \leq \rho + \# _ {\mathrm{ee}} + \# _ {\{4 \}} + \# _ {\{4 4 \}} \leq 4 (\# _ {\text { good }} + \# _ {\text { bad }} + \rho)\tag{9.57}
$$

but now for$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, where$\# _ { \{ 2 \} }$and$\# \{ 3 3 \}$etc. are the number of corresponding molecules in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$. Here the last inequality is because each {4} and {44} molecule and empty end is either good or bad by Definition 9.4. Finally, since there are only elementary components in M<sup>′</sup>, by Definition 8.11, we have

$$
\# _ {\neg \mathrm{N} \{3 \}} = \# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 \}} + \# _ {\mathrm{ee}} + \# _ {\{4 \}} + \# _ {\{4 4 \}} + \# (\text {good} \{3 \} \text {molecules}),
$$

thus$\# _ { \neg \mathrm { N } \{ 3 \} } \leq 9 ( \# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } + \# _ { \mathrm { b a d } } + \rho )$thanks to (9.57). Since we also have$\# _ { \mathrm { b a d } } \leq C ( \# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } + | H | )$by (9.51) and$| H | \leq \rho ,$we conclude that$\# _ { \neg \mathrm { N } \{ 3 \} } \leq C ( \# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } + \rho )$. This proves (9.54).

Proof part 2: decomposition of the support of Q. Recall$Q ^ { \prime }$corresponds to a sub-case in the operation sequence obtained by splittings; as in Proposition 8.18, we have$Q ^ { \prime } = Q _ { \mathrm { M } } \cdot \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { P } }$where$\mathcal { P }$represents the restriction in this sub-case. $$

where$\alpha$is the summation index,$w _ { \alpha } \geq 0$is a scalar, and$Q _ { \alpha }$are nonnegative functions that have localized support in the$x _ { e }$and$v _ { e }$variables, specified as below:

$$
Q _ {\alpha} = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D}} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} \cdot \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \big (e ^ {- \beta | v _ {e} | ^ {2} / 3} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {| x _ {e} - x _ {e} ^ {*} | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}, | v _ {e} | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}} \big).\tag{9.59}
$$

Now we proceed to prove (9.58) and (1)–(3). Recall that$Q _ { \mathbb { M } }$is given by (7.8),

$$
Q _ {\mathbb {M}} = \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D}} (\boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}) \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} (\boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E}}) \cdot \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \left| f ^ {\mathcal {A}} \big ((\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau , x _ {e} - (\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau \cdot v _ {e}, v _ {e} \big) \right|.\tag{9.61}
$$

We begin by decomposing$f ^ { A }$and then inserting into (9.61).

Decomposition of$f ^ { A }$. By (6.1), (6.2), (1.29) and (1.34), we know that$\| f ^ { A } ( \ell \tau ) \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { 2 \beta / 5 } } \le C$. The definition of$\| \cdot \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { 2 \beta / 5 } }$(1.15) implies that$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$decay exponentially in$v ,$so we may restrict$| v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$ for each bottom end e, otherwise the exponential decay will overwhelm the powers$\varepsilon ^ { - ( d - 1 ) ( | \mathcal { E } _ { * } | - \mathrm { 2 } | \mathbb { M } | ) }$in (7.6) and the desired bound becomes trivial.

Next, with the assumption that$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$is supported in$| v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, we will decompose

$$
\begin{array}{c} | f ^ {\mathcal {A}} (x, v) | \leq \sum_ {x ^ {*} \in \mathbb {Z} ^ {d}} w _ {x ^ {*}} \cdot g _ {x ^ {*}} (x, v), \\ g _ {x ^ {*}} (x, v) \leq e ^ {- (2 \beta / 5) | v | ^ {2}} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {| x - x ^ {*} | \leq C, | v | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}}, \quad \sum_ {x ^ {*} \in \mathbb {Z} ^ {d}} w _ {x ^ {*}} \leq C, \end{array}\tag{9.62}

Inserting the decomposition of$f ^ { A }$. Now, by inserting the decomposition (9.62) into (9.61), we get

$$
Q _ {\mathbb {M}} \leq \sum_ {\alpha} \underbrace {\left(\prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} w _ {x _ {e} ^ {*}}\right)} _ {w _ {\alpha}} \underbrace {\left(\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {D}} \cdot \mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} \cdot \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} g _ {x _ {e} ^ {*}} ((\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau , x _ {e} - (\ell_ {1} [ e ] - 1) \tau \cdot v _ {e} , v _ {e})\right)} _ {Q _ {\alpha}} = \sum_ {\alpha} w _ {\alpha} Q _ {\alpha},\tag{9.63}

This already establishes (9.58), and $( 1 ) - ( 2 )$also follow from (9.62) where we note that$| ( \ell _ { 1 } [ e ] - 1 ) \tau \cdot v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$

Finally we prove (3). Combining with (9.75), we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q _ {\alpha} ^ {\prime}) \leq C ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot e ^ {- (\beta / 9 6) \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} | X _ {e} | ^ {2}} \cdot \mathfrak {B} \cdot | \widetilde {\mathcal {D}} | \cdot \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} X _ {e} ^ {d} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \# _ {\neg \mathrm{N} \{3 \}}} \cdot \sup \left[ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\neg \mathrm{N} \{3 \}} \left(\mathbb {1} _ {(\heartsuit)}\right) \right] \\ \quad \leq (\mathfrak {B} \cdot | \widetilde {\mathcal {D}} |) \cdot \bigg (\prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} X _ {e} ^ {d} \cdot e ^ {- (\beta / 9 6) | X _ {e} | ^ {2}} \bigg) \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \# _ {\neg \mathrm{N} \{3 \}}} \cdot \varepsilon^ {v \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} - (d - 1) \# _ {\mathrm{bad}}}. \end{array}\tag{9.80}
$$

By Proposition 9.8 we know that$| \widetilde { D } | \cdot \mathfrak { B } \le ( C \tau ) ^ { | \mathbb { M } | } \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } ( \rho + | A | ) }$, and it is also obvious that$\Pi _ { e } ( X _ { e } ^ { d }$ $e ^ { - ( \beta / 9 6 ) | X _ { e } | ^ { 2 } } ) \le C ^ { | \mathbb { M } | }$. Recall$\# \mathrm { \neg N \{ 3 \} }$is the number of molecules in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$that are not normal {3} molecules, and we have$| A | \leq 2 \cdot \# _ { \neg \mathrm { N } \{ 3 \} }$(as an elementary component has at most two atoms). Using also (9.54), we know that$| A | + \# _ { \neg \mathrm { N } \{ 3 \} } \leq C ( \# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } + \rho )$. Inserting all the above into (9.80), we obtain

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q _ {\alpha} ^ {\prime}) \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} (\rho + \# _ {\mathrm{good}})} \cdot \varepsilon^ {v \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} - (d - 1) \# _ {\mathrm{bad}}} \cdot (C \tau) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}.\tag{9.81}
$$

Now consider (9.51) in Proposition 9.7. Since$\rho > 0$, we know the left hand side of (9.51) is at least$v / 2 ;$ by interpolation we get that this is also$\geq ( 2 v / 5 ) + ( 5 C _ { 1 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho .$Using this and (9.81), we conclude that

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q _ {\alpha} ^ {\prime}) \leq (C \tau) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot \big (| \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \varepsilon^ {\upsilon / 2} \big) ^ {\# _ {\mathrm{good}}} \cdot \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | H |} \cdot \varepsilon^ {(2 \upsilon / 5) + (5 C _ {1 3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \rho}.
$$

Since$C \tau \leq \tau ^ { 1 / 8 }$and$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } } \varepsilon ^ { v / 2 } \leq 1$, this proves (9.64) and thus completes the proof of Proposition 6.2 for$E _ { H }$

Proof part 6: the case of$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 1 } }$. Finally, to prove Proposition 6.2 for$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 1 } }$, we only need to prove (9.53) with an extra factor of$\varepsilon ^ { - C ^ { * } \mid H \mid }$on the right hand side, i.e.

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime}) \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} | / 9} \cdot \varepsilon^ {- C ^ {*} | H |} \cdot \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) | H | + (2 v / 5) + (5 C _ {1 3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \rho}.\tag{9.82}
$$

However, this follows the same arguments as in Parts 1–5 above; the only diference is that we now have an extra term$- C ^ { * } | H |$on the right hand side of (9.51), which leads to the loss$\varepsilon ^ { - C ^ { * } | H | }$. This proves Proposition 6.2 for$\mathrm { E r r ^ { 1 } }$, and completes the proof of Proposition 6.2.□

9.3. Auxiliary results in the proof of Proposition 6.2. In this subsection we state and prove the auxiliary results (Propositions 9.8 and 9.9) that are used in the proof of Proposition 6.2 in Section 9.2.

Proposition 9.8. Let M be a molecule as in Definition 3.20, which satisfies Definition 3.20 (1a) and (1c). Let$v _ { e } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$be the associated variables defined for each edge e of M, satisfying

$$
| v _ {e} | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}}, \quad | v _ {e _ {1}} | ^ {2} + | v _ {e _ {2}} | ^ {2} = | v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} | ^ {2} + | v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} | ^ {2}; \quad v _ {e _ {j}} = v _ {e _ {j} ^ {\prime}} \text {if} \mathfrak {n} \text {is O - atom}\tag{9.83}
$$

for each atom n, where$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$are the two bottom edges and$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$are the two top edges at${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$and$e _ { 1 }$is serial with$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 }$is serial with$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$as in Definition 7.3 (2). Fix also a constant$\gamma$with$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { - 1 } \leq \gamma \leq 1$ Then there exists a scalar quantity$\Re \geq 1$depending only on M, such that

$$
\prod_ {\mathfrak {n}} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \mathfrak {B} \cdot \exp \left(\gamma \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} | v _ {e} | ^ {2}\right),\tag{9.84}
$$

where the product on the left hand side of (9.84) is taken over all atoms n and$( v _ { e _ { 1 } } , v _ { e _ { 2 } } )$is as above. Moreover, this quantity B satisfies the following estimates. For any atom set$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$, we have

$$
\mathfrak {B} \cdot \left(\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}}} 1 \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M} \backslash A}\right) \leq \left(C \gamma^ {- 1 / 2} \tau\right) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} (\rho + | A |)},\tag{9.85}
$$

where the integral is taken over all variables$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } \backslash A } = ( t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) _ { \mathfrak { n } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash A } .$, and$\widetilde { \mathcal { D } }$is the projection of the set D defined in (7.5) onto the variables$\pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } \backslash A }$

Proof. We divide the proof into 4 parts.

Proof part 1: the binary tree case. In this part, we consider the case when$\mathbb { M } = T$has only one layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$and is a binary tree, where$T$has a unique highest atom m, and each atom in$T \backslash \{ \mathfrak { m } \}$has a unique parent in T.

Proof of (9.84) for binary trees. By considering$\gamma ^ { 1 / 2 } \cdot v _ { e }$instead of$v _ { e }$, we may reduce to the case$\gamma = 1$ For the domain$\mathcal { D } _ { T }$of time variables$( t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) _ { \mathfrak { n } \in T }$defined in the same way as in (7.5), we know$t _ { \mathfrak { n } } \in [ ( \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 ) \tau , \ell ^ { \prime } \tau ]$ because T only has one layer. It is easy to prove by induction that

$$
\int_ {\mathcal {D} _ {T}} 1 \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {T} = \tau^ {| T |} \cdot \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {- 1}, \quad \mathfrak {C} _ {T} := \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} \sigma (\mathfrak {n}),\tag{9.86}
$$

where$\sigma ( \mathfrak { n } )$is the number of descendant atoms of n in$T$(Definition 3.5; this includs n itself).

For any atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in T .$, by iteratively applying (9.83) for the atom n and its descendants in$T ,$we get that

$$
(1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) ^ {2} \leq 2 + 2 (| v _ {e _ {1}} | ^ {2} + | v _ {e _ {2}} | ^ {2}) \leq 2 + 2 \sum_ {(l, e)} | v _ {e} | ^ {2},\tag{9.87}
$$

where the sum is taken over all lowest atoms l of$T$that are descendants of${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$and all bottom ends e at l. Note that for each fixed e there is at most one l, and for each fixed l there are at most two e in the summation. From (9.87) we have

$$
\begin{array}{l} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) ^ {2} \leq \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} (\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {5 / 3} \cdot \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} \bigg (\frac {2}{(\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {5 / 3}} + \frac {2}{(\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {5 / 3}} \sum_ {(\mathfrak {l}, e)} | v _ {e} | ^ {2} \bigg) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {5 / 3} 2 ^ {| T |} \cdot \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} \bigg (1 + (\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {- 5 / 3} \bigg (\sum_ {(\mathfrak {l}, e)} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \bigg) ^ {3 / 2} \bigg). \end{array}\tag{9.88}
$$

where$\mathfrak { C } _ { T }$is as in (9.86), and in the last line we used$\sum x _ { j } ^ { 3 / 2 } \leq ( \sum x _ { j } ) ^ { 3 / 2 }$for$x _ { j } ~ \geq ~ 0$. By elementary inequality, for any$Z > 0$we have$1 + Z ^ { 3 / 2 } \le C e ^ { Z }$; applying this to$Z : = ( \sigma ( \mathfrak { n } ) ) ^ { - 1 0 / 9 } \sum _ { ( \mathfrak { l } , e ) } | v _ { e } | ^ { 4 / 3 }$, we get from (9.88) that

$$
\begin{array}{c} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) ^ {2} \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {5 / 3} (2 C) ^ {| T |} \exp \bigg (\sum_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} (\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {- 1 0 / 9} \sum_ {(\mathfrak {l}, e)} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \bigg) \\ = \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {5 / 3} (2 C) ^ {| T |} \exp \bigg (\sum_ {(\mathfrak {l}, e)} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \sum_ {\mathfrak {n}} (\sigma (\mathfrak {n})) ^ {- 1 0 / 9} \bigg). \end{array}\tag{9.89}
$$

Here, for fixed$( \mathfrak { l } , e )$, the summation is taken over all$\mathfrak { n } \in T$that are ancestors of l. Note that since$T$is a binary tree, each atom in$T$has at most one parent atom in T, so all such n (for fixed l) form a monotonic sequence on which the value of$\sigma ( \mathfrak { n } )$is strictly increasing. This implies that$\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( \sigma ( \mathfrak { n } ) ) ^ { - 1 0 / 9 } \le \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } n ^ { - 1 0 / 9 } \le C } \end{array}$ uniformly in (l, e), and hence

$$
\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in T} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {5 / 6} C ^ {| T |} \cdot \exp \bigg (C \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {T} ^ {-}} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \bigg),\tag{9.90}
$$

where${ \mathcal { E } } _ { T } ^ { - }$is the set of all bottom ends of atoms in$T .$

Analog of (9.85) for binary trees. In the same setting as above (where$\mathbb { M } = T$is a single layer binary tree), now let$A \subseteq T$be a fixed atom set. Next we shall prove that

$$
\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}} _ {T}} 1 \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {T \setminus A} \leq \tau^ {| T | - | A |} \cdot \mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {- 1} \cdot \frac {(| T |) !}{(| T | - | A |) !},\tag{9.91}
$$

where$\widetilde { \mathcal { D } } _ { T }$is projection of$\mathcal { D } _ { T }$(as defined above) onto the variables$\pmb { t } _ { T \backslash A }$. We will prove (9.91) by induction; the base case is trivial.

Suppose (9.91) is true for$| T | < m$, now consider some T with$| T | = m$. By time translation and dilation we may assume$\tau = 1$and$\ell ^ { \prime } = 0$so$t _ { \mathfrak { n } } \in [ 0 , 1 ]$for each n. Let the unique highest atom of$T$be m, we will assume m has 2 children atoms; the case when m has only one child atom is similar with slightly adjusted proof. Let the two children atoms of m be${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$, and let$T _ { j }$be the set of descendants of${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { j }$with $| T _ { j } | = m _ { j }$, then$m = m _ { 1 } + m _ { 2 } + 1$. Let$A _ { j } = A \cap T _ { j }$and$| A _ { j } | = k _ { j }$, we consider two cases, namely when m$\in { \cal A }$or m$\not \in A$

Suppose m$\not \in A$, then$0 \leq k _ { j } \leq m _ { j }$and$| A | : = k = k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 }$. For any$\pmb { t } _ { T \backslash A } \in \widetilde { \cal D } _ { T }$, we must have$\pmb { t } _ { T _ { j } \backslash A _ { j } } \in \widetilde { \mathcal { D } } _ { T _ { j } }$ for$j \in \{ 1 , 2 \}$, and$t _ { \mathfrak { n } } \in [ 0 , t _ { \mathfrak { m } } ]$for all${ \mathfrak { n } } \in T _ { j } \backslash A _ { j }$. By applying induction hypothesis to$( T _ { j } , A _ { j } )$and then integrating in$t _ { \mathfrak { m } } ,$we get that

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}} _ {T}} 1 \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {T \setminus A} \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {1}} ^ {- 1} \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {2}} ^ {- 1} \frac {m _ {1} ! m _ {2} !}{(m _ {1} - k _ {1}) ! (m _ {2} - k _ {2}) !} \int_ {0} ^ {1} t _ {\mathfrak {m}} ^ {m _ {1} + m _ {2} - k _ {1} - k _ {2}} \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathfrak {m}}} \\ & {\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {1}} ^ {- 1} \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {2}} ^ {- 1} \frac {m _ {1} ! m _ {2} !}{(m _ {1} - k _ {1}) ! (m _ {2} - k _ {2}) !} \frac {1}{m _ {1} + m _ {2} - k _ {1} - k _ {2} + 1}.} \end{array}\tag{9.92}
$$

Note also that

$$
\mathfrak {C} _ {T} ^ {- 1} = \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {1}} ^ {- 1} \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {2}} ^ {- 1} \cdot \frac {1}{m _ {1} + m _ {2} + 1},\tag{9.93}
$$

we see that (9.91) will follows from (9.92) and (9.93), provided we can show that

$$
\frac {m _ {1} ! m _ {2} !}{(m _ {1} - k _ {1}) ! (m _ {2} - k _ {2}) !} \leq \frac {(m _ {1} + m _ {2}) !}{(m _ {1} + m _ {2} - k _ {1} - k _ {2}) !}.\tag{9.94}
$$

Now to prove (9.94), simply note that$( x + y ) ! / x !$is increasing in$x \geq 0$for fixed$y \geq 0 ;$by applying it to $y = m _ { 2 } - k _ { 2 }$and$x = m _ { 1 } - k _ { 1 }$(and using symmetry), we see that the ratio between the left hand side and right hand side of (9.94) is maximized when x and y are both maximized, i.e.$k _ { 1 } = k _ { 2 } = 0$. In this extremal case (9.94) is trivially true, so it is true in general.

Suppose m$\in A$, then$0 \leq k _ { j } \leq m _ { j }$and$| A | : = k = k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } + 1$. By similar argument as above (except that now we do not integrate in$t _ { \mathfrak { m } }$as${ \mathfrak { m } } \in A )$, we get

$$
\int_ {\tilde {\mathcal {D}} _ {T}} 1 \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {T \setminus A} \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {1}} ^ {- 1} \mathfrak {C} _ {T _ {2}} ^ {- 1} \frac {m _ {1} ! m _ {2} !}{(m _ {1} - k _ {1}) ! (m _ {2} - k _ {2}) !}.\tag{9.95}
$$

Using also (9.93) and (9.94), this again implies (9.91).

Proof part 2: the forest case. Now consider the case when M has only one layer$\ell ^ { \prime } ,$and is a forest. By restricting to components, we may assume M is a tree (which need not be a binary tree). We shall divide the atom set of M into finitely many binary trees and upside down binary trees (where the notions of parent and child etc. are the opposite from binary trees), as follows, see Figure 17.

First choose any atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, and let$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n. This is a binary tree, because each atom has at most one parent in$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(as M has no cycle). Moreover, all bottom ends of$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$are also bottom ends of M. Consider all the atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } \not \in T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that are connected to$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$by a bond. Since M is a tree, if we remove$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$from M (and turn any bond between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$and$T _ { \mathfrak { n } }$to a free end at${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } )$, then M becomes the disjoint union of trees$\mathbb { M } ^ { j }$, where${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } \in \mathbb { M } ^ { j }$for each$j .$. Note also that each${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$has only one bond connected to$T _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$, which is turned to a bottom free end in M<sup>j</sup>.

Now for each$j ,$let$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ^ { * }$be the set of ancestors of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$in$\mathbb { M } ^ { j }$, which is now an upside down binary tree. Clearly all top ends of$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ^ { * }$are also top ends of M, and all the discussions in Step 1 above also work for upside down binary trees due to time reversal symmetry. Consider all the atoms$\mathfrak { n } _ { j k } \in \mathbb { M } ^ { j } \backslash T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ^ { * }$that are connected to$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ^ { * }$by a bond, then after removing$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } } ^ { * }$from$\mathbb { M } ^ { j }$, the$\mathbb { M } ^ { j }$will become the disjoint union of trees$\mathbb { M } ^ { j k }$ where${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j k } \in \mathbb { M } ^ { j k }$for each k. Also each${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j k }$has only one bond connected to$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } } ^ { * }$, which is turned to a top free end in$\mathbb { M } ^ { j k }$. Therefore, we can choose$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j k } }$to be the set of descendants of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j k }$in$\mathbb { M } ^ { j k }$, which is a binary tree, so that all bottom ends of$T _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j k } }$are also bottom ends of M, and so on.
