By repeating the above, we have divided the atom set of M into the disjoint union of finitely many$T ^ { ( j ) }$ where each$T ^ { ( j ) }$is either a binary tree or an upside down binary tree. If we apply (9.90) and (9.91) to each

$T ^ { ( j ) }$, we then obtain that

$$
\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \prod_ {j} \mathfrak {C} _ {T ^ {(j)}} ^ {5 / 6} \cdot C ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot \exp \left(C \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3}\right),\tag{9.96}
$$

$$
\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}}} 1 \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathbb {M} \setminus A} \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} | - | A |} \prod_ {j} \mathfrak {C} _ {T ^ {(j)}} ^ {- 1} \cdot \prod_ {j} \frac {(| T ^ {(j)} |) !}{(| T ^ {(j)} | - | A \cap T ^ {(j)} |) !} \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \prod_ {j} \mathfrak {C} _ {T ^ {(j)}} ^ {- 1} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} | A |},\tag{9.97}
$$

in view of the upper bound$| \mathbb { M } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$(see Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 7.2) and the trivial bound $\tau ^ { - 1 } \leq | \log \varepsilon | .$. Here$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } }$in (9.96) is the set of all ends of M, and$\widetilde { \mathcal { D } }$in (9.97) is the same as in (9.85).

Proof part 3: single layer case. Now consider a molecule$\mathbb { M } = \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$with a single layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$satisfying the relevant conditions in Definition 3.20 (1a) and (1c).

Consider the clusters$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$of M (Definition 3.11). For each$j ,$, we may choose at most$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) \leq \Gamma$C-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$, such that if we remove these C-atoms, and turn any bond between these atoms and other atoms n into a free end at n, then the recollision number$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$will be reduced to 0. Therefore, in the molecule $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, if we remove all such C-atoms (their total number is$\begin{array} { r } { \le \sum _ { j } \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) = \Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } } \end{array}$, see Definition 7.1), then the resulting molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$will be a forest. By applying (9.96) and (9.97) to this forest, and using (9.83) for each of the removed atoms, we get that

$$
\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \mathfrak {C} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} ^ {5 / 6} \cdot C ^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} |} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \mathfrak {R} _ {\ell^ {\prime}}} \cdot \exp \left(C \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}})} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3}\right) \cdot \exp \left(C \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} ^ {*}} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3}\right),\tag{9.98}
$$

$$
\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}}} 1 \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} \backslash A} \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} |} \cdot \mathfrak {C} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} ^ {- 1} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} | A \cap \mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}} |}.\tag{9.99}
$$

Here$\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { C } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } : = \prod _ { i } \mathfrak { C } _ { T ^ { ( j ) } } } \end{array}$as in (9.96) and (9.97) (where the decomposition is made for the resulting forest after removing these C-atoms, following Part 2), and the other notions are defined as above but associated with $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Moreover in (9.98),$\mathcal { E } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { * }$is the set of all bonds at all the C-atoms removed above, so that each such bond becomes a free end in the reduced molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(which is a forest) after removing these C-atoms.

Consider each$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ^ { * }$, which is at some C-atom n removed above. Assume that this C-atom n belongs to the cluster M . By iterating (9.83) and noticing that all collisions happen between particles in$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$, we see that

$$
\sum_ {e} | v _ {e} | ^ {2} \leq 2 \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} (\mathbb {M} _ {j})} | v _ {e} | ^ {2}, \quad \text { and   hence }\tag{9.100}
$$

$$
\sum_ {e} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \leq C \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} (\mathbb {M} _ {j})} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3},\tag{9.101}
$$

where the left hand side of (9.100) and (9.101) is the sum over (at most 4) bonds e at some fixed atom n as above. Notice that the each end in$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$naturally corresponds to an end in$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$(identify $e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } )$with the bottom end of the particle line in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that e belongs to), and each$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$has at most $\Gamma \leq C$diferent atoms n removed. We obtain, upon summing over n and then over$j ,$, that

$$

$$

so the last exponential factor on the right hand side of (9.98) can be absorbed by the one before it.

Proof part 4: general multi-layer case. Now we put together all layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and consider the general multi-layer molecule M. By applying (9.98)–(9.99) for each$\ell ^ { \prime }$we get that

$$
\prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \mathfrak {C} ^ {5 / 6} \cdot C ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} \rho} \cdot \exp \bigg (C \sum_ {\ell^ {\prime}} \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} (\mathbb {M} _ {\ell^ {\prime}})} | v _ {e} | ^ {4 / 3} \bigg),\tag{9.102}
$$

$$
\int_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {D}}} 1 \mathrm{d} t _ {\mathbb {M} \backslash A} \leq \tau^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot \mathfrak {C} ^ {- 1} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} | A |},\tag{9.103}
$$

where$\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { C } : = \prod _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \mathfrak { C } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } } \end{array}$and the other notions are defined above for M.

Now for each$( e , \ell ^ { \prime } )$such that$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$, this e is either an end in the molecule M (which we call case 1), or a bond connecting layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$and some other layer$< \ell ^ { \prime }$(which we call case 2). For case 1, recall$\gamma = 1$ we simply apply ex$\rangle ( C | v | ^ { 4 / 3 } ) \leq C \cdot \exp ( | v ^ { 2 } | / 2 0 )$to get

$$

where$\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { e \in { \mathcal E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } } | v _ { e } | ^ { 2 } = 2 \cdot \sum _ { e \in { \mathcal E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } } | v _ { e } | ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$by energy conservation. For case 2, any such bond e belongs to a particle line$p \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 } )$. Note also that the number of all such particles$p$is bounded by

following Definition 7.1. Now we apply the inequality exp$( C | v | ^ { 4 / 3 } ) \leq C ^ { * } \cdot \exp ( | v | ^ { 2 } / 2 0 d \mathfrak { L } )$(recall our convention of$C$and$C ^ { * }$in Definition 1.6 (2)), and use also (9.105), to obtain that

By energy conservation, we have

Now, we may put together (9.102),(9.104) and (9.108), and choose B to be the factor$\mathfrak { C } ^ { 5 / 6 } \cdot C ^ { | \mathbb { M } | } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$ in (9.102), multiplied by the$C ^ { | \mathbb { M } | }$and$( C ^ { * } ) ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$factors in (9.104), (9.106) and (9.108). Proposition 9.9. Let M be a molecule, and fix a cutting sequence that reduces M to$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, which contains only empty ends and elementary molecules. Let S be a subset of the set of {3} molecules in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$. For each atom n with$\{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} \in { \mathfrak { S } }$, it has a unique fixed end$e _ { 1 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$, and a unique free end$e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$that is either both top or both bottom$e _ { 1 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$. Let the collection of all such$e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$be${ \mathcal F } .$

Now suppose for each atom n with$\{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} \in { \mathfrak { S } }$we have fixed$\omega _ { \mathfrak { n } } ~ \in ~ \mathbb { S } ^ { d - 1 }$. Assume also$v _ { e } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$is the associated variable for each edge$e \in \mathbb { M }$, respectively. Moreover, assume$| v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$for each edge e of $\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$, and for each atom n with$\{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} \in { \mathfrak { S } }$and edges$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$as in Definition 3.23, assume also that

$$
v _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} = v _ {e _ {1}} - [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}} ] \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}}, \quad v _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} = v _ {e _ {2}} + [ (v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}}) \cdot \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}} ] \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}}\tag{9.109}
$$

(this is for C-atoms; for O-atoms we simply have$v _ { e _ { j } ^ { \prime } } = v _ { e _ { j } } )$. For each$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ( \mathbb { M } )$, fix

$$
X _ {e} \in [ 1, | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} ] \cap 2 ^ {\mathbb {Z}},
$$

and assume that$| v _ { e } | \le X _ { e }$. Finally let K be the number of molecules in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$that do not belong to$\mathfrak { S }$(in reality S will be the set of normal {3} molecules, so$K = \# \mathrm { \_ N } \{ 3 \}$using the notion in (9.54)).

Then, there exists a set$Y \subseteq ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) ^ { | { \mathcal { F } } | }$, which depends on$\left( \omega _ { \mathfrak { n } } \right)$and$( X _ { e } )$, and on (M, M<sup>′</sup>) and the cutting sequence, but not on the concrete choices of$( v _ { e } )$, such that

$$
(v _ {e}) _ {e \in \mathcal {F}} \in Y, | Y | \leq \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} X _ {e} ^ {d} \cdot C ^ {| \mathbb {M} |} \cdot | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} K}.\tag{9.110}
$$

Proof. For each atom n with$\{ \mathfrak { n } \} \in \mathfrak { S } ,$, let$( e _ { 1 } ( \mathfrak { n } ) , e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$and$( e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ) , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } )$be defined as in Proposition 9.9 and (9.109). Recall$\mathcal { F }$is the set of all$e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$for$\{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} \in { \mathfrak { S } }$. Let G be the set of all edges of molecules in M<sup>′</sup> that are not in S, plus the ends of M (which are preserved in cutting, so they are also free ends of M<sup>′</sup>). Note that$| \mathcal { F } | , | \mathcal { G } | \leq 1 0 | \mathbb { M } |$. The idea is to show that, with$\left( \omega _ { \mathfrak { n } } \right)$fixed and using (9.109), each vector$v _ { e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } ) }$can be written as a constant coeficient linear combination of vectors$( v _ { e ^ { \prime } } ) _ { e ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { G } }$, and

$$
\sum_ {\mathfrak {n}} \left| v _ {e _ {2} (\mathfrak {n})} \right| ^ {2} \leq \sum_ {e ^ {\prime} \in \mathcal {G}} \left| v _ {e ^ {\prime}} \right| ^ {2}.\tag{9.111}
$$

We first prove the linear relation and (9.111) as claimed above. Start from any$e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$. If n is O-atom then let$e = e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } )$; if n is C-atom then we apply (9.109) to get a linear combination of$v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ) }$and$v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ) }$(and the energy inequality$| v _ { e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } ) } | ^ { 2 } \leq | v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ) } | ^ { 2 } + | v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ) } | ^ { 2 } )$, and then let e be either$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } )$or$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } )$. If$e \in { \mathcal { G } }$then this is already what we need; if$e \not \in { \mathcal { G } }$we need to further explore from e to reach${ \mathcal { G } } ,$as follows.

Note that e is not an end in M$( \operatorname { a s } e \not \in { \mathcal { G } } )$, so it must occur during a cutting operation, say while operating on a maximal ov-segment$\sigma$(with associated notions${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \pm }$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j } )$as in Definition 8.3. It is easy to verify that e does not belong to a simple pair (Definition 8.2), so by Definition 8.3 (2), we see that the only way this cutting creates a new free end e is that${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$or${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { s } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { - }$(for example in Figure 16, we get a new free end $e _ { 5 } ^ { \prime }$due to${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 3 } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { - } )$. Assume the former by symmetry, then${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + } \in \sigma \backslash A$, so the same cutting creates a fixed end$e _ { 1 }$at${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$, with$v _ { e } = v _ { e _ { 1 } }$. If$\{ \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } \} \not \in \mathfrak { S }$, then we have$e _ { 1 } \in { \mathcal { G } }$by definition, which is what we need; thus we will assume below that$\{ \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } \} \in \mathfrak { S }$

if${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$is O-atom, then$e _ { 1 }$must be serial with a free end$e ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { . } }$, so$v _ { e } = v _ { e ^ { \prime } }$$\operatorname { I f } { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$is C-atom, then$e _ { 1 } = e _ { 1 } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } )$ so we can add in$e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) ~ \in \mathcal { F } ;$: both$v _ { e }$and$v _ { e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) }$are linear combinations of$v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) }$and$v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) }$, and $| v _ { e } | ^ { 2 } + | v _ { e _ { 2 } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) } | ^ { 2 } = | v _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) } | ^ { 2 } + | v _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } ) } | ^ { 2 }$, then we can choose$e ^ { \prime }$be either$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } )$or$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } ( \mathfrak { n } ^ { + } )$. In either case, if $e ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { G }$then this is what we need; if not then we can explore from$e ^ { \prime }$as above. In the end, every exploration will stop at some$e ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { G }$, which proves the desired linear relation and (9.111).

Now, by (9.111), we have$( v _ { e } ) _ { e \in \mathcal { F } } = \mathcal { P } \big ( ( v _ { e ^ { \prime } } ) _ { e ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { G } } \big )$for some constant matrix$\mathcal { P }$which matrix norm$\| \mathcal { P } \| \leq 1$ Note that$| v _ { e ^ { \prime } } | \le X _ { e ^ { \prime } }$is$e ^ { \prime }$is an end in M, and$| v _ { e ^ { \prime } } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$if$e ^ { \prime }$belongs to a molecule in M<sup>′</sup> that is not in${ \mathfrak { S } } ,$, and the number of the latter case does not exceed 10K. It follows that the vector$( v _ { e ^ { \prime } } ) _ { e ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { G } }$belongs to the union of at most

$$
A := C ^ {| \mathcal {G} |} | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*} K} \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}}} X _ {e} ^ {d}
$$

fixed unit boxes in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d | \mathcal { G } | }$<sup>|</sup>. However, the image of any unit box in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d | \mathcal { G } | }$under$\mathcal { P }$is contained in a ball of radius$( d | \mathcal { G } | ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d | \mathcal { F } | }$, which is covered by at most

C ^ {F} \cdot (F + G) ^ {F / 2} \cdot \operatorname{Vol} (\text { unit   ball   in } \mathbb {R} ^ {F}) = C ^ {F} \cdot (F + G) ^ {F / 2} \cdot \pi^ {F / 2} \cdot (\Gamma (F / 2 + 1)) ^ {- 1} \leq C ^ {F + G}
$$

unit boxes, where$G : = d | { \mathcal { G } } |$and$F : = d | { \mathcal { F } } |$. It then follows that$( v _ { e } ) _ { e \in \mathcal { F } }$belongs to the union of at most $C ^ { d ( | \mathcal { F } | + | \mathcal { G } | ) }$· A fixed unit boxes in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d | \mathcal { F } | }$, so (9.110) follows.□

## 10. Preparations for the algorithm

From this section until Section 13, we will prove Proposition 9.7, the main goal of the third part of the paper. In this section, we make some preparations for the proof by restating the properties of the molecule M in Proposition 9.7 (originally stated in Definition 3.20) in a more convenient way for the algorithm.

Start from the initial links$\mathcal { L } ;$we shall replace it by some new initial link set$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$where each particle line belongs to at most two new initial links in${ \widetilde { \widehat { \cal L } } } .$This is because, see the proof of Proposition 12.17, for any initial link, we will gain a power of ε from the particle line in it that is cut$a f t e r$the other; then the condition for$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$ensures that the number of gains from this is comparable with the number of initial links.

Proposition 10.1. Recall the set$\mathcal { L }$of initial links (see Proposition 5.18), let the set of particle lines involved in$\mathcal { L }$be$H _ { 0 }$. Then we have

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\mathcal {L}} ^ {\varepsilon} \leq \sum_ {\widetilde {\mathcal {L}}} \mathbb {1} _ {\widetilde {\mathcal {L}}} ^ {\varepsilon +}.\tag{10.1}
$$

Here$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon }$is defined as in (5.72),$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$is a set of pairs$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$where$p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } \in H _ { 0 }$satisfying that each particle line $p \in H _ { 0 }$belongs to one$o r$two pairs in${ \widetilde { \mathcal { L } } } ,$and$\mathbb { I } _ { \widetilde { \mathcal { L } } } ^ { \varepsilon + }$is defined as

$$
\mathbb {1} _ {\widetilde {\mathcal {L}}} ^ {\varepsilon +} = \prod_ {(p _ {1}, p _ {2}) \in \widetilde {\mathcal {L}}} \mathbb {1} _ {e _ {1} \sim_ {\text {in}} p _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon +} \quad \text {and} \quad \mathbb {1} _ {e _ {1} \sim_ {\text {in}} p _ {2}} ^ {\varepsilon +} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \quad | x _ {p _ {1}} - x _ {p _ {2}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}, \\ \varepsilon^ {v} & \quad | x _ {p _ {1}} - x _ {p _ {2}} | \geq \varepsilon^ {1 - v}, \end{array} \right.\tag{10.2}
$$

Proof. For fixed values of$( x _ { p } ) _ { p \in H _ { 0 } }$, we only need to prove that there exists$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$such that$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon } ( x _ { p } ) \leq \mathbb { 1 } _ { \widetilde { r } } ^ { \varepsilon + } ( x _ { p } )$ Define a graph$\mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$which is a subgraph of${ \mathcal { L } } ,$such that$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } ) \ \in \ { \mathcal { L } } _ { 0 }$if and only if$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } ) \in \mathsf { \tilde { L } }$and $| x _ { p _ { 1 } } - x _ { p _ { 2 } } | \leq \varepsilon$. Clearly we may restrict to a single component of the forest$\mathcal { L }$(which is a tree), then in this component,$\mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$is obtained from L by deleting those edges$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$with$| x _ { p _ { 1 } } - x _ { p _ { 2 } } | \geq \varepsilon$. Let the number of deleted edges be$q ,$then$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon } ( x _ { p } ) = \varepsilon ^ { v q }$by definition. On the other hand,$\mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$has exactly$q + 1$connected components (as it is formed by deleting q edges from a tree), and for any$( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } )$that belong to the same component, we must have$| x _ { p _ { 1 } } - x _ { p _ { 2 } } | \leq \varepsilon | H _ { 0 } | \ll \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$by triangle inequality. Now we simply list all the particle lines in$H _ { 0 }$by enumerating each component of$\mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$one after another, and construct$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$by forming an edge between any two adjacent particle lines in the above list, then it is easy to see that$| x _ { p _ { 1 } } - x _ { p _ { 2 } } | \geq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$occurs at most q times (when entering new components), which implies$\mathbb { 1 } _ { \widetilde { \mathcal { L } } } ^ { \varepsilon + } ( x _ { p } ) \geq \varepsilon ^ { v q } = \mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathcal { L } } ^ { \varepsilon } ( x _ { p } )$, as desired. □

Remark 10.2. In view of Proposition 10.1, below we will replace$\mathcal { L }$by$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$in all instances, and refer to$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } }$ as the (new) initial links, and change Definition 9.4 etc. using these new initial links. Note that (i) the number of choices of$\widetilde { \mathcal { L } } \mathrm { \Phi } \left( \mathrm { i . e } \right.$. the number of terms in the summation (10.2)) is bounded by$( C | H _ { 0 } | ) !$. Since $| H _ { 0 } | \le \rho \le | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, this resulting combinatorial factor is bounded by$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$which can be absorbed by Proposition 7.2. (ii) The proof of Proposition 6.2 in Section 9 is not afected by these new initial links. For example, in Proposition 9.2 (3), we are only assuming the weaker assumption$| x - x ^ { \prime } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - v }$consistent with $\mathbb { I } _ { \widetilde { \mathcal { L } } } ^ { \varepsilon + }$, so any good molecule with respect to the new initial links still carries the same power gain as in (9.78).

Now we can state the main result of this section, namely Proposition 10.4 below.

Proposition 10.4. Let$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$as in Definition 3.20 (1) and$r ( \mathbb { M } ) = H$. Then we have the following:

(1) The total number of atoms and particle lines in M is bounded by$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$

(2) No two atoms can be connected by two diferent ov-segments.<sup>11</sup>

(3) Any cycle in a single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$must be formed by ov-segments connecting C-atoms in the same cluster. In particular, for any cycle in a single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and any O-atom in this cycle, the two bonds of the cycle at this O-atom must be serial. see Figure 18.

(4) For any cluster$\mathbb { Q }$in each layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, we have that$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } ) \leq \Gamma$(Definition 3.13). Recall that a cluster $\mathbb { Q }$or component is cyclic (or recollisional) if$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } ) > 0$, i.e. if it contains a cycle.

Properties (5)–(7) below correspond to the particle line sets$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$and$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$(Definition 3.18).

(5) Each particle line p must belong to some$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for some ℓ<sup>′</sup>. If p intersects$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(Definition 3.19), then$\pmb { p } \in p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$. If$\pmb { p }$contains an atom in both$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 2 } }$, then$\pmb { p } \in p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for all$\ell ^ { \prime } \in [ \ell _ { 1 } : \ell _ { 2 } ]$ (6) We have$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) = H$, and$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) = p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) \cap p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } )$for$1 \leq \ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell - 1$. Define also$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { 0 } ) = H _ { 0 }$

(7) For$1 \leq \ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell ,$each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$must intersect a particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$. Each particle line in $p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$is either connected to a particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, or belongs to$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$. Proof. We first prove (1)–(8), then prove the harder (9). The proof in the$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Delta _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$case is the same (since Definition 3.20 (1a)–(1d) are the same except that (1d) now requires$\ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell - 1 )$

Proof of (1)–(8). For (1): this is already proved in Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 7.2.

For (2): this follows from the correspondence between molecules and physical trajectories in Definition 3.8, and the fact that two (physical) particles in$\mathbb { R } ^ { d }$cannot collide/overlap and immediately collide/overlap again without other any other collision in between.

For (3): recall Definition 3.11. We know$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$can be constructed, starting from the C-molecule with only the clusters, by adding the O-atoms corresponding to the overlaps joining diferent clusters, according to cluster graph of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Since this cluster graph is a forest (Definition 3.20 (1c)), we know that the process of adding O-atoms will not generate new cycles in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, and will only insert O-atoms into edges of existing cycles (turning these edges into ov-segments). Therefore the first statement in (3) is true. The second statement follows from the first, as the O-atom must be an interior atom of an ov-segment connecting two C-atoms.

For (4): this is just Definition 3.20 (1a).

For (5): this follows directly from Definition 3.18.

For (6): this follows directly from Definition 3.18 (see also Definition 3.3) that$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) = r ( \mathbb { M } ) = H$, and $r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) = p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) \cap p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } )$

For (7): this is just Definition 3.20 (1b).

For (8): this directly follows from Proposition 10.1.

Proof of (9). Fix any$\pmb { p } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$. If p is connected to another particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$then we are done. If not, by Definition 3.20 (1d), there exists$p _ { 1 } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 } )$such that p is either equal to or connected to${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. We then replace p by${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$and$\ell ^ { \prime }$by$\ell ^ { \prime } - 1$and repeat the above discussion: either ${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$is connected to${ \pmb p } _ { 1 } \neq { \pmb p } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 } )$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - 1 }$, or we can find$\mathbf { \mathit { p } } _ { 2 }$, and so on.

In the end, either we reach$\pmb { p } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { 0 } ) = H _ { 0 }$, or we get$p _ { i } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i } )$for some$0 \leq i < \ell ^ { \prime }$, which is connected to${ \pmb p } _ { i } \neq { \pmb p } _ { i } ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i } )$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i }$. In the former case, either$\mathbf { \Delta } _ { \mathbf { \mathcal { p } } } = \mathbf { \Delta } _ { \mathbf { \mathcal { p } } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } }$or$\pmb { p }$is connected to$\pmb { p } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$via $\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] } ;$; by Proposition 10.4 (8), this$\pmb { p } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$is involved in an initial link, so p forms an initial link within$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$ by definition.

Now assume we get$\mathbf { \nabla } _ { \mathbf { p } _ { i } }$with$0 \leq i < \ell ^ { \prime }$as said above. By (7) we just proved (and note that$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i } ) \subseteq$ $p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i + 1 } ) )$, there exists$\pmb { p } _ { i - 1 } ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i + 1 } )$such that$\pmb { p } _ { i } ^ { \prime }$either equals or is connected to$\pmb { p } _ { i - 1 } ^ { \prime }$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - i + 1 }$. We then replace$\pmb { p } _ { i } ^ { \prime }$by$\pmb { p } _ { i - 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$\ell ^ { \prime } - i$by$\ell ^ { \prime } - i + 1$and repeat this process, and subsequently find$\pmb { p } _ { i - 2 } ^ { \prime } , \cdots , \pmb { p } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$ see Figure 19. Note that$p ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$

Now, if$\pmb { p } \neq \pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$, then we can transit from p to${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$and then$p _ { 2 } , \cdots , p _ { i }$in this order, and then transit to $\mathbf { \mathit { p } } _ { i } ,$and then transit to$\pmb { p } _ { i - 1 } ^ { \prime } , \cdots , \pmb { p } _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$in this order. In each transit step, the two particle lines involved are either equal or connected via bonds within a subset of$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] } ;$; putting together, we get that p and ${ \pmb p } \ne { \pmb p } ^ { \prime } \in r ( { \mathbb M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$are connected via$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$

If instead$\mathbf { \nabla } \mathbf { p } = \mathbf { \nabla } p ^ { \prime } .$, note that${ \mathbf { } } p _ { i } \neq { \mathbf { } } p _ { i } ^ { \prime } .$so we choose the smallest$1 \leq n \leq i$such that${ \pmb p } _ { n } \neq { \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$. In this case, we know that${ \pmb p } _ { n }$and${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$are both connected to$\pmb { p } _ { n - 1 }$via$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - n + 1 }$, so${ \pmb p } _ { n }$is also connected to${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$via $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - n + 1 }$(see Remark 10.5 below). Moreover${ \pmb p } _ { n }$is also connected to${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$via$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } - n ] }$, by transiting from${ \pmb p } _ { n }$ to$\left( \pmb { p } _ { n + 1 } , \cdots , \pmb { p } _ { i } \right)$in this order and then to$\left( \pmb { p } _ { i } ^ { \prime } , \pmb { p } _ { i - 1 } ^ { \prime } , \cdots , \pmb { p } _ { n } ^ { \prime } \right)$in this order similar to the above paragraph. Then, by putting together a chain of bonds in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } - n + 1 }$connecting${ \pmb p } _ { n }$to${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$, another chain of bonds in $\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } - n ] }$connecting${ \pmb p } _ { n }$to${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$, and possibly a chain of bonds within the particle line${ \pmb p } _ { n }$and another chain of bonds within the particle line${ \pmb p } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$, we obtain a cycle in$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } - n + 1 ] } \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$. Since$\pmb { p }$is connected to${ \pmb p } _ { n }$(and thus to this cycle) via$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$by transiting from$\pmb { p }$to$p _ { 1 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot p _ { n }$in this order similar to the above paragraph, we conclude that$\pmb { p }$is connected to cycle within$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$. This completes the proof.□

To end this section, we record some intuitive facts about molecules, particle lines and cuttings, which will be used frequently in the algorithm below.

Remark 10.5. Let A be a layer interval$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { 1 } : \ell _ { 2 } ] }$(Definition 10.3), or any union of connected components of a layer interval, or the same for thin layers (defined in Definition 12.8 below). It is easy to see that: for any atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \in A$that belong to the same particle line, and any atom m in the same particle line between n and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$, we must have${ \mathfrak { m } } \in A$. This implies that (i) any particle line$\pmb { p }$can intersect at most one component of A, and (ii) if two particle lines$\mathbf { \boldsymbol { p } } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { \boldsymbol { p } } _ { 2 }$are both connected to a particle line p via A (Definition 3.19), then ${ \pmb p } _ { 1 }$and$\mathbf { \mathit { p } } _ { 2 }$are also connected via A. This is used in the proof of Proposition 10.4 (9) above; see Figure 19.

Remark 10.6. The following fact will be convenient to note: suppose we cut$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$as$f r e e ,$, then this may divide the remaining set$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$into connected components; however, any$f u l l$component of$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$must also be a full component of M before cutting A as free (in other words, any newly created connected component must have at least one fixed end). This is because, when any bond or ov-segment is broken in cutting A as free, we get a fixed end at every atom in this ov-segment that belongs to$\mathbb { M } \backslash A ,$, see Remark 8.6.

Remark 10.7. In the algorithm below, we usually adopt the following convention: once we cut out any elementary molecule$S ,$or cut out any subset S (as free or as fixed) and subsequently cut it into elementary molecules, we will ignore this S for the rest of the cutting sequence and consider the remaining molecule $\mathbb { M } \backslash S$only. For example, when we say “keep cutting deg 2 atoms as free until there is no more deg 2 atom”, we always mean there is no more deg 2 atom in the remaining molecule.

## 11. Main thread of the algorithm

We now start the proof of Proposition 9.7. Most of the proof below will focus on the case$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ;$the case$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { F } _ { \Delta _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$is left to the end of Section 13.5, and will only take two paragraphs. In this section, we first discuss a simplified setting which contains most of the main ideas.

11.1. Toy models. To prove Proposition 9.7, we need to construct an operation sequence (with cutting, deleting and splitting). This will be done using a number of cutting algorithms, which will be presented in Sections 12–13.

The full cutting algorithms are quite complicated; however, there is a much simpler main thread, and many of the complications actually come from the additional structures and conditions (“accessories”) that have to be added to this main thread. In this section, we present the proof in a simplified scenario, which basically isolates this main thread. The accessories needed in full generality will be discussed in Section 11.7.

Throughout this section, we will make the following two simplifications (and more later):

(1) M has no O-atoms, all {33} molecules are good, and$H _ { 0 } = \varnothing$(see Proposition 10.4 (6));

(2) Each layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$of M is a forest.

Here, regarding (1), recall that {33} molecules are good provided certain non-degeneracy conditions are met (which is diferent for {33A} and {33B} molecules, see (9.47)–(9.48) in Definition 9.4). As such, simplification (1) allows us to ignore any O-atoms, degeneracies and initial (time$t = 0 )$cumulants, and (2) allows us to ignore any cycles (or “recollisions”) happening within each layer.

Given a molecule M satisfying Proposition 10.4 and (1)–(2), the goal of this section is to construct a cutting sequence that cuts M into elementary molecules, such that (recall$v = 3 ^ { - d - 1 } )$)

$$
(v / 2) \cdot \# _ {\{3 3 \}} - d \cdot \# _ {\{4 \}} \geq c \cdot \rho ,\tag{11.1}
$$

where$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} }$is the number of {33} molecules etc., c is a positive constant and$\rho$is in Definition 7.1 (the splitting and deletion of O-atoms is not needed in this simplified model; also note that there cannot be any empty end if$H _ { 0 } = \varnothing$, which easily follows from Proposition 10.4 (9)).

In Sections 11.2–11.5, we will consider a further simplified case, when M contains only two layers (for treatment of multi-layer case, see Section 11.6). We make the following definition:

Definition 11.1. We say M is a 2-layer model, if it satisfies (1)–(2), and that

(3) M can be written as$\mathbb { M } = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, such that no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is parent of an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$;

(4) Each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a tree, has no fixed end, and the number of bonds connecting$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ is at least$\rho .$

Note that in practice, the$\rho$in (4) may be replaced by some diferent quantity, but they will always be comparable, so this will not afect the proof.

In our proof, the 2-layer model in Definition 11.1 will be further divided into 3 cases, corresponding to toy models I–III defined below. This classification is based on the following two considerations:

(1) Consider the set of atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that are adjacent to two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$by two bonds. Is this set big or small relative to$\rho ?$

The pink dots represent patterns that can be repeated.

(2) Consider all the atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that are adjacent to at least one atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$by at least one bond. Are they all connected to each other, or are they separated by other atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } ?$

The reason for considering these two questions will be clear later. For convenience, in this section we will refer to the atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that are adjacent to two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as 2-connections, and denote their number by$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } }$. We also define the set of atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that are adjacent to at least one atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$by X (note that$| X | \gtrsim \rho )$, and define the number of connected components of X (with X viewed by itself, without passing through atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash X )$by$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$. We now define a 2-layer molecule to be:

• Toy model I: if$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$and$X = \mathbb { M } _ { U }$. This case involves the core arguments in our algorithm in its simplest form, and will be proved in Section 11.2.

• Toy model I plus: if$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \ll | X |$(no 2-connections, X has few components). This is an extension of the toy model I, and can be treated in similar manners, in Section 11.3. Here we need to introduce the new idea of UP algorithm, which will play an important role in the later proofs.

• Toy model$I I \colon \mathrm { i f } \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \gtrsim | X |$(no 2-connections, X has many components). This requires a diferent argument, which involves making a clever choice in the UP algorithm introduced above, see Section 11.4.

• Toy model III: if$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \gtrsim | X |$(many 2-connections). This relies on a simpler argument, which again involves making suitable choices in the UP algorithm, see Section 11.5.

See Figure 20 for examples of toy models I–III (we distinguish toy models I and I plus only for convenience of exposition). Also the case when$0 < \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \ll | X |$, which is missing in the toy models, can be treated similarly to toy models I–II but with an extra step of removing 2-connections, see Section 11.7.4.

Once all the toy models (and hence the 2-layer model) have been addressed in Sections 11.2–11.5, we can then treat the multi-layer case in Section 11.6. This relies on the process of layer selection, which efectively reduces any multi-layer M to (basically) a 2-layer model, for which the proofs in Sections 11.2–11.5 apply.

Finally, in Section 11.7 we discuss the simplifications made in (1)–(4) above compared to the full generality case, as well as the corresponding accessories (additions, extra conditions and proofs) that are needed to treat the full generality setting.

Before proceeding, we make one remark about the presentation in this section and in Sections 12–13: in this section, the cases are arranged for exposition purposes, for example we present the 2-layer model before layer selection, and present toy models I and I plus before the other toy models, in order to showcase the core ideas of our proof as early as possible. However, in Sections 12–13 we need to present the materials in logical order, so we need to introduce layer selection (Section 12.4) before the toy models (Section 13), and toy model III (Definition 13.1–Proposition 13.2) before toy model I plus (Definition 13.12–Proposition 13.13), etc.

To make the proof easier to read, each time we discuss any argument in Sections 12–13 that has a counterpart in this section, we will explicitly point out which argument in this section does it correspond to. See Table 1 for a summary of the toy models and layer selection, and where each of them occurs in Sections 12–13. Also, in Table 2 we list the simplifications made in Definition 11.1, the corresponding accessories needed in the general setting, and where each of them occurs in Sections 12–13.

11.2. Toy model I. In this subsection we consider the following (first) toy model:

Definition 11.2. We say M is a toy model I, if it is a 2-layer model as in Definition 11.1, and that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has exactly one bond connecting to an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \ ( { \mathrm { i . e . } } \ \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$and$X = \mathbb { M } _ { U } )$).

Definition 11.3. Let$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$be part of the 2-layer model as in Definition 11.1 (or any resulting molecule after an operation sequence). We define$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$to be proper, if it does not contain deg 1 or 2 atoms, does not contain two adjacent deg 3 atoms, and does not contain two deg 3 atoms which are both adjacent to the same deg 4 atom, see Figure 21.

![](images/page_101_image_3.jpg)

Figure 21. Examples of {33} and {343} molecules (left), and proper molecules (right, see Definition 11.3). Note these notions are applied to$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ,$in which the top/bottom distinction is less important, hence we draw an equivalent simplified picture below, with no distinction of top/bottom, and with the deg (i.e. degree) of each atom indicated. Similar simplified illustrations will occur a few times below.

If M is a toy model I, we define the following algorithm applied to it:

Definition 11.4 (algorithm for toy model I). Let M be a toy model I. We define the following cutting sequence. For an example see Figure 22:

(1) If not all atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut, then choose a lowest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$that has not been cut (i.e. either n has not child in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$or all its children in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut).

(2) If n is adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { m } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$which has deg 3, then cut {n, m} as free and cut m as free from {n, m} if n has deg$4 ;$otherwise just cut n as free.

(3) If$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$contains two adjacent deg 3 atoms (say r and$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } )$, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } \}$as free; repeat until$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no adjacent deg 3 atoms.

(4) If$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$contains two degree 3 atoms (say r and$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } )$both adjacent to the same deg 4 atom (say$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } )$ then cut$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$as free and cut r as free from$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$; then go to$( 3 )  { - } ( 4 )$and repeat, until$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ becomes proper (Definition 11.3).

(5) Go to (1) and choose the next lowest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$that has not been cut, and so on.

(6) Suppose all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut. If$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is proper, then cut any deg 3 atom; if not, then go to$( 3 )  { - } ( 4 )$and repeat to remove them, and next cut any deg 3 atom, and so on.

Remark 11.5. In Definition 11.4, we are essentially applying a “naive” algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$where we simply cut a lowest atom each time, and a “greedy” algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$where we exploit a {33} molecule (or what we call a {343} molecule<sup>12</sup> where two deg 3 atoms are adjacent to the same deg 4 atom). As mentioned above, this is the core idea of our proof, in its bare simplest form. It is a simple special case of the MAINUD algorithm, which corresponds to the toy model I plus in Section 11.3.

Before stating the main result for the algorithm in Definition 11.2, we first prove a useful lemma that will be applied frequently below, see Figure 23.

Lemma 11.6. Suppose M is a forest and we cut a connected subset$S \subseteq \mathbb { M }$as free (for example, when S contains a single atom, or 2 atoms connected by a bond, or 3 atoms connected by 2 bonds, etc.). Then, for each atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash S$that is connected to an atom in S by a (pre-cutting) bond e, the post-cutting molecule $\mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$has exactly one component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } \ni { \mathfrak { q } } ,$which is in bijection with q (and q is the unique atom in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$that is adjacent to S pre-cutting, via the bond e). When viewed in$X _ { q } ,$the bond e is viewed as a free end at q before cutting, and is turned into a fixed end after cutting.

![](images/page_103_image_0.jpg)

Figure 23. An illustration of Lemma 11.6. Here$S$is a connected subset, and there are bijections between$\mathfrak { q }$and$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$, where${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$is connected to$S$by a bond$e ,$and$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$is the component containing q after cutting$S$as free. When viewed in$X _ { q } ,$the operation of cutting$S$as free creates exactly one fixed end in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$. All these crucially depend on the fact that$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$have no cycles.

Proof. This follows from the property of forests. In fact, any$\mathfrak { q } _ { 1 }$and$\mathfrak { q } _ { 2 }$(with corresponding bonds$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 2 } )$ must belong to diferent components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$after cutting$S ;$if not, then (pre-cutting) they can be connected by a path involving atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$, but they can also be connected by a path with all intermediate atoms being in S (using the bonds$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 2 }$and the connectivity of S by itself), which produces a cycle and contradicts the forest assumption. Thus, for each q we get a unique post-cutting component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$, such that e is the only pre-cutting bond between$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$and S. Clearly, when viewed in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$, the efect of cutting S as free is equivalent to turning one and only one free end at q (the one corresponding to$e )$into a fixed end. □

Proposition 11.7. Let M be a toy model I, and we apply the algorithm defined in Definition 11.4. Then in this process we only obtain elementary molecules, and we have

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} = 1, \qquad \# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq (| \mathbb {M} _ {U} | - 1) / 5.\tag{11.2}
$$

Since$\left| \mathbb { M } _ { U } \right| = \left| X \right| \gtrsim \rho \gg 1$, this clearly implies (11.1).

Proof. Recall Definition 11.4 (1)–(6). We divide the proof into 4 parts.

Proof part 1. We first prove that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is contained in an elementary molecule (after cutting). By the choices we make in (1) and (5) in Definition 11.4, we know that for each${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, at the time it is cut, it must be a lowest atom that still remains in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } ;$thus no child of it still remains in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$ so cutting n will not introduce any top fixed end in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(and neither does cutting anything in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$. This means that$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$will not contain any top fixed end throughout the process. Since each${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$is either cut by itself (when we cut {n} as free in Definition 11.4 (2)) or belongs to a {33} molecule (when we cut {n, m} as free in Definition 11.4 (2)), it is clear by definition of elementary molecules that n always belongs to an elementary molecule.

Proof part 2. We next prove that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is contained in an elementary molecule. Note that $\mathbb { M } _ { D }$initially is a tree, and will remain a forest in the whole cutting process (cutting an atom will not create any cycle, but may cause a tree to become a disconnected forest). Now consider each step in Definition 11.4 (2) involving${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, at which timeM$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$must be proper by the construction of our algorithm. Consider the possible efect of this step on$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(we may assume that n is connected to one atom m$\in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$by a bond, otherwise cutting n will have no efect on$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, see Figure 24:

(a) If we cut n as free (which means m has deg 4), then when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, this step simply turns one and only one free end at${ \mathfrak { m } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$into a fixed end, turning m from deg 4 to deg 3.

(b) If we cut$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { m } \}$as free (which means m has deg 3), then when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, this step simply cuts m, which has deg 3, as free from$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Here in (a), we note that m must have deg 4 before cutting n (otherwise m must have deg 3 because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is proper, in which case we will cut {n, m} by Definition 11.4 (2)); also when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, the bond between n and m is initially viewed as a free end at m, and is then turned into a fixed end after cutting n as free, turning m from deg 4 to deg 3. Likewise m must have deg 3 in (b), and when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, cutting {n, m} as free is equivalent to cutting {m} as free because n has no other bonds connecting to other atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Lemma 11.8. Suppose$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is proper at some point of the algorithm, and becomes non-proper after either (a) or (b). Then,$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$will once more become proper after applying Definition 11.4 (3)–(4), via cuttings of {33} and {343} molecules only (with each {343} molecule further cut into a {3} and a {33} molecule), and without seeing any deg 2 atom, see Figure 25 for an illustration.

Proof. Note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is always a forest, so we can apply Lemma 11.6. Note that right before performing (b) at a deg 3 atom m, any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$adjacent to m must have deg 4 (because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is proper). Then by Lemma 11.6,$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$will break into at most 2 components after performing (b), and the efect of (b) when viewed in each component is equivalent to (a). Therefore, we only need to prove Lemma 11.8 for (a).

Assume now$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes non-proper, say a {33} molecule forms, after (a). Let this molecule be$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } \}$ where$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$has deg 3 before (a), while r has deg 4 before (a) and is turned into deg 3 after (a). Then, before (a), any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$adjacent to r or$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$must have deg 4 (see Figure 26) because otherwise we either have two adjacent deg 3 atoms before (a), or have two deg 3 atoms adjacent to the same deg 4 atom before (a), contradicting properness. Therefore, by Lemma 11.6, we see that cutting the {33} molecule breaks$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into at most 4 components, and the efect of this cutting when viewed in each component is again equivalent to (a). We then induct on the size of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$and apply induction hypothesis to each of these components, to conclude the proof.

Finally, assume$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes non-proper, but with no {33} molecule forming, after (a). In this case there must be a {343} molecule forming, say$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$, where$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$and${ \mathfrak { r } } ^ { \prime \prime }$respectively have deg 4 and 3 before$\mathrm { ( a ) }$ and r has deg 4 before$\mathrm { ( a ) }$and is turned into deg 3 after (a). Then, before$( a )$, any atom adjacent to$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$or ${ \mathfrak { r } } ^ { \prime \prime }$must have deg$\it 4$(see Figure 26) for the same reason as above thanks to properness. Moreover, before (a), any atom adjacent to r must also have deg 4, because otherwise we would get a {33} molecule after (a), contradicting our assumption. Therefore, by Lemma 11.6, we see that cutting the {343} molecule breaks$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ into at most 6 components, and the efect of this cutting when viewed in each component is again equivalent to (a). We then conclude the proof by the same induction as above. This proves Lemma 11.8.□

Proof part 3. With Parts 1 and 2 of the proof, we now know that every resulting molecule is elementary; it sufices to calculate$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$and$\# \{ 3 3 \}$. We first show that$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$. Since the first atom cut in Definition 11.4 (2) must have deg$^ { 4 , }$it sufices to show that$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1$. Therefore, if n has any child in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$at all before any cutting, then it cannot have deg 4 when it is cut.

On the other hand, before any cutting,$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$can have at most one atom without child in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(see Figure 27); if not, say there exist two such atoms n and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$, then consider a path$( \mathfrak { n } = \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } = \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$between n and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$within$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(since$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is a tree). Then${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$must be parent of n as n has no child in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and then${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$ must be parent of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$as${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$has a child${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$and another child in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$by Definition 11.2, and so on. In the end${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } = { \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$must be parent of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j - 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, which contradicts the assumption on${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$. This proves$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$

\lambda := \# _ {\deg 3} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp}},

11.3. Toy model I plus. In this subsection we extend the toy model I to allow more general connections between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Definition 11.9. We say M is a toy model I plus, if it is a 2-layer model as in Definition 11.1, and each atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$has at most one bond connecting to an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(i.e.$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0 )$, and the number of connected components of X satisfies

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (X)} \ll | X |,\tag{11.5}
$$

where X is defined at the beginning of this note. Here, if two atoms in X can only be connected via atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash X$, then they belong to diferent components of X.

Let us explain the intuition behind Definition 11.9, in particular the role of (11.5). In the case of toy model I, we have$X = \mathbb { M } _ { U }$which is connected, hence$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } = 1$. Moreover, as in Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.7, we see that$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has at most one lowest atom (i.e. atom without child in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } ;$in fact it is not hard to see that$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$must have an “upside down binary tree” shape). This latter fact allows us to apply a “naive” strategy in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$where we always cut the lowest remaining atom (and avoid any top fixed ends), without producing too many$\{ \mathcal { } \}$atoms.

In the current case,$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$may have many lowest atoms, so we cannot always choose and cut a lowest remaining atom. Instead, we improve the strategy by choosing a lowest remaining deg 3 atom n (here we do not consider deg 2 atoms, as they will always be lowest in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and always have to be cut at top priority). Now cutting n may create top fixed ends, but only at descendants of n (which all have deg 4 when n is chosen). As such, we need to subsequently cut all descendants of n after cutting n. This leads to the idea of the UP algorithm, see Definition 11.10 below, which is another basic ingredient in our proof.

Note, however, that this UP algorithm cannot be simply combined with the “greedy” algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ as in Definition 11.4, because n may have (deg 4) descendants in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and this naive attempt may break the key monotonicity property (see Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 11.14) and lead to non-elementary molecules. As such, we should only apply UP at places in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$which will not afect$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ,$, i.e. in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash X$ Within X we still apply the naive strategy, which may lead to {4} molecules due to X.

We can then see the role of (11.5) and the dichotomy concerning$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } ;$in fact, same as in Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.7, each component of X can have at most one lowest atom. In the naive strategy, this leads to {4} molecules whose number is comparable to$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$. Under the assumption (11.5), this is negeligible compared to the number of good {33} molecules, which will be comparable to |X| (i.e. the number of bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$

With the above intuition, we start by defining the UP algorithm in the toy model case. For the full version in the real problem, see Definition 12.1.

Definition 11.10 (The UP algorithm, toy model case). Let M be any molecule which does not have top fixed end. Define the following cutting sequence. For an example see Figure 28:

![](images/page_107_image_6.jpg)

Figure 28. The UP algorithm (Definition 11.10). As in the above figures, the red box indicates the atom(s) to be cut next, the green box indicates the atom(s) in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(see Definition 11.10 (2)), which will be cut after cutting n. Note also when n and its parent${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { + }$(or child $\mathfrak { n } ^ { - } )$form a {33} molecule, we should cut them together; see Definition 11.10 (3).

(1) If M has a deg 2 atom, then cut it as free. Repeat until M does not have deg 2 atoms.

(2) Choose a lowest deg 3 atom n that has not bee cut (or a lowest atom if M has no deg 3 atoms). Let $S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n. This n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is fixed until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a highest atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If m has deg 3 and has a parent${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$or child m<sup>−</sup> that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut, then go to (1)–(2) and choose the next n, and so on.

Remark 11.11. The UP algorithm is a combination of a “global low-to-high” (where each time we select the lowest remaining deg 3 atom in Definition 11.10 (2)) and “local high-to-low” procedure (where each time we cut the highest remaining atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$in Definition 11.10 (3)). This leads to a key monotonicity property, see Proposition 11.12.

The step (3) in Definition 11.10 may seem complicated, we explain it as follows: let m be the highest remaining atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$, the simple option is to just cut m as free. However, in the case described in Definition 11.10 (3), the${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \pm }$will become deg 2 once m is cut as free; moreover${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { - } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$will be a highest remaining atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$, and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + } \not \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$will occur as a deg 2 atom in Definition 11.10 (1) once all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut. As such, this deg 2 atom${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \pm }$have to be cut at top priority, so instead of cutting {m} we can combine this with the cutting of${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \pm }$, which also forms a good {33} molecule$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$. This then leads to the step (3) in Definition 11.10.

We next prove a key monotonicity property of the UP algorithm and a suficient condition for it to produce at least one {33} molecule (in fact {33A} molecule). See Proposition 12.2 for the full version.

Proposition 11.12. Let M be as in Definition 11.10 and connected (otherwise consider each component of M). Then after applying algorithm UP to M (and same for DOWN):

(1) We have the following monotonicity property, which we refer to as (MONO-toy): at any time, any atom in$( \mathbb { M } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has no top fixed end, and any atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has no bottom fixed end. In particular, applying UP only produces elementary molecules.

(2) We have$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1$, and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$if and only if M is full.

In (3) below we assume M has no deg 2 atoms.

(3) If M contains a cycle or contains at least two deg 3 atoms, then$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq 1$. If not (i.e. M is a tree and contains at most one deg 3 atom), then all the elementary molecules are {3} molecules with at most one exception of {4} molecule.

Proof. Proof of (1). We first prove (MONO-toy), which implies all components are elementary (since each atom is either cut by itself or belongs to a {33} molecule, due to (1)–(3) in Definition 11.10). Initially there is no$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and M has no top fixed end by assumption, so it sufices to prove that (MONO-toy) is perserved. First, any deg 2 atom n cut in Definition 11.10 (1) must have two bottom fixed ends by (MONO-toy), so it has no child remaining when it is cut, thus cutting it will not create any top fixed end.

Now let n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be as in Definition 11.10 (2), and m be a highest remaining atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$as in Definition 11.10 (3). When n is chosen in Definition 11.10 (2), all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$must have deg 4 by construction, and thus have no bottom fixed end. Consider the operation of cutting m as free in Definition 11.10 (3). We then know that that this cutting does not create any bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(as m is highest), and does not create any top fixed end in$( \mathbb { M } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(as any child of m must belong to$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$, see Figure 29). The same holds for the operation of cutting$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$, because this is equivalent to cutting {m} and then cutting a deg 2 atom (either${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + } \not \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$with two bottom fixed ends or${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { - } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$with two top fixed ends). This proves that (MONO-toy) is perserved, as desired.

Proof of (2). Note that after the first cutting, M will always contain an atom that is not deg 4 (cf. Remark 10.6). By construction, this means that the n chosen in Definition 11.10 (2) will always be deg 3; moreover, any m$\in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$that is cut in Definition 11.10 (3) also cannot be deg 4, because m has a parent in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$which must have been cut before m thanks to the highest assumption of m. Thus only the first atom can produce a possible {4} molecule, so$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1 \#$; moreover$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$if and only if the first atom cut has deg 4, i.e. when M is full.

Proof of (3). Suppose M has no deg 2 atom, we first prove that either$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq 1$, or all resulting molecules are {4} and {3} (with$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1 )$). If not, then we must have a {2} molecule. Consider the first atom m that has deg 2 when we cut it, and consider the cutting operation that turns m into deg 2, which must be cutting some deg 3 atom p as free (this p cannot have deg 4, because a degree 4 atom is cut only when no degree 3 atoms are present, and in this case cutting a degree 4 atom cannot produce a degree 2 atom). This cutting creates a fixed end at m, so this p must be a parent or child of m; moreover this m and this p must both be deg 3 at the time of cutting p, but this violates Definition 11.10 (3).

![](images/page_109_image_0.jpg)

Figure 29. Illustration of the (MONO-toy) property of the UP algorithm (Proposition 11.12). Left: when we choose n in Definition 11.10 (2), there is no top fixed end outside $S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$and no fixed end at all in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(i.e. all deg 4). Right: when we cut a highest remaining atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$, we only get top fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and bottom fixed end outside$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$

Finally we prove$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } = 0$if and only if M is a tree and has at most one deg 3 atom. For this, consider the increment of the quantity$\sigma : = \# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } } - 3 \# _ { \mathrm { a t o m } }$, where$\# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } }$is the number of bonds plus the number of free ends (not counting fixed ends) and$\# _ { \mathrm { a t o m } }$is the number of remaining atoms. It is easy to see that cutting each {2}, {3}, {33} and {4} molecule increases σ by 1, 0, 1 and −1 respectively. Since finally$\sigma = 0$ we see that$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } - ( \# _ { \{ 2 \} } + \# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } ) = \sigma _ { \mathrm { i n i t } }$(initial value of σ).

Note that initially$\# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } } = \# \mathrm { d e g } - \# \mathrm { b o n d }$where$\# \mathrm { d e g }$is the total degree of all atoms (not counting fixed ends) and$\# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } }$is the number of bonds (because each bond contributes twice to the degrees), so $\sigma _ { \mathrm { i n i t } } = ( | \mathbb { M } | - \# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } } ) - | \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } |$where$\left| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right|$is the number of (initially) deg 3 atoms in M. Moreover by connectedness we have$\# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } } \geq | \mathbb { M } | - 1$with equality if and only if M is a tree, and note also$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ (and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$if and only if$| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | = 0$by the same proof in Part 2), it is then easy to see that #$\mathbf { \partial } _ { \{ 2 \} } + \# \mathbf { \partial } _ { \{ 3 3 \} } = 0$ if and only if M is a tree and$| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | \le 1$. This completes the proof.□

Now we can define the algorithm for toy model I plus. As described in the above heuristics, this features a naive algorithm (always cutting the lowest) in X, an UP algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash X$, and a greedy algorithm in M . Up to some simplifications, this is just the MAINUD algorithm, which is the main algorithm in Section 13, see Definition 13.12. Note also that the part of Definition 11.13 involving$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is exactly the same as Definition 11.4; the only diference occurs in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$

Definition 11.13 (Algorithm for toy model I plus). Let M be a toy model I plus with X be defined in the beginning of this note (this X is fixed throughout the algorithm). We define the following cutting sequence. For an example see Figures 30–31:

(1) If$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has a deg 2 atom, then cut it as free. Repeat until$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$does not have deg 2 atoms.

(2) Consider the set of all (remaining) atoms that either belong to X, or has deg 3; choose n to be a lowest atom in this set (if this set is empty then choose n to be any lowest atom). Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and fix n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$until the end of (6).

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a highest atom p in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If p is adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$which has deg 3, then cut$\{ { \mathfrak { p } } , { \mathfrak { q } } \}$as free and cut q as free from {p, q} if p has deg $4 ;$otherwise just cut p as free.

(4) If$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes non-proper, then perform the same steps$( 3 )  { - } ( 4 )$in Definition 11.4 until it becomes proper again. Then go to (3) and repeat, until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(5) When all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut, go to (1)–(2) and choose the next n, and so on.

(6) When all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut, perform the same step (6) in Definition 11.4 to finish of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Here, the next atom n we choose is not the unique deg 3 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, but rather the atom in X below${ \mathrm { i t } } ,$see Definition 11.13 (2). This leads to another {4} loss, but the total loss is bounded by$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } = 2$. In the end, we subsequently cut two deg 2 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and two deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, to conclude.

Proposition 11.14. Let M be a toy model I plus, and we apply the algorithm defined in Definition 11.13. Then in this process we only obtain elementary molecules, and we have

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} \leq \# _ {\operatorname{comp} (X)}, \quad \# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq (| X | - 1) / 5 - \# _ {\operatorname{comp} (X)}.\tag{11.6}
$$

Since$| X | \gtrsim \rho \gg 1$and using (11.5), this clearly implies (11.1).

Proof. We divide the proof into 4 parts just as Proposition 11.7.

Proof part 1. We show that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is contained in an elementary molecule. As in Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 11.12, this follows from the same (MONO-toy) property but for$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$only: any atom in$( \mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has no top fixed end, and any atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has no bottom fixed end.

To prove the monotonicity property, we first note that, for any n chosen in Definition 11.13 (2) and at the time it is chosen, each atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has deg 4 and thus has no bottom fixed end. Then consider the process of cutting in Definition 11.13 (3) and below, see Figure 32. Following exactly Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 11.12, we see that cutting any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$in this process does not create any top fixed end in$( \mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$or any bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$; moreover, for the cutting of any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$in this process (such as the one in Definition 11.13 (4)), it only creates bottom fixed ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and only at atoms in$( \mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$. This is because$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$contains no atom in X by construction, and thus has no bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, hence no fixed end can be created at any atom in this set when cutting anything in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ This proves (MONO-toy) for$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$

![](images/page_112_image_1.jpg)

This is essentially the same as the right half of Figure 29, except the green bonds connecting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$to atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(those atoms must be in X). By our choice,$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$is disjoint with$X ,$, so none of these bonds involve any atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(once n has been cut). Thus, if we do any cutting in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(as in Definition 11.13 (4)), this only creates bottom ends outside$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$, hence preserving the monotonicity property in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$

Proof part 2. We show that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is contained in an elementary molecule. Since the part of Definition 11.13 involving$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is exactly the same as Definition 11.4, this part is also exactly the same as Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 11.7.

Proof part 3. We show that #$\{ 4 \} \le \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$. Same as Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 11.12, we see that any${ \mathfrak { p } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$in Definition 11.13 (3) cannot have deg 4 when it is cut. Therefore, the only possible {4} atoms must come from those n chosen in Definition 11.13 (2). By our choice in Definition 11.13 (2), such n must belong to X and must be lowest atoms in X, i.e. it belongs to X but does not have any child in X before any cutting.

Now we claim that any two lowest atoms in X must belong to diferent components of X (see Figure 27). If not, say n and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$are connected by a path$( \mathfrak { n } = \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } = \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$in X, then arguing as Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.7 and noticing that each atom in X has a child in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, we deduce that each${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i }$must be parent of$\mathfrak { n } _ { i - 1 }$which then leads to contradiction with properties of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } = { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$. We then conclude that the number of lowest atoms in X does not exceed$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$, hence$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$

Proof part 4. Finally we show that$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq ( | X | - 1 ) / 5 - \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$. Since the part of Definition 11.13 involving$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is exactly the same as Definition 11.4, this part is essentially the same as Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 11.7. There is only one diference: in the current case, each step of cutting {p, q} as free in Definition 11.13 (3) (which corresponds to the operation (b) in Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 11.7 when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$may produce two {3} molecules instead of one {33} molecule, but this only happens when<sup>13</sup> p has deg 4, and the number of such exceptions is bounded by$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) }$following Part 3 above. Therefore, instead of (11.3) we have

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \# _ {(b)} + \# _ {\mathrm{cut} \{3 3 \}} + \# _ {\mathrm{cut} \{3 4 3 \}} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (X)},\tag{11.7}
$$

and the same proof then yields that, instead of$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq ( | X | - 1 ) / 5$as in (11.2), we now have$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq$ $( | X | - 1 ) / 5 - \# \mathrm { c o m p } ( X )$. This completes the proof.□
