11.4. Toy model II. In this subsection we introduce the toy model II, which is opposite to toy model I plus via the dichotomy, where we assume$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \gtrsim | X |$instead of$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } \ll | X |$in Definition 11.9.

Definition 11.15. We say M is a toy model II, if it satisfies all the assumptions in Definition 11.9 for toy model I plus with the same notations, except that (11.5) is replaced by$| X | \ge 2$and

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (X)} \gtrsim | X |.\tag{11.8}
$$

Let us explain the strategy for toy model II, which will be completely diferent from toy models I and I plus. Here we will not gain from the greedy algorithm in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ;$instead we first cut all of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free without exploiting any gain, and then gain from$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$under the assumption (11.8). Note that, after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free, there will not be any deg 2 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and the deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are exactly those in X.

The intuition is that, due to the lower bound of the number of components if X given by (11.8), the deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are now separated by deg 4 atoms. Essentially, we expect that for such molecules, we can design a cutting algorithm with minimal loss caused {4} molecules, such that each connected component of the set of deg 3 atoms provides a good {33} molecule. In fact, this can be achieved by a clever choice in the UP algorithm.

We next introduce the main algorithm in this case (together with an auxiliary lemma needed in this algorithm). Up to simplifications, this is just the 3COMPUP algorithm in Definition 13.6.

Lemma 11.16. Suppose M is a molecule that is a tree, contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms and has no top fixed end. Let the set of deg 3 atoms in M be${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$with$| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | \geq 2$. Define a set$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$to be no-bottom if any child of any atom in A must also be in A (see Figure 33). Then, there always exists a connected, no-bottom subset$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$with$\left| A \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| = 2$

![](images/page_113_chart_7.jpg)

Figure 33. An example of connected, no-bottom sets in Lemma 11.16; this one is a union of two intersecting descendant sets$S _ { \mathfrak { m } }$and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. In general each such set is a union of descendant sets$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$with n forming a connected set; see the proof of Lemma 11.16.

Proof. For any${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n (including n itself), then it is always connected and no-bottom. If there exists n such that$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| \geq 2$, then choose a lowest such n. Since n has no top fixed end, we know that either (i) n has one child n , or (ii) n has deg 4 and has two children${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$. In either case, by assumption we have$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| \leq 1$for each j, which then implies$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| \le 2$because $S _ { \mathfrak { n } } = ( \cup _ { j } S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ) \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$. This implies$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| = 2 .$, as desired.

Now assume$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| \le 1$for each${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$. If$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| = 1$, there is a unique${ \mathfrak { p } } = { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ) \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap { \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 } ;$; now consider all atom pairs$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$such that p(n) and${ \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } )$both exist and are diferent (which exist because$\left| { \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 } \right| \geq$ 2), and one such pair$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$that are connected by a shortest path in M. Let this path be$\left( \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \mathfrak { n } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } = \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \right)$ then for each$0 \textless i \textless j$we must have either$S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } = \emptyset$or${ \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ) = { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } )$(otherwise the pair$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } _ { i } )$ corresponds to a shorter path, contradiction). Now let$A = \cup _ { i = 0 } ^ { j } S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } }$, it is clear that A is connected, nobottom and$A \cap \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } = \{ { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ) , { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ) \}$, as desired.□

Definition 11.17 (The 3COMPUP algorithm, toy model case). Let M be a molecule that is a tree, contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms and has no top fixed end. Let the set of deg 3 atoms in M be${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$with $\left| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right| \geq 2$. Define the following cutting sequence. For an example see Figure 34:

![](images/page_114_image_1.jpg)

Figure 34. Algorithm for toy model II, applied to the example in Figure 20. Here we first cut all of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free. Then, each time we choose a connected, no-bottom subset A that contains exactly two deg 3 atoms, see Definition 11.17 ((1)). We then apply UP to cut all atoms in A (cf. Figure 28 for the application of UP) and repeat. Note that each application of UP guarantees at least one {33} molecule.

(1) Apply Lemma 11.16 to M and select a connected no-bottom subset A. This set is fixed until the end of (5).

(2) Choose a lowest deg 3 atom n in A that has not been cut. Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n. This n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$are fixed until the end of (3).

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a highest atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If m has deg 3 and has a parent${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$or child m<sup>−</sup> that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(4) If M has deg 2 atom, then cut it; repeat until M has no deg 2 atoms. Then go to (2) and choose the next n, and so on.

(5) When all atoms in A have been cut, we subsequently cut all deg 2 atoms as in (4), and then cut all components of M with only one deg 3 atom using UP.

(6) Go to (1) and select the next A from one of the remaining components of M, and so on.

Remark 11.18. Let us explain the ideas in Lemma 11.16 and Definition 11.17. Note that steps$( 2 ) - ( 4 )$in Definition 11.17 are exactly the same as UP but applied to a particular set A, so we can view 3COMPUP as a clever way of carrying out UP. The role of the set A is explained as follows: first it is connected (otherwise we can cut each of its components separately); it should also be no-bottom, because when cutting any atom we should also cut its descendants to guarantee the monotonicity property. Finally we need it to contain two deg 3 atoms so that this sequence of cutting will produce at least one {33} molecule, and we need exactly two deg 3 atoms so that we do not waste too many components of the deg-3-atom set (which are the key objects leading to the gain).

Proposition 11.19. Let M be a toy model II. We first cut$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free and cut it into elementary molecules by DOWN (i.e. the dual of UP with all directions reversed), then apply 3COMPUP (Definition 11.17) to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. Then all resulting components are elementary, and we have

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} = 1, \quad \# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \# _ {\operatorname{comp} (X)} / 1 0.\tag{11.9}
$$

Since$| X | \gtrsim \rho \gg 1$and using (11.8), this clearly implies (11.1).

Proof. Note that steps (2)–(4) in Definition 11.17 are exactly the same as UP, so the proof that all molecules are elementary (as well as$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$which comes only from$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$follows in the same way as Proposition 11.12. We now focus on the proof that #$\{ 3 3 \} \geq \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } / 1 0$

For any molecule M, define$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p ( M ) } }$to be the number of components of M, and$\# _ { 3 \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } ) }$to be the number of components of the set of deg 3 atoms in M, and

$$
\lambda (\mathbb {M}) := \frac {1}{5} \# _ {\operatorname{comp} (\mathbb {M})} + \frac {1}{1 0} \# _ {3 \operatorname{comp} (\mathbb {M})}.\tag{11.10}
$$

In Definition 11.17 (applied to$\mathbb { M } _ { U } )$, the whole algorithm consists of finitely many loops where one loop is formed by steps (1)–(5) in Definition 11.17. Consider each such loop which reduces M to M<sup>′</sup>, we shall prove the following:

(♣) If M is a tree, has no top fixed end and contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms with at least two deg 3 atoms, then each component of M<sup>′</sup> satisfies the same property. Moreover for this loop we have

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \lambda (\mathbb {M}) - \lambda (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}).\tag{11.11}
$$

Note that adding up (11.11) leads to the desired lower bound of$\# \{ 3 3 \}$(initially$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has no deg 2 atoms nor top fixed end, and$\# _ { \mathrm { 3 c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } = \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( X ) } )$, thus it sufices to prove (♣) for a given loop. We divide the proof into 4 parts.

Proof part 1. We prove that each component of M<sup>′</sup> satisfies the desired properties. This is obvious, as the lack of top fixed ends follows from the same proof as Proposition 11.12, and the lack of deg 2 atoms and components with only one deg 3 atom follows from the cuttings done in Definition 11.17 (5).

Proof part 2. Now we need to prove (11.11). We start by making some preparations. Note that A is a connected subset of M; by Lemma 11.6 in the proof of Lemma 11.8, each atom m$\in \mathbb { M } \backslash A$that is connected to an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } = { \mathfrak { n } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } )$in A by a pre-loop bond e corresponds to a unique component$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$after cutting the atoms in A as free, see Figure 35 (the loop will in fact cut as free more atoms). Note also that m must be a parent of n due to the no-bottom property of A.

Let${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$be the set of deg 3 atoms in M (before executing the loop), and consider all components of$\mathbb { M } _ { 3 }$ that intersect A or are connected to A by a bond. We know A has exactly two atoms in M ; apart from the one or two components that contain these two atoms, each component under consideration must be a subset of a unique$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$where m has deg 3 and${ \mathfrak { n } } = { \mathfrak { n } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } )$has deg 4 (call it$Y _ { \mathfrak { m } } )$. Let B be the union of these components with A (Figure 35). We claim that after steps$( 1 ) - ( 4 )$in Definition 11.17 and cutting the deg 2 atoms in Definition 11.17 (5), exactly those atoms in B have been cut as free.

![](images/page_116_image_0.jpg)

Figure 35. Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 11.19. Here A is the connected, no-bottom set as in Lemma$1 1 . 1 6 ;$various atoms m (together with the corresponding component$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$as in Lemma 11.6 are drawn, each of which connected to its child${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$by a bond. Apart from 2 exceptions, this n will have deg 4. If m has deg 4 we do nothing; if m has deg 3, we take all the cubsequently connected deg 3 atoms in$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$and call them$Y _ { \mathfrak { m } }$(i.e. the blue circle within the green circle$X _ { \mathfrak { m } } )$. The B is defined as the union of A and all blue circles. Within one loop (1)–(5) in Definition 11.17, we cut everything in A, and subsequently everything in the blue circles as deg 2 (or as part of {33} molecule). That is, we cut everything in B and nothing else (as cutting B only turns deg 4 atoms into deg 3 but does not produce further deg 2 atom).

In fact, the atoms A must have been cut by definition. For any atom in the$\mathbb { M } _ { 3 }$components forming$B ,$ by definition it is connected to an atom in A by a chain of deg 3 atoms; once the atom in A has been cut, the atoms on this chain will successively become deg 2, so they must have been cut (either in Definition 11.17 $( 4 )  { - } ( 5 )$, or as part of {33} molecule in Definition 11.17 (3)). On the other hand, each atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash B$has at most one bond connecting to B (as B is connected and M is a tree), and must be deg 4 if it has one such bond (otherwise it would belong to one of the$\mathbb { M } _ { 3 }$components forming B), so each atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash B$will have deg 3 or 4 after cutting B as free, thus it will not be cut in Definition 11.17 (1)–(4) or in cutting the deg 2 atoms in Definition 11.17 (5).

Proof part 3. Next we obtain a lower bound on$\# \{ 3 3 \}$. Note that A contains two deg 3 atoms, we can show that$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq 1$in the same way as in Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.12. Moreover, since A contains exactly two deg 3 atoms, by arguing as in Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 11.12 and calculating the quantity σ defined there but within A, we can show that, apart from at most two exceptions, each deg 4 atom in A will have deg 3 when it is cut.

Now let λ be the number of${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$components forming B. With at most two exceptions, each such component corresponds to a deg 3 atom m$\in X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$together with its deg 4 child${ \mathfrak { n } } = { \mathfrak { n } } ( { \mathfrak { m } } ) \in A$as in Part 2 above. With at most two more exceptions, this n will have deg 3 when it is cut, at which time m also has deg 3 (see Figure 36); then by Definition 11.17 (3), we know that n must belong to a {33} molecule (which may or may not be$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { m } \} ,$). Note that each {33} molecule can be so obtained by at most one n, and each n can be obtained by at most two m (hence at most two components), we conclude that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \max \left(1, \frac {\lambda - 2}{2} - 2\right).\tag{11.12}
$$

Proof part 4. Now we consider the components of M<sup>′</sup> and${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 } ^ { \prime }$(set of deg 3 atoms in M<sup>′</sup>). Note that M<sup>′</sup> is formed from M by cutting B as free and then removing all components with only one deg 3 atom. Since

![](images/page_117_image_0.jpg)

Figure 36. Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.19: here${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$is connected to${ \mathfrak { m } } \in X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$ which has deg 3, as in Figure 35. With at most 2 more exceptions, this n will also have deg 3 when it is cut (as we are essentially doing UP within$A ,$see Proposition 11.12), which leads to a {33} molecule formed by n and m.

B is connected, by applying Lemma 11.6 in the proof of Lemma 11.8 again, we see that each component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$ of M<sup>′</sup> corresponds to a unique atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash B$that is adjacent to an atom in$B ,$see Figure 37. Let$\mu$be the number of such bonds (i.e. corresponding to those new components with at least two deg 3 atoms after cutting B), then we have

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} = 1 - \mu .\tag{11.13}
$$

Finally, consider the set of deg 3 atoms, i.e.${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$and${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 } ^ { \prime }$, and their components. The components of$\mathbb { M } _ { 3 }$ includes those λ components forming B as in Part 2 (which have been cut when forming$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } )$, and the other components which are contained in some$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$defined above. Note that for each new component Y formed after cutting B that contains only one deg 3 atom, it will be removed and will not occur in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } ;$however, all atoms in Y originally have deg 4 before any cutting, so initially Y also has no contribution to #<sub>3comp(M)</sub>, and thus we can ignore such$Y .$

By Lemma 11.6, when viewed in each$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } ,$, the efect of cutting B exactly turns one free end into fixed end (turning one deg 4 atom into deg 3). Therefore the part of${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 } ^ { \prime }$within$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$is formed by adding one deg 3 atom into the existing part of${ \mathbb { M } } _ { 3 }$within$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$. This new deg 3 atom may decrease$\# _ { 3 \mathrm { c o m p } ( X _ { \mathfrak { q } } ) }$(i.e. the number of components of the set of deg 3 atoms in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } )$by joining existing components together, but this decrease is at most$\mathcal { Q }$because this new deg 3 atom can join at most 3 components into 1. From this, and accounting for the λ components removed when cutting$B ,$we deduce that

$$
\# _ {3 \mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {3 \mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \leq \lambda + 2 \mu .\tag{11.14}
$$

Putting together (11.10) and (11.12)–(11.14), we deduce that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda (\mathbb {M}) - \lambda (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}) = \frac {1}{5} \big (\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \big) + \frac {1}{1 0} \big (\# _ {3 \mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {3 \mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \big) \\ \qquad \leq \frac {1}{5} + \frac {\lambda}{1 0} \leq \max \left(1, \frac {\lambda - 6}{2}\right) \leq \# _ {\{3 3 \}}. \end{array}\tag{11.15}
$$

This proves (11.11) and completes the proof of Proposition 11.19.

11.5. Toy model III. In this subsection we introduce the toy model III. Note that in both toy models I plus and II, we are assuming the absence of 2-connections, i.e.$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$. Now we define the toy models III, which are (essentially) opposite to toy models I plus and II via the dichotomy, where we assume<sup>14</sup> $\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \gtrsim | X |$instead of$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } = 0$

Definition 11.20. We say M is a toy model III, if it is a simplified 2-layer model in Definition 11.1, and

$$
\# _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} \gtrsim | X |,\tag{11.16}
$$

where$\# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } }$and X are defined at the beginning of this note.

The strategy for toy models III is simple: we work in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as$\operatorname { i f } \mathbb { M } _ { U }$were absent, and apply the DOWN algorithm (the dual of UP) to it. Now consider any 2-connection${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, which will become deg 2 when all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$have been cut. Assume n is adjacent to two atoms${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { m } } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and assume${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$is cut before$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$in the DOWN algorithm applied to$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. Then, right before$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$is cut, this$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$will have deg 3 (say) by Proposition 11.12; also since${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$has been cut at this time, now n must also have deg 3, which leads to a {33} molecule, so we simply cut it and enjoy the gain. This way we guarantee that each 2-connection belongs to a {33} molecule, which is suficient under the assumption (11.16). We shall refer to this as the 2CONNDN algorithm (and the dual version 2CONNUP), see Definition 13.1 for the full version (which is more complicated due to the various necessary additions including the O-atoms).

Definition 11.21 (Algorithm for toy model III). Let M be toy model III. We define the following cutting sequence. For an example see Figure 38:

(1) If$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has a deg 2 atom, then cut it as free. Repeat until$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$does not have deg 2 atoms.

(2) Choose a highest deg 3 atom n in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that has not bee cut (or a highest atom if$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no deg 3 atoms). Let$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of ancestors of n in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. This n and$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is fixed until all atoms in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a lowest atom m in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If m has deg 3 and has a parent${ \mathfrak { p } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { p } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut, then go to$( 1 ) - ( 2 )$and choose the next${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$and so on.

(4) When all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$have been cut, finish of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$by applying the UP algorithm.

Note that steps (1)–(3) in Definition 11.21 are essentially just DOWN (i.e. the dual of UP) applied to $\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, except we propritize the {33} molecules formed by an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$with an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$

Proposition 11.22. Let M be toy model III. Then, after applying the cutting sequence defined in Definition 11.21, all molecules we get are elementary, and we have

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} = 1, \quad \# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \frac {1}{2} \cdot \# _ {2 \text {conn}}.\tag{11.17}
$$

Here we perform DOWN which is the dual of UP in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, so in Definition 11.10 (2) in UP algorithm we choose the highest deg 3 atom instead of the lowest, and in in Definition 11.10 (3) in UP algorithm we choose the lowest remaining atom instead of the highest, etc. Here green box indicates atoms in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(the set of ancestors of n), and when an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$forms a {33} molecule with an atom$\mathfrak { m } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$we always cut it. In the end we see that each 2-connection (pink atom) belongs to one {33} molecule, as desired. As the gain is already enough, the rest can be cut into elementary molecules using UP in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and DOWN in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Proof. Since steps (1)–(3) in Definition 11.21 are essentially the same as in DOWN, it is easy to prove all molecules we get are elementary and #$\dot { \{ 4 \} } = 1$, in the same way as the proof of Proposition 11.12. Now we only need to prove that$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } / 2$

Let${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$be any 2-connection, which is connected to two atoms${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { m } } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$by two bonds. Assume ${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$is cut before${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 2 }$in Definition 11.21 (they cannot be cut at the same time, as Definition 11.21 (3) does not provide an option to cut a {33} molecule with both atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$). Arguing in the same way as in Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 11.12, we know that m cannot have deg 4 when it is cut. On the other hand, note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a tree initially without deg 3 atoms; by arguing in the same way as in Part 4 of the proof of Proposition 11.12 and calculating the quantity σ defined there but within$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, we conclude that$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$also cannot have deg 2 when it is cut.

Therefore, m must have deg 3 when it is cut; at this time n must also have deg 3 because${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$has been cut, $\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$has not, and n also has two top edges (not fixed ends) that are not afected, see Figure 39. By Definition 11.21 (3) we conclude that$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$must belong to a {33} molecule, which means that n must be adjacent with an$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$atom in some {33} molecule. Since this is true for each 2-connection, and each {33} molecule may correspond to at most two 2-connections in this way (i.e. given the {33} molecule there can be at most two n that are adjacent with the$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$atom in this {33} molecule), we conclude that$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } \geq \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } / 2$□

Then at the time $\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$is cut, this$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 }$has deg 3 due to properties of DOWN (Proposition 11.12), and n also has deg 3 because${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$has been cut.

11.6. Reduction to 2-layers: layer selection. In Sections 11.2–11.5 we have considered the 2-layer models in Definition 11.1. In fact, this two-layer case already captures most of the essential dificulties in the multi-layer case, and a simple process allows us to reduce the general L-layer case (where L is any large constant) to the 2-layer case. This is refered to as layer selection, which we define as follows; for the precise definition see Definition 12.12.

Definition 11.23. Let M satisfy Proposition 10.4 and simplifications (1)–(2) in Section 11.1. Recall the set $r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } )$of root particles at layer ℓ (Definition 3.18), and$s _ { \ell } = | r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) |$; they are the particle lines that cross into layer ℓ. Assume also$| H | = s _ { \ell } \ll \rho$(the case when$| H | \gtrsim \rho$is easy due to the positive term$| H |$in (9.51); see Proposition 12.3). We define the layer selection process as follows, see Figure 40:

(1) Choose$\ell _ { U }$such that

$$
\rho^ {\prime} := s _ {\ell_ {U} - 1} \sim \max _ {\ell^ {\prime}} s _ {\ell^ {\prime}} \sim \rho , \qquad \rho^ {\prime} \gg \max _ {\ell^ {\prime} \geq \ell_ {U}} s _ {\ell^ {\prime}};\tag{11.18}
$$

here the first condition in (11.18) states that the majority of crossings happen between layers$\ell _ { U }$and $\ell _ { U } - 1$, and the second condition states that the crossings in layers above$\ell _ { U }$are negligible.

(2) Consider each of the$s \ell _ { U } - 1$particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$. For$\ell _ { D } < \ell _ { U } ,$, define$v _ { \ell _ { D } } ^ { * }$to be the number of particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$that are connected to either a particle line in in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$or to a cycle within$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) } ;$in other words, we start from layer$\ell _ { U } - 1$and move down, keeping track of the number of crossings that are connected to other crossings or to a cycle at each layer. Note that $v _ { 1 } ^ { * } = s _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 }$by Proposition 10.4 (9) (and$H _ { 0 } = \varnothing )$; now as in (1), we choose$\ell _ { D }$such that

$$
\rho^ {\prime \prime} := v _ {\ell_ {D}} ^ {*} \sim s _ {\ell_ {U} - 1} = \rho^ {\prime}, \quad \rho^ {\prime \prime} \gg \max _ {\ell^ {\prime \prime} > \ell_ {D}} v _ {\ell^ {\prime \prime}} ^ {*}.\tag{11.19}
$$

(3) Now we focus on the layers$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] } : = \cup _ { \ell _ { D } \leq \ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell _ { U } } \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, and ignore all other layers. Consider each component$Z$of the set$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$. If Z intersects at least two particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$or contains a cycle, then by the choice of$\ell _ { D }$in$( 2 )$, the number of such exceptional components is$\le v _ { \ell _ { D } + 1 } ^ { * } \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime }$ which is negligible. We will assume this number is zero (otherwise we need an additional cutting and pre-processing step, see Section 11.7.4 below).

(4) Define the result of layer selection, to be$\mathbb { M } _ { U D } : = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, where$\mathbb { M } _ { U } : = \mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] }$and M${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { \phi } } } } _ { D } : = \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { D } }$

Proposition 11.24. Assume M satisfies Proposition 10.4 and simplifications (1)–(2) in Section 11.1, and $| H | \ll \rho ,$and assume that the number of exceptional components is zero in Definition 11.23 (3). Then the process in Definition 11.23 is well-defined, and for$\mathbb { M } _ { U D } = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$in Definition 11.23 (4), we have that

• Each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest with no fixed end, the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$being$\ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime }$ and no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a parent of an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } ;$

• There exist at least$\rho ^ { \prime \prime }$bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and each such bond is connected to another bond between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, by a path within$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Proof. To prove that the procedure in Definition 11.23 is well-defined, we just need to prove the existence of$\ell _ { U }$in Definition 11.23 (1) and$\ell _ { D }$in Definition 11.23 (2). In fact, we can choose two large constants (see Definition 12.12 and Proposition 12.13 for more details)$C \gg ( C ^ { \prime } ) ^ { \ell }$such that

$$
\ell_ {U} - 1 := \max \left\{\ell^ {\prime}: s _ {\ell^ {\prime}} \geq C ^ {- \ell^ {\prime}} \cdot \rho \right\}, \quad \ell_ {D} := \max \left\{\ell^ {\prime \prime} <   \ell_ {U}: v _ {\ell^ {\prime \prime}} ^ {*} \geq (C ^ {\prime}) ^ {- \ell^ {\prime \prime}} \cdot \rho^ {\prime} \right\}.\tag{11.20}
$$

Note that$\rho \sim$max<sub>ℓ</sub>′ s<sub>ℓ</sub>′ by (7.1) (as$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } = 0$by assumption) and$s _ { \ell } = | H | \ll C ^ { - \ell } \cdot \rho$by assumption, so$\ell _ { U }$ exists; similarly$\ell _ { D }$exists because$v _ { 1 } ^ { * } = \rho ^ { \prime }$by Proposition 10.4 (9).

Now, we have assumed$v _ { \ell _ { D } + 1 } ^ { \ast } = 0 \ \mathrm { ( i . e ) }$. no exceptional component) in Definition 11.23 (3). It is obvious that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest (by simplification (2) in Section 11.1),$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no fixed end (because nothing is cut in$\mathbb { M } _ { U D } = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, and no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is parent of an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(because the layers forming $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are above that forming$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$

We next show that$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is a forest. In fact, each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$must intersect a particle line in $r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$(it must intersect a particle line in$p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for some$\ell ^ { \prime } < \ell _ { U }$by Proposition 10.4 (5); by applying Proposition 10.4 (7) we know that this component must also intersect a particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) \subseteq p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } )$ by repeating this and using Remark 10.5, we eventually get to a particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } ) )$. As there is no exceptional component in Definition 11.23 (3), we know that each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$is a tree by itself, and intersects a unique particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } } )$. Since$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } }$is a forest by itself, we see that$\mathbb { M } _ { U } = \mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] }$is also a forest (namely, if we start with a forest, and attach a number of trees to it with each tree connected to the original forest by a unique edge, then the result is still a forest).

We next show that the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$does not exceed$s _ { \ell _ { U } }$, which is$\ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime }$because

$$
s _ {\ell_ {U}} \leq C ^ {- 1} \cdot s _ {\ell_ {U} - 1} = C ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho^ {\prime} \leq C ^ {- 1} \cdot (C ^ {\prime}) ^ {\ell} \cdot \rho^ {\prime \prime} \ll \rho^ {\prime \prime}
$$

by (11.20) and$C \gg ( C ^ { \prime } ) ^ { \ell }$. In fact, by the same arguments for$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$as above, we see that each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] }$must intersect a particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } } )$, so the number of these components is bounded by $| r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } } ) | = s _ { \ell _ { U } }$by Remark 10.5.

Finally, consider each of the$\rho ^ { \prime \prime } = v _ { \ell _ { D } } ^ { * }$particle lines that is connected to either a particle line in in $r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$or to a cycle within$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$, say$\mathbf { \delta } _ { p . }$By definition there exists a path going from an atom on $\pmb { p }$to an atom on either a cycle or another particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } )$. This path must enter$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { D } } .$, because the above-stated property of$\pmb { p }$will not hold without layer$\ell _ { D } ;$moreover it also must exist$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { D } }$(including exiting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$when getting onto another particle line in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } - 1 } ) )$, because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$by itself does not contain a cycle. By considering the first entry and first exit at$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, we obtain two bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that are connected within M$_ { D } ;$moreover the first entry bond must be connected to$\pmb { p }$via$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$, and is thus in bijection with$\mathbf { \delta } _ { p . }$This proves the desired result, namely the existence of at least$\rho ^ { \prime \prime }$bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$ and$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, each of which being connected to another by a path within$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$□

Remark 11.25. We make two remarks concerning Definition 11.23 and Proposition 11.24.

(1) In Definition 11.23, we focus on$\mathbb { M } _ { U D } = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D } = \mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] }$and ignore other layers. In practice, we need to cut$\mathbb { M } _ { [ \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ] }$as free from M and cut the other layers into elementary components (first $\mathbb { M } _ { > \ell _ { U } }$using UP, then$\mathbb { M } _ { < \ell _ { D } }$using DOWN). This may create some {4} molecules, but their number is easily bounded using Proposition 11.12 and the upper bound on the number of components of $\mathbb { M } _ { > \ell _ { U } }$and M (see Definition 12.14 and Proposition 12.15).

(2) Compared to Definition 11.1, the$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$in Proposition 11.24 are forests instead of trees. However, the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is$\ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime }$by Proposition 11.24 and is thus negligible; on the other hand,$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$may have many components, but this is compensated by the fact that the $\rho ^ { \prime \prime }$bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$in Proposition 11.24 are connected within$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. Indeed, in the case when$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has many components, this (in fact a related property of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, see Proposition 12.15 (3b)) allows us to first cut$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$as free and gain from subsequently cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, see Proposition 13.3.

Remark 11.26. In practice, there are two complications to layer selection: first, if some single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$ contains cycles (without simplification (2) in Section 11.1), then we need an extra layer refining process (see Definition 12.12), which is discussed in Section 11.7.2. Second, if$v _ { \ell _ { D } + 1 } ^ { * } \neq 0$(i.e. there are exceptional components in Definition 11.23 (3), though their number is still$\ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime }$and negligible), we need to first cut them as free before defining$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(Definition 12.14). This will create some {4} molecules but their number is bounded (see Propositions 12.13 and 12.15), and will also introduce fixed ends to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ which necessitates the pre-processing step, see discussions in Section 11.7.4.

11.7. Additions in the general case. In this subsection, we discuss the additional “accessories” needed to address the general case, without the simplifications (1)–(2) in Section 11.1. These should be viewed as branches that are attached to the main thread of proof, which are less essential but necessary. These accessories are listed in Table 2, and will be discussed in Sections 11.7.1–11.7.4 below.

11.7.1. O-atoms and ov-segments. First, in the real problem, the molecule M may contain O-atoms, and the cutting operation in this case is more complicated (see Definition 8.3 (2) compared to Definition 8.3 (1)).

As we already see in Definition 8.3, the notion of ov-segments is important in the analysis of O-atoms, and should be viewed as a generalization of edges/bonds. In Definition 8.4, we have introduced the notions of being ov-adjacent, ov-parent and ov-child, and ov-components etc., which are direct generalizations of adjacent, parent and child, and connected components. Fortunately, in almost all cases, this generalization does not cause any essential change to the proof; we simply translate every sentence in the proofs in Sections 11.2–11.5 into the language of ov-segments, with “adjacent” replaced by “ov-adjacent” and “components” replaced by “ov-components”, etc. As an example, by replacing “connected” with “ov-connected” and “bond” with “ov-segment” in Lemma 11.6, we obtain the following statement, which is just Lemma 13.4:

• Suppose we cut$S \subseteq \mathbb { M }$as free, where S is an ov-connected subset of M and M is a tree. Then, for each atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash S$that is connected to an atom in$S$by a (pre-cutting) ov-segment e, the post-cutting molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has exactly one component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$corresponding to q. Moreover, when viewed in $X _ { \mathfrak { q } } ,$the operation of cutting S turns exactly one free end at q into a fixed end.

11.7.2. Reducing each layer to a tree: layer refining. In both the toy models in Sections 11.2–11.5 and layer selection in Section 11.6, it is crucial that each layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$of M is a forest. In reality, to deal with the case where some$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$contains cycles, we need to define the layer refining process as follows.

Recall (Proposition 10.4 (3)–(4)) that each$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$is formed by joining finitely many C-molecules by$\mathrm { O } _ { - }$ atoms, such that each C-molecule has circuit rank$\rho ( W ) \leq \Gamma$, and joining these C-molecules by O-atoms does not add any cycle. We start with the following simple intuitive lemma:

• For each molecule M with at most Γ independent cycles, we can always divide it into at most$\Gamma + 1$ subsets$\mathbb { M } _ { j } ( 1 \leq j \leq \Gamma + 1 )$, such that each subset is a tree, and no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { i }$can be parent of atom in M<sub>j</sub> for$i < j$

For the proof of the above lemma, see Lemma 12.7. Now, to complete the layer refining process for each single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, we need to delete some O-atoms to ensure each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$has$\rho$value at most$\Gamma ,$ and then apply this lemma to divide it into at most Γ + 1 thin layers, such that each thin layer is now a forest. For details see Definition 12.8 and Proposition 12.9. This then allows us to repeat the layer selection process in Section 11.6; the use of thin layers instead of layers leads to one extra step in layer selection, but this is easily adjusted, see Definition 12.12.

We remark that the above layer refining process does require the total number of independent cycles in these single-layer C-molecules to be negligible (compared to$\rho )$. When this total number of cycles is large, we can perform an alternative cutting sequence that exploits these cycles, see Propositions 12.10 and 12.11. This requires layer refining of a subset of layers and also leads to a minor auxiliary notion of primitivity, see Definition 12.4 and Lemma 12.6.

11.7.3. Strong and weak degeneracies. In Definition 11.1 we have assumed that all {33} molecules are good. In reality there may be exceptions to this when the$( x _ { e } , v _ { e } )$for fixed ends e at this {33} molecule takes some very specific values, as stated in the definition of good molecules (Definition 9.4). For example, a {33A} molecule will not be good, if

$$
\left| x _ {e _ {1}} - x _ {e _ {7}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \text { and } \quad \left| v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {7}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v},\tag{11.21}
$$

where$e _ { 1 }$and$e _ { 7 }$are the two fixed ends of the {33} molecule.

As such, we define a strong degeneracy to be an instance where (11.21) happens at two edges that would become the two fixed ends$i f$we cut the two atoms as a {33A} molecule; see Definition 12.4. Similarly we can define the notion of weak degeneracy associated with the {33B} molecules, which involves one or two atoms and some conditions opposite to the ones stated in Definition 9.4; see Definition 12.16. Note that these definitions only involve certain edges and atoms in M, and is not a priori associated with any concrete cutting sequence. This provides the flexibility, so that we can classify the degeneracies and non-degeneracies before performing any cutting, and perform diferent cutting operations according to diferent cases, which allows us to minimize the need of backtracking.

Our strategy is that, when there are many degeneracies, we shall perform an alternative cutting sequence, where we do not gain from {33} molecules but instead gain from the extra degeneracy assumptions such as (11.21). Compared to the sophisticated algorithms exploiting {33} molecules, this alternative cutting sequence essentially follows the simple procedure where we cut every atom by itself, so that most of them are cut as {3} molecules. Usually integrating a {3} molecule does not gain any power, but if this {3} molecule contains an edge or atom that is involved in some degeneracy condition like (11.21), then it is clear that this {3} molecule integration should gain some power, which makes it a good molecule, see Definition 9.4.

In practice, there will be two places in the overall algorithm where we need to consider degeneracies: the first time for strong degeneracies, see Proposition 12.5 and the second time for weak degeneracies, see

Proposition 12.17. If there are many (strong or weak) degeneracies, then we can apply the alternative cutting sequence to conclude; if there are few (strong and weak) degeneracies, then their efect will be negligible and we can get rid of them and proceed with the main thread of our algorithm.

11.7.4. Additional ingredients and pre-processing. Finally, we discuss a few minor ingredients that are needed in the full case, that are not discussed in Sections 11.7.1–11.7.3 above.

(a) Initial cumulants. In this section we have assumed$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { 0 } ) = H _ { 0 } = \emptyset$in Proposition$1 0 . 4 ;$in reality this $H _ { 0 }$may exist, which corresponds to the initial (time$t = 0 )$cumulants. This may afect the layer selection process, as it is now possible in Proposition 10.4 (9) that most particle lines in$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$form initial links instead of being connected to other particle lines or cycles. In this case we simply exploit the initial link condition to obtain good {3} molecules (see Definition 9.4); the will be quite easy, see Proposition 12.17.

(b) Cutting exceptional components. Recall the notion of exceptional components in Definition 11.23 (3); in Section 11.6 we have assumed there is no such exceptional components, so$\mathbb { M } _ { U } = \mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { U } } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell _ { D } : \ell _ { U } ) }$is a forest (Proposition 11.24). In general, when such exceptional components exist (but with a negligible number), we need to first cut them as free, before defining$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$which can be forests. This cutting process is described in Definition 12.14; it may create some {4} molecules, but their number can be bounded in Propositions 12.13 and 12.15. It may also introduce fixed ends to$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, which then requires the pre-processing step to treat, see (d) below.

(c) Cutting 2-connections. Recall that in the 2-layer models, there is a case when the number of$2 \AA ^ { - }$ connections satisfies$0 < \# _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } \ll | X |$(see Section 11.5), which is not covered in any toy model. In this case we first cut all these 2-connections as free, so no more 2-connections remain in the resulting molecule; this corresponds to Stage 1 in the proof of Proposition 12.18 in Section 13.5. After this, there will be fixed ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$similar to (b) above, so we should apply the extra pre-processing step (see (d) below).

(d) Pre-processing. In Definition 11.1, we have assumed that the 2-layer molecule M has no fixed ends; however, in reality, such fixed ends may exist as shown in (b)–(c) above, which also leads to fixed ends and deg 3 atoms after we subsequently cut all deg 2 atoms. In fact those fixed ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$will not matter as there will not be any top fixed ends; however the fixed ends in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$may afect the properness of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(which is needed in the MAINUD algorithm) and needs to be addressed.

In this case, depending on the number of components of deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(similar to the dichotomy in Sections 11.3–11.4), we either apply 3COMPDN (i.e. the dual of 3COMPUP) in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$similar to Section 11.4 with enough gain (this corresponds to Stage 2 in Section 13.5, or apply an extra pre-processing step to turn$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into a proper molecule (this corresponds to Stage 3) . The pre-processing depends on a specific process SELECT, see Definition 13.10 and Proposition 13.11.

After pre-processing, we are then ready to apply the dichotomy in Sections 11.3–11.4, to reduce to either toy model II (corresponding to Stage 5), or toy model I plus (corresponding to Stage 6). Finally, note that the pre-processing step may also cause some complications, as the set X involved in the dichotomy needs to be replaced by some natural modification$X _ { 1 }$, which will be explained in details in the MAINUD, see the definition of$X _ { 0 }$and$X _ { 1 }$in Definition 13.12, and Stage 4.

11.7.5. Strategy flowchart. We present a flowchart summarizing the proof of Proposition 9.7, see Figure 41.

## 12. Cutting algorithm I: reduction to UD molecules

In this section and Section 13 we will construct the cutting algorithm in Proposition 9.7. As already mentioned in the beginning of Section 11, these algorithms and arguments will be presented in a diferent order from Section 11, to be consistent with the logical flow of the proof. The goal of this section is to prove several cases of Proposition 9.7, namely Propositions 12.3, 12.5, 12.11 and 12.17, and reduce Proposition 9.7 to Proposition 12.18, by getting rid of degeneracies (Propositions 12.5 and 12.17), introducing layer refinement (Section 12.3) and layer selection (Section 12.4).

![](images/page_125_image_0.jpg)

Figure 41. Yes/No flow chart for the proof of Proposition 9.7. Here each green box indicates end of a proof path; each “Do” describes the algorithm, process or steps we take, and “Define” indicates the new notions defined. The notions of strongly degenerate, primitive and weakly degenerate (abbreviated str. deg., prm. and wea. deg.) pairs are defined in Definitions 12.4 and 12.16; the other notions are defined at the place indicated. The “many/large/small” etc. are all relative to$\rho ;$for the precise threshold of these statements, see the corresponding propositions.

12.1. The UP algorithm and the large |H| case. In this subsection, we prove the first case of Proposition 9.7, namely Proposition 12.3, where we assume |H| is large. We start by introducing the full version of algorithm UP, which is a direct extension of its toy model version in Definition 11.10, by replacing parent/child with ov-parent/ov-child (cf. Section 11.7.1). This is a general purpose or “default” algorithm that minimizes the number of {4} molecules, which also guarantees suficiently many good molecules only in some cases. However, this algorithm alone is enough to treat the simple scenarios studied in this section. Moreover, even in later cases where other algorithms are needed to achieve gain in a key subset of the molecule, it is usually helpful to use UP (or its dual DOWN) to finish the decomposition of the remaining parts of the molecule without loss.

Definition 12.1 (The algorithm UP). Define the following cutting algorithm UP. It takes as input any (regular) molecule M, which has no top fixed end at any C-atom (we henceforth abbreviate it as C-top fixed ends; same for C-bottom fixed ends). For any such M, we define the cutting sequence as follows:

(1) If M contains any deg 2 atom n, then cut it as free, and repeat until there is no deg 2 atom left.

(2) Consider the set of all remaining deg 3 atoms in M (i.e. those deg 3 that have not been cut), and choose a lowest atom n in this set. If M has no deg 3 atoms, then choose a lowest atom n in M. Let $S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n (including n); this n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$will be fixed until the end of (3).

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a highest remaining atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$. If m has deg 3, and either an ov-parent${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$or an ov-child$\mathfrak { m } ^ { - }$of m also has deg 3, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$or$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { - } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut. Then go to (1).

We also define the dual algorithm DOWN, by reversing the notions of parent/child, lowest/highest, top/bottom etc. It applies to any molecule that has no C-bottom fixed end.

The next proposition is the full version of Proposition 11.12.

Proposition 12.2. Let M be any molecule as in Definition 12.1. We may assume M is connected (otherwise consider each component of M). Then after applying algorithm UP to M (and same for DOWN):

(1) We have the following monotonicity property (MONO): throughout the process of UP, the set $S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$will not have any C-bottom fixed end, and$( \mathbb { M } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$will not have any C-top fixed end (in particular, when all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut and before the next n is chosen in Definition 12.1 (2), there is no C-top fixed end in whole M). In particular, the molecule M is cut into elementary molecules, and$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0 .$

(2) We have$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq 1$, and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$if and only if M is full.

In (3)–(4) below we assume M has no deg 2 atoms.

(3) If M contains a cycle or contains at least two deg 3 atoms, then$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } \geq 1$. If not (i.e. M is a tree and contains at most one deg 3 atom), then all the elementary molecules are {3} molecules with at most one exception which might be a {4} molecule.

(4) If M contains at most one deg 3 atom and contains a cycle, then we can split into 2 sub-cases such that for each sub-case we have$\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } \geq 1$

Proof. We first make some comments on the result and the proof. Here, compared to (MONO-toy) in Proposition 11.12, the (MONO) property changes the absence of fixed ends to the absence of C-fixed ends, because of the presence of O-atoms (we do not need to worry about fixed ends at O-atoms because they cannot afect any other atom; see Remark 8.7).

The main new ingredient compared to Proposition 11.12 is (4), which guarantees a good molecule instead of just a {33A} molecule, and is thus useful in strongly degenerate cases (Definition 12.4, Proposition 12.5) where {33A} molecules might not be good. The proof of (4) also provides an example how the splitting into sub-cases in Proposition 9.7 works, by decomposing 1 into suitable indicator functions with prescribed supports. Apart from these, the proof is essentially the same as Proposition 11.12.

Proof of (1). We first prove (MONO). Note that this statement is true initially, as M has no C-top fixed end. Moreover at each time of choosing n in Definition 12.1 (2), there is also no C-bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$, because all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$must have deg 4 (since n is the lowest deg 3 atom). Therefore, it sufices to show that (MONO) is preserved. For this, first note that if n has deg 2 as in Definition 12.1 (1), and has no C-top fixed end, then cutting n as free will only generate bottom fixed ends at its ov-parents (cf. Remark 8.7), so the absence of C-top fixed end in the whole molecule is preserved.

Next, suppose n is chosen as in Definition 12.1 (2), and m is a highest remaining atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$as in Definition 12.1 (3). If we cut m as free, this does not create any C-bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(because m is a highest remaining atom, so any ov-parent of m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$has already been cut), and does not create any C-top fixed end in$( \mathbb { M } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(because any ov-child atom of m must again be in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \} )$), so (MONO) is preserved.

The same can be proved for the operation of cutting$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$or$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { - } \}$; let us consider$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$as the other case is similar. Here, cutting$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$may create bottom fixed ends at ov-parents of m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$, but none of them belong to$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$(so$( \mathrm { M O N O } )$is not afected), because m is a highest remaining atom (so no ov-parent of m still remains in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$in particular${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + } \not \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$and no ov-parent of${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$can be in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$. Moreover, cutting$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$may create top fixed ends at ov-children of m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$, but they all have to be in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$ (so again (MONO) is not afected). This last statement is obvious for m as m$\in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. As for${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$, since it has deg 3, has no C-top fixed end, and has one ov-child being m, we know it must have a bottom fixed end (or is O-atom, cf. Remark 8.7). Since m is ov-child of${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$, we know that any other ov-child of${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$must belong to the maximal ov-segment containing${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$and m. Using the structure of ov-segments, we know that any other ov-child of${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$that is C-atom must occur at the bottom of this ov-segment, thus it must be an ov-child of m and belong to$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$. This shows (MONO) is preserved in the whole process, thus it is true for all time.

Now, note that by construction, any atom in M is either cut by itself, or belongs to a {33} molecule. By (MONO), all the single-atom molecules we cut must have deg at least 2, and those of deg 2 must have two fixed ends either both being top or both being bottom (or non-serial for O-atoms, due to regularity). Similarly, all the {33} molecules$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { + } \}$and$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { - } \}$cut in Definition 12.1 (3) must be {33A}, because at the time it is cut, (MONO) implies that the${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + } \not \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$must be an ov-parent of m with no C-top fixed end, and$\mathfrak { m } ^ { - } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$must be an ov-child of m with no C-bottom fixed end (in particular, if we cut m as free from$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$, then$\{ \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$will become an elementary {2} molecule). This proves that all molecules we cut are elementary, and$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$

Proof of (2). If M has only deg 4 atoms, then the first cutting in M must create a {4} molecule; at any time thereafter, M will contain at least one non-deg-4 atom (cf. Remark 10.6), and by Definition 12.1 $( 2 )  { - } ( 3 )$, any subsequent cutting will not create any {4} molecule (the n chosen in Definition 12.1 (2) must have deg$_ { 3 ; }$also any${ \mathfrak { m } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$will have deg at most 3 when it is cut in Definition 12.1 (3), because m has an ov-parent in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has already been cut before). The same holds true for any M that contains non-deg-4 atoms initially, in which case we do not get any {4} molecule. This proves (2).

Proof of (3). Here and in the proof of (4) below we assume M has no deg 2 atoms. We claim that if $\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } = 0$then necessarily also$\# _ { \{ 2 \} } = 0$. Assume the contrary, consider the first atom m that has deg 2 when it is cut, and consider the cutting operation that turns m into deg 2, which must be cutting a single atom p (otherwise p would belong to a {33A} molecule). Note that m must have deg 3 at the time p is cut (because cutting p only generates one fixed end at m, see Proposition 10.4 (2)), and p also has deg 3 or 4 when it is cut (it cannot have deg 2 because m is the first). If p has deg 4 when it is cut (so {p} is cut as a {4} molecule), then by the proof in (2) we know that all atoms must have deg 4 initially, and p must the first atom cut; but that would imply that m has deg 4 at the time p is cut, contradiction.

We now know that {p} is cut as a {3} molecule, and both p and m have deg 3 at the time p is cut. As p must be an ov-parent or ov-child of m at this time (because cutting p creates a fixed end at m), by Definition 12.1 (3), we know that we should have cut p together with another atom instead of cutting it alone as a {3} molecule, contradiction.

Next, define$\sigma : = \# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } } - 3 | \mathbb { M } |$and consider its increment under cutting operations, where$\# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } }$is the number of bonds plus the number of free ends (not counting fixed ends), and |M| is the number of (remaining) atoms in M. It is straightforward to check that cutting a {2}, {33}, {3} and {4} molecule increases the value of σ by 1, 1, 0 and −1. For example, cutting a {4} molecule turns 4 bonds/free ends into fixed ends when there is no O-atom (the case of O-atoms is similar and the result is the same) which decreases$\# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } }$by 4, and also decreases |M| by 1, leading to$\Delta \sigma = - 1$. In view of the initial and final values of$\sigma _ { : }$, we then get

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} - (\# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 A \}}) = \sigma_ {\mathrm{init}} = | \mathbb {M} | - | \mathbb {M} _ {3} | - \# _ {\mathrm{bond}},\tag{12.1}
$$

where$\sigma _ { \mathrm { i n i t } }$is the initial value of$\sigma$(with final value$\sigma _ { \mathrm { f i n } } = 0 )$,$\# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } }$is the number of bonds (initially) in M and$\left| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } \right|$is the number of deg 3 atoms; here the last equality is because each atom has deg 3 or 4, and each bond is exactly counted twice, so$\# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } } = \mathrm { ( t o t a l ~ d e g ~ }$of all$\mathrm { a t o m s ) - \# _ { b o n d } = 4 | \mathbb { M } | - | \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | - \# _ { b o n d } } .$

Since M is connected, we know$| \mathbb { M } | - \# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } } \leq 1$, with equality if and only if M is a tree. Now, if $\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } = 0$(thus$\# _ { \{ 2 \} } = 0 )$, then we have$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } + | \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | = | \mathbb { M } | - \# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } }$by (12.1), which is only possible when $| \mathbb { M } | - \# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } } = 1$(so M is a tree) and$| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | \le 1 ;$; conversely, if M is a tree and has at most one deg 3 atom, then$| \mathbb { M } | - \# _ { \mathrm { b o n d } } = 1$and$| \mathbb { M } _ { 3 } | + \# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$by (2), so we get$\# _ { \{ 2 \} } = \# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } = 0$. This proves (3).

Proof of (4). Finally we prove (4). Following UP, we first cut${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$as free, which is either the only deg 3 atom, or some deg 4 atom in M; note that this does not create any deg 2 atom (because it creates at most one fixed end at any atom, see Proposition 10.4 (2)). In the subsequent cuttings, consider the first {33A} molecule (which exists due to (2)) and the two fixed ends$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } )$at it, which are created when cutting previous atoms${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$as free, and neither${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$nor${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$has deg 2 when it is cut, by the same proof in (3). If${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \neq { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$, say${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$is cut before${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 } .$then there exist two free ends$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$in the elementary molecules$\displaystyle \{ { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \}$ and$\displaystyle \left. \mathfrak { p } _ { 2 } \right.$respectively (i.e. with$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$belonging to the same ov-segment as$e _ { 1 }$in the original molecule, and same for$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } )$, such that$z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } = z _ { e _ { 1 } }$and$z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } = z _ { e _ { 2 } }$(cf. Remark 8.17; see also Figure 42).

![](images/page_128_image_3.jpg)

Figure 42. The proof of Proposition 12.2 (4). Here both${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } = { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$is cut as free before the $\mathrm { \{ 3 3 A \} }$molecule$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$(and thus$\prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \ \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$as in Definition$8 . 1 6 )$, so there exist free ends$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$in$\displaystyle \left\{ { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \right\}$such that we have$z _ { e _ { 1 } } = z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$and$z _ { e _ { 2 } } = z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$for the fixed ends$e _ { 1 }$and $e _ { 2 }$in$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \}$(cf. Remark 8.17), which leads to the splitting.

We perform the splitting by considering the dichotomy:

$$
\text { either } \quad | x _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} | \leq \varepsilon^ {1 - v} \quad \text { or } \quad | x _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}} - x _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}} | > \varepsilon^ {1 - v}.
$$

In the former case, we may insert the corresponding indicator function, and this extra restriction implies that$\displaystyle \left. \mathfrak { p } _ { 2 } \right.$is cut as a good {3} molecule due to Definition 9.4 (note that${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$is cut before$\mathfrak { p } _ { 2 } )$. In the latter case we have$| x _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } | = | x _ { e _ { 1 } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } } | > \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$, and this extra restriction implies that the {33A} molecule is good due to Definition 9.4.

Similarly, if${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } = { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$, then both$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$are free ends at${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$. Moreover, if${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$is an O-atom, then$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$ cannot be serial (otherwise the two atoms in the {33A} molecule are connected by an ov-segment containing both$( e _ { 1 } , e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } )$and$( e _ { 2 } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } )$and goes through${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$, so they are connected by two diferent ov-segments, violating Proposition 10.4 (2)). We then perform the same splitting; if$| x _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$, then$\displaystyle \left\{ { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 } \right\}$is cut as a good {3} or {4} molecule due to Definition 9.4; if$| x _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } | = | x _ { e _ { 1 } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } } | > \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$, then again the {33A} molecule is good due to Definition 9.4. This completes the proof.□

Now, with the UP algorithm, we can already prove the first simple case of Proposition 9.7, namely when $| H | \geq ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ,$see Proposition 12.3. In this case the proof is easy due to the positive term$| H |$in (9.51).

Proposition 12.3. Proposition 9.7 is true in the case when$| H | \geq ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho .$

Proof. Under the assumption$| H | \geq ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho .$, we simply cut the whole molecule M using UP. By Definition 9.4 we know that$\# _ { \mathrm { b a d } } = \# _ { \{ 4 \} } + \# _ { \mathrm { e e } }$, where$\# \mathrm { { e e } }$is the number of empty ends. Recall (9.51) in Proposition

9.7. We shall prove that$\nu : = | H | - \# _ { \left\{ 4 \right\} } - \# _ { \mathrm { e e } } \geq 0$, and that (note that$d - 1 \geq 1$and$C _ { 1 3 } ^ { * } \gg C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * }$, so (12.2) is stronger than (9.51))

$$

$$

In the proof below, in Part 1 we will show$\nu \geq 0$by using Proposition 12.2 and bounding the number of connected components of M by$| H |$(the empty ends will be trivial), which is done by repeatedly iterating Proposition 10.4 (5)–(7) and showing that every component of M must intersect a particle line in$H ,$a process we call the (PL) argument below. In Parts 2–3, by using Proposition 10.4 (9), we will show that either$\nu \gtrsim | H |$(i.e. the number of components of M is strictly less than$| H | )$, or a constant percentage of these components contain cycles or initial links. In the former case we already gain enough powers, while in the latter case we can obtain suficiently many good molecules either by Proposition 12.2 (4) or by exploiting the initial links.

Proof part 1. We first prove$\nu \geq 0$. By Proposition 12.2 (2) we have$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq \# \mathrm { c o m p } .$, where$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } }$is the number of components of$\mathbb { M } ,$so it sufices to show$\# \mathrm { c o m p } + \# \mathrm { e e } \leq | H |$. Here we present an argument which will be used many times later in diferent variants, which we refer to as the (PL) argument below (see Figure 43). Start from any component W of M; by Proposition$1 0 . 4 \ : ( 5 )$, this$W$must intersect a particle line $\pmb { p } \in p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for some$\ell ^ { \prime } .$. By Proposition 10.4 (7), this$\pmb { p }$is equal to or connected to some$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } )$via $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 } ;$in either case$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$also intersects W (note that each particle line can intersect at most one component of$\mathbb { M } ,$, see Remark 10.5). We then replace$\pmb { p }$by$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$and repeat the same argument to get$p ^ { \prime \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } + 2 } )$and so on, in the end we see that W must intersect a particle line$\pmb { q } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell } ) = H$(in particular this$q \in H$is not an empty end). Since each$\pmb q$intersects at most one component of M, this shows that$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } }$is bounded by the number of particle lines in H that are not empty ends.

Proof part 2. Now we have$\nu \geq | H | - \# \mathrm { c o m p } - \# \mathrm { e e } \geq 0$, it sufices to prove (12.2). Define

• X to be the number of particle lines in H that are connected to another particle line in H via M,

We claim that

In fact, by Proposition 10.4 (9), each particle line p in H either (i) belongs to the X particle lines listed above, or (ii) is not connected to other particle lines in H but is connected to a cycle, or (iii) does not belong to (i) or (ii) but forms an initial link. In (iii), suppose p forms an initial link that involves$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$as in Definition 3.19, then each$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$corresponds to a unique p (otherwise they are again in (i)), and the number of$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$is at most$2 Z + 2 \cdot \# \mathrm { e e }$(those$Z$initial links not involving empty ends contribute at most 2Z choices of$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$, and those initial links involving empty ends contribute at most $4 \cdot \# _ { \mathrm { e e } }$choices of$\pmb { p } ^ { \prime }$because each empty end belongs to at most two initial links). Consider all components of M (indexed by some α), and the number of particle lines in H intersecting each component (denoted by$m _ { \alpha } )$; by the above proof we have$m _ { \alpha } \geq 1$. Proof part 3. Next we prove that

$$

As the left hand side of (12.6) is strictly positive and is trivially$\geq 1$, this proves (12.2).

12.2. Strong degeneracies. From now on we only need to consider the case$| H | < ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } { \cdot } \rho$in Proposition $9 . 7$(we will make this assumption until the end of Section 13), and the goal is to prove (9.51). $$
(v / 2) \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{good}} - d \cdot \# _ {\{4 \}} \geq (C _ {1 3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho .\tag{12.7}
$$

In this subsection we treat the case of suficiently many strong degeneracies (Definition 12.4 below), see Proposition 12.5 (also cf. Section 11.7.3). For technical reasons (explained in the proof of Proposition 12.5 below) we also need the extra notion of primitivity in Definition 12.4 below.

Definition 12.4. Let M be a molecule as in Proposition 10.4. Define a pair of atoms$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$in M to be strongly degenerate if

(i) They are ov-adjacent and in the same layer$( \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ] = \ell [ { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } ] )$

(ii) There exist edges$( e , e ^ { \prime } )$at n and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$respectively, such that cutting$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$as free in M and turning $( e , e ^ { \prime } )$into fixed ends results in a {33A} molecule, as in Definition 8.11;

We also define an atom pair$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$in M to be primitive, if they are in the same layer$\left( \ell [ \mathfrak { n } ] = \ell [ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } ] \right)$, n is ov-parent of${ \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ,$and there do not exist C-atoms${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j } \left( 1 \leq j \leq r \right)$with$r \geq 1$, such that$\mathfrak { q } _ { j + 1 }$is ov-child of${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j }$ for each$j$with${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { 0 } = { \mathfrak { n } }$and$\mathfrak { q } _ { r + 1 } = \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime }$

Proposition 12.5. Recall Definition 12.4. Suppose we make the further restriction that M contains at least$( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho$disjoint strongly degenerate primitive pairs (by inserting the corresponding indicator function $\mathbb { 1 } _ { \mathrm { s t r . d e g . p r m } } \big )$, then Proposition 9.7 is true.

Proof. Recall$| H | < ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho$and the goal is to prove (12.7). The idea is to restrict suficiently many strong degeneracies to a single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(by definition, the two atoms in any strongly degenerate pair must be in the same layer), and cut most of the atoms involved in these degeneracies as {3} molecules which will be good due to the extra restrictions given by strong degeneracy, see Choice 3 below. If this is not possible, then there must exist suficiently many cycles in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(i.e.$Y \gtrsim \rho$in our notions below), so we can try to gain from the cyclic clusters using Proposition 12.2 (4), see Choice 2. If this is also not possible, then$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$ must have many components (i.e.$X \gtrsim \rho$in our notions below); in this case we can cut each pair of strongly degenerate atoms as a good {44} molecule, see Choice 1. However, we need to make sure that cutting this {44} molecule does not violate the (MONO) property needed to execute the UP algorithm, which then naturally leads to the notion of primitive atom pairs in Definition 12.4.

First assume there exists at least$\mathfrak { A } : = ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { \ast } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho$disjoint strongly degenerate primitive pairs. By splitting into at most$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \mathfrak { A } }$sub-cases (i.e. decomposing 1 into the corresponding indicator functions), we may fix one choice of these pairs. By using pigeonhole principle and replacing A with${ \mathfrak { L } } ^ { - 1 } \cdot { \mathfrak { A } }$, we may restrict all these atom pairs$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$to a single layer, say$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Define$\mathbb { Q }$to be the union of all connected omponents of $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that contain at least one strongly degenerate primitive pair$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$. We then

(i) Cut$\mathbb { Q }$as free, then cut$\mathbb { M } _ { > \ell ^ { \prime } }$as free from$\mathbb { M } \backslash \mathbb { Q }$and cut it into elementary molecules using UP;

(ii) Then cut$\mathbb { M } _ { < \ell ^ { \prime } } \cup ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \backslash \mathbb { Q } )$into elementary molecules using DOWN.

It is easy to see that this can always be done, and the contribution of these steps (i.e. coming from atoms outside$\mathbb { Q } )$to$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$is at most$2 | H |$. This because the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { > \ell ^ { \prime } } \mathrm { ~ i s \le ~ } | H |$by repeating the (PL) argument in the proof of Proposition 12.3 (i.e. starting with a particle line intersecting one component and iteratively applying Proposition 10.4 (7)), and moreover each$f u l l$component of$\mathbb { M } _ { < \ell ^ { \prime } } \cup ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \backslash \mathbb { Q } )$after the rest has been cut must also be a full component in the original molecule$\mathbb { M }$(see Remark 10.6) and there are at most$| H |$of them, so the upper bound on$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$follows from Proposition 12.2 (2).

Now we only need to cut$\mathbb { Q }$into elementary molecules. For each connected component$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$of$\mathbb { Q } ,$consider the clusters in$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$as defined in Proposition 10.4 (4) (i.e. ov-components of the set of C-atoms in$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime } )$; denote these clusters by$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$, then$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$is formed by joining these$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$with O-atoms. Denote by$X$the number of components of$\mathbb { Q } ,$and by$Y$the total number of$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$that are cyclic (i.e.$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } _ { j } ) > 0$or$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$contains a cycle).

Depending on the sizes of X and$Y _ { \textrm { : } }$we may then choose to perform one of the following three cutting sequences.

Choice 1: in this choice we will gain from X. For each component$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$of$\mathbb { Q } .$choose one pair$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$in${ \mathrm { i t } } ,$ then cut$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$as free (Figure 45), which is a good {44} molecule due to the restrictions$| x _ { e _ { j } } - x _ { e _ { i } ^ { \prime } } | \overset { \cdot } { \leq } \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$ and$| v _ { e _ { j } } - v _ { e _ { i } ^ { \prime } } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { 1 - \upsilon }$. Recall that$S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } }$is the set of descendants of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$. We next prove that${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$has no ov-parent ${ \mathfrak { q } } \neq { \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$that is a C-atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } }$. In fact, if such a q exists, then q is a descendant of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$, so there exist a path from${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$to q by iteratively taking children. This path forms a cycle together with the ov-segments from q to ${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$and from${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$. As the cycle belongs to a single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, by Proposition 10.4 (3) it must be formed by ov-segments connecting C-atoms; in particular, by considering the path between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$and q, we see that the ${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j }$must exist as in Definition 12.4, so$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$is not primitive, contradicting our assumption that$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$ is a strongly degenerate primitive pair.

Now, we have proved that the above q does not exist; this implies that, after cutting$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$as free, there is no C-top fixed end in$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n _ { \lambda } } }$(recall that${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \in S _ { { \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } } )$, and no C-bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } }$, in particular the monotonicity property (MONO) in Proposition 12.2 is true. Since this property is preserved under UP, we can then repeat the steps in Definition 12.1 (3) and subsequently apply UP to the rest of$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$to cut it into elementary molecules. By applying this to each component$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$of$\mathbb { Q } ,$, we obtain$\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } \geq X$and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 0$
