$$
\sigma_ {\text { init }} = | \mathbb {Q} ^ {\prime} | - \# _ {\text { bond }} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {q} (1 - \rho (\mathbb {Q} _ {j})) - (q - 1) = 1 - \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {q} \rho (\mathbb {Q} _ {j}),\tag{12.9}
$$

where$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } _ { j } )$is the circuit rank of the C-molecule$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$(to see this, just note that joining two C-molecules by an O-atom decreases the value of$| \mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime } | - \# \mathrm { b o n d }$by 1 as it increases |Q<sup>′</sup>| by 1 and increases$- \# \mathrm { _ { b o n d } }$by 2, while value of$| \mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime } | - \# \mathrm { b o n d }$before introducing any O-atom equals$\scriptstyle \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { q } ( 1 - \rho ( \mathbb { Q } _ { j } ) )$by definition).

Now by adding up (12.8) and (12.9) for each component$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$, and note that$0 \leq \rho ( \mathbb { Q } _ { j } ) \leq \Gamma$with$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } _ { j } ) > 0$ if and only if$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$is cyclic, we conclude that

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} - (\# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 A \}}) \geq X - \Gamma \cdot Y
$$

(recall X is the number of components$\mathbb { Q } ^ { \prime }$, and$Y$is the number of cyclic$\mathbb { Q } _ { j } )$; since also$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq X$, we then have

$$
\left(\text { number   of   molecules   that   are   not } \{3 \}\right) = \# _ {\{4 \}} + \left(\# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 A \}}\right) \leq X + \Gamma \cdot Y.
$$

In particular, by excluding this many exceptions, we see that the number of pairs$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$such that both${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$ and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$are cut as$\{ \boldsymbol { \mathcal { 3 } } \}$molecules is at least${ \mathfrak { L } } ^ { - 1 } \cdot { \mathfrak { A } } - 2 ( X + \Gamma Y )$

For each such pair$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$, if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$is cut before${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$, since$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$is cut as a {3} molecule, we know that$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$ must be good due to the restriction$| x _ { e _ { j } } - x _ { e _ { i } ^ { \prime } } | \leq \varepsilon ^ { \mathrm { { i } } - { \upsilon } }$and Definition 9.4. Here when${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime }$is O-atom, the edge $e _ { j } ^ { \prime }$cannot be serial with the bonds between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ^ { \prime } .$otherwise$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \}$will not be regular (and thus not a {33A} molecule) after turning$e _ { j } ^ { \prime }$into a fixed end. In this way we get$\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } \geq \mathfrak { L } ^ { - 1 } \cdot \mathfrak { A } - 2 ( X + \Gamma Y )$and $\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq X$

Summing up, by choosing one of the Choices 1–3, we get

$$
\begin{array}{l} (v / 2) \cdot (\# _ {\text { good }}) - d \cdot \# _ {\{4 \}} \geq \max \left((v / 2) X, (v / 2) Y - d \cdot X, (\mathfrak {L} ^ {- 1} v / 2) \mathfrak {A} - (d + 1) (X + \Gamma Y)\right) \geq (C _ {2} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \mathfrak {A}, \\ \text { which   proves   (12.7)   as } \mathfrak {A} = (C _ {1 2} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \rho . \end{array}\tag{12.10}
$$

Note that Proposition 12.5 deals with the case where there exist many strongly degenerate primitive pairs. As for the non-primitive pairs, it turns out that they always lead to good molecules if they are cut as {33A} as shown in the following lemma.

Lemma 12.6. For each {33A} molecule$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$obtained in any cutting sequence after any deletion of$O \mathrm { . }$ atoms, if the atom pair$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is not primitive in M before any operation, then by splitting into 2 sub-cases, we can either make this {33A} molecule good, or cut it into a good {3} and a normal {2} molecule.

Proof. Consider any {33A} molecule$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$that is not primitive before any operation, and let${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j }$be as in Definition 12.4. Note that n and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$must belong to the same (original) layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(otherwise$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is good by Definition 9.4), and so does every${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j }$. Consider the cycle formed by the ov-segments from${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j }$to$\mathfrak { q } _ { j + 1 }$(with ${ \mathfrak { n } } = { \mathfrak { q } } _ { 0 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } = { \mathfrak { q } } _ { r + 1 } )$and from$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$to n, which is contained in the single layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. By Proposition 10.4 (3), we see that both n and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$must be C-atom. Moreover the C-atoms${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { j } ,$and the ov-adjacency relations between them, are not afected by deletion of O-atoms. Now, consider the C-atom${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { 1 }$which is ov-child of${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$ and$\mathfrak { q } _ { r }$which is ov-parent of$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$(they could be the same atom).

Consider any cutting sequence. If${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { 1 }$, or any (O-) atom r in the ov-segment between$\mathfrak { q } _ { 1 }$and n is cut before$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$(i.e. belongs to a molecule after cutting that is$\prec _ { \mathrm { c u t } } \{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \} )$, then we can make the splitting depending on whether$\mathrm { ( i ) } \ \lvert t _ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \rvert \geq \varepsilon ^ { v }$or (ii)$\lvert t _ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \rvert \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$. In case (i) the$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is already good by Definition 9.4; in case (ii), due to the ov-child relations we have

$$
t _ {\mathfrak {n}} \geq t _ {\mathfrak {r}} \geq t _ {\mathfrak {q} _ {1}} \geq \dots \geq t _ {\mathfrak {q} _ {r + 1}} = t _ {\mathfrak {n} ^ {\prime}},
$$

in particular$\lvert t _ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \rvert \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$implies that

$$
\left| t _ {\mathfrak {n}} - t _ {\mathfrak {r}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {v}, \quad \left| t _ {\mathfrak {n} ^ {\prime}} - t _ {\mathfrak {r}} \right| \leq \varepsilon^ {v}.
$$

Now we may cut either n or$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$from$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$as a {3} molecule such that the remaining atom becomes a {2} molecule (one of the two choices must be possible due to the definition of {33A} molecules), then this {3} molecule will be good by Definition 9.4, so the lemma is proved.

In the same way, if$\mathfrak { q } _ { r }$, or any (O-) atom r in the ov-segment between$\mathfrak { q } _ { r }$and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$is cut before$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$, then the lemma is also proved by the same arguments as above.

Finally, if none of${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { q } } _ { r }$and none of the above-mentioned O-atoms is cut before$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$, then at the time $\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is cut, the atom n cannot have any bottom fixed end (because it is ov-parent of$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$, and the ov-segment between n and$\mathfrak { q } _ { 1 }$does not lead to any fixed end at n as the other atoms on this ov-segment are all cut after n); in the same way n<sup>′</sup> has no top fixed end at the time$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is cut. However$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is a {33} molecule, which means that n must have a top fixed end and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$has a bottom fixed end, and thus$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$will be a {33B} molecule instead of {33A}, contradiction. This completes the proof.□

Reduction 1. With Propositions 12.3 and 12.5 and Lemma 12.6 proved, from now on, we may always assume in Proposition 9.7 tha$| H | \leq ( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho$and the number of disjoint strongly degenerate primitive pairs is at most$( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho .$

Using also Lemma 12.6, we see that each {33A} molecule must be good with at most$( C _ { 1 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \rho$exceptions (these exceptions are when the corresponding atom pair is both strongly degenerate and primitive; if it is not strongly degenerate then we get a good molecule by Definition 9.4, if it is not primitive we get a good molecule by Lemma 12.6).

As such, we see that Proposition 9.7 will follow if we can prove that

$$
(v / 2) \cdot (\# _ {\mathrm{good}}) - d \cdot (\# _ {\{4 \}}) \geq (C _ {1 1} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho\tag{12.11}
$$

under the assumption that all {33A} molecules are good, which we will assume throughout the rest of the proof.

12.3. Layer refinement and the large R case. The goal of this subsection is to introduce the layer refining process (discussed in Section 11.7.2) and prove the next case of Proposition 9.7 when R is large, namely Proposition 12.11. The following lemma is already stated in Section 11.7.2:

Lemma 12.7. Let M be a connected molecule with$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) \leq \Gamma$, see Definition 3.13. Then we can divide M into at most$\Gamma + 1$disjoint subsets$\mathbb { M } _ { ( k ) }$for$1 \leq k \leq \gamma \leq \Gamma + 1$, such that (i) each$\mathbb { M } _ { ( k ) }$is a tree, and (ii) if$k < k ^ { \prime }$then no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { ( k ) }$can be parent of any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { ( k ^ { \prime } ) }$. See Figure 47. Note that, unlike the original layer defined by time intervals, there is no time inequality between atoms in diferent thin layers within the same original layer, other than those coming from parent-child relations.

Figure 47. Left: example of layer refining (Lemma 12.7, each thin layer is a forest). Right: the proof of Lemma 12.7. Note that${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$are connected by a path above n (forming a cycle); also$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$consists of those atoms that can be connected to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$without entering$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$

Proof. We induct on$\rho ( \mathbb { M } )$. If$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) = 0$then M is a tree and there is nothing to prove. If$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) > 0$, then M must contain a cycle of atoms. Let a lowest atom in this cycle be n, which is adjacent to two atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$ and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$in this cycle, then both${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$must be parents of n. Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n (including n itself), we then define

M<sub>high</sub> := m ∈ M : m is connected to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$by a path not containing atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$

(12.12)

and$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } : = \mathbb { M } \backslash \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$, see Figure 47. Note in particular$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$and$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } } \ \left( \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } } \right.$because any atom in the cycle other than n cannot belong to$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$. Clearly$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$is connected, because for any m$\in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$and any${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$on the path connecting m to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$defined by (12.12), we must also have$\mathfrak { m } ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 }$by definition, so each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$is connected to$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$by a path completely within$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$

To prove$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$is connected, choose any atom$\mathfrak { m } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. Since M is connected, there is a path in M connecting m to n. Let the first atom in this path (starting from m) that belongs to$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be p, and consider any atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \neq { \mathfrak { p } }$between m and p on this path, then m is connected to q by a path not containing atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$, which means${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$(as${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$would imply m${ \bf \Psi } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } } )$. Thus we know each m$\in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is connected to an atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$by a path completely within$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$, but$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is connected (every atom in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is connected to n by a path completely within$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$, so$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$is also connected.

Moreover, if an atom$\mathfrak { m } _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$is connected to an atom$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$by a bond, then we must have ${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 2 } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$(otherwise$\mathfrak { m } _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$would imply$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } } )$. This means m must be a parent of m , since otherwise${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { 1 }$is a child of m<sub>2</sub>, so$\mathfrak { m } _ { 2 } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$implies$\mathfrak { m } _ { 1 } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$, which is impossible. Finally, since there are at least two bonds between$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$(those connecting n to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and n<sub>2</sub>), we see that

$$
| \mathbb {M} | = | \mathbb {M} _ {\mathrm{high}} | + | \mathbb {M} _ {\mathrm{low}} |, | \mathcal {B} | \geq | \mathcal {B} _ {\mathrm{high}} | + | \mathcal {B} _ {\mathrm{low}} | + 2 \Rightarrow \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {\mathrm{high}}) + \rho (\mathbb {M} _ {\mathrm{low}}) \leq \rho (\mathbb {M}) - 1 \leq \Gamma - 1,
$$

where B (resp.$B _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$and$\boldsymbol { B } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } )$is the set of bonds in M (resp.$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } )$. We now apply induction hypothesis to$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } .$, and note that no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } }$is parent of an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } }$, to divide M into at most$\left( \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { h i g h } } ) + 1 \right) + \left( \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { l o w } } ) + 1 \right) \leq \Gamma + 1$subsets that satisfy requirements (i) and (ii), so the proof is complete.□

With Lemma 12.7 we can then define the full layer refining process. The idea is to delete those O-atoms joining two cyclic clusters (or cyclic components), so that each component contains at most one cyclic cluster after the deletions; in particular each component will have$\rho$value at most Γ, so we can apply Lemma 12.7 to each component.

Definition 12.8 (Layer refining). Let M be a molecule formed by layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, as in Proposition 10.4. We define the following operation of layer refining to turn$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$into a new layered molecule$\widetilde { \mathbb { M } } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Here the atoms and edges of$\widetilde { \mathbb { M } } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$are the same as$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$except some O-atoms being deleted as in Definition 8.1 (for convenience, we will not distinguish between$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$and$\widetilde { \mathbb { M } } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$below), but the layering of the atoms are diferent: the atoms in$\widetilde { \mathbb { M } } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$are divided into at most$\Gamma + 2$disjoint subsets, each of them indicated by a refined layer number. We will call these thin layers. The layer refining process is defined as follows:

(1) Recall all the clusters (i.e. C-molecules) in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. We repeatedly delete O-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, as long as each deletion disconnects two cyclic clusters$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$(i.e. these two clusters belong to diferent components after deletion), until no more O-atoms can be deleted. For each connected component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that does not contain a cyclic cluster, we assign thin layer$( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 )$to all its atoms; note that with this definition, the thin layer$( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 )$plays a special role diferent from those thin layers$( \ell ^ { \prime } , k )$for$k \geq 1$

(2) Apply Lemma 12.7 to each component$\mathbb { Q }$of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that contains a cyclic cluster (we are guaranteed to have$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } ) \leq \Gamma$, which will be proved in Proposition 12.9 below), to divide it into$\mathbb { Q } _ { k }$, where $1 \leq k \leq \Gamma + 1$. Then, for each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, assign it thin layer$( \ell ^ { \prime } , k )$if it belongs to$\mathbb { Q } _ { k }$for some component$\mathbb { Q } .$

The thin layers defined above are linearly ordered by lexicographic ordering (where we first compare$\ell ^ { \prime }$ and then compare$k )$; if layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$is not refined, we identify it with$( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 )$. Note that the original layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$ precisely contains all the thin layers$( \ell ^ { \prime } , k )$. For any$\zeta$and$\xi ,$we define$\mathbb { M } _ { \zeta } ^ { T }$to be the set of atoms with thin layer$\zeta ;$the associated notions$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \zeta : \xi ) } ^ { T } , \mathbb { M } _ { [ \zeta : \eta ] } ^ { T }$etc. are defined similarly.

In Proposition 12.9 below we state and prove some properties of the molecule M after layer refining. The important points are that (a) each thin layer after refinement is a forest, see Proposition 12.9 (3)–(4); (b) the number of O-atoms deleted is bounded by$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } : = \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$for the refined layers$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$, see Proposition 12.9 (1); and$( \mathrm { c ) }$the original properties of M (notably Proposition 10.4$( 5 ) \mathrm { - } ( 7 )$and (9)) still hold after layer refining, with a number of exceptions that is bounded by the number of deleted O-atoms, see Proposition 12.9 (5)–(8).

The proof of$\mathrm { { ( a ) - ( b ) } }$above relies on the construction in Definition 12.8, in particular the fact that we delete all O-atoms joining two cyclic clusters, so each component contains at most one cyclic cluster after layer refining; see Parts 1–2 in the proof of Proposition 12.9 below. The proof of (c) is straightforward, basically because deleting each O-atom creates at most two exceptions to the relevant properties in Proposition 12.9 (5)–(8), see Part 3 in the proof of Proposition 12.9 below.

Proposition 12.9. If we perform the layer refining for$\ell ^ { \prime }$as in Definition 12.8, then

(1) The number of O-atoms deleted in the process is at most$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } : = \rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$

(2) After deleting the O-atoms, each component Q of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that contains a cyclic cluster satisfies$\rho ( \mathbb { Q } ) \leq \Gamma$2 in particular Lemma 12.7 is applicable in Definition 12.8.

(3) Each$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T }$(where$1 \leq k \leq \Gamma + 1 )$is a forest, and has most$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$connected components.

(4)$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$is a forest, and the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$is not more than the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$before refining.

Now consider the result of refining any set of layers in M, which we still denote by M for convenience. Then we have the followings

(5) For$\zeta < \xi ,$, no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \zeta } ^ { T }$can be parent of any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \xi } ^ { T }$

(6) Each connected component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$(where$\ell ^ { \prime } \leq \ell )$must intersect some particle line$\pmb { p } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$

(7) With at most$2 \mathfrak { R } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$exceptions, for each particle line$\pmb { p } \in p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$, either p intersects a component of $\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$, or it intersects a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T }$for some$1 \leq k \leq \Gamma + 1 , \mathrm { o r } \ p \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$

(8) Recall$\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { R } = \sum _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \mathfrak { R } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } } \end{array}$. For each$\ell ^ { \prime } < \ell ,$with at most 2R exceptions, each particle line$\pmb { p } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$either forms an initial link within$\mathbb { M } _ { < ( \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 , 0 ) } ^ { T }$, or is connected to a cycle or another particle line$p ^ { \prime } \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$ via the subset$\mathbb { M } _ { < ( \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 , 0 ) } ^ { T } .$

Proof. Proof part 1. First note the following facts about the refinement in Definition 12.8:

(i) Deleting any O-atom o in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$always breaks a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$into two;

(ii) Each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$that does not contain a cyclic cluster remain the same after refining. Each of the other components after refining contains a unique cyclic cluster.

In fact, (i) is true because if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$are the two atoms adjacent to o along two ov-segments in two diferent particle lines, then they cannot be connected after deleting o, otherwise we get a cycle (before deleting o) in view of the two bonds from o to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } ( j \in \{ 1 , 2 \} )$, such that the two bonds at o are not serial in the cycle, contradicting Proposition 10.4 (3). Also (ii) is obvious by our construction (each component not containing cyclic clusters is not afected, and each component after refining cannot contain two cyclic clusters, otherwise we would be able to delete one more O-atom).

Proof part 2. Next we prove (1)–(4). Note first that the number of cyclic clusters in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$does not exceed$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(because each cyclic cluster contributes one the to the value of$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } ) )$. Now (1) is easy because each deletion increases the number of cyclic components by 1 (due to (i) above), and this number cannot exceed$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$which is the total number of cyclic clusters (imagine we delete all O-atoms, then the number of cyclic components would be equal to$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$, so the number of O-atoms deleted cannot exceed$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$. Moreover, (2) follows from the fact that each component contains only one cyclic cluster (the other clusters are trees and do not add to the$\rho$value, and joining the clusters by O-atoms also does not increase the$\rho$value).

Also (4) is obvious because$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$has not been afected by the deletion of O-atoms, and is a forest because it does not contain any cyclic cluster (cf. Proposition 10.4 (3)). As for (3), the number of components of $\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T } \left( k \geq 1 \right)$is at most$\Re _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$because this is an upper bound for the number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$containing one cyclic cluster; also each$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T } \left( k \geq 1 \right)$is a forest which directly follows from Lemma 12.7.

Proof part 3. Now we prove (5)–(8), where we perform layer refining to any set of layers$\ell ^ { \prime } ,$and denote the result still by M. To prove (5), due to the lexicographic ordering of thin layers, we only need to prove it for a single layer$\ell ^ { \prime }$, and we only need to consider those components containing one cyclic cluster$\mathbb { Q } _ { j }$ (otherwise all thin layers are$( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) )$. But by definition, this follows from Lemma 12.7 (for each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$and the fact that no bond exists between diferent components of$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$

Next we prove (6)–(7). Note that particle lines can be defined in the same way before and after the refinement, since deleting an O-atom corresponds to removing one atom from a particle line$\pmb { p }$and merging two consecutive edges. From Proposition 10.4 (5)–(7) we already know that before layer refining, any connected component in$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$must intersect some particle line$\pmb { p }$with$p \in r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$. This then proves (6) because$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , 0 ) } ^ { T }$is not afected by layer refining: there is no bond connecting it to any$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T }$for$k > 0$, and it also does not contain any of the O-atoms deleted in the refinement process. Similarly (7) follows from Proposition 10.4 (5)–(7): any particle line$\pmb { p } \in p ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$must either belong to$r ( \mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } )$, or intersects$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$(which is then divided into$\mathbb { M } _ { ( \ell ^ { \prime } , k ) } ^ { T }$for$0 \leq k \leq \Gamma + 1 )$. The only exceptions are those containing one of the deleted O-atoms, but the number of these particle lines is at most$2 \mathfrak { R } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } }$as each O-atom belongs to at most two particle lines.

Finally we prove (8). Note that before layer refining, this just corresponds to Proposition 10.4 (9); however, after the layer refinement, we have deleted at most R O-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$(note that by our conventions,$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$ is just$\mathbb { M } _ { < ( \ell ^ { \prime } + 1 , 0 ) } ^ { T }$after the refinement). If we add back these O-atoms one by one, then each time we create at most one cycle in one component, or merge at most two components of$\mathbb { M } _ { [ 1 : \ell ^ { \prime } ] }$, and does not afect any initial link. Define a particle line$\pmb { p }$to be single if it does not satisfy the requirement of (8), then adding back one O-atom at most reduces the number of single particle lines by 2 (for example, if adding back an O-atom merges two components, then it may turn two single particle lines into non-single as they are now connected to each other; the other particle lines are unafected, as they cannot intersect the relevant components by the single assumption). By Proposition 10.4 (9), it then follows that the number of single particle lines is at most 2R, as desired.□

Before stating and proving Proposition 12.11 below (i.e. the case$\Re \gtrsim \rho )$, we need one more auxiliary result concerning a special case of UP. The intuition will be explained in the proof of Proposition 12.11.

Proposition 12.10. Suppose M is a full molecule divided into two subsets$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, such that$( \mathrm { i } ) \mathbb { M } _ { U }$is a forest, and (ii) no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is parent of atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. Then, see Figure 48, after applying the algorithm UP, we have that$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$, and

$$
\# _ {\{4 \}} \leq \# _ {\operatorname{comp} (\mathbb {M})}, \quad \text { and } \quad \# _ {\{3 3 A \}} \geq \# _ {\operatorname{cyc.comp} (\mathbb {M} _ {D})} / 4.\tag{12.13}

Here the cyclic clusters in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$are shown, with${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$being the first atom in each component that has deg 2 when cut, and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$is its ov-parent; see the proof of Proposition 12.10 below.

Proof. The statements about #$\{ 3 3 B \}  , \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} }$and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$already follow from Proposition 12.2. Now we prove the statement about$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} }$. First we prove the following claim: if A is a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contains a cycle, and no atom in A belongs to a {33A} molecule, then at least one atom in A must be deg 2 when it is cut. To prove this claim, choose a cycle θ within A, we may think of θ as formed by ov-segments, and consider the endpoints of these ov-segments. Let n be the one among these endpoints that is cut after all the other endpoints, then n is ov-adjacent to other endpoints which are cut before n, which creates two fixed ends at n, so n must be deg 2 when it is cut.

Now, if A is as above, and suppose${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$is the first atom in A that has deg 2 when it is cut, and consider the cutting operation that turns n into deg 2. Then this cutting operation must involve an atom p that is ov-adjacent to n; note that this p belongs to either A or$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. If${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A$, then p cannot be deg 2 when it is cut (as n is the first); this p also cannot be deg 4 when it is cut (because we cut deg 4 only when every atom has deg 4, and cutting a deg 4 atom p cannot turn the deg 4 atom n into deg 2, cf. Proposition 10.4 (2)), so it must be deg 3 when it is cut, but n also must has deg 3 when p is cut, which violates Definition 12.1 (3).

Therefore we must have${ \mathfrak { p } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$. Since p is cut before n, it cannot be cut in Definition 12.1 (1) (as cutting any deg 2 C-atom in Definition 12.1 (1) requires that this atom has two bottom fixed ends, see also Remark 8.7), nor can it have deg 4 when it is cut (for the same reason as in the last paragraph). Suppose p belongs to$S _ { \mathfrak { q } }$for some q as in Definition 12.1 (3), since$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is a forest, we know that p has at most one parent in $S _ { \mathfrak { q } }$(otherwise we have two diferent paths going from p to q that form a cycle in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } )$, so it must have deg 3 when it is cut (the top edge at p corresponding to the non$S _ { \mathfrak { q } }$parent, as well as the two bottom edges at p, are not fixed when p is cut; see Figure 49), while at the same time n also has deg 3. By Definition 12.1 (3), we then know that p belongs to a {33A} molecule.

As a conclusion, we know that each component A of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contains a cycle, must either contain one atom in a {33A} molecule, or intersect a particle line of some atom in some {33A} molecule. Clearly each {33A} molecule can be so obtained by at most 4 components (as each particle line can intersect at most one component of${ \mathbb { M } } _ { D } .$, see Remark 10.5), so we get$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } \geq \# _ { \mathrm { c y c . c o m p ( M } _ { D } ) } / 4$□

12.4. Layer selection and weak degeneracies. From now on we will focus on proving (12.11) under the assumptions in Reduction 1. The goal of this subsection is to reduce this result to Proposition 12.18 (and prove Proposition 12.17 which contains the simple cases of initial cumulant and weak degeneracies), by applying the procedure of layer selection (discussed in Section 11.6).

The full layer selection process, defined in Definition 12.12 below, is essentially the same as the toy version in Definition 11.23 in Section 11. The only diference is that we need to perform layer refining for layers $\mathbb { M } _ { \ell ^ { \prime } } \left( \ell ^ { \prime } \le \ell _ { 1 } \right)$, which leads to an extra step of picking a thin layer$\zeta _ { U }$within layer$\mathbb { M } _ { \ell _ { 1 } }$, see Definition 12.12 (2). ## 13. Cutting algorithm II: analyzing UD molecules

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 12.18 for the two-layer molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$, by introducing the various algorithms corresponding to the toy models in Section 11. To simplify notation in this section, if a molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { U D } = \mathbb { M } _ { U } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$satisfies that (a) each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest and has no deg 2 atoms, and (b) no atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is parent of any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } .$, then we say it is a UD molecule. If in addition$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has no C-top fixed end and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no C-bottom fixed end, then we say$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$is canonical.

Reduction 2. Our proof below relies on the properties (3a)–(3c) in Proposition 12.15. For convenience we record them here:

(i) Each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest and has no deg 2 atoms. No atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a parent of any atom in $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and${ \mathbb M } _ { U } ~ ( \mathrm { r e s p . ~ } { \mathbb M } _ { D } )$has no C-top (resp. C-bottom) fixed end.

(ii) The number of full components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is at most$1 0 ( C _ { 5 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$. Each component in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$either has at least two bonds connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, or has one bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and one deg 3 atom.

(iii) There exist at least$( \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime } / 4 )$many UD connections, such that each UD connection is either connected to another UD connection via$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, or has its$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$endpoint belonging to component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contains a deg 3 atom.

13.1. The 2CONNUP algorithm and toy model III. We start by introducing the full 2CONNUP algorithm corresponding to toy model III. Compared to the toy version (Definition 11.21), the main extra ingredient is Definition 13.1 (1); see the proof of Proposition 13.2 for more explanations.

Definition 13.1 (The algorithm 2CONNUP). Define the following cutting algorithm 2CONNUP. It takes as input any canonical UD molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$, such that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no full component that has no bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. Define$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 1 }$to be the set of atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$that have deg 3 and are ov-adjacent to one atom m$\in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, such that no other$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$atom on the ov-segment between n and m has deg 3. Define$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$ to be the set of atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$that are ov-adjacent to two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$along two diferent particle lines, and$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } = \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } ^ { 1 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } ^ { 2 }$. For any such$\mathbb { M } = \mathbb { M } _ { U D }$, we define the cutting sequence as follows:

(1) If any (maximal) ov-segment contains at least$A : = 3 2 v ^ { - 2 }$atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$, then we choose$\mathfrak { n } _ { 0 }$to be any one of these atoms, and cut it as free. Repeat until no such ov-segment exists.

(2) If M contains any deg 2 atom n, then cut it as free, and repeat until there is no deg 2 atom left.

(3) Choose a lowest deg 3 atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$among all remaining deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(or a lowest atom in $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$if$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has no deg 3 atom). Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } ;$this n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$will be fixed until the end of (4).

(4) Now, starting from n, each time choose a highest atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. If m has deg 3, and m is ov-adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } }$that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ { \mathfrak { m } } , { \mathfrak { p } } \}$as free. Otherwise just cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$has been cut. Then$_ \mathrm { g o }$to (2).

(5) Repeat (2)–(4) until all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$has been cut. Then apply algorithm DOWN to cut the rest of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into elementary molecules.

We also define the dual algorithm 2CONNDN, by reversing the roles of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$and the notions of parent/child etc., just as how we define DOWN from UP in Definition 12.1.

The key estimate for the algorithm 2CONNUP is stated in the following proposition, which is the full version of Proposition 11.22 in Section 11.

Proposition 13.2. For the algorithm 2CONNUP, we have$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$, and

$$
(v / 2) \cdot \# _ {\{3 3 A \}} - d \cdot \# _ {\{4 \}} \geq C ^ {- 1} (| \mathbb {M} _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} ^ {1} | + | \mathbb {M} _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} ^ {2} |) - C \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{fucp} (\mathbb {M} _ {U})},\tag{13.1}
$$

where$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$is the number of full components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(note the diference with$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$, i.e. the number of all components). Recall also the notion of constant C in Definition 1.6 (2). Similar results hold for the dual algorithm 2CONNDN, if we reverse the roles of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Proof. We first explain the relevance of Definition 13.1 (1), see Figure 56. Note that, in Definition 11.21 where there is no O-atom, each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$is adjacent to two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, so there cannot be a bond containing two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$; however, now an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$is only ov-adjacent to two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$ so there might be other atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$within the ov-segment between it and atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$

![](images/page_151_image_7.jpg)

Figure 56. Illustration of Definition 13.1 (1). Here$( \lambda _ { 0 } , \lambda _ { j } , \lambda _ { j } ^ { \prime } )$are the ov-segments in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ connecting an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. They intersect at diferent$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$atoms; see also the auxiliary graph$G$on the right (G-edges correspond to intersections of these ov-segments in $\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } )$. Now$\lambda _ { 0 }$contains many atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$(i.e. has large degree in$G )$, so we choose one atom (the one with$\lambda _ { 3 }$here) and cut it, breaking both$\lambda _ { 0 }$and$\lambda _ { 3 }$but not the others. The point is that (i) the number of such operations is negligible, (ii) each operation breaks two ov-segments, so the total number of ov-segments broken is also negligible, and (iii) after Definition 13.1 (1), each ov-segment contains at most$O ( 1 )$atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$, so the same algorithm 2CONNUP will sufice. See Part 1 of the proof below.

If we still argue naively as in Definition 11.21, it might happen that we break an ov-segment containing many atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } ,$turning them into deg 2 simultaneously. This is undesirable, as we expect each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$to contribute a {33A} molecule in the proof of Proposition 11.22. To resolve this, we would like that each ov-segment contains at most$O ( 1 )$(more precisely$A = 3 2 v ^ { - 2 } )$atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } ;$this leads to the process in Definition 13.1 (1), where we cut and break any ov-segments not satisfying the above assumptions, so that the same arguments in Definition 11.21 will be suficient after such cuttings.

On the other hand, since$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no cycle, it is easy to see that we can define an auxiliary graph G in Part 1 below (with G-nodes being ov-segments and G-edges being atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$that are intersections of these ov-segments) which is a forest, so the average number of$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$atoms on all ov-segments is less than 2. As such, the number of ov-segments broken in Definition 13.1 (1) will be negligible and does not afect the subsequent proof, see the calculations in Part 2 below.

Proof part 1. We claim that throughout the algorithm 2CONNUP, the (MONO) property in Proposition 12.2 is preserved in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no C-bottom fixed end. In fact, the (MONO) property is proved in the same way as in Proposition 12.2 (which is also not afected by cutting the M atoms in Definition 13.1 (1), as they do not create C-top fixed end in$\mathbb { M } _ { U } )$. Regarding$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, note that cutting atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, or atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$which has two ov-segments connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U } .$, will not introduce C-bottom fixed end in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ;$as for cutting {m, p} as free in Definition 13.1 (4), it can be viewed as first cutting m and then cutting p, and p must be O-atom or have two top fixed ends (cf. Remark 8.7) when it is cut, so cutting p also does not introduce C-bottom fixed end in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. It then follows that we only have {2}, {3}, {4} and {33A} molecules, thus$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$. Now we only need to prove (13.1).

Consider the set L of all the maximal ov-segments λ that contain at least one atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and at least one atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } .$. Clearly each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } ^ { j } ( j \in \{ 1 , 2 \} )$) belongs to exactly j ov-segments in$\mathcal { L } ;$we define $\lambda \sim \lambda ^ { \prime }$if they intersects at an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$(note that they cannot intersect at two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$due to Proposition 10.4 (2)). There cannot exist$\lambda _ { 1 } , \cdots , \lambda _ { q } \in \mathcal { L }$such that$\lambda _ { j } \sim \lambda _ { j + 1 }$with$\lambda _ { q + 1 } = \lambda _ { 1 }$(otherwise, say$\lambda _ { j }$intersects$\lambda _ { j + 1 }$at atom$\mathfrak { n } _ { j } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$, then the ov-segments between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j + 1 }$along$\lambda _ { j + 1 }$forms a cycle in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, contradicting that M<sub>D</sub> is a tree). In other words, if we define the auxiliary graph G with G-nodes$\lambda \in { \mathcal { L } }$and G-edges$( \lambda , \lambda ^ { \prime } )$where$\lambda \sim \lambda ^ { \prime }$, then this G is a forest, see Figure 57.

Recall by Definition 8.3 that, if any atom (or any two atoms) in$\lambda \in { \mathcal { L } }$is cut as free, then we either get a {33A} molecule, or get a fixed end at each remaining atom in λ. In this case we say λ is broken. Note that each cutting in Definition 13.1 (1)–(4) breaks at most two λ, and each cutting in Definition 13.1 (2) does not break any λ. Moreover, if a cutting in Definition 13.1 (2)–(4) breaks some λ, then this breaking must be due to cutting an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(this is because, in Definition 13.1 (4), if we cut$\{ { \mathfrak { m } } , { \mathfrak { p } } \}$as free, then this is equivalent to first cutting m and then cut p, and p will have deg 2 when it is cut, so cutting p will not break any$\lambda \in { \mathcal { L } } )$. In particular, if a cutting in Definition 13.1 (2)–(4) breaks both λ and$\lambda ^ { \prime } ,$then they must intersect at an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, so we must have$\lambda \not \sim \lambda ^ { \prime }$by Proposition 10.4 (2).

Now suppose$\lambda \sim \lambda ^ { \prime }$, and λ is broken before λ<sup>′</sup>, and λ<sup>′</sup> is broken in a cutting operation in Definition 13.1 (4), then this cutting operation must involve some m$\in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$that belongs to λ<sup>′</sup>. Suppose m$\mathbf { \Sigma } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is as in Definition 13.1 (4) and does not have deg$^ { 4 , }$since$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is a forest, we know that m has at most one parent in $S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$, so m must have deg 3 when it is cut in Definition 13.1 (4) (because m has two bottom non-fixed edges and one top non-fixed edge corresponding to its parent not in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } .$just as before). Let$\mathfrak { p } = \lambda \cap \lambda ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } ,$ then the previously broken λ provides a fixed end at p, so p also has deg 3 at the time when m is cut. By construction in Definition 13.1 (4), we get a {33A} molecule with higher atom m, such that${ \mathfrak { m } } \in \lambda ^ { \prime }$. In the same way, if λ contains an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 1 }$and is broken in a cutting operation in Definition 13.1 (4) with m not having deg 4, then we also get a {33A} molecule with higher atom m, such that${ \mathfrak { m } } \in \lambda$

Proof part 2. Let${ \mathcal { L } } _ { 0 } \subseteq { \mathcal { L } }$be the set of ov-segments selected in Definition 13.1 (1), and$\mathcal { L } _ { 1 } \supseteq \mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$be the set of all ov-segments λ that are broken in Definition 13.1 (1), then we have$| \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } | \leq 2 | \mathcal { L } _ { 0 } |$. Recall the auxiliary graph G defined above; let$\mathcal { N } ( \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } )$be the set of G-nodes in$\mathcal { L } \backslash \mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$that are adjacent to a G-node in $\mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$, and let$\mathcal { P } _ { 1 }$be the set of G-edges connecting a G-node in$\mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$to a G-node in$\mathcal { L } \backslash \mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$. We claim that

$$
| \mathcal {P} _ {1} | \leq | \mathcal {N} (\mathcal {L} _ {1}) | + | \mathcal {L} _ {1} |, \quad | \mathcal {P} _ {1} | \geq A | \mathcal {L} _ {0} | - 2 | \mathcal {L} _ {1} | \geq (A / 2 - 2) | \mathcal {L} _ {1} |.\tag{13.2}
$$

Here, the first inequality in (13.2) follows because the subgraph${ \mathcal { N } } ( { \mathcal { L } } _ { 1 } ) \cup { \mathcal { L } } _ { 1 } \subseteq G$of the auxiliary graph contains no cycle (and is a forest); the second inequality is because each G-node$\lambda \in \mathcal { L } _ { 0 }$has at least A diferent G-edges, and that each G-edge in$\mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$is counted twice when adding up the G-degrees of G-nodes in$\mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$, and their number is bounded by$| { \mathcal { L } } _ { 1 } |$. Moreover, let$( \lambda _ { 1 } , \cdots , \lambda _ { s } )$be the permutation of$\lambda \in \mathcal { L } \backslash \mathcal { L } _ { 1 }$ ordered by time of breaking in Definition 13.1 (2)–(4), then by construction in Definition 13.1 (1), each$\lambda _ { j }$is adjacent to at most A diferent G-nodes$\lambda _ { k } \left( k \neq j \right)$in G. Let$\mathcal { P } _ { 2 }$be the set of G-edges among these$\lambda _ { j }$, then $| \mathcal { P } _ { 1 } | + | \mathcal { P } _ { 2 } | \ge | \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } | - | \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } |$(where$| \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } |$is the total number of G-edges, as each G-edge corresponds to an intersection of two$\lambda _ { j } )$

Now, by the discussion in Part 1 above, for each$\lambda \in \mathcal { N } ( \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } )$, and each λ containing an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 1 } .$and each$\lambda = \lambda _ { j }$that is adjacent to some$\lambda _ { k } \left( k < j \right)$in G, if λ is broken in a cutting operation in Definition 13.1 (4) with m not having deg 4, we get a {33A} molecule corresponding to λ when it is broken, and each {33A} molecule can be so obtained from at most two such λ (as shown in Part 1, this λ must contain the higher atom m in this {33A} molecule, so it has at most 2 choices). In the case$\lambda = \lambda _ { j }$, each j also corresponds to at most A diferent G-edges$( \lambda _ { j } , \lambda _ { k } )$. This implies (using also the first inequality in (13.2)) that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 A \}} \geq \frac {1}{2} \max \left(| \mathcal {P} _ {1} | - | \mathcal {L} _ {1} |, | \mathbb {M} _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} ^ {1} |, A ^ {- 1} | \mathcal {P} _ {2} |\right) - \# _ {\mathrm{exc}}.\tag{13.3}
$$

Here we use$| \mathcal { P } _ { 1 } | - | \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } | \leq | \mathcal { N } ( \mathcal { L } _ { 1 } ) |$, and that the number of$\lambda = \lambda _ { j }$adjacent to some$\lambda _ { k } \left( k < j \right)$in G is at least$A ^ { - 1 } | \mathcal { P } _ { 2 } | .$. Moreover$\# _ { \mathrm { e x c } }$is the number of atoms cut in Definition 13.1 (1) plus the number of deg 4 atoms cut in Definition 13.1 (4) (each of them may break two λ which count as exceptions; also cutting any deg 2 atom in Definition 13.1 (2) will not break any λ).

because (i) any new component of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$generated in the cutting sequence cannot be full (cf. Remark 10.6, and (ii) any component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$also cannot be full when all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are cut. Proposition 13.3. Proposition 12.18 is true if either$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \geq ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, or$\mathrm { i f } \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$ and$| \overline { { { \mathbb { M } } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } | \geq ( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, where$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$is defined as in Definition 13.1, but with the roles of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ reversed.

Proof. Our goal is to prove that

$$
(v / 2) \cdot (\# _ {\mathrm{good}}) - d \cdot (\# _ {\{4 \}}) \geq (C _ {4} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho^ {\prime \prime \prime}.\tag{13.4}
$$

Consider all components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, if at least half of them contain an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } : = \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } ^ { 1 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } } ^ { 2 } ,$ then we have$| \mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } | \geq \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } / 2$. In this case we apply 2CONNUP to$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$, by Proposition 13.2 we have

$$
(v / 2) \cdot (\# _ {\mathrm{good}}) - d \cdot (\# _ {\{4 \}}) \geq C ^ {- 1} | \mathbb {M} _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} | - C \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{fucp} (\mathbb {M} _ {U})} \geq \left(C ^ {- 1} (C _ {3} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} - C (C _ {5} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1}\right) \cdot \rho^ {\prime \prime \prime}\tag{13.5}
$$

(where the upper bound of$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$follows from Reduction$2 \ ( \mathrm { i i } ) )$), which implies (13.4).

If at least half of the components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$do not contain an atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { { c o n n } } }$, then we shall cut$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$as free and cut it into elementary molecules using UP. Then, for each of these at least half components$X \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { D }$ it will not contain any deg 2 atom (because this component does not contain any atom in either$\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 1 }$or $\mathbb { M } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } ) \mathrm { . }$; moreover, this X may be divided into new components due to the broken ov-segments, but each new component will contain at least one deg 3 atom (cf. Remark 10.6), and at least one new component will contain at least two deg 3 atoms. This last fact is because at least two atoms in X will become deg 3 after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(i.e. has deg 3 or has a bond with$\mathbb { M } _ { U } )$by Reduction 2 (ii); by considering a path in X between these two atoms before cutting and whether or where this path breaks after cutting, we can obtain a component of X after cutting that contains two deg 3 atoms (as the atom where the path breaks must have a fixed end).

We then cut each resulting component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into elementary molecules using DOWN. By Proposition 12.2, and note that all {33A} molecules are treated as good, we get that$\# \mathrm { g o o d } \geq \# \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) / 2$and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq$ $\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$(this is because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no full component after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, due to Remark 10.6 and Reduction 2 (ii)), so (13.4) follows in the same way as (13.5).

Proof part 2. Assume$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$and$| \overline { { { \mathbb { M } } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } | \geq ( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$. We first cut as free each full component in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$that has no bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(and then cut it into elementary molecules using UP), to make$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$satisfy the assumptions of Definition 13.1 after reversing the roles of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. Then we apply 2CONNDN to$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$. Proposition 13.2 then gives that (note$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq \# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } )$

which implies (13.4). Here, we used the bound on$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$provided by Reduction 2 (ii).

Reduction 3. With Proposition 13.3, in the remaining proof of Proposition 12.18, we may now assume for $\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$, in addition to Reduction 2 (i)–(iii):

• That$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, and the number of weakly degenerate atoms and pairs in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is less than$( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime } .$

13.2. The 3COMPUP algorithm. The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 12.18 under the assumption of Reductions 2 and 3. This proof will be presented, following Stages 1–6, in Section 13.5. Before this, we first introduce the remaining ingredients needed in the proof; in this subsection we define the full 3COMPUP algorithm (see Definition 13.6) corresponding to toy model II ((see Stage 5 in Section 13.5), which is a direct extension of the toy version in Definition 11.17 by including O-atoms and translating into the ov-segment language (cf. Section 11.7.1). Apart from this translation, Definition 13.6 and Proposition 13.7 are exactly the same as Definition 11.17 and Proposition 11.19 in Section 11. Before proceeding, we state and prove the full version of Lemma 11.6 in Section 11 in the presence of O-atoms (by translating adjacency to ov-adjacency etc.).

Lemma 13.4. Let M be a molecule that is a tree, and$S \subseteq \mathbb { M }$is an ov-connected set. Suppose we cut$S$as free from M. Then, for each atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash S$that is ov-adjacent to an atom in S before cutting, there is a unique component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } \subseteq \mathbb { M } \backslash S$after cutting that contains${ \mathfrak { q } } .$This$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$is in bijection with${ \mathfrak { q } } ,$and when viewed in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$, the operation of cutting S creates only one fixed end in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$at${ \mathfrak { q } } ,$see Figure 58.

![](images/page_155_image_1.jpg)

Figure 58. Illustration of Lemma 13.4. The main diferences with Lemma 11.6 are that (i) now S is allowed to be ov-connected instead of connected (with possible O-atoms in between which also belong to diferent components after cutting S as free), and (ii) each ov-adjacent atom q (not necessarily adjacent) now leads to its own component. For example, the q and ${ \mathfrak { q } } ^ { \prime }$will belong to diferent components after cutting S as free, but again each component has exactly one new fixed end.

Proof. Consider all the ov-segments connecting an atom in S to another atom (in$S$or not in S), and all atoms (including the intermediate O-atoms) on these ov-segments. Let the set of all such ov-segments (and the bonds contained in these ov-segments) be Λ, and the set of all these atoms be$Z \supseteq S$, then the atoms in$Z \backslash S$are precisely all the atoms q as stated. Note that all the bonds in Λ with an endpoint in$\mathbb { M } \backslash S$are broken after cutting S as free; we claim that at this time, any two diferent atoms$\mathfrak { q } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { q } _ { 2 } \in Z \backslash S$must be in two diferent components of$\mathbb { M } \backslash S .$. In fact, if not, then they are connected in$\mathbb { M } \backslash S$by a path of bonds not containing any bond in Λ. However,${ \mathfrak { q } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { q } } _ { 2 } \in Z$are also connected by another path containing only bonds in Λ, using that S is ov-connected. This then produces a cycle in M, contradiction.

Now we have proved that${ \mathfrak { q } } \mapsto X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$is a bijection, and for each$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$, the only atom in it that is ov-adjacent to an atom in S is${ \mathfrak { q } } .$As such, cutting S as free only creates fixed end at q and not at any other atom in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$ If we get more than one fixed end at q, then q must be ov-adjacent to two atoms in${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } \in S$along two diferent ov-segments (note: breaking two bonds at q that belong to the same ov-segment creates only one fixed end at${ \mathfrak { q } } ,$see Definition 8.3). Note that${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$is connected to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$by a path of bonds in$\Lambda ;$since${ \mathfrak { q } } \notin S$, we know that q either does not occur in this path, or occurs in this path but as one of the intermediate O-atoms (so the two bonds at q in this path must be serial). However, the two ov-segments connecting q to${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j }$also form a path between${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } .$, in which the two bonds at q are not serial. Thus these two paths cannot coincide, which again produces a cycle in M. This contradiction then proves that cutting S as free produces only one fixed end at q (and in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } )$, as desired.□

Lemma 13.5. Suppose M is a molecule that is a tree, contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms and has no C-top fixed end. Let the set of deg 3 atoms in M be$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$and assume$| \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | \geq 2$. Define a set$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$to be nobottom if any child of any atom in A must also be in A. Then, there always exists a connected, no-bottom subset$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$with$| A \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | = 2$

Proof. For any${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n, then it is always connected and no-bottom. If there exists n such that$\left| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } \right| \geq 2$, then choose a lowest such n. Since n is either O-atom or has no top fixed end, we know that either (i) n has one child${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$, or (ii) n has deg 4 and has two children$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$. In either case, by assumption we have$| S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | \le 1$for each$j ,$which then implies$\vert S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } \vert \le 2$because $S _ { \mathfrak { n } } = ( \cup _ { j } S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { j } } ) \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$. This implies$\vert S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } \vert = 2 .$as desired.

Now assume$| S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | \le 1$for each${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$$\mathrm { I f ~ } | S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | = 1$, there is a unique${ \mathfrak { p } } = { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ) \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \cap$ $\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } ;$now consider all atom pairs$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$such that${ \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } )$and${ \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } )$both exist and are diferent (which exist because$| \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } | \ge 2 )$, and one such pair$( \mathtt { n } , \mathtt { n } ^ { \prime } )$that are connected by a shortest path in M. Let this path be $( \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \mathfrak { n } , \cdot \cdot \mathbf { \Omega } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j } = \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } )$, then for each$0 < i < j$we must have either$S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } } \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } = \emptyset \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ) = { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } )$(otherwise the pair$( \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } _ { i } )$corresponds to a shorter path, contradiction). Now let$A = \cup _ { i = 0 } ^ { j } S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { i } }$, it is clear that A is connected, no-bottom and$A \cap \mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } = \{ { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n } } ) , { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } ) \}$, as desired.□

Definition 13.6 (The 3COMPUP algorithm). Let M be a molecule which is a forest, contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms and has no$\mathrm { C - t o p }$fixed end, and assume that each component of M contains at least two deg 3 atoms. Let the set of deg 3 atoms in M be$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$. Define the following cutting sequence:

(1) Apply Lemma 13.5 to one component of M and select a connected no-bottom subset A. This set is fixed until the end of (5).

(2) Choose a lowest deg 3 atom n in A that has not been cut. Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n (note that$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \subseteq A )$. This n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$are fixed until the end of (3).

(3) Starting from n, each time choose a highest atom m in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If m has deg 3 and has an ov-parent${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { + }$or ov-child m<sup>−</sup> that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { m } ^ { \pm } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(4) If M has deg 2 atom, then cut it; repeat until M has no deg 2 atoms. Then go to (2).

(5) When all atoms in A have been cut, we subsequently cut all remaining deg 2 atoms in M as in (4), and then cut all components of M with only one deg 3 atom using UP.

(6) Go to (1) and select the next A from one of the remaining components of M, and so on.

Proposition 13.7. Let M be as in Definition 13.6. Define$\# _ { \mathrm { { 3 o v c p } ( M ) } }$to be the number of ov-components of $\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$(the det of deg 3 atoms in M), and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p ( M ) } }$to be the number of components of M. Then M is cut into elementary molecules after 3COMPUP (Definition 13.6), and we have

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 B \}} = \# _ {\{4 4 \}} = \# _ {\{4 \}} = 0; \qquad \# _ {\{3 3 A \}} \geq \frac {1}{1 0} \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{3ovcp} (\mathbb {M})} + \frac {1}{5} \cdot \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})}.\tag{13.7}
$$

Proof. Note that steps$( 2 )  { - } ( 3 )$in Definition 13.6 are exactly the same as those UP (see Definition 12.1 $( 2 )  { - } ( 3 )$, note also the step of cutting deg 2 atoms is done in Definition 13.6 (5)), but applied to A only. Since A is no-bottom which means$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \subseteq A$whenever${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$, it is easy to see (following the same proof as Proposition 12.2) that the (MONO) property is preserved, and thus M is cut into elementary molecules only, and$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 0$. We now focus on the proof of (13.7).

Note that the algorithm 3COMPUP consists of finitely many loops where one loop is formed by steps (1)–(5) in Definition 13.6, and (say) turns M into$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$. Define λ(M) to be the right hand side of the last inequality in (13.7), then we only need to consider each single loop (1)–(5) in Definition 13.6, and prove that:

(♣) If M is a forest, has no top fixed end and contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms with each component containing at least two deg 3 atoms, then the result M<sup>′</sup> after executing the loop (1)–(5) in Definition 13.6 satisfies the same property. Moreover for this loop we have

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \lambda (\mathbb {M}) - \lambda (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}).\tag{13.8}
$$

Note that adding up (13.8) leads to the desired lower bound of$\# \{ 3 3 \}$, thus it sufices to prove$( \clubsuit )$for a given loop. We divide the proof into 4 parts, which exactly correspond to the 4 parts of the proof in toy model II (Proposition 11.19).

Proof part 1. We prove that each component of M<sup>′</sup> satisfies the desired properties. This is obvious, as the lack of top fixed ends follows from the same proof as Proposition 12.2, and the lack of deg 2 atoms and components with only one deg 3 atom follows from the cuttings done in Definition 13.6 (5).

Proof part 2. Now we need to prove (13.8). We start by making some preparations. Note that A is an ov-connected subset of M; by Lemma 13.4, each atom${ \mathfrak { m } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash A$that is ov-adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$by a pre-loop ov-segment corresponds to a unique component$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$after cutting the atoms in A as free (the loop will in fact cut as free more atoms). Note also that m must be an ov-parent of n as A has no bottom.

Let$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$be the set of deg 3 atoms in M (before executing the loop), and consider all ov-components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$that intersect A or are ov-adjacent to A by an ov-segment (we call them good). We know A has exactly two atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } ;$apart from the one or two ov-components that contain these two atoms, for any atom in any other good ov-component, it must belong to$X _ { \mathfrak { m } }$for a unique m, and this m must have deg 3 (otherwise the ov-component will not be ov-adjacent to A), with the corresponding n having deg 4. This is similar to the scenario in toy model II, see Figure 59. Let B be the union of all good ov-components and A. We claim that after steps (1)–(4) in Definition 13.6 and cutting the deg 2 atoms in Definition 13.6 (5), exactly those atoms in B have been cut as free.

Figure 59. The set A and ov-components of deg 3 atoms forming B, in Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 13.7. This is basically the same as in toy model II (Figure 35), except now the notion of adjacency and components are replaced by ov-adjacency and ov-components.

In fact, the atoms A must have been cut by definition. For any atom in a good ov-component of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$ by definition it is connected to an atom in A by a sequence of deg 3 atoms with each consecutive ones being ov-adjacent; once the atom in A has been cut, the atoms on this chain will successively become deg 2, so they must have been cut (either in Definition 13.6 (4)–(5), or as part of {33} molecule in Definition 13.6 (3)). On the other hand, each atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash B$has at most one ov-segment connecting to B (as B is ov-connected and M is a tree, cf. the proof of Lemma 13.4), and must be deg 4 if it has one such ov-segment (otherwise it would belong to one of the good ov-components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } )$, so each atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash B$will have deg 3 or 4 after cutting B as free, thus it will not be cut in steps (1)–(4) in Definition 13.6 or in cutting the deg 2 atoms in Definition 13.6 (5).

Proof part 3. Next we obtain a lower bound on$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} }$. As A contains two deg 3 atoms, we can show that #$\{ 3 3 \} \geq 1$in the same way as Proposition 12.2 (3). Moreover, since A contains exactly two deg 3 atoms, by arguing as in the proof of Proposition 12.2 (3) and calculating the quantity σ defined there but within A, we can show that, apart from at most two exceptions, each deg 4 atom in A will have deg 3 when it is cut.

Now let λ be the number of good ov-components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$(i.t. those forming B). By the discussions in Part 2 above, with at most two exceptions, each such ov-component must contain some m which has deg 3 and is an ov-parent of an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A$of deg 4; consider then the maximal ov-segment σ containing m and n, note that each σ corresponds to at most one good ov-component (if σ is given, then any deg 3 atoms on σ must be ov-adjacent to each other and thus belong to the same ov-component), so the number of such ov-segments$\sigma$is at least λ. We claim that with at most two more exceptions, the first atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in \sigma$that is cut, must belong to a {33A} molecule. In fact, we must have${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A$by Definition 13.6 (3); with at most two exceptions we may assume p has deg 3 when it is cut. At this time the m (which is ov-parent of p) also has deg 3 (because the only way m is ov-connected to A is by the ov-segment between m and n, cf. Lemma 13.4), so by Definition 13.6 (3), we know that p must belong to a {33} molecule (which may or may not be {p, m}). Since each {33} molecule can be so obtained from at most two σ, we thus obtain that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \max \left(1, \frac {\lambda - 2}{2} - 2\right).\tag{13.9}
$$

Proof part 4. Now consider the components of$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime }$and ov-components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } ^ { \prime }$(set of deg 3 atoms in M<sup>′</sup>). Note that M<sup>′</sup> is formed from M by cutting B as free and then removing all components with only one deg 3 atom. Since B is ov-connected, by applying Lemma 13.4 again, we see that each component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$of M<sup>′</sup> corresponds to a unique atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash B$that is ov-adjacent to an atom in B. Let$\mu$be the number of such atoms (i.e. corresponding to those new components with at least two deg 3 atoms after cutting B), then

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} = 1 - \mu .\tag{13.10}
$$

Finally, consider the set of deg 3 atoms, i.e.$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } ^ { \prime }$, and their ov-components. The ov-components of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$includes those λ ov-components forming B as in Part 3 (which have been cut when forming M<sup>′</sup>), and the other ov-components which are contained in some$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$defined above. Note that for each new component Y formed after cutting B that contains only one deg 3 atom, it will be removed and will not occur in$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } ;$ however, all atoms in Y originally have deg 4 before any cutting, so initially Y also has no contribution to $\# _ { \mathrm { { 3 o v c p } ( M ) } }$, and thus we can ignore such Y .

By Lemma 13.4, when viewed in each$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$, the efect of cutting B exactly turns one free end into fixed end (turning one deg 4 atom into deg 3). Therefore the part of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) } ^ { \prime }$within$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$is formed by adding one deg 3 atom into the existing part of$\mathbb { M } _ { ( 3 ) }$within$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$This new deg 3 atom may decrease$\# _ { \mathrm { 3 o v c p } ( X _ { \mathfrak { q } } ) }$(i.e. the number of ov-components of the set of deg 3 atoms in$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } )$by joining existing ov-components together, but this decrease is at most 2 because this new deg 3 atom can join at most 3 ov-components into 1, see Figure 60. From this, and accounting for the λ ov-components removed when cutting B, we deduce that

$$
\# _ {3 \mathrm{ovcp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {3 \mathrm{ovcp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \leq \lambda + 2 \mu .\tag{13.11}
$$

Putting together (13.9)–(13.11), and using the definition of λ(M), we deduce that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda (\mathbb {M}) - \lambda (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}) = \frac {1}{5} \big (\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \big) + \frac {1}{1 0} \big (\# _ {3 \mathrm{ovcp} (\mathbb {M})} - \# _ {3 \mathrm{ovcp} (\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime})} \big) \\ \qquad \leq \frac {1}{5} + \frac {\lambda}{1 0} \leq \max \left(1, \frac {\lambda - 6}{2}\right) \leq \# _ {\{3 3 \}}. \end{array}\tag{13.12}
$$

This proves (13.8) and completes the proof of Proposition 13.7.
