13.3. Pre-processing. In this subsection we introduce the pre-processing step, discussed in Section 11.7.4 (d). We start with the notion of ov-proper, which is the extension of proper in Definition 11.3.

Definition 13.8. Let M be a molecule, we say it is ov-proper, if it is a forest, contains only deg 3 and 4 atoms, and the ov-distance (Definition 8.4) between any two deg 3 atoms is at least 3.

Note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$may have fixed ends as the result of the cuttings in Definition 12.14 (and further cuttings of 2-connections, see Stage 1 in Section 13.5), and might not be ov-proper. The idea of pre-processing is to turn$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into ov-proper again by cutting as free a suitable set S. Namely, given a subset of atoms in $Z \cup Y \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { D }$(which in practice will include the deg 3 atoms and weakly degenerate atoms (Definition 12.16)), we define a function SELECT (Definition 13.10) which outputs a set$S \supseteq Z \cup Y$, such that cutting$S$as free turns$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into ov-proper, see Proposition 13.11 (1). Moreover, since the$U D$connections are important in the algorithm MAINUD below, we also prove a result on how cutting S as free may afect the UD connections, see Proposition 13.11 (2).

The idea of the SELECT function is a simple greedy algorithm. Start with the set$Z \cup Y$and its$\mathrm { O V ^ { - } }$ components. If cutting$Z \cup Y$as free would create (deg 2 atom or) two deg 3 atoms with ov-distance$\leq 2 .$ then there must exist two ov-components$A , B \subseteq Z \cup Y$with ov-distance$\leq 4$. We then add to$Z \cup Y$the intermediate atoms in the shortest path of ov-segments between$A$and$B$to bring them together, and repeat this process until it is no longer possible. In the end we get$S = \mathbf { S E L E C T } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , Z , Y )$such that cutting S as free makes$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ov-proper; see Definition 13.10 and Proposition 13.11 (1). As for Proposition 13.11 (2), the proof relies on Lemma 13.9 below, which is in the same spirit as the proof of uniqueness of lowest atom in Part 3 of the proof of Proposition 11.7 in Section 11.

Lemma 13.9. Let$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$be a UD molecule such that$\mathbb { M } _ { D } = \emptyset$, and$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$does not have C-top fixed end. Suppose$A \subseteq \mathbb { M } _ { U }$is ov-connected within$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(cf. Definition$8 . 4 )$such that each atom in A has deg 3. Then A contains a unique lowest atom n, such that (i) each atom m$\in { \cal A }$is obtained from n by iteratively taking ov-parents in A, and (ii) each ov-child of${ \mathfrak { m } } \in A$is either one of the terms preceding m in the ov-parent sequence defined in (i), or an O-atom between two consecutive terms preceding m, or an ov-child of n.

Similarly, if we assume$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \neq \emptyset$, A is ov-connected within$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, each atom of$A$is C-atom, and each deg 4 atom of A has at most one ov-child in$A ,$, then conclusion (i) is still true.

Proof. Choose a lowest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in A .$We will prove (i), which also establishes the uniqueness of n, and prove (ii) in the process. For any m$\in \ A$, since A is ov-connected, there exists a sequence${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j } \in A \left( 0 \leq j \leq r \right)$ such that$( { \mathfrak { p } } _ { 0 } , { \mathfrak { p } } _ { r } ) = ( { \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { m } } )$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j + 1 }$is ov-adjacent to${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j } ;$we may assume this sequence is shortest. Since n is lowest, p<sub>1</sub> must be ov-parent of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 0 } = { \mathfrak { n } } ;$since${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$has deg 3 (thus it is O-atom or has one bottom fixed end, cf. Remark$8 . 7 ,$, we know that${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$must be ov-parent of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$(otherwise${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$is ov-child of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$along the same maximal ov-segment containing${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$and p<sub>0</sub>, which means${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 }$is ov-adjacent to${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 0 }$and we can skip${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 1 }$to get a shorter sequence), and for the same reason${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 3 }$must be ov-parent of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { 2 } .$, and so on. This proves (i). Then (ii) follows from the same proof (any ov-child of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$either belongs to the ov-segment between${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$and${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j - 1 }$, or is an ov-child of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j - 1 }$so we can keep iterating). The proof of$\mathrm { ( i ) }$in the case$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \neq \emptyset$is similar, where we note that${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$has at most one ov-child in A in the case when${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$has deg 4, so${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j + 1 }$still cannot be ov-child of${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j }$if ${ \mathfrak { p } } _ { j + 1 } \in A$and is C-atom.□

Definition 13.10 (The function SELECT). Let M be any UD molecule, such that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has no deg 2 atoms, and has no C-bottom fixed end. Let$Z$be the set of deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and Y be a subset of the set of deg 4 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. Given$( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , Z , Y )$, we define a set$S : = \mathbf { S E L E C T } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , Z , Y )$as follows, see Figure 61:

(1) Consider all the ov-components of$Z \cup Y$in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(this means we only consider the O-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ when defining ov-connectedness in Definition 8.4), which is a finite collection of disjoint subsets of $\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$

(2) If any two of these subsets, say A and B, have the shortest ov-distance (within$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$which is at most 4, then we choose the shortest path between an atom in A and an atom in$B _ { : }$, which can be divided into at most 4 ov-segments. Write this path as$\left( \mathfrak { n } _ { 0 } , \cdots , \mathfrak { n } _ { q } \right)$, where$q \leq 4$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 0 } \in A$ $\mathfrak { n } _ { q } \in B$, and each$( \mathfrak { n } _ { j } , \mathfrak { n } _ { j + 1 } )$is an ov-segment. Then replace the two sets A and B by a single set $A \cup B \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \mathfrak { n } _ { q - 1 } \}$

(3) Repeat (2) until this can no longer be done$( { \mathrm { i . e . } }$. when only one set is left, or any two sets have of distance at least 5). Then output$S : = \mathbf { S E L E C T } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , Z , Y )$as the union of all the current sets.

Proposition 13.11. Let the function SELECT be as in Definition 13.10. Then we have the followings:

(1) After cutting$S : = \mathbf { S E L E C T } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , Z , Y )$from M as free, then the set$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$in the resulting molecule $\mathbb { M } \backslash S$is ov-proper (Definition 13.8). Note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$may have both C-top and C-bottom fixed ends, however this is compensated by the good property of being ov-proper.

![](images/page_160_image_0.jpg)

Figure 61. Top: the process of constructing the SELECT function in Definition 13.10 (for two ov-components A and B with ov-distance$\leq ~ 4$, add the intermediate atoms in the ov-segments connecting them, until this cannot be done anymore). Bottom: proof of Proposition 13.11 (1); if m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to the same component A, then we get a cycle from${ \mathfrak { m } } \to { \mathfrak { n } } \to \cdots \to { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \to { \mathfrak { m ^ { \prime } } } \to \cdots \to { \mathfrak { m } }$(the path from${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$to m belongs to$A )$

(2) Consider all the maximal ov-segments in M that contains at least one atom in$S$and one atom in $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. Then the number of these maximal ov-segments does not exceed$1 0 ( \# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) } + | Y | )$, where $\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) }$is the number of ov-components of$Z$(i.e. the set of all deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, where the ov-components are determined by considering$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$only.

Proof. Proof of (1). At the end of the construction in Definition 13.10 (3), we get a number of disjoint subsets, such that each one is ov-connected and the ov-distance between each two of them is at least 5, and S is the union of all these subsets. Note also that the sub-molecule M \S of the molecule formed by cutting S as free from M, is equal to the molecule formed by cutting$S$as free from$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Now suppose after cutting S as free, there exist two deg 3 atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$of ov-distance at most 2; the case of a deg 2 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } \backslash S$can be treated similarly. Since${ \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \notin S .$, they must have deg 4 initially in $\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. As they become deg 3 after cutting S as free, we know that for each of n and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$, it must be ov-adjacent to an atom in S. Assume n is ov-adjacent to${ \mathfrak { m } } \in S .$and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$is ov-adjacent to$\mathfrak { m } ^ { \prime } \in S$. If m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to two diferent subsets A and$B$defined above, then the ov-distance between m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$(and hence the ov-distance between A and B) is at most$1 + 2 + 1 = 4$, contradicting the assumption about these subsets.

Therefore, we know that m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to the same set A defined above. But then there exists a path$\mu _ { 1 } : \mathfrak { m } \to \mathfrak { n } \to \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \to \mathfrak { m } ^ { \prime }$(composed of ov-segments), and another path$\mu _ { 2 }$between m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$, which is composed of ov-segments connecting atoms in$S$(because m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to the same ov-component A of S). The path$\mu _ { 1 }$cannot be expressed in this way (because the atoms n,$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$separating the diferent ov-segments, as well as the possible atom ov-adjacent to both n and${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } ,$all belong to$\mathbb { M } \backslash S )$, unless this whole path belongs to a single ov-segment connecting m and m<sup>′</sup> (meaning the atoms n,$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$etc., all belong to this single ov-segment connecting m and$\mathfrak { m } ^ { \prime } )$, but in this latter case the path$\mathfrak { n } \to \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$would no longer exist after cutting S as free (see Definition 8.3). Consequently, we know that the paths$\mu _ { 1 }$and$\mu _ { 2 }$cannot coincide, but then they will form a cycle, which contradicts the fact that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest.

Proof of (2). In each step in Definition 13.10 (2) we add at most 3 atoms to the union of the current subsets. Moreover, the number of such steps that can be carried out cannot exceed the initial number of subsets (as each step reduces the number of subsets by at least 1), which is the number of ov-components of $Z \cup Y$, and is at most$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) } + | Y |$. This means that the number of newly added atoms in the construction of S (starting from$Z \cup Y )$is at most$3 ( \# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) } + | Y | )$.

Therefore, we only need to consider the required maximal ov-segments that contains an atom in$Z .$In each such maximal ov-segment, we have an atom m belonging to an ov-component$W$of$Z ,$which has an ov-parent in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$. By (the dual version of) Lemma 13.9 (ii), this ov-parent of m, which does not belong to$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, must also be an ov-parent of the unique highest atom n of$W ;$therefore this maximal ov-segment must contain n. As each ov-component W contains a unique highest atom n, and each atom belongs to at most two maximal ov-segments, we conclude that the number of such maximal ov-segments does not exceed $2 \cdot \# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) } \left( \operatorname { a s } \# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( Z ) } \right.$is the number of ov-components of Z in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, as desired.□

13.4. The MAINUD algorithm. In this section we introduce the last ingredient, which is also the central algorithm in our proof, namely the MAINUD algorithm corresponding to toy model I plus (see Stage 6 in Section 13.5). In Definition 13.12 below, we present the full version of this algorithm. Compared to the toy version (Definition 11.13), the main diference (apart from standard translations into ov-segment language) is that, the set X in Definition 11.13 is replaced by the set$X _ { 1 }$(see Definition 13.12 below). The reason has to do with the main dichotomy between toy models I plus and II in Section 11 (basically$X _ { 1 }$is the set of deg 3 atoms after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free, which plays the same role as the X in Section 11); see the discussion before Stages 1–6 in Section 13.5. Apart from this, Definition 13.12, Proposition 13.13 and its proof are essentially the same as their toy versions (Definition 11.13, Proposition 11.14) in Section 11.

Definition 13.12 (The algorithm MAINUD). Define the following cutting algorithm MAINUD. It takes as input any UD molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$that satisfies the following assumptions:

(i)$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$contains no C-top fixed end, and$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } = \mathcal { O }$, where$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$is defined as in Proposition 13.3.

(ii)$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is ov-proper (Definition 13.8), and does not have any full component that is not connected to $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$by a bond.

For any such M, we define the sets$X _ { 0 }$and$X _ { 1 }$of C-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$as follows (see Figure 62):

• Define${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ^ { 0 }$if n has deg 3 and has one ov-child in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

• Define${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ^ { q }$, if$\mathfrak { n } \ \in \ X _ { 0 } ^ { q - 1 }$, or n has deg 3 and has one ov-child in$X _ { 0 } ^ { q - 1 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, or if n has two ov-children in$X _ { 0 } ^ { q - 1 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$along two ov-segments in two diferent particle lines. Then define $X _ { 0 } = \cup _ { q \geq 0 } X _ { 0 } ^ { q }$

• With$X _ { 0 }$fixed, define${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 1 }$if and only if${ \mathfrak { n } } \not \in X _ { 0 }$, and n either has deg 3 or has one ov-child in $X _ { 0 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D }$

![](images/page_161_image_9.jpg)

Figure 62. The sets$X _ { 0 }$and$X _ { 1 }$in Definition 13.12, constructed by definition. The main point (which will be used in Stage 5 in Section 13.5) is that, after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free, (i) all atoms in$X _ { 0 }$(pink) will be subsequently cut as deg 2, (ii)$X _ { 1 }$(yellow) is precisely the set of deg 3 C-atoms, (iii) the number of ov-components does not decrease if we add the new deg 3 O-atoms (blue) to$X _ { 1 }$

Note these sets are fixed throughout the cutting sequence below. Define the following cutting sequence:

(1) If$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$contains any deg 2 atom n, then cut it as free, and repeat until there is no deg 2 atom left.

(2) Consider the set of all (remaining) atoms that either belong to$X _ { 0 } \cup X _ { 1 }$, or has deg 3; choose n to be a lowest atom in this set (if this set is empty then choose n to be any lowest atom). Let$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of descendants of n in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and fix n and$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$until the end of (6).

(3) Starting from n, choose a highest atom p in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ;$if p is ov-adjacent to a deg 3 atom${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, then cut $\{ { \mathfrak { p } } , { \mathfrak { q } } \}$as free, and cut q as free from {p, q} is p has deg 4. Otherwise cut p as free.

(4) If any two deg 3 atoms$( \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } )$in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes ov-adjacent, then choose$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } \}$such that this ovsegment contains the fewest bond, and cut$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } \}$as free. Repeat until no such instances exist.

(5) If the ov-distance of any two deg 3 atoms$( \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } )$in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes 2 (within$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, say r and r<sup>′</sup> are both ov-adjacent to some$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$, then cut$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$as free and then cut r as free from$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$. Go to (4). Repeat until$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes ov-proper.

(6) When$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes proper, go to (3). Repeat until all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut.

(7) When all atoms in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut, go to (1). Repeat until all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut.

(8) When all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$have been cut, choose any deg 3 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$and cut it as free. If the ov-distance between any two deg 3 atoms becomes at most 2, go to (4) and repeat (4)–(5) until$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ becomes proper again. Then choose and cut the next deg 3 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and so on.

Proposition 13.13. Let M be any UD molecule that satisfies (i)–(ii) in Definition 13.12. Consider the number of UD connections e that are either (i) connected to some other UD connection via$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, or (ii) connected to a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contains deg 3 atoms. We call such UD connections good and let the number of them be$\# _ { \mathrm { U D } }$

Let$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$be the number of full components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and let$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) }$be the number of ov-components of the set$X _ { 1 }$defined in Definition 13.12. Then, for the algorithm MAINUD, we have$\# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$, and each {33B} molecule must have both its atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, and that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 A \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 B \}} \geq \frac {1}{5} \cdot (\# _ {\mathrm{UD}} - \# _ {\mathrm{fucp} (\mathbb {M} _ {U})} - \# _ {\mathrm{ovcp} (X _ {1})}), \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \# _ {\{4 \}} \leq \# _ {\mathrm{fucp} (\mathbb {M} _ {U})} + \# _ {\mathrm{ovcp} (X _ {1})}.\tag{13.13}
$$

Proof. We divide the proof into 4 parts, which exactly correspond to the 4 parts of the proof in toy model I plus (Proposition 11.14); the presentation of Part 4 is slightly diferent, but essentially it is the same counting argument (involving the same quantity$\# \mathrm { d e g 3 } - \# \mathrm { c o m p } )$

Proof part 1. We prove the (MONO) property as in Proposition 12.2: at any time in the cutting sequence, there is no C-top fixed end in$( \mathbb { M } _ { U } \backslash S _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$and no C-bottom fixed end in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$. In fact, when we choose n as in Definition 13.12 (2), every atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$must have deg 4. In the process of Definition 13.12 (3)–(6), if we only consider the cutting within$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, then the desired property follows from the same proof as in Proposition 12.2. Now suppose an arbitrary set of atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$are also cut in the process, then this will only create C-bottom fixed ends, and only at C-atoms t that are ov-adjacent to some atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ By definition we must have$\mathfrak { t } \in X _ { 0 } \cup X _ { 1 }$, and thus$\mathfrak { t } \not \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$by our choice, so it does not afect the desired (MONO) property. Similarly, for any {33} molecule$\{ { \mathfrak { p } } , { \mathfrak { q } } \}$cut in (3), the p must either be O-atom or${ \mathfrak { p } } = { \mathfrak { n } }$ so this {33} molecule must be {33A} (as p has not C-top fixed end).

Proof part 2. We prove that each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$belongs to a {3} or {33} molecule (which can be either {33A} or {33B}). In fact, note first that initially M<sub>D</sub> is ov-proper (thus has no deg 2 atom), and does not have full components not connected to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$by a bond (thus will not have any full component after cutting $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$as free), so the cuttings in Definition 13.12 (8) will not create any {4} molecule.

Next, note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$initially is a forest, and will remain a forest in the whole cutting process (cutting an atom will not create any cycle, but may cause a tree to become a disconnected forest). Now consider each cutting step in Definition 13.12 (3) involving${ \mathfrak { p } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$, at which time$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$must be proper by the construction in Definition 13.12 (4)–(6). This p has at most one ov-segment connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, because$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } = \mathcal { O }$by Definition 13.12 (i). If no such ov-segment exists, then cutting p does not afect$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$. If one such ov-segment exists, then the efect of the cutting step in Definition 13.12 (3) on$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, has the following two possibilities:

(a) If we cut p as free (which means all atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ov-adjacent to p have deg 4), then this step breaks $\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into connected components$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$which are in bijection with atoms${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$ov-adjacent to p, and this cutting creates only one fixed end at q when viewed within$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$, turning it from deg 4 to deg 3.

(b) If we cut$\{ { \mathfrak { p } } , { \mathfrak { q } } \}$as free (which means${ \mathfrak { q } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$is ov-adjacent to p and has deg 3), then when viewed in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } ,$this step equivalent to cutting q (which has deg 3) as free in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$

Here (a) follows from the same proof in Lemma 13.4 (i.e. q in bijection with$X _ { \mathfrak { q } } .$, in which only one fixed end is created at q) as$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest. In (b), the efect of cutting$\{ { \mathfrak { p } } , { \mathfrak { q } } \}$as free to$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is equivalent to cutting {q} as free, because p has no other ov-segment connecting to other atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(apart from those on the ov-segment containing q).

Now, regarding the efects described in$\mathrm { { ( a ) - ( b ) } }$, we have the following lemma, which is extension of Lemma 11.8 in the proof of Proposition 11.7:

Lemma 13.14. Suppose$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is proper at some point of the algorithm, and becomes non-proper after either (a) or (b). Then,$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$will once more become proper after applying Definition 13.12 (4)–(5), via cuttings of {3} and {33} molecules only, and without seeing any deg$\mathcal { Q }$atom.

Proof. Note that$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is always a forest, and our proof will crucially rely on Lemma 13.4. Consider first (a): when viewed within each resulting component$X _ { \mathfrak { q } }$, its efect is simply switching one free end at a deg 4 atom into a fixed end, turning it into deg 3. We call the latter step (∗). As for (b), right before performing it at a deg 3 atom${ \mathfrak { q } } ,$any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that is ov-adjacent to q must have deg 4 (because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is ov-proper). By Lemma 13.4, M<sub>D</sub> will break into finitely many components after performing (b), and the efect of (b) when viewed within each component is again step (∗). Therefore we only need to prove Lemma 13.14 for step (∗).

Assume now$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes non-proper, with two ov-adjacent deg 3 atoms (say r and$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } )$, after step (∗). We may assume$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$has deg 3 before (∗), while r has deg 4 before (∗) and is turned into deg 3 after (∗). Then, before (∗), any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$ov-adjacent to r or$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$must have deg 4, because otherwise we either have two ov-adjacent deg 3 atoms before$( * )$, or have two deg 3 atoms ov-adjacent to the same deg 4 atom before (a), contradicting properness. Therefore, by Lemma 13.4, we see that cutting the {33} molecule breaks$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into finitely many components, and the efect of this cutting when viewed in each component is again equivalent to step (∗). We then induct on the size of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$and apply induction hypothesis to each of these components, to conclude the proof of Lemma 13.14.

Now suppose$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes non-proper, without two ov-adjacent deg 3 atoms, after (∗). In this case there must be two deg 3 atoms, say r and${ \mathfrak { r } } ^ { \prime \prime }$, that are both ov-adjacent to a deg 4 atom$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } .$. We may assume$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$and ${ \mathfrak { r } } ^ { \prime \prime }$respectively have deg 4 and 3 before (∗), and r has deg 4 before (∗) and is turned into deg 3 after (∗). Then, before (∗), any atom ov-adjacent to$\mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime }$or${ \mathfrak { r } } ^ { \prime \prime }$must have deg$\it 4$for the same reason as above thanks to properness. Moreover, before (∗), any atom adjacent to r must also have deg 4, because otherwise we would get two ov-adjacent deg 3 atoms after (∗), contradicting our assumption. Therefore, by Lemma 13.4, we see that cutting$\{ \mathfrak { r } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime } , \mathfrak { r } ^ { \prime \prime } \}$breaks$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$into finitely many components, and the efect of this cutting when viewed in each component is again equivalent to (∗). We then conclude the proof by the same induction as above. This completes the proof of Lemma 13.14.□

Now, with Lemma 13.14, we can finish Part 2 of the proof, i.e. each atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is contained in a {3} or {33} molecule. In fact, those cut in Definition 13.12 (3) clearly belong to {33} molecule. Those cut in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5) also belong to {3} or {33} molecules by Lemma 13.14. Finally, those cut in Definition 13.12 (8) either belong to {3} molecule, or are cut in the process of applying Definition 13.12 (4)–(5) and thus belong to {3} or {33} molecules by Lemma 13.14.

Proof part 3. We prove that the number of deg 4 atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { U }$cut in Definition 13.12 (3) is at most $\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } + \# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) }$. In fact, such n must be the atom chosen in Definition 13.12 (2) (the${ \mathfrak { p } } \in S _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$in (3) will not be cut as deg 4 because it has an ov-parent in$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$which must be cut before p). Moreover, there are two possibilities when this n can has deg 4: either the component of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$containing n contains only deg 4 atoms, or n is the lowest remaining atom in$X _ { 0 } \cup X _ { 1 }$and has deg 4. The former case leads to at most $\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) }$choices for n.

In the latter case, n must have deg 4 and must not have any ov-child in$X _ { 0 } \cup X _ { 1 }$(otherwise this ov-child must have been cut before n as n is the lowest remaining atom in$X _ { 0 } \cup X _ { 1 }$, so n would not have deg 4), which means that n$\not \in X _ { 0 }$by definition of$X _ { 0 }$(and that$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } = \mathcal { O } )$. Therefore${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 1 }$, and it must belong to one of the initial ov-components of$X _ { 1 }$, say A. Since n has no ov-child in A, by Lemma 13.9 (i), it must be the unique lowest atom in$A$(here A satisfies the assumption of Lemma 13.9, because each deg 4 atom in$X _ { 1 }$ must have an ov-child in$X _ { 0 } \cup \mathbb { M } _ { D } ,$thus has at most one ov-child in$X _ { 1 } )$, which leads to at most$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) }$ choices for n due to the same number of choices of A. Putting together, this finishes Part 3 of the proof.

Proof part 4. We now complete the proof of (13.13). The bound for$\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$follows directly from Part 3, as no deg 4 atom can be cut in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5), or Definition 13.12 (8) (as shown in Part 2). To prove the lower bound for$\# _ { \{ 3 3 \} }$(which is$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } + \# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } )$, note that with at most$\mu : = \# _ { \operatorname { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } + \# _ { \operatorname { o v c p } ( X _ { 2 } ) }$ exceptions, each {3} molecule in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$created in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5) is always paired with a {33} molecule (the exceptions correspond to those atoms p in Definition 13.12 (3) with deg 4, which may cause q to be cut as a {3} molecule without a pairing {33} molecule), so the number of atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$cut in these steps is at most$3 \cdot \# _ { \{ 3 3 \} } + \mu$

Now consider the #<sub>UD</sub> good UD connections and the corresponding atoms${ \mathfrak { r } } \in \mathbb { M } _ { D }$. If any such r is not cut in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5), then in the molecule$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$after Definition 13.12 (7), this r must be a deg 3 atom (it cannot be deg 4 as it belong to a UD connection, and cannot be deg 2 because$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is ov-proper by Part 2), and must belong to a component of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contains at least two deg 3 atoms (by considering the pre-algorithm path connecting r to a deg 3 atom or another UD connection, and the possible place where a bond of this path is broken; note that a broken bond creates a fixed end and thus deg 3 atom). We collect all these atoms r (which are not cut in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5)), with the number of them being $\geq \# \mathrm { w D } - ( 3 \cdot \# \{ 3 3 \} + \mu )$by the above proof, and consider all the components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(after Definition 13.12 $( 7 ) )$containing them; let the number of deg 3 atoms in each of these components be$m _ { j } \geq 2$, then after Definition 13.12 (7) we have that (note that each component in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$will have at least one deg 3 atom after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, see Remark 10.6):

$$
\# _ {\deg 3} - \# _ {\mathrm{comp}} \geq \sum_ {j} (m _ {j} - 1) \geq \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {j} m _ {j} \geq (\# _ {\mathrm{UD}} - 3 \cdot \# _ {\{3 3 \}} - \mu) / 2,\tag{13.14}
$$

where$\# \mathrm { d e g 3 }$and$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } }$are the number of deg 3 atoms and number of components respectively. Then, consider the increment of the left hand side of (13.14) in each cutting in Definition 13.12 (8). Using Definition $8 . 3$, and noting that each such cut can only create one fixed end at one deg 4 atom (adding only one deg 3 atom) in each resulting (extra) component, we can verify that this is invariant after cutting one deg 3 atom, and decreases by 1 after each cutting in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5). Since this value should be come 0 after all atoms of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$have been cut, we conclude that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \frac {1}{2} (\# _ {\mathrm{UD}} - 3 \cdot \# _ {\{3 3 \}} - \mu),
$$

and therefore

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 \}} \geq \frac {1}{5} \cdot (\# _ {\mathrm{UD}} - \mu).
$$

This completes the proof.

13.5. Toy model I plus/II dichotomy, and finishing the proof. We now put everything together and finish the proof of Proposition 12.18. Now we may assume (i)–(iii) in Reduction 2, as well as Reduction 3 (otherwise Proposition 12.18 already follows from Proposition 13.3); namely, we assume that

• Each of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a forest and has no deg 2 atoms. No atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is a parent of any atom in $\mathbb { M } _ { U } .$, and$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(resp.$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$has no C-top (resp. C-bottom) fixed end.

• The number of full components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$is$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } \leq 1 0 ( C _ { 5 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$. Each component in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$has either at least two bonds connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, or one bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and one deg 3 atom.

• The number of good UD connections (i.e. UD connections that are connected to either another UD connection or a deg 3 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { D } .$, see Proposition 13.13) satisfy$\# \mathrm { { U D } } \geq \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime } / 4$

• The number of components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is$\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, and the number of weakly degenerate atoms and pairs in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is less than$( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime } .$

• We have$| \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } | \leq ( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, with the set$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$defined in Proposition 13.3.

Proof of Proposition 12.18. Before proceeding with Stages 1–6 below, we first briefly summarize our strategy, how the diferent toy models (I plus and II) in Section 11 occur in the proof, and how the diferent algorithms (3COMPUP and MAINUD) are used. First note that, from the above assumptions, each of $\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$is essentially a tree (with negligible full components), with negligible number of 2-connections in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$, and suficiently many good UD connections (all relative to$\rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime } ;$same below).

In Stage 1, we first cut as free all 2-connections (i.e. atoms in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } )$in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and subsequently cut any deg 2 atoms. This allows to completely get rid of 2-connections in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$at a loss of negligible {4} molecules. The quantity #<sub>UD</sub> (i.e. the number of good$U D$connections) may decrease, but the decrease is again negligible, so we still have$\# \mathrm { { u p } } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$after this stage.

Now, let Z be the set of deg 3 atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(in reality this needs slight modification to avoid components with only one deg 3 atom, which we omit here). Consider$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( \overline { { Z } } ) }$which is the number of ov-components of Z; if$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( \overline { { Z } } ) } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, then in Stage 2, we can apply 3COMPDN (the dual of 3COMPUP) to$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, which is already suficient by Proposition 13.7.

Therefore, we may assume$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( \overline { { Z } } ) } \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$. Now in Stage 3, we perform pre-processing to get rid of$\overline { { Z } }$ as well as the set Y of weakly degenerate atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, by cutting as free the set$S = \mathbf { S E L E C T } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } , \overline { { Z } } , \overline { { Y } } )$ defined in Definition 13.10. By assumption we have$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( \overline { { Z } } ) } \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$and$| \overline { { Y } } | \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, so by Proposition 13.11, $\mathbb { M } _ { D }$becomes ov-proper after cutting S as free, and the decrease of$\# _ { \mathrm { U D } }$is still negligible, so we still have $\# \mathrm { { u p } } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$after this stage.

At this point we can see the dichotomy that distinguishes the cases of toy model I plus (where we apply MAINUD) and toy model II (where we apply 3COMPUP). Let$X _ { 0 }$and$X _ { 1 }$be defined as in Definition 13.12; by definition, it is easy to see that if we cut$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free, then the C-atoms in$X _ { 0 }$are subsequently cut as deg 2, and the deg 3 C-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$are exactly those in$X _ { 1 }$(the O-atoms in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$will not matter in this discussion). As such, this$X _ { 1 }$plays the role of the set X in toy model II (see the discussion below Definition 11.15), so our dichotomy will be based on the value of$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) }$, the number of ov-components of$X _ { 1 }$(which is the analog of the number of components of X in Section 11).

Before proceeding, however, we need one more step: in order to apply 3COMPUP, we need that each component of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$after cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free (and subsequently cutting deg 2 atoms) to contain at least two deg 3 atoms. If a component A violates this, it is easy to see that before cutting$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$, the set A has only one bond connecting to$\mathbb { M } \backslash A$. This leads to Stage 4, where we get rid of these sets A by cutting them as fixed, which allows us to apply 3COMPUP when needed. It is easy to see that we still have$\# \mathrm { { U D } } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$

Now we can consider the dichotomy discussed above: if$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, then in Stage 5 we cut$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$as free and apply 3COMPUP to$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(as in toy model II), which is suficient by Proposition 13.7. Finally, if $\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) } \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, then in Stage 6 we apply MAINUD to$M _ { U D }$(as in toy model I plus). Note that M$\mathbfcal { D }$ is ov-proper and has no weak degeneracy atom thanks to Stage 3, so any {33} molecule will be good. We then apply Proposition 13.13, and use that$\# \mathrm { { U D } } \gtrsim \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$and$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( X _ { 1 } ) } \ll \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$, to conclude the proof.

Stage 1. We cut each atom in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$as free (see Figure 63). If any atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$becomes deg 2, we also cut it as free, until$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$contains no deg 2 atoms. Note that the contribution of these operations to $\# _ { \{ 4 \} }$is at most$| \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } | \leq ( C _ { 2 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$

![](images/page_165_image_8.jpg)

Figure 63. Cutting atoms in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } \ ( \mathrm { r e d } )$and subsequent deg 2 atoms (blue) in Stage 1. Note that cutting each red breaks at most 2 UD connections (cutting each blue breaks none), and any good UD connection that is not broken shall remain good.

By definition of${ \overline { { \mathbb { M } } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } ,$cutting any atom in it as free does not create any C-top fixed atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$or any C-bottom fixed atom in${ \mathbb { M } } _ { D } .$, and neither does any subsequent operations cutting deg 2 atoms (because, when we subsequently cut any deg 2 atom in$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$(resp.$\mathbb { M } _ { D } )$, it must be O-atom or has two bottom (resp. top) fixed ends, so cutting it will not create any top (resp. bottom) fixed end). Moreover, consider any UD connection e and the maximal ov-segment containing$e ;$cutting each atom in$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 }$breaks at most two such ov-segments (where breaking means cutting an atom in this ov-segment as free), and any subsequent cutting of deg 2 atoms cannot break any such ov-segment (for the same reason as above).

If the ov-segment containing e is not broken, then e will remain a good UD connection if it is initially so. In fact, consider the component X of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$containing the$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$endpoint of$e ;$if$X$is not afected in the cutting (i.e. no atom in X is cut and no fixed end is created in X) then e will remain good as it is; if X is afected then the new component containing the$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$endpoint of e must contain a deg 3 atom.

Therefore, after Stage 1, we still have

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{UD}} \geq \rho^ {\prime \prime \prime} / 4 - 2 | \overline {{\mathbb {M}}} _ {2 \mathrm{conn}} ^ {2} | \geq \rho^ {\prime \prime \prime} / 5.\tag{13.15}
$$

Moreover, after Stage 1,$\mathbb { M } _ { U D }$is still a canonical UD molecule, and now$\overline { { \mathbb { M } } } _ { 2 \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { 2 } = \mathcal { O }$. The number of full components of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$still satisfy that$\# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { U } ) } + \# _ { \mathrm { f u c p } ( \mathbb { M } _ { D } ) } \leq 4 ( C _ { 3 } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \rho ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$

Stage 2. Now consider all the components of$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$that contain at least two deg 3 atoms, and all the deg 3 atoms contained in one such component. Let the set of all such deg 3 atoms be${ \overline { { Z } } } _ { 0 } .$, and let$\overline { { Y } }$be the union of all weakly degenerate atoms and atom pairs in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$(see Proposition 12.17). Let the number of ov-components of$\overline { { Z } } _ { 0 }$in$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$be$\# _ { \mathrm { o v c p } ( \overline { { Z } } _ { 0 } ) }$as in Propositions 13.7 and 13.11.

## 14. Proof of the$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$estimates

In this section, we prove Proposition 6.1. By induction, we only need to prove$( 6 . 1 ) \mathrm { - } ( 6 . 2 )$for$\ell \tau .$assuming that they are already true for$( \ell - 1 ) \tau$. \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} (x, v) = (- 1) ^ {| \mathbb {M} | \circ} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q _ {\mathbb {M}}) (x - \tau v, v), \quad | \mathcal {I N} _ {\mathbb {M}} | (x, v) = \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} | Q _ {\mathbb {M}} | (x - \tau v, v),

(14.2)

where$| \mathbb { M } | _ { \mathrm { o } }$is the number of O-atoms in M.

In the rest of this section, we will perform the above change of variables and thereby assume$\ell = 1$. Now, using (14.2), we can rewrite the sum (3.16) as

are the leading and sub-leading terms in$f ^ { \mathcal { A } }$respectively.

We will study the leading term$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$in Section 14.1, and establish its asymptotics (see (14.27)) in Section 14.2. 14.1. The leading terms. Start with the term$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$in (14.4). Here M is a tree as$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) = 0$and M is connected (by Definition 3.20 (1b), note M has only one root particle line); moreover, it is straightforward to verify that M is a tree and$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } < \Lambda _ { \ell }$actually implies$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } }$. Therefore, the summation in$f ^ { \lambda , \mathrm { l e d } } \ \mathrm { i n }$ (14.4) is taken with only the assumptions that M is a tree and$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } < \Lambda _ { \ell }$. Note also that$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = | \mathbb { M } | + 1$ (i.e. number of collisions equals number of particles minus 1, in the absence of recollisions).

Now we introduce the following definition.

Definition 14.1. Let M be a molecule with single layer ℓ and one root particle line, which we denote by ${ \pmb { p } } _ { \mathrm { r t } }$. Define the highest atom in${ \pmb { p } } _ { \mathrm { r t } }$to be${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { \mathrm { r t } }$, and the top end in${ \pmb { p } } _ { \mathrm { r t } }$to be$e _ { \mathrm { r t } }$, which is the unique fixed end of M.

Define${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$to be the set of trees M with$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) = 0$and$| \mathbb { M } | = n$(with$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = n + 1 < \Lambda )$. Define also${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n } ^ { * }$ to be the subset of${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$formed by those M such that every atom in M is a descendant of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { \mathrm { r t } }$

It is known in [7] that the contribution of the molecules$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } \backslash \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$to$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$in (14.4) is zero, due to a simple cancellation between the terms. We now present this argument, in a similar manner to [7].

Proposition 14.2. There is an involution$\mathbb { M } \mapsto \mathbb { M } ^ { \mathrm { t w i } }$from$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } \backslash \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$to itself, such that$| \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } | _ { 0 } = | \mathbb { M } | _ { 0 } \pm 1$ and${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ) = { \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$for$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M } ^ { \mathrm { { t w i } } }$. In particular, this implies that

$$
\sum_ {\mathbb {M} \in \mathfrak {M} _ {n} \setminus \mathfrak {M} _ {n} ^ {*}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathbb {M} | \circ} \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q _ {\mathbb {M}}) = 0.\tag{14.5}
$$

Proof. If$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } \backslash \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$, then$\mathbb { M } \ne S _ { \mathfrak { n _ { t } } }$(where$S _ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the set of descendants of n, see Definition 3.5). Choose a highest atom m$\in \mathbb { M } \backslash S _ { \mathrm { t r } }$. If there is more than one m, we can select one in an arbitrary way (for example by introducing the artificial total ordering in Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 7.5 and select the highest m). Then define$\mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } = \mathbb { M } ^ { \mathrm { t w i } }$to be formed from M by turning m into a$\mathrm { C } / \mathrm { O }$atom m<sup>′</sup> if m is originally an $\mathrm { O } / \mathrm { C }$atom.

Clearly$| \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } | _ { 0 } = | \mathbb { M } | _ { 0 } \pm 1$. To prove${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ) = { \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$, note that m$\in \mathbb { M }$(and$\mathfrak { m } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } )$has no parent, thus it has two top free ends$e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$and$e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$(the fixed end$e _ { \mathrm { r t } } \not \in \{ e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \} \big )$. Now we compare the integrals$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } )$ and$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$as in (7.6). Note that$Q _ { \mathbb { M } } = Q _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } }$does not depend on$z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$and$z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$, thus the only diference in the two integrals occurs in the$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { m } }$and$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { m ^ { \prime } } }$factors. However, by (7.15), if we integrate out the variables $\left( z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } , t _ { \mathfrak { m } } \right)$, then the result would be the same for C and O-atoms, provided that the$Q$in (7.15) does not depend on$z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } }$and$z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } }$(which is true in our case). This proves${ \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } ^ { \prime } } ) = { \mathcal { T } } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$, then (14.5) follows consequently.□

Thanks to (14.5), we can rewrite the sum in$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$in (14.4) as

$$
f ^ {\mathcal {A}, \text {led}} (x, v) = g (x - \tau v, v) + \sum_ {1 \leq n <   \Lambda_ {\ell} - 1} \sum_ {\mathbb {M} \in \mathfrak {M} _ {n} ^ {*}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathbb {M} | _ {\mathrm{O}}} \cdot \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (Q _ {\mathbb {M}}) (x - \tau v, v).\tag{14.6}

Note that, for$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$, we have$\mathbb { M } = S _ { \mathfrak { n } _ { \mathrm { t r } } }$is a binary tree in the sense that each atom other than${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { \mathrm { t r } }$has a unique parent (and one top fixed end), and two bottom free ends/children in total. As such, it will be convenient to rename the variables at the node n as

$$
\left(z _ {e _ {1}}, z _ {e _ {2}}, z _ {e _ {1} ^ {\prime}}, z _ {e _ {2} ^ {\prime}}\right) \leftrightarrow \left(z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}\right)\tag{14.7}
$$

where$z _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the variable corresponding to the top free end at$\mathfrak { n } , \ z _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the one corresponding to the bond connecting n to its parent (or the free end$e _ { \mathrm { t r } }$when${ \mathfrak { n } } = { \mathfrak { n } } _ { \mathrm { t r } } ) , z _ { 4 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the one corresponding to the bottom edge at n that is serial to the top free end, and$z _ { 3 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$is the remaining variable. Given the symmetries of$\Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } } ,$, we always have$\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \Delta } _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( z _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 3 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 4 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } ) = \pmb { \Delta } _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( z _ { e _ { 1 } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } } , z _ { e _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } } , z _ { e _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } } ) } \end{array}$

Next, we will split$g = f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau ) + g _ { \mathrm { r e m } }$for each input factor in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$in (14.6). We expect those terms containing at least one$g _ { \mathrm { r e m } }$should vanish in the limit, in view of (6.2) satisfied by$g _ { \mathrm { r e m } } ;$to prove this, we need the next proposition.

Proposition 14.3. Let$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$, and let$\widetilde { Q }$be defined as in (14.1) but with the input factors$g$replaced by $h _ { e }$which depends on e. Recall also the$\beta _ { \ell }$as in (1.34), and define$\widetilde { \beta } _ { \ell } : = ( \beta _ { \ell } + \beta _ { \ell - 1 } ) / 2$. Then we have

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\widetilde {Q}) (x - \tau v, v) \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell}}} \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot C ^ {n} \tau^ {n / 2} \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \| h _ {e} \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\beta_ {\ell - 1}}}.\tag{14.8}
$$

Proof. Recall that$\widetilde { \beta } _ { \ell } = \beta _ { \ell - 1 } - ( \beta / 4 0 \mathfrak { L } )$by definition. We divide the proof into 3 parts.

Proof part 1: adjusting Maxwellian weights. Without loss of generality, we may assume$h _ { e } \geq 0$ and$\| h _ { e } \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta _ { \ell - 1 } } } = 1$for all$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$. Recall$\mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { \pm }$is the set of all top/bottom ends of M, and$e _ { \mathrm { t r } } \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + }$is the unique fixed end; by energy conservation we have$\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { e \in { \mathcal E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } } | v _ { e } | ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { e \in { \mathcal E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { + } } } \end{array}$. Using also the notion$z _ { j } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$in (14.7), this implies that

$$
\sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \beta_ {\ell - 1} | v _ {e} | ^ {2} = \widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell} | v | ^ {2} + \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} \frac {\beta}{4 0 \mathfrak {L}} | v _ {e} | ^ {2} + \sum_ {\mathfrak {n}} \widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell} | v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} | ^ {2},\tag{14.9}
$$

where$v = v _ { e _ { \mathrm { t r } } }$is the output variable in the function$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( \widetilde { Q } ) ( x - \tau v , v )$. Since$\| h \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta } } = \| e ^ { \beta | v | ^ { 2 } } h \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { 0 } }$by (1.15), we can replace$h _ { e } \ b y \ e ^ { \beta \ell - 1 \left| v _ { e } \right| ^ { 2 } } h _ { e }$and apply (14.9), to reduce (14.8) to the following estimate:

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {\prime} (\widetilde {Q}) (x - \tau v, v) \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {0}} \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \cdot C ^ {n} \tau^ {n / 2}, \quad \mathrm{given} \| h _ {e} \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {0}} = 1,\tag{14.10}
$$

where$\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { Z } _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \prime } ( \widetilde { Q } ) = \mathcal { Z } _ { \mathbb { M } } \left( \widetilde { Q } \cdot \prod _ { \mathfrak { n } } e ^ { - \widetilde { \beta } _ { \ell } \lvert v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } \rvert ^ { 2 } } \cdot \prod _ { e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - } } e ^ { - ( \beta / 4 0 \mathfrak { L } ) \lvert v _ { e } \rvert ^ { 2 } } \right) . } \end{array}$

Proof part 2: decomposition of$\widetilde { Q }$. By the exponential decay in the formula of$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ^ { \prime } ( \widetilde { Q } )$, it is easy to see that we can restrict the support of$Q$to$| v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$for each$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$, and therefore for all$e \in { \mathcal { E } }$by energy conservation, in the same way as in Part 2 of the proof of Proposition 6.2. Moreover, by repeating the same proof there (in Section 9.2), we can also decompose

$$

$$

where each$\widetilde { Q } _ { \alpha }$is uniformly bounded and is supported in the set$| x _ { e } - x _ { e } ^ { * } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$for each$e \in \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$, with some choice of$( x _ { e } ^ { * } )$depending on$\alpha .$

Since$| v _ { e } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$, this support condition implies that$| x _ { e _ { \mathrm { t r } } } - x _ { e _ { 0 } } ^ { * } | \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$where$e _ { 0 }$is the bottom end of the root particle line$( e _ { \mathrm { t r } }$is its top end). As we have$x = x _ { e _ { \mathrm { t r } } } + \tau \cdot v _ { e _ { \mathrm { t r } } }$for the variable x in (14.8), we know that for each$\alpha .$, this x belongs to a fixed ball of radius$| \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$. This ball can be divided into $\leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } }$unit cubes, so under this support condition we have$\| f \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { 0 } } \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } } \cdot \| f \| _ { L ^ { \infty } }$due to (1.15).

Summing up, using (14.11) and the above discussions, we see that (14.10) would follow if we can prove the following estimate (uniformly in α):

Proof part 3: estimating the integral. To prove (14.12), we first invoke (9.90) in Proposition 9.8 with $v _ { e }$replaced by${ \mathfrak { L } } ^ { - 1 / 2 } v _ { e }$, which allows us to bound the product of the cross-sections in the$\Delta ( \cdots )$factors by

\prod_ {\mathfrak {n}} (1 + | v _ {e _ {1}} - v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq \mathfrak {L} ^ {n / 2} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n}} (1 + | \mathfrak {L} ^ {- 1 / 2} v _ {e _ {1}} - \mathfrak {L} ^ {- 1 / 2} v _ {e _ {2}} |) \leq C ^ {n} \mathfrak {L} ^ {n / 2} \cdot \mathfrak {C} _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {5 / 6} \cdot \exp \left(\frac {\beta}{4 0 \mathfrak {L}} \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\mathrm{end}} ^ {-}} | v _ {e} | ^ {2}\right),

Here we have used the elementary inequality ex$\mathsf { p } ( C | v | ^ { 4 / 3 } ) \leq C \exp ( ( \beta / 4 0 ) | v | ^ { 2 } )$. This allows to bound

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {\prime} (\widetilde {Q} _ {\alpha}) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq C ^ {n} \mathfrak {L} ^ {n / 2} \cdot \mathfrak {C} _ {\mathbb {M}} ^ {5 / 6} \cdot \left(\int_ {\mathcal {D}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}\right) \cdot \sup _ {\boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}} \in \mathcal {D}} \| V _ {n} (z, \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}) \| _ {L ^ {\infty}},} \\ & {\quad V _ {n} (z, \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}) = \varepsilon^ {- (d - 1) n} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {*}} |} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} e ^ {- \widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell} | v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} | ^ {2}} \pmb {\Delta} ^ {\dagger} (z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \mathrm{d} z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} \mathrm{d} z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} \mathrm{d} z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}},} \end{array}
$$

where$\mathcal { D }$is as in (7.5) but with$\ell ^ { \prime }$replaced by 1, and$\Delta ^ { \dagger }$is as in$( 7 . 3 ) \mathrm { - } ( 7 . 4 )$but without the$[ ( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) \cdot \omega ] _ { - }$ factor, and we have relabeled the variables at each atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$using the variables$z _ { j } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$as in$( 1 4 . 7 )$. Note also that$| \mathcal { E } _ { * } | - 2 | \mathbb { M } | = n$in (7.6) using Part 1 of the proof of Proposition 7.5 (and$| \mathcal { E } | - | \mathcal { E } _ { * } | = 1$and$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } = n + 1 )$ Since$\mathfrak { C } _ { \mathbb { M } } \geq 1$and$\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \mathcal { D } } \mathrm { d } t _ { \mathrm { M } } = \boldsymbol { \tau } ^ { n } \cdot \boldsymbol { \mathfrak { C } } _ { \mathrm { M } } ^ { - 1 } } \end{array}$by (9.86), and recall that$\tau { \mathfrak { L } } = t _ { \mathrm { f i n } } \leq C$, we see that (14.12) will follow once we show that$\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } } \in \mathcal { D } } \| V _ { n } ( z , \pmb { t } _ { \mathbb { M } } ) \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } \leq C ^ { n } } \end{array}$. The latter is straightforward as one calculates the integrals from top to bottom in the binary tree M as follows: for each$\mathfrak { n } \in \mathbb { M }$, we fix$z _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$and integrate in the variables$\left( z _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 3 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 4 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } \right)$, noting that for any node${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$we have

by a simple variant of (9.5). This finishes the proof.

Now, using Proposition 14.3, we may split$g = f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau ) + g _ { \mathrm { r e m } } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$for each input factor in in $\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } ( Q _ { \mathbb { M } } )$in (14.6). Define$f _ { 1 } ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$to be the same as in (14.6) but with all input factors$g = f ^ { A } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$ replaced by$f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$. By Proposition 14.3 and (6.2) and (1.29), it is easy to see that

$$
\left\| f ^ {\mathcal {A}, \text {led}} - f _ {1} ^ {\mathcal {A}, \text {led}} \right\| _ {\operatorname{Bol} ^ {\beta_ {\ell}}} \leq | \log \varepsilon | ^ {C ^ {*}} \sum_ {n \geq 0} (C \tau^ {1 / 2}) ^ {n} \cdot \varepsilon^ {\theta_ {\ell - 1}} \leq \varepsilon^ {\theta_ {\ell}} / 1 0.\tag{14.13}

Here we have used the fact that the number of molecules$\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n } ^ { * }$is bounded by$C ^ { n }$, which follows from the well-known upper bound for the number of binary trees.

14.2. Approximation by Boltzmann iterates. In view of (14.13), now we only need to estimate$f _ { 1 } ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$ In this subsection, we will approximate it by the iterates, up to order$\Lambda - 2 .$, of the Boltzmann equation. To do this, we first perform a change of variables in the integral appearing in the definition of$f _ { 1 } ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$. We adopt the same relabeling of the variables$z _ { j } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$at each atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M }$, then there are two cases of$\Delta = \Delta _ { \mathfrak { n } }$in (14.6):

• When n is C-atom, we have$\Delta _ { + }$defined by

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \boldsymbol {\Delta} _ {+} (z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) := & \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \big) \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + [ (v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \cdot \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (v _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - [ (v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \omega ] \omega \big) \\ & \times \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) | - \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big [ (v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \omega \big ] _ {+}; \end{array}\tag{14.14}
$$

• When n is O-atom, we have$\Delta _ { - }$defined by

$$
\begin{array}{r l r} & & {\pmb {\Delta} _ {-} (z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) := \pmb {\delta} (x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \pmb {\delta} (x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \pmb {\delta} (v _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \pmb {\delta} (v _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}})} \\ & & {\times \pmb {\delta} (| x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) | - \varepsilon) \cdot [ (v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) \cdot \omega ] _ {+}.} \end{array}\tag{14.15}
$$

Here we have used that$\left[ \left( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } \right) \cdot \omega \right] _ { - } = \left[ \left( v _ { 3 } ^ { \mathtt { n } } - v _ { 4 } ^ { \mathtt { n } } \right) \cdot \omega \right] _ { - } = \left[ \left( v _ { 1 } ^ { \mathtt { n } } - v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathtt { n } } \right) \cdot \omega \right] _ { - }$1for the given relabeling in (14.7); also recall that$\omega : = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { e _ { 1 } } - x _ { e _ { 2 } } + t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { e _ { 1 } } - v _ { e _ { 2 } } ) ) = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } ( x _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - x _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } + t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - v _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } ) )$. Now, recall that the integration of the$\Delta _ { \pm }$factor at each atom is performed by first integrating in$( z _ { 3 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 4 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } )$(with$( z _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } , z _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } )$fixed), followed by integrating in$z _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$followed by that in$z _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$and$t _ { \mathfrak { n } }$. Since the integral over$x _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } }$involves a δ measure supported on a sphere centered at$x _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - v _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } )$, we can make the change variables$x _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } = x _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - v _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } ) + \varepsilon \omega _ { \mathfrak { n } }$as in the proof of Proposition 9.1, and write

$$
\boldsymbol {\delta} \big (| x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} + t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) | - \varepsilon \big) = \varepsilon^ {d - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \boldsymbol {\delta} \big (x _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - x _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - t _ {\mathfrak {n}} (v _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}} - v _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}) + \varepsilon \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}} \big)   \mathrm{d} \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}}.

As a result, we can now rewrite the integral defining$f _ { 1 } ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} f _ {1} ^ {\mathcal {A}, \text {led}} (x, v) = f \big ((\ell - 1) \tau , x - \tau v, v \big) + \sum_ {1 \leq n <   \Lambda_ {\ell} - 1} \sum_ {\mathbb {M} \in \mathfrak {M} _ {n} ^ {*}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathbb {M} | _ {\mathrm{o}}} \cdot \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\widetilde {Q} _ {\mathbb {M}}) (x - \tau v, v), \\ \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\widetilde {Q} _ {\mathbb {M}}) := \int_ {\mathcal {D}} \int_ {(\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {*} |}} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \widetilde {\Delta} _ {\pm} (z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {end}} ^ {-}} f ((\ell - 1) \tau , z _ {e})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {*}}   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {\omega} _ {\mathbb {M}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}, \end{array}\tag{14.16}
$$

where$\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { d } \omega _ { \mathcal { M } } : = \prod _ { \mathfrak { n } \in \mathcal { M } } \mathrm { d } \omega _ { \mathfrak { n } } } \end{array}$and$\widetilde { \Delta } _ { \pm }$is the same as$\Delta _ { \pm }$in (14.14)–(14.15) except that$\omega$is replaced by$\omega _ { \mathfrak { n } }$ and the last δ in both expressions is replaced by$\delta ( x _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - x _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ( v _ { 2 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } - v _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { n } } ) + \varepsilon \omega _ { \mathfrak { n } } )$

Next, we will explain the relation of the above expansion in (14.16) with the Duhamel expansion of the solution$f ( t , z )$to the Boltzmann equation on the interval$[ ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , \ell \tau ]$

Proposition 14.4. The solution$f ( s , z )$of the Botlzmann equation on the interval$[ ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , \ell \tau ]$can be written as$f ( s , z ) : = F ( s - ( \ell - 1 ) \tau , x - s v + ( \ell - 1 ) \tau v , v )$where$F ( t , z )$is defined for$t \in [ 0 , \tau ]$as

$$
\begin{array}{l} F (t, z) := F ^ {(\mathrm{app})} + F ^ {(\mathrm{rem})}, \\ F ^ {(\mathrm{app})} := f ((\ell - 1) \tau , z) + \sum_ {1 \leq k <   \Lambda_ {\ell} - 1} F ^ {(k)} (t, z), \qquad F ^ {(\mathrm{rem})} := \sum_ {k \geq \Lambda_ {\ell} - 1} F ^ {(k)} (t, z), \end{array}\tag{14.17}
$$

and$F ^ { ( k ) } ( t , z )$is defined by

$$
\begin{array}{l} F ^ {(k)} (t, z) := \sum_ {\mathbb {M} \in \mathfrak {M} _ {k} ^ {*}} (- 1) ^ {| \mathbb {M} | _ {\mathrm{O}}} \cdot \widetilde {\mathcal {I}} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\widetilde {Q} _ {\mathbb {M}}) (t, z), \\ \widetilde {\mathcal {I}} _ {\mathbb {M}} (\widetilde {Q} _ {\mathbb {M}}) := \int_ {\mathcal {D} ^ {t}} \int_ {(\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}) ^ {| \mathbb {M} |}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d | \mathcal {E} _ {* |}}} \prod_ {\mathfrak {n} \in \mathbb {M}} \widetilde {\boldsymbol {\Delta}} _ {\pm} ^ {(0)} (z _ {1} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {2} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {3} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, z _ {4} ^ {\mathfrak {n}}, \omega_ {\mathfrak {n}}, t _ {\mathfrak {n}}) \prod_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {and}} ^ {-}} f ((\ell - 1) \tau , z _ {e})   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} _ {\mathcal {E} _ {*}}   \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {\omega} _ {\mathbb {M}} \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {t} _ {\mathbb {M}}. \end{array}\tag{14.18}
$$

$$

Proof. First notice that F satisfies the following integral equation on the interval$[ 0 , \tau ]$

$$
\begin{array}{l} F (t, z) = f ((\ell - 1) \tau , z) + \mathcal {C} (F, F) (t, z), \\ \mathcal {C} (f, g) (t, z) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \left[ (v - v _ {1}) \cdot \omega \right] _ {+} \cdot \left(f (s, x + v s - v ^ {\prime} s, v ^ {\prime}) g (s, x + v s - v _ {1} ^ {\prime} s, v _ {1} ^ {\prime}) \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ = \sum_ {(\pm)} \pm \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {6 d}} \widetilde {\boldsymbol {\Delta}} _ {\pm} ^ {(0)} (z, z _ {2}, z _ {3}, z _ {4}, s) \cdot f (s, z _ {3}) \cdot g (s, z _ {4}) \prod_ {i = 2} ^ {4} d z _ {i} d \omega d s, \end{array}\tag{14.20}

where$v ^ { \prime } , v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime }$are defined from$( v , v _ { 1 } )$as in (1.14).

Next, notice that$F ^ { ( k ) }$defined in (14.18) satisfies the following rrecurrence relation:

which can be checked readily by induction using the last equation in (14.20). Here we note that each molecule $\mathbb { M } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { k } ^ { \ast }$consists of one highest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { \mathrm { t r } }$which is either C-atom (corresponding to$\tilde { \Delta } _ { + } ^ { ( 0 ) }$in (14.20)) or$\mathrm { O } _ { - }$ atom (corresponding to$\widetilde { \Delta } _ { - } ^ { ( 0 ) }$in (14.20)), and two sub-molecules$\mathbb { M } ^ { i } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { k } ^ { * }$which are the sets of descendants of the two children${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i }$of$\mathfrak { n } ^ { * }$, with$k _ { 1 } + k _ { 2 } = k - 1$. The convergence of the infinite series$\textstyle \sum _ { k = 0 } ^ { \infty } F ^ { ( k ) }$then follows, once we establish (14.19), in view that$\mathfrak { M } _ { k }$ contains$O ( C ^ { k } )$molecules (by counting binary trees), and our choice of$\tau .$. The fact that this sum solves (14.20) follows by writing down the equation satisfied by$\begin{array} { r } { F ^ { \leq k } = \sum _ { j < k } F ^ { ( i ) } } \end{array}$, which reads

As such, it remains to justify (14.19). But, this follows from exactly the same proof of Proposition 14.3, only with$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$replaced by$\widetilde { \cal T } _ { \mathbb { M } }$□

Now we can compare$f _ { 1 } ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { l e d } }$with$f ( \ell \tau )$. The key step is contained in the next proposition.

14.3. The sub-leading terms. We now turn to$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { s u b } }$in (14.3)–(14.4). This is a sum over molecules M. Let$| { \mathbb { M } } | = n$and$\rho ( \mathbb { M } ) = \rho ,$note that either$\rho > 0$or$| \mathbb { M } | _ { p } \geq \Lambda _ { \ell }$by definition of$f ^ { \mathcal { A } , \mathrm { s u b } }$(if$\mathbb { M } \in \mathcal { T } _ { \Lambda _ { \ell } } ^ { \mathrm { e r r } }$then the extra O-atom creates a cycle). The same proof of Proposition 7.2 allows us to bound the number of molecules M by$C ^ { n } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$, so it sufices to bound each individual term$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } | Q _ { \mathbb { M } } |$. Just as in the proof of Proposition 6.2 (see Section 9.2), it sufices to construct an operation sequence (after turning M into regular, see Point 4 below) that produces at most$C ^ { n } | \log \varepsilon | ^ { C ^ { * } \rho }$sub-cases, and prove that each sub-case satisfies (cf. (9.53))

$$
\| \mathcal {I} _ {\mathbb {M} ^ {\prime}} | Q ^ {\prime} | (x - \tau v, v) \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\tilde {\beta} _ {\ell}}} \leq \tau^ {n / 9} \cdot \varepsilon^ {(v / 3) + (C _ {1 4} ^ {*}) ^ {- 1} \cdot \rho}.\tag{14.28}
$$

The proof of (14.28) will follow the same arguments as in Sections 9–13. We will only elaborate on the few places where the proof needs to be adapted to the current setting.

Point 1: adjusting Maxwellian weights. Start with the input factors$g = f ^ { A } ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$in$\mathcal { T } _ { \mathbb { M } } | Q _ { \mathbb { M } } |$. We decompose$g = f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau ) + g _ { \mathrm { r e m } }$as before, where$f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$and$g _ { \mathrm { r e m } }$satisfy (1.29) and (6.2) respectively. Let$\mathcal { V } \subseteq \mathcal { E } _ { \mathrm { e n d } } ^ { - }$be such that we have$g _ { \mathrm { r e m } }$for$e \in \mathcal { V }$and$f ( ( \ell - 1 ) \tau )$for$e \notin \mathcal { V }$, then we already gain a factor $\varepsilon ^ { \theta _ { \ell - 1 } \cdot | \nu | }$from the inputs in$\nu .$

Next, we use$\| h \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta } } = \| e ^ { \beta | v | ^ { 2 } } h \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { 0 } }$to reduce the$\mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta }$norms to$\mathrm { B o l } ^ { 0 }$norms. $$
\sum_ {e \in \mathcal {V}} \beta_ {\ell - 1} | v _ {e} | ^ {2} + \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {end}} ^ {-} \setminus \mathcal {V}} \beta | v _ {e} | ^ {2} \geq \widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell} | v | ^ {2} + \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {V}} (\beta / 4 0 \mathfrak {L}) | v _ {e} | ^ {2} + \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {end}} ^ {-} \setminus \mathcal {V}} (\beta / 2) | v _ {e} | ^ {2} + (\beta / 4 0 \mathfrak {L}) | v | ^ {2} + \sum_ {e \in \mathcal {E} _ {\text {end}} ^ {+} \setminus \{e _ {\text {tr}} \}} \widetilde {\beta} _ {\ell} | v _ {e} | ^ {2},
$$

Before getting to the proof of Proposition 15.1, we first briefly explain the strategy.

Cutting deg 3 and deg 2 atoms. A naive idea to exploit the recollisions is to keep cutting deg 3 atoms (the first being deg 4), until hitting a recollision and getting a {33} molecule. The main dificulty here, also the main dificulty in general, is that we may be forced to cut long sequences of deg 2 atoms without any gain. Let the set of deg 3 atoms being cut be A, then the set of subsequent deg 2 atoms being cut is obtained by starting from A and iteratively taking atoms with 2 bonds with previous atoms, which is just$X ( A )$in the notion of Definition 15.3.

We note that each atom in A is cut as deg 3, so it has only one bond connecting to previously cut atoms; in particular keep adding atoms in A will not create any new cycle, and we can think of these sets A as close to being trees (i.e. with$\rho ( A )$controlled). On the other hand, adding each atom in$X ( A )$will create one new cycle and increase the$\rho$value by 1. Finally, in choosing the set A we can optimize this process by each time cutting the highest (or lowest) deg 3 atom as in UP, which will ensure this set A is transversal<sup>18</sup> as in Definition 15.3.

We now define the transversal subsets A of M, and prove some properties.

Definition 15.3. Let M be a full molecule of C-atoms, and$A \subseteq \mathbb { M }$is an atom set. For any transversal set A, define the set$X _ { 0 } ( A )$such that, an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ( A )$if and only if${ \mathfrak { n } } \not \in A$and n has two bonds connected to two atoms in A. Inductively define$X _ { q } ( A )$such that,${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { q } ( A )$if and only if${ \mathfrak { n } } \not \in A .$, and either${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { q - 1 } ( A )$, or n has two bonds connected to two atoms in$X _ { q - 1 } ( A ) \cup A$. Define $X ( A ) = \cup _ { q \geq 0 } X _ { q } ( A )$, see Figure 65.
