(1) We can always choose$( A ^ { + } , A ^ { - } )$in Definition 15.3 such that each component of$A ^ { + }$has at least one bond connected to A.

(2) Define the sets$X _ { q } ^ { \pm } ( A )$in the same way as$X _ { q } ( A )$, but with the sentence$^ { 6 6 } \mathfrak { n }$has two bonds connected to two atoms in${ \dot { X } } _ { q - 1 } ( A ) \cup A ^ { \prime \prime }$replaced by$^ { 6 6 } \mathfrak { n }$has two children (or two parents) in$X _ { q - 1 } ^ { \pm } ( A ) \cup A ^ { \prime }$ Then we have$X _ { q } ^ { \pm } ( A ) = X _ { q } ( A ) \cap A ^ { \pm }$. Define$X ^ { \pm } ( A ) = \cup _ { q \geq 0 } X _ { q } ^ { \pm } ( A )$, then$X ^ { \pm } ( A ) = X \dot { ( } A ) \cap A ^ { \pm }$

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">A<sup>−</sup> = ∅ (resp. A<sup>+</sup> = ∅)</span></small>

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">no-bottom (resp. no-top) subsets are transversal sets where , so the general notion of transversality then arises naturally as combination of both.</span></small>

(3) The set$X ( A ) \cup A$is also connected and transversal. Moreover any atom in$\mathbb { M } \backslash ( X ( A ) \cup A )$has at most one bond with atoms in$X ( A ) \cup A$, so$X _ { 0 } ( X ( A ) \cup A ) = \varnothing$

(4) Recall$\rho ( A )$defined in Definition 3.13. Then there exists a connected transversal set$B \supseteq A$, such that$\rho ( B ) = \rho ( A )$, and either$B = \mathbb { M }$or$X _ { 0 } ( B ) \neq \emptyset$

Proof. Proof of (1). Suppose$A ^ { + }$has a component U that is not connected to A by a bond, then we replace $A ^ { + } \ \mathrm { b y } \ A ^ { + } \backslash U$and$A ^ { - }$by$A ^ { - } \cup U$, which still satisfies the requirements for$( A ^ { + } , A ^ { - } )$in Definition 15.3, but the number of components of$A ^ { + }$decreases by 1. Repeat until each component of$A ^ { + }$is connected to A by a bond$( \mathrm { o r } \ A ^ { + }$becomes empty).

Proof of (2). First$X _ { q } ^ { \pm } ( A ) \subseteq X _ { q } ( A ) \cap A ^ { \pm }$, which easily follows from definition and induction. To prove the opposite direction, first if an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ( A )$belongs to$A ^ { \pm }$, then n must have two children (or two parents) in A so${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ^ { \pm } ( A )$. We then proceed by induction: suppose$X _ { q - 1 } ^ { \pm } ( A ) = X _ { q - 1 } ( A ) \cap A ^ { \pm }$, now consider$\mathfrak { n } \in ( X _ { q } ( A ) \cap A ^ { + } ) \backslash X _ { q - 1 } ( A )$which has two adjacent atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$and${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$in$X _ { q - 1 } ( A ) \cup A$. If${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$belongs to$A ^ { - }$, then n must be child of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$(it is easy to see that both parents of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } \in A ^ { - }$must be in$A \cup A ^ { - } )$and thus n$\in A ^ { - }$which is impossible. This means$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 } \in A ^ { + } \cup A$and same for${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 }$. Since$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 , 2 } \in X _ { q - 1 } ( A ) \cup A$, we know by induction hypothesis that$\mathfrak { n } _ { 1 , 2 } \in X _ { q - 1 } ^ { + } ( A ) \cup A$, thus${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { q } ( A )$by definition. Same is true for$A ^ { - }$

Proof of (3). Connectedness is obvious by definition. To prove transversality, we simply decompose $\mathbb { M } \backslash ( A \cup X ( A ) ) = B ^ { + } \cup B ^ { - }$, where$B = A ^ { + } \backslash X ^ { + } ( A )$and$B ^ { - } = A ^ { - } \backslash X ^ { - } ( A )$. This then satisfies the requirements (using the fact that any child (or parent) of any atom n$\in X ^ { \pm } ( A )$must belong to$X ^ { \pm } ( A ) \cup A )$. The second statement follows from the definition of$X ( A )$in Definition 15.3.

Proof of (4). Suppose A is connected and transversal; we may assume$A \neq \mathbb { M }$and$X _ { 0 } ( A ) = \varnothing$(otherwise choose$B = A )$. Since M is connected, there must exist an atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash A$that is either a parent or child of an atom in A. We may assume it is a parent, and then choose a lowest atom${ \mathfrak { n } } \in \mathbb { M } \backslash A$among these parents. Since$X _ { 0 } ( A ) = \varnothing$, we know that n has only one bond with atoms in$A ;$let$A _ { 1 } = A \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$, then$A _ { 1 }$ is connected and$\rho ( A _ { 1 } ) = \rho ( A )$, see Figure 66.

Figure 66. Proof of Proposition 15.4 (4): n is a lowest parent of atom in$A ,$which is natural in terms of the UP or DOWN algorithm; C is the set of descendants of n in$A ^ { + }$

Now we claim that$A _ { 1 }$is transversal. To see this, define C to be the set of atoms m$\in A ^ { + } \backslash \{ \mathfrak { n } \}$that are descendants of${ \mathfrak { n } } ,$and decompose$\mathbb { M } \backslash A _ { 1 } = A _ { 1 } ^ { + } \cup A _ { 1 } ^ { - }$, where$A _ { 1 } ^ { + } = A ^ { + } \backslash ( C \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } \} )$) and$A _ { 1 } ^ { - } = A ^ { - } \cup C$. It is clear by checking all cases that no atom in$A _ { 1 }$can be parent of any atom in$A _ { 1 } ^ { + }$, and no atom in$A ^ { - }$can be parent of any atom in$A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 1 } ^ { + }$. If an atom m$\in C$is parent of some atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A _ { 1 } ^ { + }$, then${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A ^ { + } \backslash C .$, but m$\in C$and p is child of m, so we also have${ \mathfrak { p } } \in C .$contradiction. Finally if m$\in C$is parent of${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A _ { 1 } = A \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$, clearly ${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A$, but then m is also parent of an atom in$A ,$contradicting the lowest assumption of n.

Now we know that$A _ { 1 }$is also connected transversal; by replacing A by$A _ { 1 }$and repeating the above discussion, we eventually will reach some B such that either$B = \mathbb { M }$or$X _ { 0 } ( B ) \neq \emptyset$, as desired.□

Now we define the algorithm TRANSDN, which is analogous to the 2CONNDN algorithm and is applicable in the case when$\vert X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) \vert$(corresponding to the 2-connections in toy model III) is large.

Definition 15.5 (Algorithm TRANSDN). Suppose M is connected full molecule and A is a connected transversal subset. We may choose$( A ^ { + } , A ^ { - } )$as in Proposition 15.4 (1). Define the following algorithm:

(1) If A contains any deg 2 atom n, then cut it as free, and repeat until there is no deg 2 atom left.

(2) Choose a highest atom n in the set of all deg 3 atoms in A (or a highest atom in A, if A only contains deg 4 atoms). Let$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$be the set of ancestors of n in A.

(3) Starting from n, choose a lowest atom m in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$that has not been cut. If m has deg 3, and is adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$that also has deg 3, then cut$\{ { \mathfrak { m } } , { \mathfrak { p } } \}$as free; otherwise cut m as free. Repeat until all atoms in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } }$have been cut. Then go to (1).

(4) Repeat (1)–(3) until all atoms in A have been cut. Then cut the remaining part of$A ^ { + }$as free and cut it into elementary components using UP, then cut A<sup>−</sup> into elementary components using DOWN.

We also define the dual algorithm TRANSUP by reversing the notions of parent/child etc. Note that we replace$A ^ { + }$and$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$by$A ^ { - }$and$X _ { 0 } ^ { - } ( A )$, and also replace$A ^ { + }$by$A ^ { - }$in Proposition 15.4 (1).

Proposition 15.6. For the algorithm TRANSDN (and same for TRANSUP), we have$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } =$ 0 and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$, and$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} } \geq | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) | / 2 - \rho ( A ) - 1$

Proof. It is clear, in the same way as in the proof of Proposition 12.2, that during the process, there is no bottom fixed end in$( A \backslash Z _ { \mathfrak { n } } ) \cup \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$or in$A ^ { - }$, and there is no top fixed end in$Z _ { \mathfrak { n } } \backslash \{ { \mathfrak { n } } \}$or in$A ^ { + }$, so $\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$. Moreover$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$because no component of the remaining part of$A ^ { + }$after Definition 15.5 (3) can be full when it is first cut in Definition 15.5 (4) (thanks to Proposition 15.4 (1)), and no component of$A ^ { - }$can be full when it is first cut in Definition 15.5 (4) (thanks to M being connected).

To prove the lower bound for$\# _ { \{ 3 3 A \} }$, note that only one atom in A belongs to a {4} molecule (as A is connected). Let the number of atoms in A that belongs to a {2} molecule be$q ,$then by considering the increment of the same quantity$\sigma : = \# _ { \mathrm { b o / f r } } - 3 | \mathbb { M } |$and applying the same arguments in the proof of Proposition 12.2 (but restrected to$A )$, and noticing that initially all atoms in A have deg 4, we deduce that

$$
\# _ {\{2 \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 \}} - \# _ {\{4 \}} = - \sigma_ {\mathrm{init}} = \# _ {\mathrm{bond}} - | A | = \rho (A) - 1,
$$

and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$, hence$q \le \rho ( A )$. Then, for each${ \mathfrak { n } } \in X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$, which is adjacent to two atoms${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 } , { \mathfrak { n } } _ { 2 } \in A$by two bonds, assume say$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$is cut after${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { 1 }$. The total number of such$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$is at least$\vert X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) \vert / 2$as each$\mathfrak { n } _ { 2 }$can be obtained from at most two n. For each such n<sub>2</sub>, the corresponding n must have deg 3 when it is cut, so by Definition 15.5 (3), it must belong to either$\{ 4 \} \mathrm { - , o r ~ \{ 2 \} \mathrm { - , ~ o r ~ \{ 3 3 A \} } }$molecule. Using the upper bound for the number of {4} and {2} molecules, this completes the proof.□

Next we define the SELECT2 function, which is an extension of the SELECT function in the case when A may contain cycles (but with$\rho ( A )$bounded). The proof follows similar ideas, except for the extra step (3), which is needed because of the possible cycle in A.

Definition 15.7 (The function SELECT2). Let A be a connected molecule with only C-atoms, no bottom fixed end, and no deg 2 atoms. Let Z be the set of deg 3 atoms in A, and let Y be a subset of atoms in A such that A becomes a forest after removing the atoms in Y. We define the function SELECT2 = SELECT2(A, Z, Y) as follows, see Figure 67.

(1) Consider all the components of$Z \cup Y$in A, which is a finite collection of disjoint subsets of A.

(2) Since A only has C-atoms, the shortest ov-distance between sets (Definition 8.4) coincides with the standard definition of distance on a graph. If any two of the subsets in (1), say U and V, have the shortest distance (within A) which is at most 4, then we choose one shortest path between an atom in U and an atom in V, and let the atoms on this path be${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { j } .$. Then replace the two sets U and V by a single set which is$U \cup V \cup \{ \mathfrak { n } _ { j } \}$

(3) Repeat (2) until this can no longer be done. Next, if a single subset U contains two atoms (which may be the same) that are connected by a path of length at most 4 with none of the intermediate atoms belonging to$U$or any other subset, then add the atoms on this path to U. If this causes the shortest distance between two subsets to be$\leq 4$, then proceed to (2) and repeat it as above.

(4) When no scenario in (2) or (3) occurs, we output$S : = \mathbf { S E L E C T 2 } ( A , Z , Y )$as the union of all the current sets.

Proposition 15.8. The molecule A becomes a proper forest after cutting S as free, and we also have $| S | \leq 1 0 ( | Y | + | Z | + \rho ( A ) )$

Proof. The proof is essentially the same as Proposition 13.11. First A becomes a forest after cutting S as free, because$Y \subseteq S$. Also A becomes proper after cutting S as free, due to the same reason in the proof of Proposition 13.11; in the language of that proof, the absence of the scenario in Definition 15.7 (2) prevents the case when m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to two diferent components U and$V ,$and the absence of the scenario in Definition 15.7 (3) prevents the case when m and${ \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \prime }$belong to the same components$U .$

As for the upper bound for |S|, simply note that each single step in Definition 15.7 (2)–(3) adds at most 3 atoms to S. Moreover each single step in Definition 15.7 (2) decreases the number of subsets by 1 (as it connectes U and V together) and does not decrease$\rho ( S )$(as$\rho ( S )$is the number of independent cycles, so adding more atoms cannot decrease$\rho ( S ) )$. Each single step in Definition 15.7 (3) does not change the number of subsets, but adds one more cycle to$S ;$in particular adding this cycle increases the value of$\rho ( S )$ by at least 1. Putting together, we know that the value of

$$
\gamma := (\text { number   of   sets   in } S) - \rho (S)
$$

decreases by at least 1 in each step Definition 15.7$( 2 )  { - } ( 3 )$. Since we always have$\rho ( S ) \leq \rho ( A )$because$S \subseteq A$ (again it is easy to see that adding one atom or arbitrarily many atoms does not decrease the$\rho$value), we know that the initial value of$\gamma \ { \mathrm { i s } } \leq | Y | + | Z |$and the final value of γ is$\geq - \rho ( A )$, which means that the total number of steps in Definition 15.7 (3) is bounded by$| Y | + | Z | + \rho ( A )$, hence the result.□

Now we can define the algorithm MAINTRUP, which is the main algorithm in this section. It has two options, Option 1, which is applied only in the (simple) weakly degenerate case, and essentially trivially cuts most atoms in A as {3} molecules, so one can gain from extra restrictions from weak degeneracies. In Option 2, which is the main part, we basically combine Stage 1 (cutting 2-connections in$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) )$and Stage 3 (pre-processing) in the proof of Proposition 12.18 at the end of Section 13, and the MAINUD algorithm in toy model I plus, but wih the roles of$\mathbb { M } _ { U }$and$\mathbb { M } _ { D }$played by$X ^ { + } ( A )$and X respectively.

Definition 15.9 (Algorithm MAINTRUP). Suppose M is a connected full molecule and A is a connected transversal subset. We may choose$( A ^ { + } , A ^ { - } )$as in Proposition 15.4 (1). Let the number of bonds connecting an atom in$X ^ { + } ( A )$to an atom in A be$\# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { + }$. It is easy to prove that there exists a set$Y _ { 0 } \subseteq A$of at most $\rho ( A )$atoms, such that A becomes a forest after cutting atoms in$Y _ { 0 }$as free. Moreover, by splitting into at most$C ^ { | { \cal A } | + \rho ( { \cal A } ) }$sub-cases, we can identify a set of weakly degenerate atoms and atom pairs in A in the sense of Proposition 12.17; let$Y _ { 1 } \subseteq A$be the atoms involved in these weak degeneracies. We define the following algorithm, which contains two Options that we can choose at the beginning.

In Option 1 we do the followings:

(1) Cut A as free, then cut it into elementary components using UP.

(2) Then cut$A ^ { + }$as free and cut it into elementary components using UP, then cut$A ^ { - }$into elementary components using DOWN.

In Option 2 we do the followings:

(1) Cut all atoms in$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$as free. If any atom in A becomes deg 2, also cut it as free until A has no deg 2 atom.

(2) If A remains connected after the above step, let Z be the set of deg 3 atoms in A, and Y be those atoms in$Y _ { 0 } \cup Y _ { 1 }$that have not been cut. Define$S = \mathbf { S E L E C T 2 } ( A , Z , Y )$as in Definition 15.7, then cut S as free and cut it into elementary components using DOWN. If A is not connected, apply this step to each connected component of A.

(3) If not all atoms in$X ^ { + } ( A )$have been cut, then choose a lowest atom n in$X ^ { + } ( A )$that has not been cut. If n is adjacent to an atom${ \mathfrak { p } } \in A$that has deg 3, then cut {n, p} as free; otherwise cut n as free. If A becomes non-proper (Definition 11.3) then repeat the steps in Definition 13.12 (4)–(5) until A becomes proper again.

(4) Repeat (3) until all atoms in$X ^ { + } ( A )$have been cut. Then repeat the step in Definition 13.12 (8) until all atoms in A have been cut.

(5) Finally, cut (the remaining parts of)$A ^ { + }$as free and cut it into elementary components using UP, and then cut A<sup>−</sup> into elementary components using DOWN.

We define the dual algorithm MAINTRDN in the same way$( \mathrm { s o \ \# _ { c o n n } ^ { + } }$is replaced by$\# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { - } \mathrm { e t c . } )$

Proposition 15.10. In Option 1 of MAINTRUP in Definition 15.9 (same for MAINTRDN), we have

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 B \}} = \# _ {\{4 4 \}} = 0, \quad \# _ {\{4 \}} = 1; \qquad \# _ {\mathrm{good}} \geq \frac {1}{1 0} \cdot | Y _ {1} | - \rho (A) - 1.\tag{15.7}
$$

In Option 2 of of MAINTRUP in Definition 15.9, we have$\# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$and all {33B} molecules are good, and moreover

$$
\begin{array}{c} \# _ {\{3 3 A \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 B \}} \geq \frac {1}{1 0} \cdot \big (\# _ {\mathrm{conn}} ^ {+} - 1 0 ^ {5} (| Y _ {1} | + \rho (A) + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |) \big), \\ \# _ {\{4 \}} \leq | Y _ {1} | + \rho (A) + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |. \end{array}\tag{15.8}
$$

Proof. The case of Option 1 is easy;$\# _ { \{ 3 3 B \} } = \# _ { \{ 4 4 \} } = 0$is obvious by definition, and$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } = 1$because A is connected and$A ^ { + }$satisfies the assumption in Proposition 15.4 (1), in the same way as in the proof of Proposition 15.6. Moreover, each atom in A belongs to a {4} or{3} or {2} or {33A} molecule, and the total number of {2} and {33A} molecules is equal to$\rho ( A )$(see the proof of Proposition 15.6). For any atom n that belongs to a {3} molecule, if it is a weakly degenerate atom, or if it is part of a weakly degenerate pair and is cut after the other atom n<sup>′</sup> of the pair, then {n} must be a good component by Definition 9.4 (3a). This gives at least$| Y _ { 1 } | / 1 0 - \rho ( A ) - 1$good components, as desired.

In the case of Option 2, note that in the whole process, there is no top fixed end in$A ^ { + }$and no bottom fixed end in$A ^ { - } ;$this is because for the lowest atom n in$X ^ { + } ( A )$chosen in Definition 15.9 (3), any child of n must either belong to A or belong to$X ^ { + } ( A )$(and thus will have already been cut). Moreover, any n chosen in this step either has deg 2 and no bond connecting to A or has deg 3 and exactly one bond connecting to A (because all atoms in$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$have been cut in Definition 15.9 (1)). Also any {33} molecule $\{ { \mathfrak { n } } , { \mathfrak { p } } \}$cut in this way must be {33A} molecule, and no full component can be cut (hence no$\{ 4 \}$molecule created) in Definition 15.9 (5). Therefore, all {33B} molecule must have both atoms in$A ,$and the only {4} molecules created are those created in Definition 15.9 (1) (contributing at most$\vert X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) \vert$many {4} molecules) and Definition 15.9 (2) (contributing at most$| Y _ { 1 } | + \rho ( A )$many {4} molecules), hence the upper bound$\# _ { \{ 4 \} } \leq | Y _ { 1 } | + \rho ( A ) + | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) |$

Now we prove the lower bound on$\# \{ 3 3 \}$. Note that after Definition 15.9 (1), there is no bottom fixed end in A (and hence none in$S )$, so we can cut$S$into elementary components using DOWN as in Definition 15.9 (2). By definition of$Y _ { 0 }$and$Y _ { 1 }$, and by Proposition 15.8, we know that after Definition 15.9 (2) is finished, A will become a forest which is proper, and contains no weakly degenerate atoms or atom pairs.

Next we prove an upper bound on |S|; let$Z _ { 0 }$be the set of atoms in A cut in Definition 15.9 (1), then $| Z | \le 4 ( | Z _ { 0 } | + | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) | )$(because the deg 3 atoms in$Z$must be adjacent to one of the atoms in$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$or $Z _ { 0 }$that has been cut) and$| S | \le 1 0 ( 4 | Z _ { 0 } | + 4 | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) | + | Y _ { 1 } | + 2 \rho ( A ) )$by Proposition 15.8.$\mathrm { B y }$Definition 15.9 (1), we know that each atom in$Z _ { 0 }$must have two parents with each of them in either$Z _ { 0 }$or$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A )$. This then leads to$\rho ( Z _ { 0 } ) \ge | Z _ { 0 } | - 2 | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) |$(by counting the total number of top bonds at all atoms of$Z _ { 0 }$, note that each bond is counted only once, and the number of such bonds that do not connect two atoms in$Z _ { 0 }$is at most$2 | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) | )$. Since also$\rho ( Z _ { 0 } ) \leq \rho ( A )$(because$Z _ { 0 } \subseteq A )$, we know$| Z _ { 0 } | \le \rho ( A ) + 2 | X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) |$|, thus

$$
| S | \leq 2 \cdot 1 0 ^ {2} (\rho (A) + | Y _ {1} | + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |).
$$

Now, after cutting$X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) \cup Z _ { 0 } \cup S$as free, the number of bonds connecting an atom in A to an atom in $X ^ { + } ( A )$is still at least

$$
(\# _ {\mathrm{conn}} ^ {+}) ^ {\prime} = \# _ {\mathrm{conn}} ^ {+} - 2 (| X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) | + | Z _ {0} | + | S |) \geq \# _ {\mathrm{conn}} ^ {+} - 1 0 ^ {4} (\rho (A) + | Y _ {1} | + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |).
$$

At this point we can apply the same arguments as in the proof of Proposition 13.13 (especially using Part 2 of the proof and (13.14)) to show that

$$
\# _ {\{3 3 A \}} + \# _ {\{3 3 B \}} \geq \frac {1}{1 0} \cdot \big (\# _ {\mathrm{conn}} ^ {+} - 1 0 ^ {5} (\rho (A) + | Y _ {1} | + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |) \big).\tag{15.9}
$$

Here the role of UD connections is played by the$( \# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { + } ) ^ { \prime }$bonds connecting an atom in$A$to an atom in $X ^ { + } ( A )$. Note that after cutting$S$as free, the number of components of A is at most

$$
\# _ {\mathrm{comp} (A)} \leq 1 + 4 (| X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) | + | S | + | Z _ {0} |) \leq 1 0 ^ {5} (\rho (A) + | Y _ {1} | + | X _ {0} ^ {+} (A) |),
$$

so among these$( \# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { + } ) ^ { \prime }$bonds (we denote this set by$Q )$, there exists a subset$Q ^ { \prime } \subseteq Q$of at least$( \# _ { \mathrm { c o n n } } ^ { + } ) ^ { \prime } -$ $\# _ { \mathrm { c o m p } ( A ) }$bonds, such that each bond in$Q ^ { \prime }$is connected to some other bond in$Q$via A (which matches the definition of UD connections). The same proof for Proposition 13.13 then applies, which leads to (15.9). This completes the proof.□

Now, we can finally prove Proposition 15.1.

Proof of Proposition 15.1. First assume M contains at least one strongly degenerate primitive pair$( \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { n } )$ then we can cut$\{ \mathfrak { m } , \mathfrak { n } \}$as free and cut the rest of M into elementary components using either UP or DOWN (cf. proof of Proposition 12.5, Choice 1). This creates one good {44} molecule and no {4} molecule (as M is connected), so$\# _ { \mathrm { g o o d } } \geq 1$and$\# _ { \mathrm { b a d } } = 0$, which implies (15.1).

Now assume M contains no strongly degenerate primitive pair, then we can show (by splitting into two sub-cases) that each {33A} molecule is either good or can be cut into one {2} and one good {3}-atom. The proof is similar to Lemma 12.6; suppose this {33A} molecule is$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$where n is parent of${ \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime } .$, then we may assume this is strongly degenerate and$\lvert t _ { \mathfrak { n } } - t _ { \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } } } \rvert \leq \varepsilon ^ { v }$otherwise this is already good by Definition 9.4. Now our assumption implies that$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$must be non-primitive; in the absence of C-atoms, this implies that there exists another chain of atoms going from n to n<sup>′</sup> by iteratively taking children. If any atom q in this chain is cut before$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$, then the inequality$t _ { \mathfrak { n } } \geq t _ { \mathfrak { q } } \geq t _ { \mathfrak { n } } ^ { \prime }$allows us to argue as in the proof of Lemma 12.6 to get a good molecule; if not, this means that at the time$\{ \mathfrak { n } , \mathfrak { n } ^ { \prime } \}$is cut, n still has two children$\mathrm { ( i . e . ~ } \mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$and a child on the chain), and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$still has two parents (i.e. n and a parent on the chain), which means that n must have a top fixed end and$\mathfrak { n ^ { \prime } }$must have a bottom fixed end, but this contradicts that {n, n<sup>′</sup>} is {33A} molecule.

Therefore, from now on, we will treat {33A} molecules as good. We start by choosing a connected transversal subset$A _ { 1 }$of M which is a tree$( { \mathrm { i . e . ~ } } \rho ( A _ { 1 } ) = 0 )$and either$A _ { 1 } = \mathbb { M }$or$X _ { 0 } ( A _ { 1 } ) \neq \emptyset$; the existence of such$A _ { 1 }$follows in the same way as in Proposition 15.4 (4) starting from a single atom with no children. If$A _ { 1 } \neq \mathbb { M }$, let$X _ { 1 } = X ( A _ { 1 } )$, then$A _ { 1 } \cup X _ { 1 }$is connected transversal by Proposition 15.4 (3), so we can find $A _ { 2 } \supseteq A _ { 1 } \cup X _ { 1 }$starting from$A _ { 1 } \cup X _ { 1 }$, using Proposition 15.4 (4). If$A _ { 2 } \neq \mathbb { M }$, then let$X _ { 2 } = X ( A _ { 2 } )$and find $A _ { 3 }$by Proposition 15.4 (4), then define$X _ { 3 } = X ( A _ { 3 } )$and so on, see Figure 68.

Recall the function$G ( q ) = ( 2 q + 1 ) \cdot { \binom { q } { 2 } } \cdot ( 3 2 q ^ { 3 / 2 } ) ^ { q ^ { 2 } }$as in Proposition 15.2. Define$D = K _ { 1 } : = ( 6 0 d ) ^ { 6 0 d }$ and$K _ { j + 1 } = ( 6 0 d \cdot G ( ( 6 0 d K _ { j } ) ^ { 6 0 d } ) ) ^ { 6 0 d }$for$j \geq 1$. We will assume$\Gamma > ( 6 0 d ) ^ { 6 0 d } K _ { D }$, and consider several cases.

Note that if we cut$A _ { 1 }$, then$X _ { 1 }$, then$A _ { 2 } \backslash ( A _ { 1 } \cup X _ { 1 } )$, then$X _ { 2 }$etc., then we get a {33} molecule when cutting each$X _ { j }$

We then perform the following cutting sequence:

Starting from$j = 1$, for each$j ,$cut the atoms$( { \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ^ { j } : i \leq | B _ { j } | )$as free in the increasing order of i. However, if${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ^ { j }$is adjacent to${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { j }$and${ \mathfrak { m } } _ { j }$has deg 3 when we cut${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ^ { j }$, then we cut$\{ \mathfrak { n } _ { i } ^ { j } , \mathfrak { m } _ { j } \}$instead of${ \mathfrak { n } } _ { i } ^ { j }$. We then

• Run algorithm TRANSUP and apply Proposition 15.6 if$| X _ { 0 } ^ { + } ( A ) | \geq ( 3 0 d ) ^ { 3 0 d } \cdot K _ { j }$

## Appendix A. Some auxiliary results

In this appendix, we first prove some basic properties of the extended (E-) and truncated$\left( \mathrm { T - ~ o r ~ } ( \Lambda , \Gamma ) - \right)$ dynamics, in Proposition 4.5.

Proof of Proposition 4.5. We need to prove the following statements$( 1 ) - ( 5 )$. Note that the flow property for$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$in (4.3) follows from the same property for$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$and the definition (3.4) of$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$, since

$$
\sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t + s) \boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {1}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) \boldsymbol {z} ^ {1} = \boldsymbol {z}} \sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (s) \boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} = \boldsymbol {z} ^ {1}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0});
$$

also the equality$\begin{array} { r } { S _ { N } ^ { E } ( t ) f = S _ { N } ( t ) f } \end{array}$in Proposition 4.5 (2) follows from the previous statement concerning $\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$and$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ( t )$, in the same way as in the proof of (4.7) in Proposition 4.7.

(1) For E- and T-dynamics, the initial configurations in which two collisions happen at the same time, or an infinite number of collisions happen in a finite time interval, or some collision happens at a fixed time, form a Lebesgue zero set.

(2) Apart from Lebesgue zero sets, the mapping$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$defined by the E-dynamics (Definition 4.1, Proposition 4.5 (2)) satisfies the flow property in (4.3).

(3) If the initial configuration$z ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { D } _ { N }$, then the E-dynamics and the O-dynamics coincide.

(4) In the$( \Lambda , \Gamma )$-dynamics, the size and recollision number of any cluster$\mathbb { M } _ { j }$of the topological reduction M always satisfy that$| \mathbb { M } _ { j } | \le \Lambda$and$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) \leq \Gamma$

(5) The equality (4.4) holds for both E- and T-dynamics.

(6) For${ \mathrm { O } } _ { - } ,$E- and T-dynamics, the total number of collisions has an absolute upper bound that depends only on d and N.

Proof of (1). This follows from the same proof as in [1].

Proof of (2)–(3). Notice that by Definition 4.1, the motion of the particles starting from any time t depends only on the configuration of the system at time t but not on the collision history before time t. The flow property in (2) then follows. Moreover, by Definition 4.1, we know that if the distance between any two particles i and$j$ever becomes$\geq \varepsilon$along the E-dynamics, then their distance will remain$\geq \varepsilon$for the rest of time; therefore, if the distance between any two particles is$> \varepsilon$initially, then all these distances will remain $\geq \varepsilon { \mathrm { ~ f o r e v e r } } ,$so the E-dynamics coincide with the O-dynamics, which proves (3).

Proof of (4). This follows from the definition of$( \Lambda , \Gamma )$-truncated dynamics (Definition 4.3): it is easy to see that any collision that is allowed cannot cause$| \mathbb { M } _ { j } | > \Lambda$or$\rho ( \mathbb { M } _ { j } ) > \Gamma$, due to the definition of the condition Pro in (4.2).

Proof of (5). We prove it for$\mathcal { S } _ { N } ^ { E }$, and the$S _ { N } ^ { \Lambda , \Gamma }$case is the same. By listing all the collisions and time ordering them, we can divide$\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 d N }$into a countable union of disjoint open sets$( O _ { \alpha } ) _ { \alpha \in \mathbb { N } }$, where on each$O _ { \alpha }$ the E-dynamics contain only a fixed set of collisions between fixed particles with a fixed time ordering. The mapping$\mathcal { H } _ { N } ^ { E } ( t )$, when restricted to$O _ { \alpha } .$, is injective and volume preserving; we denote it by$\mathcal { H } ^ { t }$. Then

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}} (\mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) f) (\boldsymbol {z}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}} \left(\sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}: \mathcal {H} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0})\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} = \sum_ {\alpha} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}} \left(\sum_ {\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} \in O _ {\alpha}: \mathcal {H} ^ {t} (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) = \boldsymbol {z}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0})\right) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z}.\tag{A.1}
$$

The above sum in$z ^ { 0 }$contains at most one element, and is nonzero if and only i$\mathrm { ~ : ~ } z \in { \mathcal { H } } ^ { t } ( O _ { \alpha } )$. By the above, the mapping$\mathcal { H } ^ { t }$is a volume preserving bijection between$O _ { \alpha }$and${ \mathcal { H } } ^ { t } ( O _ { \alpha } )$. Therefore,

$$
\int \mathcal {S} _ {N} ^ {E} (t) f (\boldsymbol {z}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} = \sum_ {\alpha} \int_ {\mathcal {H} ^ {t} (O _ {\alpha})} f ((\mathcal {H} ^ {t}) ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {z}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} = \sum_ {\alpha} \int_ {O _ {\alpha}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} ^ {0} = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}} f (\boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}) \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol {z} ^ {0}.\tag{A.2}
$$

Proof of (6). For the O-dynamics this follows from [15]; in fact the upper bound is explicit$( 3 2 N ^ { 3 / 2 } ) ^ { N ^ { 2 } }$ For the (Λ, Γ)-truncated dynamics this follows directly from (5). Consider now the E-dynamics. We know that in the E-dynamics, for each pair of particles, their distance remains$< \varepsilon$until some time when their distance becomes$\varepsilon ,$and their distance remains$\geq \varepsilon$afterwards. There are at most$\textstyle { \binom { q } { 2 } }$such transition times, and in any time interval$I = ( t ^ { \prime } , t ^ { \prime \prime } )$between each two consecutive transition times$t ^ { \prime }$and$t ^ { \prime \prime }$, the set of particle pairs with distance$< \varepsilon ,$say K, remains fixed.

Note that, see [15], the O-dynamics can be viewed as the billiard motion on the billiard table

$$
\mathcal {D} := \bigcap_ {1 \leq i <   j \leq N} \mathcal {D} _ {i j}; \quad \mathcal {D} _ {i j} = \left\{\boldsymbol {z} \in \mathbb {R} ^ {2 d N}: | x _ {i} - x _ {j} | \geq \varepsilon \right\}.
$$

The proof in [15] shows that the number of boundary reflections of this billiard ball is at most$( 3 2 N ^ { 3 / 2 } ) ^ { N ^ { 2 } }$ by establishing some geometric properties of$\mathcal { D } .$

Now the same result in [15] still holds, if one replaces D by$\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime } : = \bigcap _ { ( i , j ) \in K ^ { c } } \mathcal { D } _ { i j } ; } \end{array}$; indeed$\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$is just the intersection of a sub-collection of the full collection of balls defining${ \mathcal { D } } ,$and it can be checked that the same proof in [15] carries over. This then gives an upper bound on the number of collisions in the$E _ { - }$ dynamics within any interval$I ,$because this dynamics exactly corresponds to the billiard motion on the billiard table$\mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$(the billiard is also restricted to the sets$\mathcal { D } _ { i j } ^ { c }$for$( i , j ) \in K$, but the boundaries of these sets are not involved in any reflections, as the billiard ball never reach the boundary of any of these sets within time interval$I )$. The desired result for the E-dynamics then follows with the absolute upper bound $\begin{array} { r } { G _ { 0 } ( d , N ) = \binom { N } { 2 } \cdot ( 3 2 N ^ { 3 / 2 } ) ^ { N ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}$□

Fina${ \mathrm { l y } } ,$we state and prove a result concerning the preservation of the norm$\mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta }$used in Theorem 1.

Proposition A.1. Recall the norm$\mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta }$defined in (1.15). Suppose$n = n ( t , x , v )$is a positive solution to the Boltzmann equation (1.13), and let$\beta = \beta ( t )$be a fixed, strictly positive, strictly decreasing function with$\beta ( 0 ) \ge \beta > 0$and$\beta ^ { \prime } ( t ) \leq - c < 0$for some constant c. Assume n satisfies that

$$
\sup _ {t \in [ 0, T ]} \left\| e ^ {\beta (t) | v | ^ {2}} n (t) \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq A <   \infty ,\tag{A.3}
$$

and that

$$
\| n (0) \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\beta (0)}} + \| \nabla_ {x} n (0) \| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\beta (0)}} \leq B <   \infty ,\tag{A.4}
$$

then for any$t \in [ 0 , T ]$we have

$$
\left\| n (t) \right\| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\beta (t)}} + \left\| \nabla_ {x} n (t) \right\| _ {\mathrm{Bol} ^ {\beta (t)}} \lesssim B,\tag{A.5}
$$

where the constants in$\lesssim$may depend on$( A , \beta , c , T )$

Proof. First we prove (A.5) for$n ( t )$. Define$\| n ( t ) \| _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta ( t ) } } : = M _ { 0 } ( t )$, by (1.13) we have

$$
\begin{array}{c} n (t, x, v) = n (0, x - t v, v) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \big ((v - v _ {1}) \cdot \omega \big) _ {+} \cdot \big \{n (s, x - (t - s) v, v ^ {\prime}) n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1} ^ {\prime}) \\ - n (s, x - (t - s) v, v) n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1}) \big \}   \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {1} \mathrm{d} s. \end{array}\tag{A.6}
$$

We focus on the Duhamel term (denote it by$n ^ { ( 1 ) } )$. Using that$| v | ^ { 2 } + | v _ { 1 } | ^ { 2 } = | v ^ { \prime } | ^ { 2 } + | v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } | ^ { 2 }$, we get that

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {\beta (t) | v | ^ {2}} n ^ {(1)} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} e ^ {- \beta (t) | v _ {1} | ^ {2}} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \big ((v - v _ {1}) \cdot \omega \big) _ {+} \cdot e ^ {(\beta (t) - \beta (s)) (| v | ^ {2} + | v _ {1} | ^ {2})} \\ \times \left\{e ^ {\beta (s) | v ^ {\prime} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v ^ {\prime}) \cdot e ^ {\beta (s) | v _ {1} ^ {\prime} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1} ^ {\prime}) \right. \\ \left. - e ^ {\beta (s) | v | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v) \cdot e ^ {\beta (s) | v _ {1} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1}) \right\} \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {1} \mathrm{d} s. \end{array}\tag{A.7}
$$

Note that$\beta ( t ) \geq \beta$and$\beta ( t ) - \beta ( s ) \leq - c ( t - s )$, it is easy to see that

$$
\left(\left(v - v _ {1}\right) \cdot \omega\right) _ {+} \cdot e ^ {(\beta (t) - \beta (s)) (| v | ^ {2} + | v _ {1} | ^ {2}) / 2} \lesssim_ {\beta , c} (t - s) ^ {- 1 / 2}.
$$

Let$K \in 2 ^ { \mathbb { N } }$be such that$( t - s ) \operatorname* { m a x } ( | v | , | v _ { 1 } | ) \sim ( t - s ) \operatorname* { m a x } ( | v ^ { \prime } | , | v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } | ) \sim K$(with ∼ replaced by$\lesssim \mathrm { i f } ~ K = 1 )$ then from (A.7) we have

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & e ^ {\beta (t) | v | ^ {2}} n ^ {(1)} \lesssim_ {\beta , c, T} \sum_ {K} e ^ {- \theta K ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} (t - s) ^ {- 1 / 2} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} e ^ {- \beta | v _ {1} | ^ {2}} \mathbb {1} _ {(t - s) \max (| v |, | v _ {1} |) \lesssim K} \\ & \qquad \times \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} \bigl \{e ^ {\beta (s) | v ^ {\prime} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v ^ {\prime}) \cdot e ^ {\beta (s) | v _ {1} ^ {\prime} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1} ^ {\prime}) \\ & \qquad + e ^ {\beta (s) | v | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v) \cdot e ^ {\beta (s) | v _ {1} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v _ {1}) \bigr \} \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {1} \mathrm{d} s, \end{array}\tag{A.8}
$$

where$\theta \gtrsim _ { \beta , c T } 1$is a positive constant. In (A.8), if$k \in  { \mathbb { Z } ^ { d } }$is fixed and$| x - k | \leq 1$, then for$y = x - ( t - s ) v$ we have$| y - k | \lesssim K$, therefore we have

$$
e ^ {\beta (s) | v ^ {\prime} | ^ {2}} n (s, x - (t - s) v, v ^ {\prime}) \leq \sum_ {k ^ {\prime} \in \mathbb {Z} ^ {d}, | k ^ {\prime} - k | \lesssim K} G _ {k ^ {\prime}} (s),\tag{A.9}
$$

for some$G _ { k ^ { \prime } } ( s )$satisfying$\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k ^ { \prime } } G _ { k ^ { \prime } } ( s ) \ \lesssim \ \Vert n ( s ) \Vert _ { \mathrm { B o l } ^ { \beta ( s ) } } \ \leq \ M _ { 0 } ( s ) } \end{array}$. The other three terms satisfy the same estimate; moreover, by (A.3) we also have$e ^ { \beta ( s ) | v ^ { \prime } | ^ { 2 } } n ( s , x - ( t - s ) v , v ^ { \prime } ) \leq A$and the same for the other three terms. In summary, for every$| x - k | \leq 1$and$v \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$, we have

$$
e ^ {\beta (t) | v | ^ {2}} n ^ {(1)} (x, v) \lesssim_ {\beta , c, T} \sum_ {K} e ^ {- \theta K ^ {2}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} (t - s) ^ {- 1 / 2} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {d}} e ^ {- \beta | v _ {1} | ^ {2}} \int_ {\mathbb {S} ^ {d - 1}} A \cdot \sum_ {| k ^ {\prime} - k | \leq K} G _ {k ^ {\prime}} (s)   \mathrm{d} \omega \mathrm{d} v _ {1} \mathrm{d} s.\tag{A.10}
$$

Upon taking supremum in$( x , v )$and summing in k and K, and doing the same for the transport term $n ( 0 , x - t v , v )$, we obtain that

$$
M _ {0} (t) \lesssim_ {A, \beta , c, T} B + \int_ {0} ^ {t} (t - s) ^ {- 1 / 2} M _ {0} (s) \mathrm{d} s.
$$

By Gronwall, this implies$M _ { 0 } ( t ) \lesssim _ { A , \beta , c , T }$B for any$t \in [ 0 , T ]$. Finally, for the proof of the$\nabla _ { x }$derivative, just notice that, by (1.13) we have$( \partial _ { t } + v \cdot \nabla _ { x } ) ( \nabla _ { x } n ) = \mathcal { Q } ( n , \nabla _ { x } n ) + \mathcal { Q } ( \nabla _ { x } n , n )$, so the same result holds by repeating the proof above.□

Appendix B. A dictionary between molecules and physical trajectories

| Molecule terms | Physical picture | Molecule terms | Physical picture |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C/O atoms | Collisions/overlaps | Particle line | Full trajectory of one particle (will be identified with particles) |
| Layers $\ell'$ | Time intervals $[(\ell' - 1)\tau, \ell'\tau]$ | Serial | In the same particle line (trajectory of the same particle) |
| Edges | Linear pieces (of trajectories) | Start/finish layers in $[\underline{\ell} : \ell]$ | First/last layer where the particle occurs in the dynamics |
| Bonds/ends | Linear pieces between two consecutive collisions or overlaps/first and last linear pieces | Finish layer $\ell + 1$ | (Root) particles occurring in the time $t = \ell\tau$ correlation/cumulant |
| Empty ends | Trajectories with no collisions and overlaps | Lifespan | Time layers where the particle is present in $\mathbb{M}$ (excluding $\ell + 1$) |
| Parent/child | Next/previous collision or overlap of an involved particle | Initial links | Initial closeness of particles governed by initial cumulants |
| Top/bottom edges | Post/pre collisional configurations | Ov-segments | Linear pieces of trajectories with possible overlaps in between |

Table 3. Correspondence between molecule terms and physical picture. The notations are as in Definition 3.1. There is some special convention about finish layer being ℓ + 1 (recall ℓ is the highest layer).
